text_kjv: In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah Ahaz the son of Jotham king of Judah began to reign.

commentary.narrative: This verse marks the beginning of Ahaz's reign in Judah and establishes the chronological framework for understanding his catastrophic rule. The synchronism with Pekah of Israel's seventeenth year of rule appears intentionally precise, yet scholars have long noted that the numbers in Kings' chronological system create difficulties when compared with Assyrian records of the same period. The phrase 'began to reign' (Hebrew: malakh) is the standard formula introducing a new monarch in the Deuteronomic history. Ahaz becomes king during a turbulent era when both the northern kingdom of Israel and Syria (Aram) are in their death throes, facing Assyrian expansion. This timing is crucial: Ahaz will inherit a kingdom already under existential pressure, and his response to that pressure—turning to Assyria rather than trusting in the Lord—will define his legacy.

word_study.meaning: to become king, to establish royal rule; the verb carries the sense of taking up the throne and establishing authority
word_study.significance: This verb is the standard formula in Kings for accession to power. It indicates not merely birth or designation, but the actual commencement of ruling authority. In Ahaz's case, malakh inaugurates a sixteen-year period of what the narrator will immediately judge as covenant failure.

word_study.meaning: in the year seventeen; synchronistic dating formula that anchors one king's reign to another's regnal year
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this synchronism presents chronological difficulties when compared with extra-biblical sources. Ancient chroniclers used such formulas to create a unified timeline, but the precision claimed sometimes exceeds historical reality. For the reader, this verse asks: can we trust the numerical framework, or should we focus on the narrative truth about Ahaz's covenantal failure regardless of exact dating?

cross_references.connection: Jotham's death and Ahaz's succession; the previous verse shows Jotham reigning for sixteen years before Ahaz takes the throne.
Isaiah's account of the same historical moment—the Syro-Ephraimite crisis—provides the prophetic perspective on Ahaz's reign and his crucial decision.
The parallel account in Chronicles emphasizes even more strongly Ahaz's covenant failure and the judgment that follows.
The formula 'son of Remaliah' for Pekah parallels the opening of Israel's northern kingdom's history, showing how even kings are defined by their dynastic lines.

commentary.historical_context: Ahaz ascends the throne during the final decades of the northern kingdom's existence. The mid-eighth century BCE was a period of radical imperial transformation: Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser III (745-727 BCE) was consolidating power and beginning systematic conquest of the Levant. Within Ahaz's own lifetime, Israel will fall to Assyria (722 BCE), and within a few decades, Judah will face near-extinction. The northern kingdom's kings—including Pekah—were attempting to build an anti-Assyrian coalition. Ahaz's refusal to join this coalition, combined with his subsequent appeal to Assyria for military aid, made him a vassal of Assyria but kept Judah alive. However, this political pragmatism came at an enormous theological cost: it meant importing Assyrian religious practices and abandoning the exclusive covenant with Yahweh.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of a covenant king rejecting the counsel of prophets and turning instead to human alliances appears repeatedly in the Book of Mormon. Ahaz's choice parallels King Lamoni's initial rejection of Ammon's teaching—both involve covenant people turning away from the true God toward foreign powers and practices. The Book of Mormon also shows how such choices, while sometimes producing temporary political survival, ultimately place a kingdom on a path toward spiritual and temporal destruction.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:14-16 describes how the Lord warns His people through prophets, and how rejection of that warning brings judgment. Ahaz will reject Isaiah's counsel to trust in the Lord's promise of protection (Isaiah 7:1-9); instead, he will petition Assyria for help. This pattern of rejecting prophetic counsel appears throughout D&C as a defining mark of apostasy.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Ahaz's reign marks the beginning of the corruption of Judah's Temple worship. As we will see in verses 10-18, Ahaz will alter the Temple altar to match Assyrian religious forms. This corruption of the Temple—the central sign of the covenant—represents a breaking of the innermost bond between Judah and the Lord.

commentary.christological_typology: Though Ahaz is fundamentally a negative type—his failures point to what a covenant king must not do—his reign sets the stage for the Messianic promise. Isaiah 7, spoken during Ahaz's reign, contains one of the Old Testament's most explicit Messianic declarations: 'Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel' (Isaiah 7:14). This promise arises precisely in the context of Ahaz's faithlessness, showing that the Lord's covenant will ultimately be fulfilled not through faithless kings like Ahaz, but through the promised Messiah. Jesus Christ alone fulfills what Ahaz and all mortal kings fail to accomplish: perfect obedience to the Father's will.
commentary.application: Ahaz's reign raises a piercing question for modern covenant members: When we face pressure—financial, social, professional—do we trust in the Lord's promises, or do we turn to worldly alliances that require us to compromise our values? Ahaz's choices seemed pragmatic and politically wise, yet they set Judah on a course toward judgment. The Book of Mormon and modern prophetic counsel repeatedly warn that there is no safety in compromising the covenant, no true security in alliances that require us to adopt the 'way' of the world. The application is not that we live passively, but that we seek the Lord's counsel through His prophets before making decisions that will shape our spiritual identity and that of our families and communities.

text_kjv: Twenty years old was Ahaz when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, and did not that which was right in the sight of the LORD his God, like David his father.

commentary.narrative: Verse 2 provides a biographical and moral verdict on Ahaz's reign before describing his actions in detail. He ascends the throne as a young man of twenty and rules for sixteen years—a substantial reign that allows his policies to reshape Judah's religious and political landscape. The narrator immediately delivers the covenant verdict: Ahaz 'did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God, as his ancestor David had done.' This is the Deuteronomic formula for covenant failure, and it is stated comprehensively—not that Ahaz 'sometimes failed' or 'committed certain errors,' but that he failed to do what is right in the fundamental, ongoing sense. The comparison to David is deliberate and cutting: David, despite his grave personal sins (Bathsheba, the census), maintained his overall loyalty to the covenant and the Temple; Ahaz, by contrast, actively dismantles the covenant framework itself. The phrase 'like David his father' (ke-David aviv) uses 'father' in the dynastic sense—David is the ancestor and standard against which all subsequent kings of Judah will be measured. Ahaz fails that test completely.

word_study.term_english: did not do that which was right
word_study.meaning: and he did not do the right thing; hayyashar means 'that which is straight, correct, right'—what conforms to the covenant norm
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this negative verdict formula is measured against an absolute standard. It is not a partial judgment but a comprehensive assessment of failure. The absence of any mitigating clause—no 'except for' or 'though he did accomplish'—indicates total covenant failure. This formula appears for every king of Israel and most kings of Judah; only a handful of Judean kings receive a positive verdict (such as David, Hezekiah, and Josiah).

word_study.term_english: in the sight of the LORD
word_study.meaning: in the eyes of the LORD; the metaphor of 'eyes' indicates the Lord's attention, judgment, and standards of evaluation
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes that the judgment is not the narrator's opinion but the Lord's own assessment. What is 'right in the eyes of the LORD' is an objective moral reality grounded in the covenant. The Lord sees and judges; the king's deeds cannot be hidden or reframed.

word_study.meaning: as/like David his father; 'father' here denotes dynastic ancestor and covenantal standard
word_study.significance: David is the measure of faithfulness for Judean kings. The phrase does not mean biological father (Jotham was Ahaz's father) but dynastic founder. By invoking David, the verse sets up an unbridgeable contrast: David, despite personal failings, maintained covenant loyalty; Ahaz systematically violates it. This Davidic standard runs throughout the Deuteronomic history and becomes central to the Messianic hope—the ultimate David is yet to come.

cross_references.connection: David is invoked as the model of faithfulness against which other kings are judged; this sets the pattern used for Ahaz.
The parallel account provides additional detail on Ahaz's youth and the explicit charge that he 'did not do that which was right in the sight of the LORD.'
The Davidic covenant promises that God will establish David's line forever; Ahaz's violation of that covenant raises the question of how the promise can stand when the king breaks faith.

Spoken during Ahaz's reign, Isaiah's word about the coming Immanuel is addressed to the 'house of David' and implies that the true fulfillment of the Davidic covenant lies in a future, faithful descendant—not in Ahaz.

Modern revelation teaches that influence gained through persuasion and righteousness lasts eternally, while that gained through compulsion vanishes; Ahaz's political maneuvers, lacking righteousness, will prove hollow.

commentary.historical_context: Ahaz was born around 745 BCE and became king around 735 BCE, during the height of Assyrian expansion under Tiglath-Pileser III. A twenty-year-old king in the ancient Near East was not anomalous; many came to power in their late teens or early twenties. Ahaz's sixteen-year reign (approximately 735-720 BCE) spans the precise moment when the balance of power in the Levant shifted irreversibly toward Assyria. His early years were marked by the Syro-Ephraimite crisis (described in verse 5 and Isaiah 7); his later years saw him maneuvering to survive by becoming Assyria's vassal. The Deuteronomic verdict reflects not merely political failure but religious failure: from the narrator's theological perspective, Ahaz's political choices were disastrous precisely because they involved abandoning faith in the Lord's protection and adopting the religious practices of the pagan empire.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon offers repeated examples of how younger kings often prove weaker in faith than their predecessors. The principle of generational spiritual decline appears in both 1 and 2 Nephi, where sons sometimes fail to maintain their fathers' covenant commitment. Ahaz represents this pattern: his father Jotham 'did that which was right in the sight of the LORD his God' (2 Kings 15:34), yet Ahaz, despite his father's example, chose the opposite path. Alma the Younger's early apostasy before his dramatic conversion illustrates how even those raised in covenant families can reject the faith—though Alma, unlike Ahaz, ultimately repents.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 95:8 records the Lord's rebuke to the early Saints: 'You have not kept the commandments, and must needs stand rebuked before the Lord.' Ahaz's comprehensive failure to do 'that which was right' mirrors this kind of wholesale breach of covenant. However, D&C also emphasizes that repentance remains possible if the heart turns; Ahaz, unlike later kings such as Manasseh, shows no sign of repentance during his reign.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Verse 2 sets up what will happen in verses 10-18: Ahaz's fundamental covenant failure leads him to corrupt the Temple itself. The Temple is the house of the Lord, the central place where the covenant is enacted and renewed. When a king 'does not do what is right in the sight of the LORD,' the natural consequence is the desecration of the Lord's house. This points forward to later prophetic symbolism in which the Temple becomes corrupted and ultimately destroyed—a physical manifestation of spiritual apostasy.

commentary.christological_typology: Ahaz is a negative type of kingship. Jesus Christ, born of David's line centuries later, will embody the covenant faithfulness that Ahaz rejected. Where Ahaz 'did not do that which was right in the sight of the LORD,' Christ will be the one who perfectly fulfills the covenant, who always does the will of the Father. Hebrews 10:7 applies Psalm 40:7-8 to Christ: 'I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.' Ahaz's failure of the Davidic standard becomes the foil against which the true and final King is measured.
commentary.application: The verdict on Ahaz arrives before the detailed narrative of his sins, which suggests something important: the outcome of a reign is determined by its fundamental direction and commitments, not by isolated decisions. Ahaz's choice to turn toward Assyria and away from the Lord was not a single mistake but a pattern that shaped his entire reign. For modern covenant members, this raises the question: Are we, as individuals and families, building our lives on covenantal faithfulness, or are we, like Ahaz, making choices that systematically move us away from the Lord? The judgment on Ahaz is not meant to be punitive in tone but diagnostic: it names the reality of what happens when we fail to do 'that which is right in the sight of the LORD.' The application is to examine our own lives and ask whether our choices align us with the Davidic standard of covenant faithfulness that the restored Church continues to emphasize.

text_kjv: But he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, yea, and made his son to pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the heathen, whom the LORD cast out from before the children of Israel.

commentary.narrative: Verse 3 provides the specific content of Ahaz's covenant failure. The phrase 'walked in the way of the kings of Israel' is devastating for a king of Judah. The 'way' established by Jeroboam I and followed by his successors was the path of covenant violation: the establishment of golden calves, the rejection of the Jerusalem Temple, and syncretistic worship of foreign gods. For a Judahite king to adopt the 'way of the kings of Israel' is to embrace apostasy. But the verse goes further: 'and even made his son pass through the fire.' The Covenant Rendering notes that this phrase is partly veiled in Hebrew idiom (he'evir, 'caused to pass over') but the context makes clear this refers to child sacrifice. The phrase 'according to the abominations of the heathen, whom the LORD cast out from before the children of Israel' is the crushing irony: Ahaz is adopting the very practices that justified the conquest of Canaan. The Lord drove out the Canaanites because of their detestable practices; now Ahaz, a covenant king, is imitating those practices and inflicting them on his own people. This verse represents the nadir of Judean religious practice in the pre-exile period.

word_study.meaning: and he walked in the way; derek means both a literal path and a metaphorical direction or pattern of conduct
word_study.significance: The verb 'to walk' (halak) is used throughout Kings to describe the spiritual trajectory of a reign. 'Walking in the way' of someone means adopting their pattern and values. For a Judahite king to walk in the way of Israel's kings is to abandon the unique covenant identity of the southern kingdom.

word_study.term_english: made his son to pass through the fire
word_study.term_original: וְגַם אֶת־בְּנוֹ הֶעֱבִיר בָּאֵשׁ (vegam et-beno he'evir ba-esh)
word_study.meaning: and also his son he caused to pass through the fire; the hiphil verb he'evir means 'caused to pass over/through'; ba-esh, 'in/through the fire'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this phrase is an instance of Hebrew idiom partly veiling a horrifying practice. The exact nature of the act is not elaborated here, but Deuteronomy 18:10 explicitly condemns 'one who makes his son or daughter to pass through the fire' (ma'avir et-beno va-bitro ba-esh) as abomination. The context and parallels in 2 Kings 21:6 (Manasseh) and 23:10 (Josiah's reform) make clear this refers to human sacrifice in worship of foreign deities, likely Molech. The use of 'his son' (et-beno) is personal and visceral—this is not an abstract sin but an attack on Ahaz's own family.

word_study.meaning: detestable practices, abominations; plural of to'evah, a term reserved for practices that violate the boundary between covenant and paganism
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that to'avot is not merely a term of disapproval but a category reserved for practices that are 'ontologically incompatible with covenant life.' The word appears prominently in Deuteronomy (12:31, 18:10-12) to mark the absolute limit of acceptable practice. For Ahaz to commit to'avot is to place himself outside the covenant entirely.

word_study.meaning: the nations, the heathen; goy can mean 'nation' or, when used of non-Israelites, implies those outside the covenant
word_study.significance: The phrase 'abominations of the nations' sets up a fundamental contrast: these practices belong to the goyim, to those outside the covenant. For an Israelite—much less a king—to adopt them is a radical breach of the covenant boundary.

cross_references.connection: Explicitly condemns child sacrifice ('he who causes his son or daughter to pass through the fire') as abomination; Ahaz is committing the very sin that Deuteronomy identifies as the reason the Lord drove out the Canaanites.
Manasseh, Ahaz's great-grandson, will also 'make his son pass through the fire'; this shows that Ahaz's practice establishes a pattern in the royal house.
The Lord forbids the Israelites from giving 'any of thy seed to pass through the fire to Molech'; Ahaz violates this explicit covenant command.
Josiah's reform explicitly destroys the site of Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom where such sacrifices were performed, showing that these practices persisted and were eventually purged from Judah.
Jeremiah condemns the practice of building 'high places to Baal to burn their sons with fire,' placing this sin at the heart of Judah's judgment.

commentary.historical_context: Child sacrifice in the ancient Near East was practiced by various peoples, including Canaanites, Phoenicians, and others. Archaeological evidence from sites like Carthage (Tophet) shows evidence of such practices. However, the extent to which child sacrifice was a normative part of Canaanite religion versus an extreme practice in times of crisis is debated among scholars. In the Deuteronomic history, such practices are presented as fundamentally incompatible with Israelite covenant worship. Ahaz's adoption of these practices represents the deepest possible departure from Israelite identity. The reference to 'the heathen, whom the LORD cast out from before the children of Israel' recalls the conquest narrative: the Lord dispossessed the Canaanites precisely because of their abominations. For Ahaz to imitate those practices suggests that Judah is becoming indistinguishable from the pagan nations whose displacement justified Israel's original possession of the land.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly warns against adopting the 'ways' of covenant-breaking peoples. When the Nephites turn to 'the way of the Lamanites' or embrace Gadiantons or other apostate practices, they are following precisely the pattern Ahaz embodies. Alma's teaching to Lamoni includes the warning that those who choose evil over good become 'slaves to sin' (Alma 41:11). The use of 'son' in Ahaz's case—he sacrifices his own child—parallels the spiritual death that comes to those who lead family members astray, a theme emphasized repeatedly in the Book of Mormon and modern revelation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 132:19 teaches that those who enter into the new and everlasting covenant with full hearts and commitment 'receive of the fulness of the Father.' The inverse is also true: those who turn from the covenant and embrace practices antithetical to it lose that fulness. Ahaz's adoption of practices explicitly forbidden in the covenant represents the antithesis of what the restoration teaches about faithful family life and the proper raising of children.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the place where covenant sacrifice is properly performed. Child sacrifice—whether literal or metaphorical—represents the perversion of the sacrificial system. Where the Temple teaches that the Lord's sacrifice (ultimately Christ's) is sufficient and that human life is sacred, the practice Ahaz embraces mocks this understanding. The Doctrine and Covenants teaches that the temple endowment focuses on the proper covenantal path; Ahaz represents the polar opposite, walking in a way that leads to spiritual death for himself and his family.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 3 sets up a crucial contrast with the Messiah. Jesus Christ, born of David's line, will be the final king of Israel and Judah. Where Ahaz sacrifices his own son to foreign gods, Christ's Father will offer His own Son as the ultimate and final sacrifice for the sins of all humanity. Hebrews 10:10 teaches that 'by the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.' The horrifying practice Ahaz engages in stands in absolute contrast to the voluntary, redemptive self-offering of Christ. Moreover, Matthew 26:39 records Christ in Gethsemane: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt'—the perfect submission that Ahaz, with his idolatrous practices, utterly rejects.
commentary.application: Verse 3 addresses the deepest question: how far can we drift from covenant? Ahaz's journey from king to apostate is a journey of incremental choices, each one moving him further from the Lord and deeper into practices that violate fundamental covenant boundaries. For modern members, the application is sobering: there are practices and patterns that, once embraced, place us outside the covenant in fundamental ways. The modern Church's teachings on the sanctity of children, the importance of family, and the protection of the young are direct applications of the warnings embedded in verse 3. Moreover, the teaching on the 'way' suggests that we become like what we follow. If we follow worldly ways—whether through media, associations, or lifestyle choices—we gradually become unable to recognize or value the covenant. The antidote is what Proverbs 3:5-6 teaches: 'Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.'

text_kjv: And he sacrificed and burnt incense in the high places, and on the hills, and under every green tree.

commentary.narrative: Verse 4 expands on Ahaz's religious apostasy by detailing the locations and forms of his illicit worship. The three-part formula—'high places, and on the hills, and under every green tree'—is a comprehensive description of syncretistic worship throughout Judah's territory. These locations represent what might be called the 'decentralized' worship system that opposed the Temple-centered covenant practice. High places (bamot) were worship sites, often on elevated terrain, where local populations made offerings. Deuteronomy and Kings repeatedly condemn them as incompatible with the covenant, which calls for worship at the one place the Lord will choose (the Temple in Jerusalem). The 'hills' and 'green trees' reference nature-based worship sites, including sites associated with Asherah groves and other fertility worship. The phrase 'under every green tree' echoes earlier descriptions of Judahite apostasy (see 1 Kings 14:23) and Israelite apostasy. The comprehensiveness—'every' green tree—suggests that Ahaz is not merely tolerating such worship but actively promoting it throughout his kingdom. The verbs 'sacrificed' (zabach) and 'burned incense' (qittar) are technical terms for worship acts that belong properly to the Temple. For Ahaz to perform these acts at unauthorized locations is to create a religious system that directly competes with and undermines the Temple and the covenant.

word_study.meaning: high places; elevated locations used for worship; singular bamah
word_study.significance: Bamot appear throughout Kings as the great symbol of covenant violation in Judah and Israel. Even when bamot are used nominally to worship the Lord, they are condemned because they violate the principle of centralized worship at the Temple. Their prominence in this verse indicates systemic religious apostasy.

word_study.meaning: and he burned incense; the piel of qatar, 'to burn incense'
word_study.significance: The verb qatar is the technical term for incense offering in the sacrificial system. In the Temple, incense was burned on the altar of incense as part of the daily service (Exodus 30:1-8). For Ahaz to burn incense at high places and under trees is to usurp priestly prerogatives and to conduct Temple-like worship in non-sanctioned locations. This represents not merely a 'mistake' but a fundamental restructuring of worship.

word_study.meaning: under every leafy/green tree; the phrase encompasses all such locations throughout the kingdom
word_study.significance: The term 'green' (ra'anan) refers to flourishing, living vegetation. Such trees were associated with Asherah worship and fertility cults. The universalizing word 'every' (kol) indicates that Ahaz has not merely overlooked such worship but has systematized it throughout Judah. This is comprehensive apostasy.

cross_references.connection: Uses nearly identical language to describe Rehoboam's apostasy: 'they also built them high places, and images, and groves, on every high hill, and under every green tree.'
The law commands Israel to destroy all the places where pagan nations worship and to 'serve the LORD your God in the place which he shall choose'; Ahaz does the opposite, establishing such places.
Josiah's reform will explicitly remove and destroy the high places, showing that Ahaz's legacy of bamot worship persists for generations.
Isaiah's contemporary condemnation: 'For they shall be ashamed of the oaks which ye have desired, and ye shall be confounded for the gardens that ye have chosen.'
Hosea condemns Israel's worship 'under the oaks and poplars and elms, because the shadow thereof is good'; this same practice appears in both northern and southern kingdoms.

commentary.historical_context: The high places were endemic to Canaanite and early Israelite worship before the centralization of the Temple cult. Archaeology has uncovered remains of bamot throughout Israel and Judah, some with evidence of animal sacrifice and ritual activity. While the Law (Deuteronomy 12) calls for exclusive worship at one central location, local sanctuaries persisted in both kingdoms throughout the monarchic period. Kings presents this persistence as a form of apostasy, a failure to fully embrace the covenant's demand for centralized worship. Ahaz's active promotion of such worship suggests either that he was influenced by Assyrian religious pluralism (Assyria typically tolerated multiple worship sites) or that he was attempting to gain local support by permitting traditional fertility worship. From the narrator's perspective, however, such pragmatism is indistinguishable from apostasy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The principle of 'one place' where the Lord causes His name to be remembered is central to Book of Mormon teaching. The temple at Zarahemla and later the temple in the land Bountiful serve as the covenant centers where proper worship occurs. When Nephites abandon the temple and embrace widespread local worship, they are following precisely Ahaz's path. Alma's teaching emphasizes that scattered, decentralized worship without the temple covenant framework leads to spiritual dissolution.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109:16 describes the dedication of the Kirtland Temple with the prayer that the Lord will 'visit this house, and bless this people, and let the fulness of the gospel be proclaimed by the weak and the simple before this people.' This reiterates the principle that the Lord designates a particular place and a particular people for His work. Ahaz's systematic violation of this principle—establishing worship everywhere except where the Lord commanded—represents the antithesis of what D&C teaches.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the central location where covenant worship occurs. Ahaz's multiplication of unauthorized worship sites represents a direct assault on the Temple's unique status. In restoration theology, the temple is not one option among many but the place where endowments and sealings occur—the covenant is sealed at the temple. Ahaz's approach—making worship possible anywhere, for anyone, in any form—dissolves the temple's authority and the covenant's particularity.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ will establish the ultimate temple—His own body. John 2:19-21 records: 'Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up... But he spake of the temple of his body.' Where Ahaz multiplies false worship sites, Christ becomes the one true meeting place between God and humanity. Hebrews 9:11-12 teaches that Christ, as high priest, entered into 'a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands,' offering the final and perfect sacrifice. The contrast is stark: Ahaz's worship sites are spread throughout the land, dispersing and weakening covenant identity; Christ's sacrifice and resurrection create a new and unified covenant that transcends place.
commentary.application: Verse 4 raises a critical question about spiritual authority and the danger of 'many paths.' In modern terms, Ahaz represents the approach that says 'everyone should be able to worship according to their own understanding, in their own preferred location, in their own preferred form.' From the world's perspective, this sounds inclusive and tolerant. From the covenant perspective presented in scripture, it is apostasy because it denies the Lord's right to specify how and where He will be worshipped. For modern covenant members, the application involves several dimensions: (1) The temple is not interchangeable with other places or practices—covenants are sealed there specifically. (2) The restored priesthood is not democratized or multiplied; it flows through a particular line of authority. (3) True spiritual community requires recognizing the Lord's designated location and representatives, not substituting our own preferences. The teaching can feel restrictive to modern sensibilities, but the alternative—Ahaz's approach—leads to the dissolution of the covenant and ultimately to judgment.

text_kjv: Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to war: and they besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him.
text_kjv_second: Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to war: and they besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him.

commentary.narrative: Verse 5 introduces the Syro-Ephraimite crisis, the major military and political event of the early years of Ahaz's reign (approximately 735 BCE). Rezin, king of Aram (Syria), and Pekah, king of Israel, march on Jerusalem with military intent. These two kings were attempting to force Judah into an anti-Assyrian coalition to resist the expanding Assyrian empire under Tiglath-Pileser III. Their siege of Jerusalem was meant to compel Ahaz's cooperation; when he refused to join them, they invaded. The phrase 'came up to Jerusalem to war' (ya'alu et Yerushalaim laamilkhama) is geographically and militarily precise—they marched toward the highland city to conduct a siege. However, the verse ends with 'but could not overcome him' (velo yakhlu lehillachem)—the siege failed militarily. Jerusalem held. This military failure, however, masks a political and theological disaster: though unable to take the city by military force, Rezin and Pekah's pressure drove Ahaz into the arms of Assyria, which will prove far more catastrophic for Judah's long-term future than either a siege or a coalition would have been.

word_study.meaning: came up to, marched against; the verb 'alah means 'to go up' and is used for military campaigns, especially those involving movement from lower to higher terrain
word_study.significance: The verb 'alah is used throughout Kings for military campaigns. In this context, it indicates military purpose and the traversal from lower territory toward Jerusalem, which sits on a higher elevation in the Judean hills. The movement 'up to' Jerusalem emphasizes the military threat.

word_study.meaning: and they besieged; the qal of tzur means 'to besiege, to lay siege to'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the phrase 'they besieged Ahaz' personalizes the siege—the city becomes identified with the king. Ahaz is the one under siege, not merely his city. The verb indicates an attempt to reduce the city through starvation, psychological pressure, and military blockade.

word_study.meaning: they were not able to fight/overcome; yakhol means 'to be able, to have the strength or power to'
word_study.significance: This phrase indicates that despite the siege, Rezin and Pekah lacked the military capacity to take the city. Whether due to the strength of Jerusalem's walls, the presence of garrison troops, or simply the resources required for a prolonged siege, the military outcome was clear: they could not prevail. Yet this military fact did not translate into strategic victory for Ahaz.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah's account of the same event: 'And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Ahaz, king of Judah, that Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up toward Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it.'
Isaiah's word to Ahaz during the siege: 'Take heed, and be quiet; fear not... these two fiery brands... shall not come to pass'; the Lord promised deliverance if Ahaz would trust.

The parallel account emphasizes the damage done despite the siege's failure: Pekah killed 120,000 Judahites in battle and took 200,000 captive, showing that though Jerusalem was not taken, Judah suffered grievously.
Teaching that the Lord protects His covenant people: 'And we humbly ask thee to grant, in thy great mercy, that we may be worthy of thy protection.'

commentary.historical_context: The Syro-Ephraimite War (735-733 BCE) is one of the best-documented events of Judahite history because it appears not only in Kings but in Isaiah, in 2 Chronicles, and in Assyrian records. Tiglath-Pileser III's annals mention his campaigns against these very kings and his receipt of tribute from them. The coalition that Rezin and Pekah were attempting to form was meant to resist Assyrian expansion. However, Ahaz's refusal to join them left him vulnerable—not to Rezin and Pekah militarily, but to Assyrian pressure. Within three years, both Rezin and Pekah were dead (either in battle against Assyria or deposed by Assyrian pressure), and Judah was a vassal state of Assyria. The irony is that the siege's military failure set up Ahaz's political disaster: had he joined the coalition, he might have faced Assyrian wrath; by refusing, he faced it anyway, but having refused to ally with his northern neighbors, he faced it alone.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records multiple instances where covenant people face military siege and learn that their deliverance depends on their faith rather than their military capacity. The Nephites, besieged by Lamanites, learned that 'with God is the battle' (Alma 44:3). Ahaz's situation parallels these moments, except that Ahaz learns the opposite lesson: he abandons trust in the Lord and turns to human alliances. The contrast between those who trust (like Alma) and those who do not (like Ahaz) is central to the Book of Mormon's historical theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:37 teaches: 'Therefore, be ye as wise as serpents and yet harmless as doves.' Ahaz attempts to be 'wise' through political maneuvering with Assyria, but he is neither 'harmless' (he violates the covenant) nor ultimately wise (his political moves lead to vassalage). D&C 123:1-5 emphasizes that the Lord will 'plead [the] cause' if His people remain faithful; by contrast, those who abandon the covenant find themselves without that promise.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple in Jerusalem was understood as the seat of the Lord's presence and the place of His protection. The verse notes that the siege failed to overcome the city, which many commentators have interpreted as indicating the Lord's protection of His house. However, this military protection does not translate into spiritual safety if the king (and people) abandon the covenant. The Temple's protection is conditional on covenant fidelity—a principle that will be tested more severely in later reigns.

commentary.christological_typology: The siege of Jerusalem and its deliverance foreshadow the ultimate defense of the City of David by Jesus Christ. Just as earthly Jerusalem was preserved from these ancient enemies (though at great cost), the heavenly Jerusalem—the Bride of Christ—will be preserved eternally by Christ Himself. Revelation 3:12 promises: 'Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God: and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem.' The military deliverance Ahaz experiences is temporary and does not lead to his salvation; the spiritual deliverance Christ provides is eternal.
commentary.application: Verse 5 presents a subtle but crucial teaching: military victory is not the same as theological victory, and deliverance from one threat does not guarantee wisdom or faithfulness. Ahaz is delivered from the siege, but he responds to this deliverance with further apostasy rather than with renewed covenant commitment. For modern members, this raises the question: when we experience what seems like divine protection or blessing, do we respond with deeper faithfulness, or do we become complacent and even bolder in our departures from the covenant? The teaching here is that external circumstances are not the ultimate measure of success. A life can be outwardly secure while being inwardly corrupt (as Ahaz's is). The application is to remain faithful not because we have faced a crisis that demands it, but because faithfulness to the covenant is itself the highest good. The verse also warns against seeking deliverance through human alliance instead of through the Lord. Ahaz's next move—appealing to Assyria—will prove far more costly than the siege itself.

text_kjv: At that time Rezin king of Syria recovered Elath to Syria, and drave the Jews from Elath: and the Syrians came to Elath, and dwelt there unto this day.

commentary.narrative: Verse 6 shifts focus from the main siege at Jerusalem to a concurrent military development: the loss of Elath (also spelled Eilat), Judah's crucial Red Sea port. The phrase 'at that time' (ba'et hahi) indicates this was happening during the same period as the siege of Jerusalem—simultaneous military pressure from multiple directions. Rezin recovered (or more accurately, conquered) Elath for Aram. The verb 'recovered' (shivah) might suggest Elath had been under Aramean control before; however, in context it likely means Rezin conquered/took control of the city. More significantly, Ahaz (or his forces) lost Judahite control of the city entirely. The phrase 'drave the Jews from Elath' (vaynashel et-hayeudim me-eilot) uses a forceful verb—'expelled' or 'drove out'—indicating the removal of the Judahite population. The final phrase, 'and dwelt there unto this day' (ad hayyom hazeh) is an editorial note from the narrator indicating that at the time of writing, Aram still controlled Elath or at least, the situation persisted long after Ahaz's reign. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac Peshitta read 'Edomites' (Edomim) instead of 'Arameans' (Aramim), which would make better geographical sense—Edom borders the Red Sea south of Judah, while Aram is to the north. This textual variant suggests some uncertainty about which power actually controlled Elath in the immediate aftermath, though Aram's temporary control seems likely given the broader military situation.

word_study.meaning: recovered, restored, returned; the hiphil of shuv, 'to return'
word_study.significance: The verb carries the sense of taking control or restoring to one's own possession. In this context, it indicates Rezin's conquest and securing of Elath. The use of 'recovered' rather than simply 'conquered' may suggest historical tradition that Elath had been under Aramean control at some earlier point, though the immediate context shows it was Judahite before Rezin's action.

word_study.meaning: and he expelled/drove out the Jews from Elath; nashel (qal) means 'to drive out, to expel'
word_study.significance: The verb is forceful, indicating not merely military defeat but the removal of the population. This was standard practice in ancient Near Eastern warfare—conquered territories were often depopulated or repopulated with loyal subjects. The term 'Jews' (yehudim) here denotes the inhabitants of Judah, whether ethnically Judahite or simply residents of the kingdom.

word_study.term_original: וַיֵּשְׁבוּ שָׁם עַד־הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה (vayeshvu sham ad-hayyom hazeh)
word_study.meaning: and they dwelt there to this day; an editorial formula indicating the narrator's perspective on the persistence of the situation
word_study.significance: The phrase 'to this day' (ad hayyom hazeh) is characteristic of the Deuteronomic history and indicates the narrator writing from a perspective centuries after the events described. The persistence of the situation from Ahaz's time through the narrator's time emphasizes the permanence of the loss. This is not a temporary setback but a lasting change in the political geography.

cross_references.connection: Uzziah (Azariah), an ancestor of Ahaz, 'built Elath and restored it to Judah'; Ahaz loses what his predecessor had secured.
Elath is mentioned as a location on the border of Edom; its strategic position on the Red Sea made it valuable for trade and military control.
Solomon built a fleet of ships at Elath, showing its importance as a maritime port for Judah; its loss cuts Judah off from Red Sea trade.

The parallel account notes: 'For the LORD brought Judah low because of Ahaz king of Israel; for he made Judah naked, and transgressed sore against the LORD.' Edom and Philistines also invaded during this period.

commentary.historical_context: Elath (modern Eilat/Aqaba) sits at the northern tip of the Red Sea and was a crucial trading hub in antiquity. Control of Elath provided access to trade routes to Arabia, the Red Sea, and beyond. Uzziah's rebuilding of Elath (2 Kings 14:22) was part of a program of territorial expansion and economic development. The loss of Elath to Aram during Ahaz's reign represents both a military defeat and an economic disaster—Judah loses its primary access to maritime trade. The verse's note that the situation persisted 'unto this day' suggests that Elath remained outside Judahite control for the rest of the pre-exile period. Interestingly, the textual variant (Edomites vs. Arameans) points to historical uncertainty: by the time the later books of Kings were being compiled, it may have been unclear exactly which power controlled Elath in the immediate aftermath of the Syro-Ephraimite crisis. However, the critical point—that Judah lost the city and suffered economically and strategically—is clear regardless.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The loss of Elath parallels the loss of prosperity and covenant blessings that the Book of Mormon associates with unfaithfulness. When the Nephites maintain the covenant, they 'prosper in the land' (2 Nephi 1:9; Alma 50:23); when they depart from it, they face losses—territorial, economic, and military. Ahaz's loss of Elath is part of the broader pattern of covenant unfaithfulness leading to national diminishment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:5-9 teaches that the Lord gives and the Lord takes away according to His will and the covenant fidelity of His people. The loss of Elath, coming as it does alongside Ahaz's covenant violations, illustrates this principle. The Lord does not preserve a kingdom's prosperity when the king abandons the covenant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: While Elath is not a religious site, its loss represents the diminishment of Judah's power and resources. The Temple depends, in part, on a functioning kingdom with sufficient resources to maintain it. The progressive loss of Judahite territory and wealth during and after Ahaz's reign will eventually contribute to the vulnerability that leads to the Babylonian exile. The Temple's fate is thus indirectly tied to the kingdom's territorial integrity.

commentary.christological_typology: The loss of Elath represents a loss of dominion and territorial promise. In the Messianic vision, Jesus Christ will inherit all dominion and authority. Daniel 7:14 prophesies of the Son of Man: 'And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him.' Where Ahaz loses Elath and Judah's borders shrink, Christ's kingdom expands infinitely. The restoration of all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:9-10) reverses the losses incurred by unfaithful kings like Ahaz.
commentary.application: Verse 6 teaches that covenant unfaithfulness leads not only to spiritual loss but to practical, material loss. Ahaz's apostasy sets off a cascade of military defeats and territorial shrinkage. The loss of Elath cuts off trade, impoverishes the kingdom, and weakens Judah militarily. For modern covenant members, the application extends beyond the spiritual realm: faithfulness to the covenant has real-world consequences for prosperity, security, and flourishing. The phrase 'unto this day'—indicating a permanent loss—warns that some losses, once incurred, persist. Ahaz cannot recover Elath; that port will not return to Judahite control in his lifetime. The application is that choices made in covenant unfaithfulness can have long-lasting consequences that extend far beyond the immediate moment. The temple teaching associated with the 'at-one-ment' emphasizes that we can be reconciled to God and recover what was lost spiritually; however, temporal consequences sometimes remain even after spiritual repentance. The wise course is to avoid such losses in the first place by maintaining faithfulness, rather than hoping to repair the damage afterward.

text_kjv: So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria, and out of the hand of the king of Israel, which rise up against me.

commentary.narrative:
Ahaz's decision to appeal to Tiglath-pileser represents a theological and political watershed moment in Judah's history. Facing the Syro-Ephraimite coalition (the combined forces of Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel), Ahaz rejects Isaiah's counsel to trust God and instead seeks rescue through an earthly superpower. This verse marks the beginning of Judah's fatal entanglement with Assyria—a relationship that will ultimately lead to vassalage, religious apostasy, and spiritual decline.

The language Ahaz employs—'your servant and your son'—draws directly from ancient Near Eastern treaty and vassal terminology. In the world of the second-century imperial powers, these were the binding formulas by which a lesser king bound himself to a greater one in perpetual subordination. Ahaz is not merely requesting military aid; he is formally entering Assyria's imperial system, placing himself under Tiglath-pileser's sovereignty. What makes this act particularly grave is that these very terms—'servant' and 'son'—belong to Israel's covenant relationship with God. By appropriating vassal language for an earthly king, Ahaz implicitly transfers the loyalty that belongs to the God of Israel to a pagan emperor.

The verb Ahaz uses for salvation—hoshi'eni ('rescue me')—compounds the theological tragedy. This comes from the root yasha, which throughout the Psalms and Prophets denotes divine salvation, divine deliverance from enemies. It is the verb that righteous kings use in prayer to God (Psalm 109:26, for example). Ahaz speaks to Assyria the language of prayer to God. Isaiah had offered Ahaz a sign—'Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God' (Isaiah 7:11)—but Ahaz refused, saying it would be tempting God. Now, rather than accepting God's offer of protection, he begs an earthly king for the salvation only God can provide. The irony is not merely literary; it is the theological core of the narrative: Ahaz has fundamentally misplaced his faith.

word_study.meaning: Eved ('servant') denotes political subordination, vassalage, and obedience; ben ('son') indicates a relationship of dependent loyalty within a hierarchical family structure. In ancient Near Eastern treaty contexts, these two terms together form the binding formula of vassal relationship—the vassal is both a subordinate servant and an adopted dependent of the suzerain. The phrase 'your servant and your son am I' (avdekha ubinkha ani) is the formal self-designation of a vassal committing himself to perpetual allegiance.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that these terms are deliberately chosen from covenant vocabulary. Eved and ben are the very terms the covenant reserves for Israel's relationship to God the Father. By using them for Tiglath-pileser, Ahaz misdirects the loyalty that belongs to the divine covenant. This is not a mere political alliance; it is a covenantal violation dressed in diplomatic language.

word_study.meaning: From the root yasha ('to save, deliver, rescue'), this verb appears throughout the Psalms as the cry of the righteous to God in times of distress. It means 'save me' in the fullest theological sense—deliverance from enemies, rescue from danger, divine intervention on behalf of the one who calls.
word_study.significance: Ahaz directs to the Assyrian emperor the same plea that the Psalms direct to God. This is the language of prayer, of covenant faith, of trust in divine deliverance. By petitioning Tiglath-pileser with this verb, Ahaz performs a kind of liturgical inversion: he prays to a pagan king for what only God can provide. Isaiah's offer of a sign from God (Isaiah 7) is rejected; the emperor's military response is embraced.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'palm' or 'sole of the foot,' but idiomatically 'power, control, possession, grasp.' The phrase mikkaf melekh ('from the hand/power of the king') indicates being under someone's control or grip.
word_study.significance: Ahaz seeks to escape from the 'palm' or 'grip' of two earthly kings by placing himself in the grip of a third. The imagery is one of being clutched, seized, held captive—and his solution is to exchange one captor for another, more powerful one.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah offers Ahaz a sign from God to build his faith during the same Syro-Ephraimite crisis, but Ahaz refuses, claiming it would be 'tempting the LORD.' His rejection of divine offer here makes his appeal to Assyria all the more pointed—he has chosen earthly power over faith.
The righteous use the verb 'save me' (hoshi'eni) in prayer to God: 'Help me, O LORD my God; O save me according to thy mercy.' Ahaz uses this covenantal language toward an earthly king instead.
The covenant curse warns that unfaithful Israel will serve enemies who will place an iron yoke upon their neck—a curse Ahaz now voluntarily invites by submitting to Assyria.

The parallel account in Chronicles adds that Ahaz also sent to Assyria for help while being pressed by Edomites and Philistines, showing his multiple crises—yet his response is uniformly to rely on Assyria rather than God.

The prophet later rebukes Israel's covenant infidelity: 'And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor? or what hast thou to do in the way of Assyria, to drink the waters of the river?' Ahaz's decision exemplifies this condemned pattern.

commentary.historical_context: The Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 735-732 BCE) was a crisis in which Rezin of Aram-Damascus and Pekah of the northern kingdom of Israel formed a coalition against Judah, likely trying to force Ahaz into an anti-Assyrian alliance. Tiglath-pileser III (745-727 BCE) was one of ancient Assyria's most aggressive imperial expansionists, engaged in massive campaigns of territorial conquest and population deportation. When Ahaz appeals to him, he is not approaching a friendly neighbor but an empire actively conquering the Levant. Tiglath-pileser had his own strategic interests in the region and was already moving toward Damascus independently; Ahaz's appeal provided him with a pretext and perhaps financial incentive to accelerate that campaign. The historical irony is that Tiglath-pileser would have moved against Damascus eventually, with or without Ahaz's plea—but by making it, Ahaz placed Judah firmly within Assyria's imperial orbit, creating obligations and dependencies that would bind future Judean kings and ultimately contribute to the kingdom's vulnerability. Ancient Near Eastern practice shows that vassal relationships carried heavy tribute burdens and ideological subordination; a king who styled himself 'your servant and your son' was committing to ongoing deference and financial obligation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of rejecting divine counsel in favor of seeking worldly power appears repeatedly in the Book of Mormon. King Lamoni's father initially seeks power and dominion through military conquest, though he eventually turns to God (Alma 19:36). More directly, the decline of the Nephite kingdom often follows patterns of leaders seeking alliances with worldly powers and rejecting prophetic counsel—particularly the trade and commerce that bind kingdoms together in unholy dependencies (Helaman 7:21-26). The principle that salvation comes through covenant relationship with God, not through earthly alliances, is central to Nephite theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants emphasizes that Zion stands or falls by faithfulness to covenants. Section 105:2-4 explains that the Lord's people are sometimes led captive 'because of the transgressions of [the] people.' Ahaz's decision to seek Assyrian protection rather than trust God mirrors the spiritual choice that covenants present: allegiance is indivisible. One cannot simultaneously hold covenants with God while making Assyria (or any earthly power) the ultimate source of security. D&C 111:11 teaches, 'I am in your midst, and I am the God of Israel, and the God of the whole earth, and has been sent down from heaven to prove you in all things'—a principle that directly counters Ahaz's assumption that earthly rulers are more reliable than God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple represents the place where covenants with God are made and renewed, the place where salvation is secured through ordinances. By turning to Assyria instead of God, Ahaz is essentially rejecting the Temple's offer of covenant protection and making a pagan empire his source of salvation. The subsequent desecration of the Temple altar (which occurs in verse 10-12 of this chapter) flows logically from this spiritual choice: having rejected the covenant relationship, the Temple becomes merely a building to be refashioned according to foreign religious patterns.

commentary.christological_typology: Ahaz's rejection of divine salvation in favor of worldly power is implicitly a rejection of the Messiah. Isaiah 7:14 (spoken during this very crisis) prophesies the coming of Immanuel, 'God with us'—the ultimate fulfillment of covenant salvation. Ahaz's refusal to accept the sign from Isaiah, and his turning instead to an earthly emperor, prefigures the rejection of Christ himself. Just as the Messiah would offer salvation freely but be rejected in favor of worldly powers (John 18:40—'Not this man, but Barabbas'), Ahaz rejects God's offer and chooses an earthly ruler. The covenant principle is constant: salvation comes through God's appointed means, not through human alliances.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members face versions of Ahaz's choice repeatedly: Do we trust God's covenants and promises, or do we seek security through worldly systems, status, wealth, or human alliances? The Test of Discipleship is whether our ultimate allegiance is to the covenant or to something else. When we feel threatened or insecure, do we turn to God in prayer and faith (the equivalent of asking for a sign from God), or do we immediately reach for worldly solutions—financial manipulation, social maneuvering, political power, or human approval? Ahaz's language of vassalage ('I am your servant and son') is the language of ultimate allegiance. To whom do we say these words? The covenant demands that they be directed to God alone. Every time we compromise a covenant principle to gain worldly advantage or security, we repeat Ahaz's choice.

text_kjv: And Ahaz took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the LORD, and in the treasures of the king's house, and sent it for a present to the king of Assyria.

commentary.narrative:
Having committed himself verbally to Assyria, Ahaz now backs his oath with material payment. He raids the Treasury of the Temple—the house of the LORD—and combines those sacred funds with the royal treasury to send as payment to Tiglath-pileser. The narrator's word choice is significant: he calls this payment a shochad, a 'bribe,' not a neutral 'tribute' or 'gift.' This is not merely a political transaction; it is an act of corruption—the very act the Torah forbids in Exodus 23:8 ('thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous'). The Temple treasury is being emptied to purchase the favor of a pagan king.

The phrase 'that was found in the house of the LORD' (hannimtsa beit YHWH) suggests a comprehensive raiding—Ahaz takes whatever silver and gold is available, stripping the Temple of its reserves. This is not a small diplomatic gift; it is a systematic plundering of sacred resources. The source of the funds matters theologically: the Temple treasury represents the wealth of the covenant community, the material expression of God's blessing on Israel. To empty it into the hands of a pagan emperor is to transfer the community's spiritual wealth to serve an alien power. It is, in effect, to deny that the Temple has any saving power, any efficacy, any reason to be maintained.

This verse encapsulates Ahaz's entire spiritual problem: he has concluded that the God of Israel cannot or will not save him, so he invests his trust—and his treasure—in Tiglath-pileser instead. The bribe is not merely a transaction; it is a statement of faith: 'I believe that Assyrian military power, purchased with Assyrian gold, can save me more reliably than the God of my fathers.' By raiding the Temple to pay for Assyrian protection, Ahaz has virtually admitted that the Temple's God is powerless or indifferent. His actions will have consequences: the Temple, stripped of resources and now compromised by association with Assyrian religious practices, will decline in influence and authority.

word_study.meaning: A bribe, a gift given to corrupt judgment or secure unjust favor. Unlike neutral terms like minchah ('gift') or masset ('tribute,' levy), shochad carries explicit negative moral connotation throughout Hebrew Scripture. It appears in laws prohibiting judges from accepting bribes (Exodus 23:8, Deuteronomy 16:19) and in warnings about corruption.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the narrator's choice of shochad rather than a neutral term 'signals moral judgment.' By calling Ahaz's payment a 'bribe,' the narrator explicitly condemns the transaction as corrupt. This is not the legitimate tribute a vassal pays a suzerain; it is a bribe—an attempt to purchase favor through corruption. The theological message: when a covenanted people offer their sacred wealth to a pagan king to secure protection, they are not engaging in prudent statecraft but in spiritual corruption.

word_study.meaning: Passive form of matsa ('to find, to discover, to locate'). Suggests that Ahaz takes whatever silver and gold happens to be available or in storage in the Temple—a comprehensive seizure of liquid resources.
word_study.significance: The passive form and the phrase 'that was found' emphasize the totality of the seizure. Ahaz doesn't take a portion or set aside some reserves; he empties whatever is there. The Temple treasury, which should be reserved for worship, maintenance, and covenant obligations, is transferred entirely to serve a foreign power.

word_study.meaning: The Temple, the dwelling place of God's Name, the center of Judah's covenant worship and spiritual life. All wealth held there was understood to be under God's ownership and reserved for covenant purposes.
word_study.significance: By raiding the 'house of the LORD' to pay a pagan king, Ahaz violates the sanctity of the Temple and redirects covenant resources to alien purposes. This act foreshadows the later desecration of the Temple under Manasseh and the ultimate exile of Temple treasures to Babylon.

cross_references.connection: The Torah explicitly forbids taking bribes (shochad): 'For the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.' By paying Tiglath-pileser a bribe, Ahaz violates a foundational covenant law.

Judges are warned: 'Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift (shochad).' The same term for bribe appears, showing that bribery corrupts justice and righteousness.

Asa, an earlier Judean king, sends silver and gold from the Temple treasury to Ben-hadad of Syria to break his alliance with Baasha of Israel. Like Ahaz, Asa depletes the Temple treasury to purchase foreign military aid—a pattern that shows Judah's recurring temptation to treat sacred wealth as a resource for political manipulation.

At the end of Judah's kingdom, the Babylonians 'carried all the vessels of the house of God...unto Babylon.' What Ahaz began—the departure of the Temple's wealth and treasures—is completed when enemies carry them away entirely.

Isaiah condemns a similar generation: 'Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water: Thy princes are rebellious, and companions of thieves: every one loveth gifts, and followeth after rewards.' Bribery and corruption, like Ahaz's payment to Assyria, indicate a people who have abandoned covenant faithfulness.

commentary.historical_context: The Temple treasury in ancient Judah functioned as both a religious repository and an economic reserve for the kingdom. It accumulated wealth from Temple taxes, donations, and the spoils of military campaigns dedicated to God. Kings were expected to maintain and enhance the Temple's resources, not deplete them. However, in times of crisis, Temple treasuries were sometimes raided—either by foreign invaders or by desperate rulers. Ahaz's action was unusual in that it was voluntary: he himself pillaged the Temple to pay a foreign king. This would have been shocking to the Jerusalem priesthood and the devout population. From an ancient Near Eastern perspective, it would have signaled complete capitulation: Ahaz was not negotiating as an equal or even a peer, but as a desperate supplicant willing to impoverish his own religious institution. Tiglath-pileser's policies included systematic extraction of tribute from vassals; Ahaz's payment would have been recorded (likely by Assyrian scribes) as the first installment of ongoing obligation. The emptying of the Temple treasury also had practical consequences: maintenance of the building, support of the priesthood, and the purchase of sacrificial animals all required funds. A depleted treasury would affect the daily functioning of worship.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records instances where the righteous protected and maintained sacred treasures while the wicked misused them. When the Nephites had the Liahona, the brass plates, and other sacred objects, their faithfulness protected these things; their apostasy led to loss or corruption of sacred items. Alma 37:38-40 teaches that 'by small and simple things are great things brought to pass,' and applies this to the preservation of sacred records and treasures. The opposite is also true: by small and continuous compromises (like Ahaz's raid on the Temple), spiritual institutions are degraded. King Benjamin's teaching (Mosiah 4) emphasizes that all we have is from God and should be used according to His will, not for personal or political advantage.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:78-80 speaks of the Lord's house and the law that should govern it: 'And let all they who have received the blessing of my house...remember that these blessings are sacred...and are not to be used except in obedience to my law.' Ahaz's use of Temple treasury funds for a bribe violates this principle entirely. He treats sacred resources as political capital. D&C 59:21 teaches the broader principle: 'In nothing doth man offend God, or against none is his wrath kindled, save those who confess not his hand in all things, and obey not his commandments.' Ahaz's actions show a man who does not acknowledge God's hand in his security and therefore misallocates sacred resources.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple treasury was sacred space, held in trust for covenant purposes. By emptying it to pay a foreign king, Ahaz violates the sanctity of the Temple. In Latter-day Saint understanding, the Temple is the place where members make covenants and renew their commitment to God's law. To treat Temple resources as mere political tools is to deny the Temple's sacred purpose. Ahaz's action implicitly says: 'The Temple cannot save me, so I will use its wealth to purchase salvation elsewhere.' This is a foundational rejection of Temple covenant theology.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus was offered worldly power and wealth by Satan during His temptation (Matthew 4:8-10), but He rejected it all, choosing instead to trust God and fulfill His covenant mission. In contrast, Ahaz accepts a 'temptation' of power, purchased with sacred wealth. Later, at His crucifixion, Jesus is offered 'sour wine' (a common drink offered to criminals) in a final test of whether He will accept worldly provision instead of trusting His Father. Ahaz's corruption of the Temple treasury through payment to Assyria stands as a shadow image of everything Christ's sacrifice would overcome—the perversion of sacred space and resources, the misdirection of trust away from God to earthly powers.
commentary.application: The principle embedded in this verse is direct: we cannot serve two masters, and we cannot claim to trust God while we invest our resources, time, and energy in worldly systems as our primary source of security. Ahaz's bribe to Assyria is an extreme example, but modern applications abound. Do we invest spiritually in Temple attendance and sacrament worthiness, or do we prioritize status, wealth, and professional advancement? Do we set aside resources for fast offerings and charitable giving (the modern equivalent of Temple maintenance), or do we rationalize that money is needed for personal security? Do we teach our children that their ultimate protection comes through covenant faithfulness, or through accumulating wealth, credentials, and social position? Like Ahaz, we face choices about where to place our trust and how to allocate our sacred resources (our time, talents, emotional energy, finances). Every such choice echoes his decision: Am I buying security from the world, or investing in my covenant relationship with God?

text_kjv: And the king of Assyria hearkened unto him: for the king of Assyria went up against Damascus, and took it, and carried the people of it captive to Kir, and slew Rezin.

commentary.narrative:
In this verse, Ahaz's stratagem appears to succeed in the short term. Tiglath-pileser heeds his plea and moves militarily against Damascus, conquering it, deporting its population, and executing Rezin, the king of Aram. Ahaz's immediate enemies are eliminated—at least in appearance. The political crisis that threatened Judah is resolved, and the vassal king has been effective in purchasing his own protection. From a purely military and political standpoint, Ahaz's gamble has paid off: he is no longer under attack. However, the narrator's tone is instructive: the apparent 'success' is actually the beginning of Judah's long decline into dependency and spiritual compromise.

The verb vayyishma alayv ('he listened to him') shows Tiglath-pileser responding to Ahaz's plea—but the historian makes clear that Tiglath-pileser's campaign against Damascus was likely already in motion. Tiglath-pileser III was engaged in a systematic conquest of the Levant, and Damascus was a strategic target with or without Ahaz's invitation. What Ahaz's appeal accomplished was to ensure that when Assyria conquered his enemies, Judah would be obligated to the conqueror. The Aramean kingdom is permanently crushed: the verb vayyiglehah ('he exiled them') uses the root galah, which will come to dominate the remaining chapters of Kings as it describes the deportation of Israel, Judah, and Jerusalem. Rezin's death (heimit, 'he put to death') ends the Aramean monarchy.

The deportation to Kir is particularly significant. The Covenant Rendering notes that Amos 9:7 identifies Kir as the original homeland of the Arameans: 'Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?' The Arameans are being sent back to where they came from, stripped of their kingdom and identity. This is Tiglath-pileser's standard policy: conquest, exile, and cultural erasure. And now Judah has voluntarily placed itself in relationship with a power that practices such thorough destruction. The narrator is implicitly asking: what will happen when this same power turns its attention to Judah?

word_study.meaning: To uncover, to lay bare, to exile. As a verb describing forced population transfer, it means to deport people from their land, stripping them of territory, identity, and freedom. The root meaning of 'uncovering' or 'laying bare' underlies the sense of complete exposure and loss.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that galah will 'dominate the remaining chapters of Kings.' Indeed, this verb appears in 17:6 (Israel's exile to Assyria), 24:15 (Judean exile to Babylon), and 25:21 (the final deportation after Jerusalem's fall). Every instance of galah represents a covenant people being stripped, exposed, and removed from the land. Ahaz's appeal to Tiglath-pileser sets in motion the very process that will eventually apply to Judah itself.

word_study.meaning: To cause death, to execute, to slay. The verb appears in contexts of judicial execution and military killing.
word_study.significance: Rezin's execution marks the final end of the Aramean kingdom. His death is the consequence of his opposition to Assyria. For Ahaz, Rezin's elimination is a relief—but it comes at the cost of establishing Judah as Assyria's vassal.

word_study.meaning: To listen to, to hear and respond to, to obey. In the context of international relations, it means to grant the request or comply with the plea.
word_study.significance: Tiglath-pileser listens to Ahaz's plea—but this 'listening' comes with strings attached. Ahaz has asked for Assyrian protection, and Assyria will ensure that Ahaz remains perpetually dependent on Assyrian power to maintain his position.

cross_references.connection: Amos identifies Kir as the original homeland of the Arameans: 'Have not I brought up...the Syrians from Kir?' The deportation of Damascus to Kir represents a return to origins—an undoing of the Aramean kingdom's place in history.

The same root verb (galah, 'deported') is used when Israel is exiled to Assyria: 'In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria.' The pattern established with Damascus will repeat with Israel.

During the same Syro-Ephraimite crisis, Isaiah assures Ahaz that Aram and Israel will be broken: 'Take heed, and be quiet; fear not...because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have taken evil counsel against thee...Yet the LORD hath not appointed him to the end.' Isaiah predicts the collapse of these enemies without Ahaz needing to call Assyria.

Chronicles adds context: 'Wherefore the LORD his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Syria...and Ahaz took the treasures of the house of the LORD, and of the king's house.' Ahaz's apparent success in eliminating enemies comes because he has already placed himself under Assyrian protection and paid the price.

Decades later, when Judah faces Babylon, a similar dynamic occurs: the king capitulates, sends tribute, and the Babylonian king listens—but the 'listening' leads to siege, capture, and exile, not lasting security.

commentary.historical_context: Tiglath-pileser III's campaign against Damascus occurred in 732 BCE and is confirmed by Assyrian annals and archaeological evidence. Damascus was a major center of Aramean power and a strategic hub on trade routes. Tiglath-pileser's policy toward conquered territories was systematic and brutal: military conquest, followed by the deportation of the elite classes and significant portions of the population. This served both political (removing potential resistance) and economic (providing forced labor for Assyrian imperial projects) functions. The deportations created permanent dependency: a kingdom that had lost its population and leadership could not recover or rebel. Kir, the destination of the Damascene deportees, was likely in Upper Mesopotamia (possibly near the Kur River in what is now Turkey/Armenia). By exiling Arameans to their supposed 'homeland,' Tiglath-pileser was symbolically undoing the political entity of Aram-Damascus. The complete destruction of Damascus' kingship was unusual for the period—it shows that Aramean resistance to Assyria was perceived as a serious threat. For Judah, watching this destruction was instructive: this is what happened to those who opposed Assyria, and it will happen to those who did as well.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains warnings about trusting in the arm of flesh and making alliances with foreign powers. In Helaman 13:2-5, Samuel the Lamanite condemns the Nephites for building up their own strength and wealth while rejecting the Lord's guidance. Alma 37:33-34 teaches that reliance on God's guidance prevents us from being 'led about hither and thither, carried about with every wind of doctrine.' Ahaz's reliance on Assyria mirrors the condemned pattern of seeking security through worldly alliances rather than covenant fidelity.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:2 contains a promise to the faithful: 'I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God...I came into the world...to be crucified for the sins of the world...that all those who believe and are baptized shall be saved.' In contrast, Ahaz seeks salvation (hoshi'eni) from Tiglath-pileser. The Restoration emphasizes that 'the Lord shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace' (D&C 105:14). Ahaz's failure to trust God's protection is presented as a violation of a foundational covenant principle: trust in God, not in the arm of flesh.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple represents the place where God's covenants are enacted and where the faithful encounter God's power. By turning to Assyria instead of the Temple, Ahaz implicitly rejects the Temple's efficacy. His later desecration of the Temple altar (verses 10-12) flows from this theological choice: if Assyrian protection is more reliable than God's, then Assyrian religious forms have equal or greater validity than the Temple's forms.

commentary.christological_typology: The pattern of choosing worldly power and military solutions over faith in God is fundamentally opposed to Christ's way. Jesus explicitly rejected the Zealots' approach of seeking salvation through military revolt against Rome. His temptation in the wilderness (Matthew 4) included the offer of 'all the kingdoms of the world' if He would bow to Satan—an offer to gain security through worldly power, exactly like Ahaz's appeal to Tiglath-pileser. Christ's refusal to call down legions of angels to defend Himself (Matthew 26:53) stands in stark contrast to Ahaz's call for military rescue from a pagan king.
commentary.application: When we face threats—to our finances, our reputation, our children's future, our security—do we, like Ahaz, immediately reach for worldly solutions (lawyers, financial advisors, social maneuvering, political connections), or do we first seek God's counsel through prayer and fasting? The contrast is not between foolishness and wisdom (prudent planning is appropriate), but between trust in God as the ultimate source of our security and trust in earthly powers as the ultimate source. Ahaz's problem was not that he sought Assyrian military aid; his problem was that he did so in place of, rather than in addition to, faith in God. Modern parallels: Do we accumulate wealth primarily for personal security, or as stewardship for God's purposes? Do we teach our children that their ultimate protection comes from covenant keeping, or from credentials and connections? Do we live as though God can and will fulfill His promises, or as though we must fend for ourselves? Ahaz's short-term success (Damascus is defeated) masks long-term disaster (Judah becomes Assyria's vassal). Similarly, worldly solutions may appear to work in the short term, but they bind us to dependencies that ultimately compromise our freedom and our covenant.

text_kjv: And king Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and saw an altar that was at Damascus: and king Ahaz sent to Urijah the priest the fashion of the altar, and the pattern of it, according to all the workmanship thereof.

commentary.narrative:
Ahaz's theological decline accelerates.
