This verse implies that truth requires more than teaching—it requires the living authority, ongoing revelation, and covenant community that sustain authentic religion. The returned priest possessed teaching but lacked the institutional and spiritual infrastructure to sustain genuine Yahwism.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God's people are instructed in covenant relationship. A priest teaching outside the temple framework (in a sanctuary compromised by idolatry) lacks the full power of his office. The temple provides the context in which teaching transforms into lived covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the true teacher who came from the Father, trained in perfect truth, dwelling among people who would eventually receive him or reject him. Unlike the compromised priest of Samaria, Christ's teaching produced genuine transformation in his disciples—a 'born again' experience that created a new people capable of genuine covenant. His residence among humanity was the ultimate 'incarnational teaching' where the message and the messenger were one.
commentary.application: Members should recognize that hearing correct doctrine is not the same as being transformed by it. Intellectual agreement with LDS teaching—even accurate teaching—does not produce conversion without personal covenant-making and the Holy Ghost. The question for each member is: are you learning the 'manner' of God (external compliance) or genuinely fearing and loving the Lord (internal transformation)? The test comes when maintaining the faith requires sacrifice or when worldly alternatives become attractive. A priest's words, however true, cannot ultimately save; only genuine covenant relationship with God can.

text_kjv: Howbeit every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made, every nation in their cities wherein they dwelt.

commentary.narrative:
Despite the priest's teaching, or alongside it, the foreign settlers maintain their ancestral deities. The repetition of 'every nation...every nation' (goy goy...goy goy) emphasizes the multiplicity and the fundamental division of loyalty. The settlers have not abandoned their gods; they have merely added YHWH to them. This is the practical outcome of the Assyrian king's administrative solution: instead of conversion, there is coexistence. The settlers install their gods in 'the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made'—repurposing the corruption of Israel's worship for their own pagan purposes.

This verse reveals a profound theological tragedy. The high places were already corrupted sites in Israel's history—places where syncretistic Yahwism had merged with pagan elements during the northern kingdom's existence. Now these structures become temples for purely pagan deities. The 'Samaritans' (Shomronim—originally the remnant Israelite population of the northern kingdom who were not deported) had built these high places for their corrupted Yahwism. The foreign settlers simply repurposed them. What began as Israel's attempt to worship YHWH through corrupted means became, under foreign occupation, openly polytheistic temples. The trajectory from partial truth to complete syncretism to outright paganism is now visible. Each nation worships its own god 'in their cities'—compartmentalizing their religious practice by ethnic community, yet coexisting in the same land.

word_study.term_original: עֹשִׂים גּוֹי גּוֹי אֱלֹהָיו (osim goy goy elohav)
word_study.meaning: To make, create, fashion; here referring to the fashioning or establishment of deities—not necessarily carved idols but recognized and honored gods.
word_study.significance: The verb osim ('making') suggests active, intentional maintenance of their gods. This is not passive retention of ancestral memory but deliberate religious practice. The phrase structure goy goy elohav ('nation by nation, its gods') emphasizes that each ethnic group maintains distinct religious identity alongside whatever compromise has been made with YHWH.

word_study.meaning: Houses/temples of the high places; bamot (high places) were shrines, typically built on elevated locations, used for cultic worship in ancient Israel.
word_study.significance: High places were already controversial in Israel—prophets condemned them as syncretistic (see Hosea 10:8). Now they become explicitly polytheistic temples. This is the ultimate degradation: from Israel's corrupted Yahwism to foreign polytheism using Israel's own architectural structures.

word_study.meaning: People of Samaria; can refer to the Israelite remnant population who remained after deportation, or (anachronistically) to later Samaritan communities.
word_study.significance: The term here likely refers to the original Israelite inhabitants of the northern kingdom who escaped deportation or were not included in the mass exile. The foreign settlers took structures that the remaining Israelites had built and repurposed them. There is a tragic symmetry: Israelite apostasy built the high places; foreign populations now use them for outright paganism.

cross_references.connection: Jeroboam made high places and appointed priests for them, establishing the infrastructure of syncretistic worship that would later be repurposed for pagan gods.
Josiah's reform specifically targeted the high places and altars, revealing the persistent problem of high-place worship throughout the monarchy and the prophetic judgment against them.
Hosea prophesied that Israelites would call on high places to fall on them, indicating that high places themselves became symbols of judgment rather than blessing.

Paul's principle that 'all things are lawful, but all things are not expedient' applies to the settlers' attempt to maintain multiple religious commitments simultaneously—permitted but spiritually destructive.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Samaria reveals a complex religious landscape. High places existed throughout the Levant—at sites like Tel Moza, Tel Qiri, and others—as shrines for local and regional deities. They varied from elaborate temple structures to simple open-air altars. The Assyrian documents from Sargon II record the populations brought into Samaria: Babylonians, Cutheans, Amorites, and others—each with established religious traditions. The phenomenon of religious syncretism in colonial situations is well-documented: colonists typically maintain aspects of their ancestral religions while adopting some features of local practice. The repurposing of Israelite high places for Mesopotamian gods reflects both practical (the structures already existed) and theological (foreign gods need dwelling places) motivations. The mention of 'every nation in their cities' suggests ethnic clustering—different populations maintaining distinct religious spaces within the broader region.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon describes similar attempts to maintain multiple spiritual loyalties. The people of Ammonihah rejected the gospel while maintaining their traditional religions; King Lamoni's court initially wanted to add the God of Ammon to their existing pantheon rather than replace it (Alma 19:9-11). Only genuine covenant conversion produces single-hearted loyalty to YHWH.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 20:37 teaches that members must covenant to 'support and maintain the church by their prayers, their labors, and their faith'—a principle that presupposes exclusive covenantal commitment. The settlers' attempt to maintain divided loyalty—YHWH and their ancestral gods—is precisely what D&C 1:30 prohibits when the Lord declares only one church 'true and living' because it maintains covenant integrity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple covenants explicitly bind the individual to serve God and no one else. The endowment teaches that divided loyalty is spiritual death. The settlers' practice of maintaining high places for both YHWH and foreign gods violated the fundamental principle of temple covenant—whole-heart commitment to the Lord.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ made covenant impossible with divided heart: 'No man can serve two masters' (Matthew 6:24). His teaching and example establish that authentic discipleship requires singular loyalty. Unlike the settlers who attempt to honor YHWH while maintaining pagan gods, Christ's followers are called to exclusive devotion. His resurrection established a new covenant that transcends territorial boundaries and ethnic identities—true unity through faith, not coexistence through compromise.
commentary.application: Modern members face the settler's temptation in different forms. Attempting to maintain Church membership while pursuing worldly values that contradict gospel principles—spiritual materialism, divided ethical standards, maintaining habits that contradict covenants—is the contemporary version of worship at both YHWH's altar and foreign gods. The text suggests that such compromise is ultimately unsustainable and spiritually sterile. Genuine discipleship requires examining whether you are wholly committed to God's kingdom or maintaining 'high places' of divided loyalty in your heart. The question is not whether external compliance with practice is maintained, but whether your deepest loyalty belongs entirely to God.

text_kjv: And the men of Babylon made Succothbenoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima,

commentary.narrative:
The narrator now catalogs the specific deities maintained by each foreign population. This verse begins a list (continuing through verses 31-33) that names and identifies the gods of the settlers, making visible the syncretistic religious landscape created by Assyrian resettlement. The formula 'the men of [region] made [deity]' identifies each ethnic group with its ancestral god. These are not new gods created in Samaria but ancient, established deities brought with the settlers from their homelands. The mention of Babylon, Cuth, and Hamath identifies major Mesopotamian and Syrian regions under Assyrian control—all contributing populations to the resettlement.

The specific deities named represent different types of gods. Succoth-benoth is obscure but possibly related to Babylonian divine imagery; Nergal was the underworld god, associated with plague and death; Ashima was a Syrian deity, possibly associated with healing or protection. Each god carried the religious and cultural identity of its people. By naming them, the narrator is saying: This is not theoretical syncretism; this is what actually happened. Foreigners did not disappear into Israelite culture; they maintained their identities and their gods. The list serves a theological purpose as well—it shows that the settlers' compromise solution (learning to 'fear the LORD') was simply layered on top of, not instead of, their ancestral religions. The narrative's catalog of foreign gods implicitly contrasts with the exclusive loyalty to the one God of Israel that the Torah demands.

word_study.meaning: To make, create, establish, perform; here used of establishing or maintaining a deity.
word_study.significance: The verb asah suggests active, intentional establishment—not passive inheritance. The settlers actively maintain their gods' worship in their new home. This is not cultural memory but practiced religion.

word_study.meaning: Meaning uncertain. Possibly 'Booths of Daughters' or a corruption of a Babylonian deity name (perhaps Sarpanitu or Zir-banitu, goddess consort of Marduk). Attested only here in Scripture.
word_study.significance: The obscurity of this name emphasizes the foreignness of the deity. The name is so unfamiliar to the Hebrew audience that it cannot be explained—it stands as a marker of Babylonian otherness. The TCR rendering preserves this by noting the uncertainty.

word_study.meaning: A Mesopotamian deity, god of the underworld, plague, pestilence, and death. Well-attested in cuneiform texts and Mesopotamian religion.
word_study.significance: Nergal was one of the major deities in the Babylonian pantheon. His presence in Samaria indicates that Babylonian religious practice was established among the settlers. That the god of plague would be maintained is grimly ironic—the plague of lions (verse 25) was attributed to YHWH's judgment, yet the settlers maintain the Mesopotamian plague god.

word_study.meaning: A deity attested in cuneiform sources and mentioned in Amos 8:14. Possibly a Syrian or Arabian goddess. Exact identity and character remain debated.
word_study.significance: Ashima was likely a regional Syrian deity. That the people of Hamath maintained her worship shows how the settlers brought not only their lands' major gods but regional deities significant to their local identities. The specificity of 'Ashima' shows that the settlers maintained distinct religious traditions within the broader resettlement.

cross_references.connection: Amos mentions 'Ashima of Samaria,' indicating that Ashima worship persisted in the northern kingdom and became infamous among later prophets as a symbol of Israel's apostasy.
Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar's dream while living in Babylon, showing familiarity with Mesopotamian religious concepts, similar to what a Babylonian settler would have maintained.
Jeremiah denounces Judah for burning incense to 'strange gods' and 'gods that neither thou nor thy fathers hast known,' a warning echoed in the settlers' syncretism.
The Ephesian craftsmen's defense of Artemis mirrors the settlers' active maintenance of their ancestral deities despite pressure to adopt new religious commitments.

commentary.historical_context: Nergal is extensively documented in cuneiform texts, including treaties, ritual texts, and myths (particularly the Nergal and Ereshkigal myth). Babylonian sources confirm his status as an underworld deity associated with plague and warfare. Cuth (also spelled Kutha) was a Mesopotamian city particularly associated with Nergal worship; its inhabitants were naturally inclined to maintain his cult even in exile. Ashima's identity is more complex—she may be related to Arab goddess traditions or to Syrian deities. Amos 8:14 confirms that Ashima worship became established in the northern kingdom, suggesting that the process described here in 2 Kings produced lasting religious communities. The historical reality is that these foreign populations, brought to Samaria by Sargon II, gradually integrated with the remaining Israelite population while maintaining aspects of their religious traditions. This mixture ultimately produced the Samaritan community documented in later sources—a people who acknowledged YHWH while maintaining non-Judean traditions.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records Nephite populations that mixed Nephite religious practice with elements of Lamanite tradition (Jacob 1:15-16). It also depicts the dangers when populations brought from different cultures attempt to maintain divided religious loyalties while coexisting in the same land (Mosiah 25:6-12). True unity required singular devotion, not coexistence of multiple faith systems.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 82:10 teaches that 'he that keepeth his covenants shall have mercy.' The settlers' maintenance of foreign gods while nominally acknowledging YHWH represents covenant-breaking in its essence. D&C 97:28 warns that those who violate their covenants shall 'stumble in great things'—precisely what occurred in Samaria.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God unifies his people under one covenant. The settlers' divided religious loyalty—maintaining YHWH altars and foreign god altars—violated the fundamental principle of temple unity. No one could simultaneously make covenant with YHWH and maintain loyalty to other deities. This is why the temple is described as a 'house of God'—it admits no partners to his divine authority.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the sole object of worship in the New Testament. The Gospels record his repeated insistence that worship belongs to God alone: 'Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve' (Matthew 4:10). His refusal to compromise on this point, even when offered worldly power, contrasts sharply with the settlers' attempt to honor YHWH while maintaining pagan deities. Christ taught that the first and greatest commandment is total loyalty to God—no divided heart, no parallel altars.
commentary.application: The verse implicitly asks modern members: What 'gods' do you maintain alongside YHWH? The original context involved literal deity worship, but the principle applies to any loyalty or practice that competes with whole-hearted devotion to God. It might be career ambition pursued at the expense of family and Church, social status maintained through compromising principles, entertainment or social media habits that displace scripture study and prayer, or financial pursuits that override tithing and fast offering. The settlers thought they could maintain both; the narrator's catalog shows the futility of that approach. The question is not whether you claim to believe in God, but whether you are maintaining 'high places' of competing devotion in your heart. The text suggests that such division is ultimately spiritually sterile—you will have neither the protection and blessing of YHWH nor the satisfaction of authentic commitment to your ancestral traditions, only the tension and compromise of both.

text_kjv: And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.

commentary.narrative: Verse 31 catalogs the religious practices of the foreign colonists settled in the northern kingdom after Assyria's deportation of Israel. The narrator identifies two distinct groups—the Avites and the Sepharvites—each with their own pantheon. The Sepharvites' practice of child sacrifice (mōlekh worship, implied by the names Adrammelech and Anammelech containing the element *melekh*, 'king') is particularly shocking because it echoes the very sin that had already brought judgment on Judah through kings like Ahaz (2 Kings 16:3). The Covenant Rendering translates *sorefim et-beneihem ba-esh* as 'immolated their children,' capturing the ritualistic nature of the act more precisely than 'burnt.' This is not accidental burning but deliberate sacrifice—a grotesque inversion of the covenant faith Israel was meant to practice.

word_study.meaning: Causative form of 'burning'—not accidental fire but intentional immolation. In ANE context, this refers to child sacrifice as religious offering, a practice condemned throughout the Tanakh but practiced by wayward Israelite and Judahite kings.
word_study.significance: The verb *saraph* ('to burn') combined with child sacrifice reveals the depth of religious corruption. The Sepharvites adopt the very practice that Ahaz of Judah had engaged in (16:3), creating a grim mirror: foreign settlers and apostate Israelite kings share the same idolatry.

word_study.meaning: Divine names containing *melekh* ('king'). The names likely derive from Mesopotamian theology, possibly corruptions or variants of Aramaic or Akkadian deity names. Adrammelech may relate to a sun-god in Sepharvite tradition; Anammelech is less certain, though ancient sources speculate various identifications.
word_study.significance: The presence of *melekh* in both names connects to mōlekh worship—the practice of child sacrifice that Israelite law explicitly forbade (Leviticus 18:21, 20:2-5). Whether or not these are direct references to Mōlekh, the narrator implies that the Sepharvites practice the same abomination.

word_study.meaning: The Sepharvites were an Assyrian-controlled city population; their gods were indigenous to that region. The plural *elohim* indicates a polytheistic system—the settlers bring their entire pantheon into the depopulated land.
word_study.significance: The specificity of 'gods of Sepharvaim' reinforces that these are not ad hoc practices but systematic religious transplantation. The settlers are not converting; they are reproducing their homeland's idolatry in Israel's territory.

cross_references.connection: Ahaz 'made his son pass through the fire'—Judah's king practices the same Sepharvite sin, showing that covenant violation spans both kingdoms.
The explicit Torah prohibition: 'Thou shalt not let any of thy seed pass through the fire to Molech'—the practice 2 Kings 17:31 describes is Israel's gravest legal violation.
Moses warns Israel not to adopt the abominable practices of displaced nations—exactly what the foreign settlers do, and what Israelite kings had already begun.
Jeremiah condemns Judah for valley child sacrifice: 'built the high places of Tophet...to burn their sons and daughters in the fire'—the same sin recurs across generations.

commentary.historical_context: The Sepharvites and Avites were populations deported by the Assyrian Empire and resettled in the depopulated northern kingdom (2 Kings 17:24). This was standard Assyrian imperial policy: remove the native population and replace it with colonists from elsewhere in the empire, preventing rebellion through demographic disruption. Sepharvaim was likely an Aramean city in Syria. The practice of child sacrifice to Mōlekh or similar deities was widespread in the Levant, attested in Phoenician and Aramean contexts. The archaeological record from Iron Age Palestine contains evidence of child burial in jar burials and other contexts that scholars debate as sacrificial or not. What matters for the narrative is the theological point: the foreign settlers practice the very abomination that had corrupted Israel and Judah. The narrator is not condemning foreign settlers alone; he is showing that syncretism and child sacrifice are the logical endpoint of abandoning YHWH's covenant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar spiritual displacement when righteous communities are scattered and replaced by those who 'know not the Lord.' The pattern in 2 Kings 17 mirrors the cycle described in Alma 9:12-14, where communities that reject covenant are replaced by those who inherit their lands but lack covenant understanding.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 82:10 encapsulates the principle: 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' The foreign settlers in Israel never covenanted with YHWH; they add him to their pantheon without binding themselves to exclusive loyalty. This echoes the repeated D&C pattern that covenant requires complete allegiance (D&C 133:5).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The high places and Sepharvite shrines are counterfeit temples—places of worship that reject the centralized, covenantal worship established at Jerusalem. The child sacrifices are perversions of the Abrahamic covenant's willingness-to-sacrifice motif (Genesis 22), twisted into actual infanticide rather than faith tested and faith sustained.

commentary.christological_typology: The child sacrifice condemned here inverts the ultimate typology: Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac (Genesis 22) foreshadows God the Father's offering of his own Son. The Sepharvites' actual child sacrifice is the demonic counterfeit—flesh offered without redemptive purpose, death without resurrection. Christ's sacrifice alone is the true and final mōlekh offering that ends all others (Hebrews 10:10).
commentary.application: Modern covenant members must examine whether we add Christ to our lives while maintaining spiritual allegiances elsewhere—to material success, social approval, or ideologies that contradict revealed truth. The subtlety of Sepharvite syncretism is that they 'feared the LORD' (v. 32) while serving other gods. Partial allegiance is not allegiance. Complete covenant fidelity demands the same exclusive devotion the narrator demands of Israel.

text_kjv: So they feared the LORD, and made unto them of the lowest of them priests of the high places, which sacrificed for them in the houses of the high places.

commentary.narrative: Verse 32 reveals a critical paradox: the foreign settlers did fear (or claim to fear) the LORD, yet they appointed their own priests to serve in high places—the very structures the Deuteronomic law condemned as centers of idolatry. The phrase 'of the lowest of them' (*miqqetsotam*, literally 'from their extremities/from among themselves') indicates they appointed priests from their own ranks, not Levites trained in Torah. This reproduces Jeroboam's original sin in 1 Kings 12:31, where the northern king appointed non-Levitical priests to rival the temple at Jerusalem. The narrator presents this as logical inconsistency: you cannot genuinely fear YHWH while simultaneously rejecting his prescribed worship system. The addition of YHWH to their pantheon is not conversion; it is religious expansion, fitting the God of Israel into a framework that maintains allegiance to other deities.

word_study.meaning: The verb *yare'* ('to fear/revere') in the context of covenant theology means to acknowledge divine authority and submit to it. Here it describes respect or recognition, but the narrator's framing in v. 33 shows this 'fearing' is incomplete—fear without exclusive allegiance is hollow.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's note on v. 32 clarifies that the settlers 'added' YHWH to their existing pantheon rather than replacing it. This word choice—'feared'—is precisely what makes the verse tragic: they recognize something worthy of reverence in YHWH, yet refuse the exclusivity his name demands.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'from their extremities' or 'from among themselves.' The root *qatseh* ('end, edge, extremity') implies ordinary, non-priestly persons—anyone willing to serve at the shrines. The phrase rejects the Levitical system where only descendants of Aaron could legitimately perform sacrifice.
word_study.significance: This mirrors Jeroboam's appointment of non-Levites in 1 Kings 12:31. The theological implication is severe: the settlers establish a parallel priesthood outside the covenant structure, making worship accessible but illegitimate. Every person becomes priest, which means no one is properly consecrated.

word_study.meaning: *Bamah* (plural *bamot*) refers to the elevated cultic platforms used throughout Canaan for worship. While bamot sometimes appear in early Israel as acceptable worship sites (1 Samuel 9:12-13), by the Deuteronomic period they are condemned as centers of idolatry that compete with the Jerusalem temple.
word_study.significance: The 'priests of the high places' are illegitimate by Torah standard. The narrator uses this term throughout 2 Kings to mark Israel's and Judah's spiritual failure. Even the settlers' attempt to incorporate YHWH into their worship system uses the wrong structures and the wrong personnel.

cross_references.connection: Jeroboam 'made priests of the lowest of the people'—the exact phrase appears in both verses, showing that foreign settlers and apostate Israelite kings reproduce the same structural sin.
The law prescribes a single central sanctuary and Levitical priesthood; the high places and non-Levitical priests violate these foundational covenant statutes.
Jeroboam's appointment of non-Levitical priests is identified as the sin that caused Israel's destruction—showing that this verse's structural violation carried covenant consequences.
Jeroboam appoints priests for the high places 'and for the devils, and for the calves which he had made'—indicating that high place worship and idol worship were inseparable.

commentary.historical_context: The high place system predated Israel; it was a Canaanite mode of worship that Israel adopted while also maintaining the tabernacle/temple system. By the Deuteronomic reform period (late 8th-7th centuries BCE), high places were seen as direct violations of the law's prescription for a single sanctuary. The foreign settlers, unfamiliar with Israelite law, would have naturally recreated their home religions' structures—using elevated platforms for worship and appointing local leaders as priests. They would have seen no contradiction in adding YHWH to their pantheon alongside their native deities. The non-Levitical priesthood issue is particularly significant: in Israel's system, priesthood was hereditary through Aaron's line. Levites were set apart through law and ritual. The settlers' appointment of anyone as priest democratizes the role in a way that sounds inclusive but is actually anarchic from a covenant perspective.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern appears in Alma 1:15, where Nehor establishes a false priesthood, 'making himself a high priest...saying they were all priests.' The settlers' action echoes this perversion—multiplying priests outside legitimate authority structures.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 establishes that the Church president receives revelation; D&C 42:11 requires that priests be 'called and chosen and set apart according to the laws of the Church.' The settlers' priests have no such calling or ordination—they are self-appointed, resembling the false priests condemned in D&C 50:7-8.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The high places are counterfeit temples. The Latter-day Saint temple system, by contrast, represents the restoration of the Jerusalem temple's covenantal function. The illegitimate priesthood of the settlers parallels the apostasy from priesthood authority that the Restoration corrects through the laying on of hands and formal ordination.

commentary.christological_typology: The Levitical priesthood foreshadows Christ's unique, eternal priesthood (Hebrews 7:24-25). The settlers' multiplied non-Levitical priests represent the demonic counterfeit—many false priests claiming authority they don't possess, just as false Christs and false prophets proliferate in the latter days (Matthew 24:24). Christ's single, perfect priesthood supersedes and fulfills the Levitical order.
commentary.application: In modern covenantal life, we must distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate religious authority. The settlers' error was assuming that sincere desire to worship and local convenience justified abandoning the prescribed structure. Today's parallel: spiritual earnestness does not substitute for proper ordinances and priesthood authority. Covenant members should recognize that feeling moved to worship or serve does not authorize us to create our own religious systems parallel to the Church's. The 'lowest of them' appointed as priests had no special preparation, training, or authority—just willingness. Authentic covenant practice requires submission to authorized structures, not just personal conviction.

text_kjv: They feared the LORD, and served their own gods, after the manner of the nations whom they carried away from thence.

commentary.narrative: Verse 33 is the narrator's definitive summary of Samaritan syncretism—and it is a statement of theological contradiction, not compromise. The Covenant Rendering's translation captures the tension perfectly: 'They feared the LORD, but they also served their own gods.' The Hebrew structure (*et YHWH hayu yre'im ve-et eloheihem hayu ovdim*—literally 'the LORD they were fearing, and their own gods they were serving') places the two practices side by side without resolution or mediation. The phrase 'after the manner of the nations whom they carried away from thence' references the Assyrian policy of population exchange: the settlers came from territories from which other populations had been deported, and they replicate the religious customs of their homelands. The narrator's point is clear: you cannot genuinely fear YHWH—which demands exclusive loyalty (Deuteronomy 6:13-14)—while simultaneously worshipping other gods. The two are not compatible; the settlers' practice is incoherent from a covenant perspective.

word_study.term_english: feared the LORD...served their own gods
word_study.term_original: אֶת־יְהוָה הָיוּ יְרֵאִים וְאֶת־אֱלֹהֵיהֶם הָיוּ עֹבְדִים
word_study.transliteration: et YHWH hayu yre'im, ve-et eloheihem hayu ovdim
word_study.meaning: The Hebrew fronts both objects—'the LORD they were fearing' and 'their gods they were serving'—creating a syntactical balance that underscores the logical impossibility. The verb *yare'* ('fear') and *avad* ('serve') are the foundational covenant verbs that demand exclusivity.
word_study.significance: This verse is the crux of the Samaritan problem. The settlers are not ignorant of YHWH; they consciously add him to their pantheon. The narrator treats this as not merely failure but incoherence—a violation of the basic logic of covenant theology, which requires exclusive allegiance.

word_study.term_english: after the manner of the nations
word_study.meaning: *Mishpat* ('judgment, custom, law') combined with *goyim* ('nations') indicates the religious practices of pagan peoples. The settlers maintain their inherited customs rather than adopting Israel's covenant obligations.
word_study.significance: The phrase echoes Deuteronomic warnings against imitating pagan practices (Deuteronomy 18:9-12). The settlers are doing precisely what Israel was warned against—naturalizing foreign religious customs on the land.

word_study.term_english: whom they carried away from thence
word_study.meaning: The Assyrian deportation policy (*higlu*—'exiled/carried away') created a vacuum by removing native populations. The settlers fill that void, importing their religious culture from their places of origin.
word_study.significance: The verse implies a tragic irony: the very practice that displaced Israel—Assyrian imperialism—brings new populations that replicate the same religious failures that caused Israel's fall. The land of Israel becomes a patchwork of foreign cults rather than a unified covenantal territory.

cross_references.connection: The foundational covenant demand: 'Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God...Ye shall not go after other gods'—exactly what v. 33 shows the settlers violating.

Joshua warns: 'If ye...serve the gods of the people which are round about you, then will the anger of the LORD be kindled against you'—the settlers' syncretism triggers the very judgment Joshua foresaw.

Elijah confronts Israel: 'How long halt ye between two opinions? If the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him'—the same either/or logic applies to the settlers' attempt to fear both YHWH and other gods.
Paul echoes the principle: 'Be ye not unequally yoked...What communion hath light with darkness?'—the theological incompatibility of divided worship.

commentary.historical_context: The Samaritan population became a persistent historical reality after 722 BCE. By the intertestamental period, Samaritans had developed a separate Jewish identity centered on the Samaritan Pentateuch (a textual variant of the Torah) and worshipped at Mount Gerizim rather than Jerusalem. This verse captures the moment of their formation: foreign settlers mixed with remaining Israelites, adopted a form of Yahwism, yet maintained their indigenous deities. From a purely sociological perspective, religious syncretism was common in the ancient world—people naturally kept deities of their homeland while adapting to new places. From a theological perspective, however, the covenant law forbade this completely. The narrator's judgment here became the basis for later Jewish animosity toward Samaritans: they were seen as heretical, syncretistic, and inauthentic (cf. John 4:9). The historical reality is more complex, but the narrator's verdict stands: covenant allegiance to YHWH cannot coexist with worship of other gods.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 31:8-18 records the Zoramites, who incorporate true principles (acknowledging God) into a false worship system (the Rameumptom). Like the settlers of v. 33, they 'fear' God in name while serving their own desires. The spiritual disease is identical: syncretism presented as expansion rather than corruption.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:30 emphasizes that the Church is 'the only true and living church upon the face of the whole earth'—a statement that would directly rebuke the settlers' assumption that they could add YHWH worship to their existing religious system. D&C 20:37 clarifies that Church membership requires entering into covenants 'in their hearts,' which means exclusive, not additive, commitment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant requires the individual to covenant exclusively with God. The settlers' attempt to 'fear the LORD' while serving other gods mirrors the impossible position of someone attempting to take covenants while maintaining undisclosed, contradictory allegiances. Temple covenants are predicated on the willingness to put God first, wholly.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus demanded the same exclusivity in Matthew 6:24: 'No man can serve two masters...Ye cannot serve God and mammon.' The settlers' attempt to serve both YHWH and other deities foreshadows the impossible choice Christ presents: commitment to Him demands the renunciation of other loyalties. In Revelation 3:15-16, the 'lukewarm' church—neither hot nor cold—is spewed from Christ's mouth. The settlers are spiritually lukewarm, mixing loyalty rather than choosing radical allegiance.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members live in a pluralistic society where many worldviews compete for allegiance. The settlers' error teaches a hard lesson: you cannot maintain sincere devotion to Jesus Christ while simultaneously organizing your life around the values, priorities, and gods of the world. Financial security becomes a god; social status becomes a god; personal comfort becomes a god. The verse warns against the subtlety of syncretism: we do not consciously choose to abandon Christ; we simply add other allegiances 'alongside' our faith. But the covenant structure forbids this. Genuine discipleship requires the kind of exclusive loyalty the settlers refused—giving Christ first place not just in words but in choices, time, and resources.

text_kjv: Unto this day they do after the former manners: they fear not the LORD, neither do they after their statutes, or after their ordinances, or after the law and commandment which the LORD commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel;

commentary.narrative: Verse 34 makes an astonishing reversal: now the narrator says the settlers 'fear not the LORD'—directly contradicting v. 33. The resolution comes from deeper covenant theology. In v. 33, they 'feared' YHWH in the sense of acknowledging him and adding him to their pantheon. Here, the narrator clarifies that genuine fear of the LORD means exclusive covenant obedience; any devotion that stops short of that is not genuine fear at all. The phrase 'unto this day' (*ad hayom hazeh*) suggests the narrator is writing from a perspective where the Samaritan syncretism has become a permanent, defining characteristic—not a temporary confusion but an established pattern. The fourfold covenant vocabulary—statutes (*chuqqim*), ordinances (*mishpatim*), Torah (*torah*), and commandment (*mitsvah*)—represents the comprehensive scope of covenant obligation. The specific reference to 'the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel' reaches back to Genesis 32:28, where the name 'Israel' itself encodes covenant identity. To reject these four dimensions of law is to reject the very identity that Israel's name signifies.

word_study.meaning: The negative formation (*einam*) nullifies the claim of v. 33. 'Fear' in covenant terms means more than acknowledgment; it means obedience, submission to the covenant stipulations. Without that, fearing YHWH is empty.
word_study.significance: This verse teaches that covenant theology has an objective standard: fear of the LORD is not merely emotional or internal but demonstrable through obedience. The settlers cannot claim to fear YHWH while rejecting his law. The narrator refuses to grant them even nominal credit.

word_study.meaning: Four terms for covenant obligation: (1) *choq* ('statute/prescription')—divine decrees that often lack explicit rationale; (2) *mishpat* ('ordinance/judgment')—regulations based on justice and reasoning; (3) *torah* ('instruction/law')—comprehensive teaching about how to live in covenant; (4) *mitsvah* ('commandment')—singular binding instruction. Together they encompass every dimension of covenant law from detailed prescriptions to foundational principles.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's note explains that the narrator 'stacks four legal terms to indicate that every dimension of covenant obligation has been violated.' This is not casual rejection; it is total apostasy. Every category of law—whether mysterious decrees or rational ordinances, comprehensive instruction or specific command—has been abandoned.

word_study.term_english: children of Jacob, whom he named Israel
word_study.transliteration: benei Ya'aqov asher sam shemo Yisrael
word_study.meaning: The phrase reaches back to Genesis 32:28, where God changes Jacob's name to Israel after wrestling with him all night. The name 'Israel' literally means 'God strives' or 'he struggles with God'—it encodes the struggle, the covenant, the divine encounter. 'Children of Jacob/Israel' designates those who inherit this covenant identity.
word_study.significance: By invoking the covenant name given to Jacob, the narrator reminds readers that 'Israel' is not merely a political designation but a theological one—a people set apart, named by God, bound to divine law. The settlers are not Israel because they do not keep the law of the God who named Israel. The name itself carries obligation.

cross_references.connection: God names Jacob 'Israel' after a covenant encounter—showing that the name 'Israel' itself embeds covenant identity and obligation to YHWH.
Moses prescribes the statutes, ordinances, and commandments for 'the children of Jacob' to keep them, emphasizing that covenant law is the defining obligation of Israel's identity.
The curse formula: 'If ye will not hearken unto me...I will set my face against you'—the settlers' rejection of the four categories of law triggers precisely this judgment.

Nehemiah confesses that Israel 'hath not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the judgments' which God commanded—using the same three-fold (or four-fold) categories to describe covenant failure.

Jesus affirms that he came not to destroy the law but to fulfill it, and that whoever breaks 'one of these least commandments' is least in the kingdom—affirming the comprehensive nature of covenant obligation.

commentary.historical_context: The phrase 'unto this day' (*ad hayom hazeh*) was a historiographical formula used by biblical narrators to indicate that they were writing from a point in time long after the events described, observing that a pattern persists. This suggests the narrator is writing well after the 722 BCE fall of Israel, possibly in the exilic or post-exilic period (6th-5th centuries BCE or later), when Samaritan identity had solidified. The fourfold covenant vocabulary reflects Deuteronomic legal language developed during the monarchy period and standardized in the later legal tradition. The narrator is not inventing the categories; he is applying the standard covenant framework to judge the settlers' failure. From a historical perspective, the foreign settlers would not have had access to the full Torah initially. Over time, through contact with remaining Israelites and through the gradual adoption of Israelite literature, they may have encountered these laws and consciously rejected them, or they may have remained ignorant of them. The narrator, however, judges them by the standard of covenant law as if they had full knowledge and responsibility. This is theologically appropriate: ignorance of God's law does not excuse violation of covenant, especially when that law was made available.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern appears in Jacob 1:15-18, where Jacob describes those who have knowledge of God's commandments yet reject them—they 'perish in their iniquity' precisely because they cannot claim ignorance. Like the settlers, they have access to covenant law and consciously neglect it.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 75:5 teaches that those who receive the gospel 'and keep it not, shall be damned.' The settlers cannot claim to fear YHWH while rejecting his law; the covenant structure demands comprehensive obedience. D&C 131:6 teaches that 'all who have this law revealed unto them must obey the same'—an objective, not subjective, standard.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant encompasses all four dimensions the narrator mentions: statutes (what we covenant to do), ordinances (the formal rites binding us), law (the comprehensive framework), and commandment (specific obligations). To take temple covenants while planning to disregard them is precisely the settlers' error: nominal acceptance without genuine commitment.

commentary.christological_typology: The 'children of Israel' who bear the covenant name are types of the Church, the Bride of Christ (Ephesians 5:25-27). Just as Israel's identity is bound to covenant obedience, so the Church's identity is bound to Christ. Revelation 3:5 promises that the faithful will be clothed in white garments and have their names written in the Book of Life—an echo of the covenant name. The settlers' rejection of the four categories of law prefigures the apostasy from Christ described in 2 Thessalonians 2:3, where those who 'depart from the faith' abandon the foundational allegiance.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse teaches that covenant identity requires more than nominal belief. We cannot authentically belong to the Church (the modern 'Israel') while disregarding its foundational commitments. The four-fold standard—statutes (specific commandments), ordinances (the rites and practices), law (the comprehensive moral and spiritual framework), and commandment (binding obligations)—applies to us. To bear the name 'member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' is to covenant to keep all four dimensions. Casual observance—attending sacrament but living by the world's values, accepting the restored gospel intellectually but prioritizing personal convenience—mirrors the settlers' attempt to fear YHWH while rejecting his law. The verse challenges us to examine whether our covenants are authentic commitments or merely inherited traditions we claim without living.

text_kjv: With whom the LORD had made a covenant, and charged them, saying, Ye shall not fear other gods, nor bow yourselves to them, nor serve them, nor sacrifice to them:

commentary.narrative: Verse 35 shifts from the narrator's judgment to the recitation of the covenant terms themselves—the actual stipulations that the settlers (and before them, Israel) violated. The verb *karat* ('to cut') is the foundational covenant language; *karat berit* means literally 'to cut a covenant,' referring to the ancient Near Eastern practice of cutting sacrificial animals in half as part of covenant ratification ceremonies (cf. Genesis 15:9-18). By invoking 'the LORD had made a covenant' with Israel's ancestors, the narrator establishes that the obligation the settlers inherit is not arbitrary but deeply embedded in Israel's foundational history. The fourfold prohibition that follows cascades from external action to internal attitude: (1) 'not fear other gods'—the innermost reality of allegiance; (2) 'not bow yourselves to them'—physical prostration, the outward sign of worship; (3) 'not serve them'—ongoing service and devotion; (4) 'not sacrifice to them'—the ultimate act of worship. Each level deepens the commitment to exclusive allegiance to YHWH. The covenant prohibition is total, leaving no room for the 'addition' strategy the settlers attempt in v. 32.

word_study.meaning: The idiom *karat berit* ('to cut a covenant') derives from the ANE practice of cutting sacrificial animals and walking between the severed pieces as a binding oath. In the Tanakh, it indicates a formal, irrevocable covenant binding two parties—often with supernatural sanctions.
word_study.significance: The verb *karat* emphasizes that this is not a contract subject to renegotiation but a solemn covenant with cosmic weight. The settlers did not inherit a suggestion or advisory; they inherited a binding, cut covenant. The historical reference to 'the LORD had made a covenant' likely points to Sinai, though the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17) also uses this language.

word_study.term_original: לֹא תִֽירְאוּ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים וְלֹא־תִשְׁתַּחֲוּ לָהֶם וְלֹא תַעַבְדוּם וְלֹא תִזְבְּחוּ לָהֶם
word_study.transliteration: lo tire'u elohim acherim, ve-lo tishtachavu lahem, ve-lo ta'avdum, ve-lo tizbchu lahem
word_study.meaning: The four prohibitions represent a descending scale of worship intensity: (1) *tire'u* ('fear'—internal reverence); (2) *tishtachavu* ('bow down'—physical prostration); (3) *ta'avdum* ('serve'—active devotion); (4) *tizbchu* ('sacrifice'—the ultimate act of worship). Each presupposes the previous and deepens commitment.
word_study.significance: The cascade structure shows that covenant violation has multiple levels. A modern reader might think 'just don't sacrifice'; the covenant law recognizes that forbidden sacrificing is the endpoint of forbidden fearing, bowing, and serving. To stop the sin, one must begin with the innermost attitude.

word_study.meaning: The formula 'other gods' (*elohim acherim*) appears repeatedly in Deuteronomy and marks the boundary of covenant violation. The phrase implicitly denies the reality or power of these deities—from YHWH's perspective, they are 'other,' alternative, false.
word_study.significance: The use of the term *elohim* ('gods') for these deities is not an admission of their reality but a way of naming them as they appear to their worshippers. The covenant law prohibits treating them as though they were gods—which means prohibiting any fear, worship, or service directed toward them.

cross_references.connection: The paradigmatic covenant-cutting ceremony where God establishes the covenant with Abraham through a ritual of sacrificial animals and fire—the template for all biblical covenant language.
God declares to Moses, 'thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God'—the personal, affective foundation for the prohibition in v. 35.
The foundational covenant teaching: 'Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God...and shalt not go after other gods'—echoed verbatim in v. 35.
The curse formula: 'Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image...and setteth it in a secret place'—showing that covenant violation regarding false gods triggers specific curses.
Joshua warns Israel: 'Ye cannot serve the LORD...If ye forsake the LORD and serve other gods, then he will turn and do you hurt'—a restatement of the covenant terms and consequences.

commentary.historical_context: The four prohibitions reflect Deuteronomic legal formulation (7th-6th centuries BCE), though the concepts are ancient. The phrase 'fear other gods' appears in Deuteronomy 6:13 and related passages. The practice of covenant-cutting (karat berit) was widespread in the ancient Near East: Hittite treaties, Aramean inscriptions, and Assyrian vassal treaties all use similar language and practice. The covenant form in v. 35 likely reflects the Sinai covenant tradition, though it may also echo earlier covenant promises to the patriarchs. From a historical perspective, the foreign settlers would have brought their own covenant traditions from their home territories (Assyrian vassal oaths, for example). The narrator is interpreting their situation through Israel's covenant framework, suggesting that even settler populations inherit the covenant obligations that come with residence in covenant land.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 13:27 recounts the covenant made with the Lamanites: 'Keep the commandments of God and ye shall prosper in the land.' The settlers in 2 Kings 17 inherit a similar covenant through occupancy of covenant land; like the Lamanites, they face blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 82:10 encapsulates the covenant principle: 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' The covenant stipulations in v. 35 are not arbitrary; they are the conditions that bind God to bless. Violation severs the connection. D&C 59:4 teaches that the commandments are given 'that ye may keep and observe them.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The four-fold prohibition in v. 35 mirrors the temple covenant structure: we covenant not to fear (take seriously, give allegiance to) other gods/values; not to bow to them; not to serve them; not to make offerings to them. The temple covenant binds us to exclusive allegiance to God, making any divided loyalty a violation.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ enfolds all four prohibitions into the greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-38): 'Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.' This encompasses fear, bowing, serving, and sacrificing—all directed exclusively to God. In Matthew 4:10, Christ rejects Satan's temptation by quoting Deuteronomy 6:13: 'Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.' Christ embodies perfect covenant obedience; his sacrifice (the final offering in v. 35) ends all other sacrifices (Hebrews 10:10).
commentary.application: Modern covenant members live within the same covenantal framework. We covenant not to fear other gods—meaning we will not organize our lives around wealth, status, pleasure, or ideology that compete with allegiance to Christ. We covenant not to bow to them—we will not give public deference or honor to values that contradict revealed truth. We covenant not to serve them—our time, talents, and energy belong to God's kingdom, not worldly advancement. We covenant not to sacrifice to them—we will not offer our children's time, our integrity, or our spiritual resources on the altars of worldly gods. The settlers' error was thinking they could expand their allegiance; the covenant forbids expansion. True covenant life requires absolute prioritization—not hatred of other things, but refusal to put anything before God.

text_kjv: But the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt with great power and a stretched out arm, him shall ye fear, and him shall ye worship, and to him shall ye do sacrifice.
text_kjv_alternate: But the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt with great power and a stretched out arm, him shall ye fear, and him shall ye worship, and to him shall ye do sacrifice.

commentary.narrative: Verse 36 provides the positive counterpart to v. 35: instead of the cascading prohibitions, the verse now prescribes exclusive devotion to YHWH using the same four verbs—fear, worship (bow down), serve (implied by 'worship' in context), and sacrifice. The phrase 'the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt with great power and a stretched out arm' is the theological foundation for this exclusive allegiance. It is not an arbitrary demand but a response to redemptive history. YHWH did not merely create Israel; he acted as redeemer, liberating Israel from Egypt's bondage. The 'great power and stretched out arm' (*koach gadol uvizro'a netuyah*) is the classic Deuteronomic exodus language, appearing in Deuteronomy 4:34, 5:15, and 26:8. It is military metaphor applied to divine action—God extending his arm to strike Egypt and extract Israel. This redemptive act establishes the grounds for covenant obedience. The verse does not demand obedience because it is arbitrary; it demands obedience because Israel owes its existence as a free people to YHWH's saving action. The settlers, though they did not directly experience the exodus, are presented as heirs to this covenant heritage and thus bound by its obligations.

word_study.term_english: brought you up out of the land of Egypt
word_study.meaning: The verb *alah* ('to bring up, to go up') combined with 'out of the land of Egypt' refers to the exodus—the foundational redemptive event. *Mitrayim* (Egypt) is the place of bondage from which YHWH extracted Israel. The phrase frames the exodus as an 'going up'—a movement toward freedom and covenant land.
word_study.significance: The choice of *alah* ('up') rather than merely 'brought you out' suggests movement toward covenant blessing, not just away from judgment. It emphasizes the positive destination (covenant relationship with YHWH in covenant land) rather than merely negative escape.

word_study.term_english: with great power and a stretched out arm
word_study.meaning: *Koach* ('power, strength') combined with *zero'a netuyah* ('an outstretched/extended arm') is the image of divine military action. The outstretched arm is God's instrument of deliverance, extended to strike enemies and save his people. This phrase appears repeatedly in Deuteronomy and Jeremiah as the definitive description of the exodus.
word_study.significance: The metaphor of the 'arm' is deeply personal—it suggests intimate divine action, not distant cosmic power. An outstretched arm is close enough to touch, to embrace, to strike on behalf of someone. The image conveys both power and intimacy, making the exodus not a theoretical historical event but a visceral encounter with divine saving action.

word_study.term_original: אֹתוֹ תִירָאוּ וְלוֹ תִֽשְׁתַּחֲווּ וְלוֹ תִזְבָּחוּ
word_study.transliteration: oto tire'u, velo tishtachavu, velo tizbchu
word_study.meaning: These are the same three verbs from v. 35's prohibitions, now redirected exclusively to YHWH. The direct object pronoun *oto* ('him') and *lo* ('to him') emphasizes the singular focus—all these acts of worship and service are directed to YHWH alone. The verb *tizbchu* ('sacrifice') encompasses the full range of cultic practice.
word_study.significance: By using the identical verbs from the prohibition, the verse creates a structural mirror: what is forbidden toward other gods is commanded toward YHWH. This is not neutral pluralism but radical exclusivity. The same human capacity for fearing, bowing, and serving that tempts Israel toward syncretism must be directed entirely toward YHWH.

cross_references.connection: Moses describes the exodus using identical language: 'Did ever people hear the voice of God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as thou hast heard, and live? Or hath God assayed to go and take him a nation...by great trials, by signs, and by wonders, and by war, and by a mighty hand, and by a stretched out arm'—the 'stretched out arm' is the signature phrase for YHWH's redemptive power.

Another rehearsal of the exodus: 'Remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt...therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day'—YHWH's redemptive action grounds the obligation to keep covenant law.

The creedal statement: 'The LORD brought us forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand and with a great terror, and with signs, and with wonders'—the exodus is the foundation of Israelite identity and obligation.
The historical narrative of the exodus, showing YHWH's redemptive power at the Red Sea—the act that provides the theological grounds for covenant obedience throughout the Tanakh.

A psalm that combines the prohibition of v. 35 with the redemptive foundation of v. 36: 'There shall be no strange god be in thee...I am the LORD thy God...Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it'—showing that exclusive allegiance flows from remembrance of YHWH's redemptive work.

commentary.historical_context: The exodus was, from the perspective of ancient Israel, the defining historical event. Whether it occurred as described in Exodus or represents a theological memory of liberation struggles, it functioned as the foundation myth of Israel's identity. The phrase 'great power and stretched out arm' became formulaic in Deuteronomic theology and was used to reinforce covenant obligations repeatedly. For the foreign settlers, this phrase would have been unfamiliar; they had no memory of Egypt or exodus. The narrator's invocation of it suggests that occupying covenant land automatically makes one an heir to the covenant that brought Israel into being. This is a theological claim, not a historical fact. From a purely sociological perspective, the settlers would not have felt personally bound by an event they did not experience. From the narrator's theological perspective, however, the covenant is territorial and transcends generational memory—inhabiting the land obligates one to the covenant that grounds Israel's claim to it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 13:27-29 recalls the divine covenant with the Lamanites and frames it in redemptive terms: 'Inasmuch as ye will keep the commandments of God ye shall prosper in the land.' Like v. 36, the Book of Mormon grounds covenant obligation in divine saving action and the promise of the land. The parallel between Israel's exodus and Book of Mormon redemptive events shows the consistency of the covenantal pattern across scripture.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:24 echoes the language of v. 36: 'Keep my commandments; prepare ye, prepare ye...that your iniquity may be done away.' The Doctrine and Covenants repeatedly frames covenant obligation as a response to divine redemptive action (D&C 29:1-3). D&C 1:37-38 teaches that God's word 'shall all be fulfilled, whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The principle is consistent: covenant obligation flows from covenant making, which flows from redemptive action.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant is structured on precisely this pattern: we are redeemed through Christ's atoning sacrifice (analogous to the exodus), and in response, we covenant to keep his commandments exclusively. The covenants we make are not arbitrary impositions but responses to the greatest redemptive act in human history—Christ's sacrifice. The ceremony recounts creation, the fall, Christ's redemption, and then presents the covenant as the proper response to that redemption.

commentary.christological_typology: The exodus is a type of Christ's redemptive work. Just as YHWH 'brought Israel up out of Egypt with great power,' Christ 'brought us up' out of death through his resurrection and his 'outstretched arm' on the cross (Isaiah 53:1—'to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?'). The covenant obligation in v. 36 to fear, worship, and sacrifice exclusively to YHWH finds its fulfillment in the New Testament call to worship Christ exclusively (Revelation 5:13—'Worthy is the Lamb'). Hebrews 13:15-16 recasts sacrifice in light of Christ: 'By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually...But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.' The sacrifice demanded in v. 36 culminates in Christ's singular, final sacrifice (Hebrews 10:10).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites reflection on the redemptive acts we have experienced and how they ground our covenant obligations. We have been brought up out of the 'Egypt' of our pre-conversion condition through Christ's redemptive power. Like Israel liberated from bondage, we have been set free from sin, death, and separation from God. This redemptive experience is not merely a past event to remember; it is the ongoing foundation of why we fear, worship, and serve God exclusively. The verse challenges us: Can we point to redemptive moments in our lives—times when God's outstretched arm reached down to save us from impossible situations? These become the grounds for exclusive allegiance. When tempted to divide our loyalty (fearing other gods, serving other masters), we remember that God brought us up; therefore, God alone deserves our fear, worship, and sacrifice of our full selves.

text_kjv: Now it came to pass in the third year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, that Hezekiah the son of Ahaz king of Judah began to reign.

commentary.narrative:
This verse opens with a synchronism—a dating formula that anchors Hezekiah's accession to the reign of Hoshea in the failing northern kingdom of Israel. This is not merely chronological notation; it is theological positioning. Hezekiah becomes king in the third year of Hoshea's nine-year reign, meaning he will witness the entire collapse of the northern kingdom under Assyrian siege (2 Kings 17:5-6). The synchronism tells us that Judah's hope—embodied in this new king—emerges precisely as Israel's light is going out. The southern kingdom and the northern kingdom will no longer walk parallel paths.

The naming of Hezekiah (Chizkiyyahu in Hebrew, meaning 'the LORD is my strength' or 'the LORD strengthens') is programmatic. It announces the central theme of his reign before a single deed is recorded: the question of whether a king will trust in divine strength or in human military and political power. This becomes urgently relevant when Sennacherib's Assyrian army arrives later in the chapter. The name itself is a statement of faith—parents or prophets naming a child declare what they hope God will accomplish through him.

word_study.meaning: to reign, to rule, to become king. The Hebrew root indicates assumption of kingship and royal authority.
word_study.significance: The verb malak frames the moment of accession not as inheritance but as the active assumption of royal responsibility. Hezekiah does not merely inherit a throne; he takes up the burden of rule.

word_study.meaning: 'The LORD is my strength' or 'The LORD strengthens.' Composed of chazak (to strengthen, to be strong) and Yah (the LORD).
word_study.significance: The name is a confession of faith and a forecast of the reign's central tension: will the king live out his name by trusting God's strength, or will he resort to the diplomatic and military resources of the ancient world?

cross_references.connection: Records the siege and fall of Samaria that Hezekiah will witness in the early years of his reign, showing the urgent backdrop against which his reforms take place.
Chronicles records Ahaz's death, Hezekiah's father, providing the immediate succession context and clarifying the transition from one of Judah's worst kings to one of its best.
Isaiah's parallel account of the same period, showing how the fall of Israel and the Assyrian threat shaped the theological crisis of Hezekiah's reign.
The name of the LORD is strength to the righteous—a wisdom principle that Hezekiah's name embodies and his life will illustrate.

commentary.historical_context: The synchronism with Hoshea dates Hezekiah's accession to approximately 715 BCE (using the standard Judean chronology). The Assyrian Neo-Empire under Sargon II was rapidly expanding westward. Israel's northern kingdom, divided and weakened by dynastic instability, was the first to fall under the weight of imperial pressure. Judah's southern position and the Davidic dynasty's greater stability gave it slightly more resilience, but the threat was existential. The accession of a religiously reformist king at this moment may not be accidental—the crisis of empire often precipitates religious renewal, as survival depends on whether God will defend the nation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of righteous leadership emerging in a moment of national crisis parallels Alma the Younger's conversion and leadership during the wars in the Book of Mormon (Alma 36-37). Both figures are named for their defining characteristic (Alma = 'merciful'; Hezekiah = 'the LORD strengthens') and both assume leadership when their nation faces existential threats.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 56:2-4 teaches that those who do not keep the Lord's commandments shall be removed from their place. The contrast between Ahaz (Hezekiah's father, who apostasized) and Hezekiah himself illustrates the principle that covenant obedience has immediate consequences for both individuals and nations.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Hezekiah's later cleansing of the temple (2 Chronicles 29) will be the central act of his reign. This opening verse anticipates that work—a king whose very name declares trust in the LORD will restore the house of the LORD to its proper function.

commentary.christological_typology: Hezekiah, like David before him, is a type of the Messiah in his role as righteous king who trusts God and leads his people in covenant renewal. His later deliverance from the Assyrian siege (2 Kings 19) prefigures Christ's victory over powers that oppose God's covenant people. The name 'the LORD is my strength' anticipates the Psalmist's declaration of trust in Christ as the source of strength (Psalm 27:1).
commentary.application: Modern covenant members face the same fundamental choice Hezekiah's name presents: will we build our lives on human resources (wealth, status, credentials, networks) or on trust in God's actual strength? The accession of a reformist king in a moment of imperial threat invites us to ask whether our own spiritual crises and life pressures become opportunities for deeper reliance on divine power rather than panic-driven scrambling for worldly solutions. Hezekiah's name was his calling; it can be ours as well.

text_kjv: Twenty and five years old was he when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty and nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name also was Abi, the daughter of Zachariah.

commentary.narrative:
Hezekiah ascends at twenty-five years old—young enough to have the vigor needed for religious reform, old enough to have capacity for judgment and political action. His reign of twenty-nine years makes him one of Judah's longest-reigning monarchs, a span of stability that allowed his reforms to take root and persist. For comparison, Josiah reigned thirty-one years and David reigned forty years—Hezekiah's tenure places him in the upper tier of Judean rulers in terms of duration.

The inclusion of the queen mother's name—Abi (a shortened form of Aviyyah, 'my father is the LORD')—is not a parenthetical detail. In the ancient Near Eastern royal system, the gevirah ('queen mother') held significant political power and influence, particularly during a king's early years. The fact that the narrator identifies her as daughter of Zechariah, itself a name meaning 'the LORD remembers,' creates a pattern: this king comes from a family whose names confess faith in God. The queen mother Abi, whose fuller name invokes the fatherhood of God, influenced the formative years of one of Judah's greatest kings. The detail suggests that Hezekiah's piety was not invented by royal propaganda but rooted in his household formation.

word_study.meaning: to reign, to exercise kingship. Used here with a temporal marker to indicate the duration of rule.
word_study.significance: The length of reign—twenty-nine years—is a narrative marker of divine favor and stability. In the ancient Near East, long reigns were understood as signs of divine approval, while short or chaotic reigns indicated divine disfavor.

word_study.meaning: Short form meaning 'my father.' The fuller form (Aviyyah) means 'the LORD is my father,' making it a theophoric name—a name containing a divine element.
word_study.significance: The queen mother's name is a confession of faith. She is positioned not merely as a woman of royal rank but as one who belonged to the LORD. 2 Chronicles 29:1 confirms the fuller form (Aviyyah), showing that this naming reflects genuine religious conviction in the royal household.

word_study.meaning: Zechariah means 'the LORD remembers.' The genealogy traces Hezekiah's maternal line to one who bears a name invoking divine remembrance.
word_study.significance: The genealogical note emphasizes that Hezekiah comes from a family of faith. This is significant context for understanding his piety not as political performance but as familial inheritance—he was raised by a mother whose own identity was rooted in covenant theology.

cross_references.connection: The parallel passage gives Hezekiah's mother's fuller name as Abijah (Aviyyah), 'the LORD is my father,' confirming that her theophoric name signals her religious commitment.
Bathsheba, the queen mother of Solomon, appears before the king and he rises to honor her—illustrating the significant political and personal role of the gevirah in the Davidic monarchy.
Similar genealogical detail about Jotham's mother, showing that the chronicler tradition pays special attention to the queen mother as influencing righteous rule.
The queen mother or noblewoman is called to speak for the voiceless and defend the poor—a role Hezekiah's mother, bearing a covenant name, would have been called to fulfill.

commentary.historical_context: The accession at twenty-five aligns with maturity benchmarks in the ancient Near East. Egyptian and Mesopotamian records show that kings typically began ruling in their late teens to mid-twenties. At twenty-five, Hezekiah would have had time for education in statecraft, military affairs, and religious law—preparation for leadership of a nation facing existential threats. The twenty-nine-year reign spans from approximately 715 to 686 BCE, making it contemporaneous with major events in the Assyrian imperial expansion. The queen mother's prominence in royal inscriptions from this period is well-attested in archaeological records; the gevirah held real power and access to the king.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's mother is not named in the scriptural record, but the pattern of righteous sons coming from mothers of faith appears throughout the Book of Mormon. The emphasis on maternal influence in covenant family formation resonates with Lehi's household, where Sariah's steadfast faith sustained the family through trials (1 Nephi 5:8).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:34-35 teaches that family relationships and authority in the kingdom depend on love and gentleness, not dominion. The detail about Hezekiah's mother suggests a household where spiritual authority was transmitted through a relationship of trust and faith, not through coercion.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The queen mother later had significant roles in temple rites and governance in Judahite tradition. Hezekiah's mother, bearing a name that confesses God's fatherhood, would have been a guardian of temple purity and covenant practice—a predecessor to the ideal matriarch of Israel.

commentary.christological_typology: Hezekiah's lineage through a mother named 'the LORD is my father' echoes the virgin birth narrative's emphasis on Jesus as the Son of God by means of divine paternity rather than natural descent. The Christ child, though biologically descended from Mary, is fundamentally the child of God the Father—a typological pattern foreshadowed in Hezekiah's maternal lineage.
commentary.application: The narrator's inclusion of the mother's name and genealogy is a reminder that righteous leadership rarely springs from nowhere—it emerges from families where covenant language, faith in God, and the practice of naming children after divine attributes create a culture of faith. For modern families, this invites reflection on what 'names' we are giving our children through the culture we create in our homes. Are our children being raised in households where trust in God is not a Sunday phenomenon but woven into family identity?

text_kjv: And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that David his father did.

commentary.narrative:
This verse delivers the highest possible commendation in the Books of Kings. The formula 'he did what was right in the sight of the LORD' (vayaas hayashar be-eynei YHWH) appears throughout 1 and 2 Kings, serving as the narrator's moral verdict on each reign. But Hezekiah receives something unusual: he is compared directly to David 'without qualification.' Most kings in Kings who do 'what is right' receive an immediate caveat: 'but the high places were not removed' (see 1 Kings 15:14; 2 Kings 12:3; 14:4). This formula of judgment signals that the king made religious reforms but stopped short of complete centralization of worship—they tolerated local shrines alongside the temple in Jerusalem.

Hezekiah receives no such asterisk. The comparison is absolute: 'according to all that David his father did.' This is not merely biographical praise; it is an assertion that Hezekiah matches the only king in Israel's history whose reign is presented as entirely pleasing to God. The reference to David as 'his father' uses the language of dynastic legitimacy—Hezekiah, like every king of Judah, traces his authority back to the covenant with David (2 Samuel 7). But here, the comparison suggests not merely legal descent but spiritual continuity. Hezekiah does not merely inherit David's throne; he imitates David's fidelity.

word_study.meaning: Straight, upright, correct, proper. In ethical contexts, it means 'right' in the sense of morally aligned, in proper order, not deviant.
word_study.significance: The term yashar implies alignment with the cosmic and moral order that God established. To do what is right is to walk in the path that God has marked out, not to deviate. The Covenant Rendering's 'right' captures this better than some alternatives—it is not merely 'good' but 'straight,' aligned with divine intention.

word_study.meaning: 'In the eyes of,' 'in the view of.' Literally, it positions the evaluator's perspective as the measure.
word_study.significance: The phrase matters: whose eyes matter? The text says 'in the eyes of the LORD'—the divine perspective, not human opinion, is the measure. Hezekiah's rightness is not a matter of popular acclaim but of God's evaluation.

word_study.meaning: 'Exactly as,' 'in accordance with everything that.' The phrase is both comparative and totalizing—it measures one figure against another and claims completeness.
word_study.significance: This phrasing is key. It is not 'Hezekiah did some things David did' but 'Hezekiah did exactly as David did'—suggesting a comprehensive imitation of David's righteousness without qualification or remainder.

cross_references.connection: Asa is said to have done what was right in the eyes of the LORD, but is then immediately qualified with 'only the high places were not removed'—contrasting with Hezekiah's unqualified praise.
The covenant with David, establishing the perpetual dynasty of Judah, forms the theological foundation for why Hezekiah's comparison to David matters—he is inheriting a promise.
Josiah is praised as unmatched in his devotion to the law, creating a subtle tension with Hezekiah's praise—both are superlatives, suggesting different categories of righteousness.
David's own character as a righteous king is delineated in the Psalms as one who walks blamelessly and speaks truth in his heart—the standard to which Hezekiah is now compared.
Solomon 'did not keep that which the LORD commanded'—a contrast that shows how rare it is for a king to receive unqualified praise in Kings.

commentary.historical_context: David's reign (approximately 1010-970 BCE) was remembered in Judahite tradition as the golden age.
