He is essentially saying: 'I am so confident in my power and so contemptuous of yours that I can offer you two thousand cavalry mounts knowing you don't have enough trained soldiers to use them.' The offer is designed to make Judah's military weakness visible and laughable. The phrase 'hit'arev na' ('make a wager') turns the offer into a bet—a game in which the outcome is already determined. The Rabshakeh is not seriously offering horses; he is mocking Judah's inability to field an adequate military force.

word_study.meaning: make a wager; enter into a pledge or agreement; become surety for. The verb 'arab means 'to pledge, to put up security, to make a bet.' Hit'arev is the reflexive form, 'to make a wager with someone.'
word_study.significance: The Rabshakeh frames his offer as a game or wager, transforming what appears to be an offer of military aid into a taunt. He is betting that Judah cannot field two thousand mounted cavalry—and he knows he will win the bet. The use of this term suggests that the entire negotiation is, from the Rabshakeh's perspective, a game that Judah has already lost.

word_study.meaning: horses; particularly cavalry mounts. In military contexts, susim refer to war horses, which were expensive, valuable, and required significant training to maintain.
word_study.significance: Horses in the ancient Near East were luxury items—a sign of military sophistication and wealth. To possess two thousand horses required resources that small nations like Judah simply did not have. Judah's reliance on Egypt for chariots and cavalry (mentioned in verse 24) underscores that Judah lacked the resources and military infrastructure to maintain a significant cavalry force.

word_study.meaning: riders; mounted cavalry; those who ride on horseback. A rokheb was a trained warrior on horseback.
word_study.significance: The offer exposes the fundamental weakness: even if Judah could somehow acquire horses, it lacks trained riders. The Rabshakeh is saying that Judah's military deficiency is so profound that the limiting factor is not equipment but personnel—Judah simply does not have enough trained soldiers. This is intelligence assessment expressed as mockery.

cross_references.connection: Solomon's enormous resources in horses and chariots are described as a sign of his incomparable wealth and power. By the time of Hezekiah, Judah's military capacity has declined drastically from Solomon's era, making the contrast between past power and present weakness sharp.
Verse 24 immediately returns to the theme of military inferiority, asking how Judah can turn back even one Assyrian provincial governor, given its lack of military resources.
Isaiah mocks those who trust in horses and chariots: 'We will flee upon horses... therefore shall ye flee.' Horses are presented as an illusion of security for those who do not trust in God.

The psalmist teaches: 'Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.' The Rabshakeh's mockery of horses contrasts with the psalmist's assertion that trust in horses is inferior to trust in YHWH.

commentary.historical_context: Judah in 701 BCE had been severely weakened by previous Assyrian campaigns and tributaries. Archaeological and historical evidence suggests that Hezekiah's military forces were significantly depleted compared to earlier centuries. The offer of two thousand horses is not arbitrary—two thousand trained cavalry would constitute a major military force. Egypt occasionally fielded such forces, which is why Hezekiah looked to Egypt for military support. Assyrian cavalry forces were among the most advanced in the ancient world, well-trained and equipped. The Rabshakeh's offer is made from a position of unassailable strength. He is essentially demonstrating through the absurdity of his offer that Judah is militarily helpless.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly contrasts reliance on military equipment and numbers with reliance on faith in God. When Lehi and Nephi face enemies, they do not attempt to match their enemies' military hardware but instead trust in God to make up for their deficiency. The principle is that military superiority does not guarantee victory if God is not on your side. The Rabshakeh's offer of horses assumes that military equipment determines outcomes; the Restoration teaches that faith determines outcomes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 105:19-20 teaches that those who trust in God should not rely on the 'arm of flesh'—physical military force or material resources. The Lord will fight their battles if they are faithful. Hezekiah's weakness militarily is actually positioned as a strength if he trusts fully in YHWH.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that God's power transcends human military and political power. The endowment contrasts Satan's tactics (which rely on worldly power, deception, and force) with God's power (which relies on truth, covenant, and spiritual authority). Hezekiah's choice to trust God rather than to scramble to match the Rabshakeh's military superiority is the covenant choice.

commentary.christological_typology: Satan's temptation to Christ involves offering worldly power and resources—'the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them.' The Rabshakeh's taunt about horses is similarly an offer of worldly power and the demonstration of Hezekiah's inability to match it. Christ's response, like Hezekiah's, is to reject the primacy of military/material power and to trust in God's power instead. Satan's taunt about casting himself down from the temple (testing God's protection) is parallel to the Rabshakeh's offer of horses—both are designed to make the object of faith look inadequate and the object of worldly trust look necessary.
commentary.application: This verse exposes the illusion that military superiority or material resources guarantee security. The Rabshakeh's mockery of Judah's inability to field cavalry illustrates a fundamental principle: security based on the accumulation of military or material resources is always fragile and relative—there is always someone more powerful. For modern disciples, this teaches a liberating principle: we need not match the world's accumulation of resources, power, or influence to be secure. Our security comes from covenant relationship with God, not from competitive advantage in worldly terms. The verse challenges us to examine: Am I trying to build security by accumulating worldly advantages? Am I trying to match the resources and power of others? Or am I building security on trust in God's promises? The Rabshakeh assumes that horses (military power) are the issue; Hezekiah's challenge is to recognize that the real issue is trust.

text_kjv: How then wilt thou turn away the face of one captain of the least of my master's servants, and put thy trust on Egypt for chariots and for horsemen?

commentary.narrative: The Rabshakeh's final logical move completes the rhetorical trap. He reasons with devastating simplicity: if Judah cannot defeat a single low-ranking Assyrian governor (pechat), how can it possibly resist the full might of the Assyrian empire? The logic is impeccable and emotionally devastating. The Rabshakeh is not claiming that defeating him (the Rabshakeh himself) is impossible; he is claiming that defeating even one minor provincial administrator is beyond Judah's capacity. He exposes the absurdity of Hezekiah's position: You cannot defeat my lowest-ranking servant, yet you hope to resist my master and his entire army? The verse also explicitly names Judah's last remaining hope—Egypt—and mocks it. The Rabshakeh knows that Hezekiah's secret diplomatic initiative involves seeking Egyptian chariots and cavalry. By naming this strategy openly, he strips away the veil of secrecy and exposes it to public mockery. Hezekiah's hope for Egyptian assistance is made ridiculous by the comparison: what good are Egyptian chariots against Assyrian military might? The Rabshakeh has now systematically dismantled every possible source of Hezekiah's confidence: military strength (verse 23), religious faith (verse 22), diplomatic alliance (verses 21 and 24). There is apparently nothing left to trust in.

word_study.meaning: to turn back; to repel; to defeat; literally 'to turn the face away.' Penei can mean 'face' or 'presence.' To 'turn away the face' of an enemy means to force them to retreat.
word_study.significance: The idiom suggests not merely military conflict but a reversal—making someone retreat or flee. The Rabshakeh is asking: can you make even one of my servants retreat? The question assumes that Judah cannot, and therefore that its position is hopeless.

word_study.meaning: governor; provincial administrator; military commander of a province. Pechat is an Assyrian title for a regional official responsible for administering a conquered territory.
word_study.significance: The pechat was a bureaucratic and military administrator, but not the highest-ranking officer. By identifying himself as a servant of the great king (or by identifying with the pechat class), the Rabshakeh emphasizes the hierarchy: if you cannot defeat a minor official, you certainly cannot defeat the king. The mention of 'the least of my master's servants' (et-hamqatannim, 'the smallest ones') further intensifies the taunt. Even the least-ranking Assyrian official is superior to all of Judah's military capacity.

word_study.meaning: to trust; to rely on; to place confidence in. The form here is 'you trust' (tabitach), continuing the theme of batach/bitachon throughout the speech.
word_study.significance: This is the fifth or sixth reference to bitachon/batach in the Rabshakeh's speech (verses 20, 21, 22, 24), creating an obsessive rhetorical focus on the act of trust itself. The Rabshakeh's entire strategy is to make trust impossible—to demonstrate that every possible object of trust is illusory. By the end of his speech, he wants Hezekiah to conclude that trust itself is irrational.

cross_references.connection: The parallel passage in Isaiah contains the same argument with nearly identical wording, confirming the centrality of this logical assault on Hezekiah's position.

Verse 5 defines Hezekiah as one who 'trusted in the LORD God of Israel.' Verse 24 represents the nadir of the Rabshakeh's assault—he has worked systematically to sever that trust by attacking every apparent source of security.

In the continuation of this narrative, Sennacherib sends a written message to Hezekiah making similar arguments—that no nation has ever resisted Assyria and survived, that Hezekiah's trust is therefore irrational.

Jeremiah prophesies regarding Egypt's promised aid: 'Pharaoh's army, which is come forth to help you, shall return to the land of Egypt.' Like the Rabshakeh's analysis, scripture confirms that Egypt is an unreliable ally.

commentary.historical_context: Judah's military capacity by 701 BCE was severely limited. Hezekiah had inherited a kingdom weakened by the earlier Assyrian campaigns under Tiglath-Pileser III, which had resulted in the loss of the northern kingdom (Israel) and the deportation of countless Judahites. Judah's standing army and fortified cities had been significantly impacted. Sennacherib's annals claim that he surrounded Jerusalem with such overwhelming force that Hezekiah capitulated and sent tribute. Whether this account is accurate or propaganda, the military reality was that Judah was vastly outmatched. The Assyrian army was the superpower of the age—its military technology, training, logistics, and discipline were unmatched in the Near East. The Rabshakeh's claim that Judah could not defeat even a minor Assyrian official was probably an accurate assessment of relative military capacity. Egypt's military support, while theoretically possible, was uncertain and unreliable. Historical records show that Egypt did not effectively intervene to save Judah from Sennacherib's invasion.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple instances where faithful leaders face seemingly impossible military situations and are counseled to trust in God rather than in their own military capacity. Helaman's stripling warriors (Alma 53-58) are a prime example: they trust in God and achieve victory despite being vastly outnumbered. The principle is that when human military capacity is manifestly inadequate, the possibility of divine intervention becomes clear. Hezekiah's situation is similar—his military weakness becomes the occasion for faith.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 98:37 teaches that 'the wicked shall slay the wicked' and that God will fight the battles of His people. The revelation affirms that trusting in military superiority is futile compared to trusting in God's protection. This principle applies directly to Hezekiah's situation: Judah's military inferiority is not a reason for despair but an occasion for trusting in God's superior power.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents the principle that Satan's power is limited and illusory—that Satan boasts of his power, but that power is contingent and ultimately powerless against those who are faithful. The Rabshakeh's boasting about Assyrian military superiority is exactly parallel to Satan's boasting in the temple narrative. Both are attempting to convince through the appearance of overwhelming power, but both can ultimately be resisted through covenant faith.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's temptation by Satan in the wilderness follows a similar logic of impossibility: Satan essentially argues 'If you are the Son of God, prove it by demonstrating power.' Christ's response is to refuse to test God by demanding proof of power. Similarly, Hezekiah's situation is designed to test whether he will trust God despite the apparent impossibility of his position. Both Christ and Hezekiah are being asked whether their faith survives when the logical arguments of the world seem to demonstrate that trust is irrational. Christ's path to victory does not involve winning a military or power-based confrontation with Satan but rather in maintaining faith despite the world's apparent logic.
commentary.application: This final verse of the Rabshakeh's speech presents the ultimate test of faith: What do we do when the world's logic seems irrefutable? When every apparent source of security has been dismantled? When the reasonable, intelligent assessment suggests that our position is hopeless? This is the point at which faith becomes distinguishable from mere optimism or positive thinking. At this moment, Hezekiah cannot reassure himself with military strength, diplomatic alliances, or even a comfortable theology that fits popular religious practice. He stands naked before the Rabshakeh's logic with only his covenant relationship with God. For modern disciples, this verse teaches that faith is not meant to be supported by visible, logical, worldly props. Those props are removed precisely so that we learn to trust God directly. The verse challenges us to examine: Are we trusting in things that can be taken away? Are our faith and security dependent on worldly conditions that may change? Or have we built our foundation on something that the world's logic cannot touch—our covenant with God? When all other sources of security fail, is that our moment of greatest despair or our moment of greatest faith?

text_kjv: Am I now come up without the LORD against this place to destroy it? The LORD said to me, Go up against this land, and destroy it.

commentary.narrative: The Rabshakeh makes the most audacious claim in the entire siege narrative: he asserts that YHWH himself authorized the Assyrian invasion. This is either a calculated psychological weapon, a logical inference from Assyrian military theology (that the gods ordain empire), or—most disturbingly—an unwitting truth. The prophet Isaiah will later confirm that Assyria is indeed 'the rod of my anger' (Isaiah 10:5-6), yet Assyria acts in pride and does not understand that it is God's instrument. The Rabshakeh's claim is devastatingly effective because it strikes at the heart of Judahite confidence: if YHWH has authorized this destruction, resistance becomes not merely futile but impious.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Hebrew construction here is brutal in its logic. By asserting 'the LORD said to me,' the Rabshakeh reframes the military campaign as a divine commission. He puts words in God's mouth—a grave violation in Israelite theology. Yet the narrator does not step in to deny the claim directly. Instead, the text leaves readers to wrestle with a terrifying possibility: has God truly withdrawn his protection? This silence creates psychological space for doubt within the besieged city. The propaganda works precisely because Judah's own theological tradition contains the seeds of its undoing—a God who can judge his own people through foreign powers.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: What makes verse 25 so psychologically sophisticated is that it forces the listener to choose between two interpretations, both of which undermine resistance. Either (1) the Rabshakeh is lying, in which case he is a dangerous deceiver who should not be trusted, or (2) he is telling the truth, in which case God has turned against Judah and resistance is sinful. The Rabshakeh has created a rhetorical trap from which there appears to be no escape—except through faith in God's promises despite all appearances, a faith that the narrative is testing to its limits.

word_study.meaning: literally 'without, apart from, or beside the LORD'—expressing complete separation or exclusion from divine presence or approval. The preposition 'mil' (from, out of) combined with 'balti' (without, apart) creates an emphatic negation. The rhetorical question 'Am I now come up mibladay YHWH?' flips the expected inference: no, I came with divine authorization.
word_study.significance: The term appears primarily in wisdom literature and covenant contexts to denote separation from God's will. Here, the Rabshakeh inverts its meaning, using it to claim alignment with divine purpose. In Latter-day Saint theology, being 'without the Lord' carries covenantal weight—those who break covenant lose divine protection. The Rabshakeh weaponizes this language to suggest Judah has already lost such protection.

word_study.meaning: A direct, prophetic formula typically reserved for divine commission of a prophet or king. The phrase 'YHWH said to me' appears in Isaiah (Isaiah 48:15), Jeremiah, and other prophetic books to authenticate divine calling. The Rabshakeh appropriates this most sacred formula, claiming direct divine speech—a claim that only priests and prophets could legitimately make.
word_study.significance: In Israelite theology, amar ('to say') when the subject is God is performative speech—words that enact reality and carry binding authority. The Rabshakeh's claim is not merely propaganda but theological usurpation. He is claiming the prophetic mantle for himself, essentially placing Assyrian military strategy on the same level as Mosaic law or prophetic utterance. For the Judahite ear, this would be recognized as either blasphemy or, more unsettlingly, a sign that God's voice has shifted to an unexpected speaker.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah explicitly identifies Assyria as 'the rod of mine anger' sent by God to punish faithless Israel, yet emphasizes that Assyria acts from pride and does not understand its role as God's instrument. The Rabshakeh's claim has biblical precedent, but Isaiah clarifies that Assyria will also be judged for its arrogance.

The law forbids false prophets who claim to speak words the LORD has not commanded. The Rabshakeh's claim 'the LORD said to me' would be immediately recognizable as either true prophecy or severe violation of the commandment against false witness.

The Rabshakeh will continue this argument by listing other gods who failed to deliver their peoples from Assyrian power, suggesting that YHWH will be equally powerless—a logical extension of his claim to divine authorization.

In the Restoration, the Lord clarifies that his word spoken through his servants carries his authority: 'Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The Rabshakeh inverts this principle, claiming Assyrian imperial speech is sanctioned by God.

Nephi sees the formation of a great and abominable church that combines with earthly kingdoms to corrupt and control people. The Rabshakeh's fusion of military power with false claims of divine authority prefigures this pattern of deceptive institutional power.

commentary.historical_context: The Rabshakeh's claim reflects ancient Near Eastern military theology, in which empires presented their conquests as ordained by their gods. Assyrian royal inscriptions routinely attributed military success to the will of Ashur, the national god. The Rabshakeh's statement would resonate with Assyrian soldiers in his army, who believed they were instruments of Ashur's will. However, in the context of Judah's monotheistic covenant theology, the claim is not merely propaganda but a direct assault on the theological foundations of resistance. The formula 'the LORD said to me' mimics the language of Hebrew prophecy, suggesting either that the Rabshakeh understands Israelite religious discourse well enough to weaponize it, or that the narrator is hinting at a more complex theological truth—that even pagan empires are ultimately subject to YHWH's purposes, though they do not recognize it. The cultural context matters: to an Assyrian audience, the claim is straightforward and expected; to a Judahite audience, it is either a gross lie or a terrifying theological realization.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 12:25-28, the wicked king Noah's priests attempt to deceive the people through false claims of divine authorization, using religious language to justify oppression. Like the Rabshakeh, they weaponize the language of prophecy and divine sanction to forestall resistance. Abinadi directly confronts their false claim to speak for God, declaring that their words do not align with God's actual character or covenant promises.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 52:14-15 warns against false prophets who claim divine sanction: 'Be careful that ye offend not the children of these people, I say unto you, that ye suffer not that they shall be destroyed.' The Rabshakeh's invocation of divine authority to justify destruction directly violates the Lord's actual teaching about how his servants should treat the weak and vulnerable.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, members promise to follow the voice of the living God and to discern between true and false guidance. The Rabshakeh's false claim to speak for YHWH is precisely the kind of deceptive spiritual authority that initiates encounter in the temple and are taught to reject. The test of discernment—recognizing God's true voice amid counterfeit claims—is central to the endowment experience.

commentary.christological_typology: Just as the Rabshakeh falsely claims to speak for YHWH and seeks to turn the people away from trust in God's protection, the Adversary in the last days will present false Christs and false prophets claiming divine authority (Matthew 24:24). The narrative prefigures the final spiritual test: believers must discern between true and false claims to divine sanction. Christ's ultimate victory will be the silencing of all false voices and the vindication of true faith in God—exactly what occurs when Hezekiah's prayer is answered and the Assyrian army is destroyed.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, we face constant appeals to trust in powers other than God—economic systems, political ideologies, technology, or influential figures who claim to have access to divine approval for their agenda. Like the besieged Judahites, we must practice rigorous discernment. The test is not whether an authority claims divine backing (many will), but whether their claims align with God's actual revealed character and covenants. When faced with pressure to abandon trust in God because 'even the Lord says so,' the faithful response is not to believe the claim without verification against established doctrine and the voice of living prophets. The lesson is: do not be fooled by the right vocabulary used in the wrong mouth.

text_kjv: Then said Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and Shebna, and Joah, unto Rabshakeh, Speak, I pray thee, to thy servants in the Syrian language; for we understand it: and talk not with us in the Jews' language in the ears of the people that are on the wall.

commentary.narrative: The three senior Judahite officials—Eliakim (master of the palace), Shebna (secretary), and Joah (recorder)—attempt a damage-control maneuver by requesting that the Rabshakeh switch to Aramaic, the lingua franca of international diplomacy. Their request is ostensibly diplomatic and reasonable: 'We understand Aramaic; please use it so we can conduct serious negotiations.' But the underlying admission is devastating: they are terrified that the Rabshakeh's arguments are reaching and persuading the common soldiers and civilians on the city wall. The officials are essentially confessing that the propaganda is working. Their use of the deferential plural 'speak to your servants' acknowledges Assyrian power while trying to contain the psychological damage.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'do not speak to us in the Jews' language in the ears of the people that are on the wall' reveals the true fear. The officials recognize that the Rabshakeh's rhetorical assault is more dangerous when the general population can understand every word. In an oral culture, hearing a persuasive argument in one's own language with maximum emotional impact creates a powerful effect that negotiators in an elite language might resist more easily. The request to use Aramaic is thus a plea to move the conversation into a space where only educated officials can comprehend—a space where rebuttal and context can be controlled. Ironically, by making this request, the officials publicly signal to the soldiers on the wall that the Rabshakeh's message is so compelling that it must be hidden from them.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: What Eliakim and his colleagues do not understand is that the Rabshakeh has no intention of negotiating quietly. His entire strategy depends on demoralizing the population, breaking the bonds between leaders and people, and creating a wedge between a king's promises and a people's reality. The request for Aramaic will be refused—and the refusal will itself become part of the propaganda, demonstrating that the Assyrian commander answers to no one and brooks no constraint on his speech.

word_study.meaning: The Aramaic language, which by the 8th century BCE had become the lingua franca of diplomatic and commercial exchange across the Near East. It was the language of Aramean kingdoms and of international treaties. To speak Aramaic was to speak the language of diplomacy and commerce, not passion or popular appeal.
word_study.significance: The officials' request reveals their understanding of language as having domains: Aramaic is for elite negotiation; Hebrew is for popular address. By requesting Aramaic, they are asking to move the conversation into a more controlled, technical register where rhetorical power is diminished and mutual understanding (dakah) is the goal. In Latter-day Saint context, we might compare this to discussions conducted in the language of temple ordinance versus popular speech—different registers carry different power.

word_study.term_english: do not speak to us in the Jews' language
word_study.term_original: וְאַל־תְּדַבֵּר עִמָּנוּ יְהוּדִית (ve-al tedabber immanu Yehudit)
word_study.meaning: The verb 'tedabber' (speak) is not merely communication but rhetoric and persuasion. The term 'Yehudit' (Judahite Hebrew) identifies the language specifically with the Judahite people and their identity. The plea 'do not speak to us in the Jews' language' is thus also a plea: 'do not address us as a people, do not activate our identity as the stakes of your argument.'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that Yehudit refers to the Judahite dialect of Hebrew, distinct from Samaritan Hebrew or other variants. The officials' use of the term acknowledges that language carries identity. When the Rabshakeh speaks Yehudit, he is speaking to the Judahites as a people, invoking their shared identity and covenant theology. The request to switch languages is a request to dissolve that direct identity appeal and move to abstract, depersonalized diplomacy.

word_study.term_english: in the ears of the people that are on the wall
word_study.term_original: בְּאׇזְנֵי הָעָם אֲשֶׁר עַל־הַחֹמָה (be-ozne ha-am asher al-ha-choma)
word_study.meaning: The phrase 'in the ears of' (be-ozne) is a Hebraism for 'within earshot of' or 'in the hearing of.' The word 'choma' (wall) is the city's defensive barrier, and those 'on the wall' are the soldiers and citizens who would fight to the death in a siege. The phrase creates a spatial metaphor: the officials want to keep dangerous words away from those ears that hear them most acutely.
word_study.significance: In biblical rhetoric, the ear is the organ of persuasion and covenant commitment. When the Lord says 'hear' (shema), he is calling for obedience rooted in understanding. The officials' concern about words reaching the ears of the wall-defenders shows they understand that hearing the Rabshakeh's case directly could undermine the will to resist. This is a profound statement about the power of rhetoric to shape reality in real time.

cross_references.connection: Later, in the post-exilic period, official correspondence between the Persian court and Jewish leaders also involves language choices—Aramaic for official communication. The use of Aramaic as a diplomatic language reflects broader ancient Near Eastern practice.

In Daniel's vision narrative, the wise men of Babylon address the king 'in the Aramaic tongue,' signaling that Aramaic is the language of official court communication and technical discourse, while Hebrew is the language of covenantal and prophetic speech.

The Rabshakeh's immediate response is to stand and cry out in an even louder voice 'in the Jews' language'—directly defying the request and escalating his propaganda assault, proving the officials' fears justified.

In the Book of Mormon, Alma teaches that words plant seeds that grow and yield faith. The Rabshakeh understands this principle implicitly—he knows that words in the people's own language, heard directly, will produce the emotional and intellectual effects he desires. The officials' request acknowledges this power.

The Lord teaches that truth is of God and falsehood is of the devil, and that those who speak truth speak 'that which is of God.' The officials' fear suggests they recognize that the Rabshakeh's words, though in Hebrew, carry a spirit contrary to the covenant and God's promises.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern diplomatic context, Aramaic was indeed the language of international negotiation by the 8th century BCE. The Tel Dan Stele and other inscriptions confirm that Aramaic served as a lingua franca. However, the Rabshakeh's knowledge of Hebrew suggests either that he has been briefed extensively on Judahite affairs, or that he purposefully sought to master the language in order to maximize rhetorical impact on a popular audience. Ancient siege warfare included psychological operations: demoralizing the defenders, breaking trust between commanders and soldiers, and offering terms or threatening devastation directly to those who would bear the weight of resistance. The officials' request reflects a real tactical consideration—in oral communication, the register and language of speech shaped audience reception. The fact that three high officials make this plea together suggests the seriousness with which they regarded the threat.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 28:3-9, Mormon describes how false leaders 'rob the children of men of the plain and most precious parts of the gospel' by complicating doctrine and obscuring truth. The Judahite officials' request to switch to Aramaic parallels this pattern: they want to move the truth-telling into a format where fewer will understand and fewer will be persuaded. In contrast, prophets in the Book of Mormon (like Nephi, Alma, and Abinadi) deliberately speak plainly and in the people's own language to maximize understanding and conviction.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 132:8 teaches that the Lord speaks 'that which is right.' The officials' fear that the Rabshakeh's false claims will persuade people 'in the ears of the people' reflects the principle that clear communication of doctrine—whether true or false—shapes belief and action. The lesson is that true leaders should also speak clearly and directly to the people, not hide truth in elite registers.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the endowment, covenants are made audibly and directly to the participant, not through intermediaries or esoteric language obscuring the meaning. The officials' attempt to move negotiation into Aramaic mirrors the attempt to obscure or mediate between the people and truth, whereas God's covenant is always direct and clear to the individual conscience.

commentary.christological_typology: Just as the Rabshakeh seeks to speak directly to the people in their own language in order to sway them toward despair and surrender, the Savior throughout his ministry spoke in the common language of his people, using parables, healings, and direct address to communicate eternal truth in culturally intelligible forms. The contrast between the Rabshakeh's propaganda and Christ's teaching is that Christ's words, though direct and powerful, always call people toward faith, covenant, and divine protection rather than despair and surrender. Christ's refusal to hide or complicate his message is the opposite of the officials' attempt to keep dangerous rhetoric away from common ears.
commentary.application: In modern life, we live in an environment saturated with competing messages in multiple registers. We encounter propaganda in entertainment, social media, and public discourse, often precisely calculated to reach us in the language and format most likely to influence emotion and bypass rational discernment. The Judahite officials' fear reminds us that words matter, language choices shape persuasion, and concentrated exposure to compelling false rhetoric can undermine faith. The lesson is not to retreat into isolation or elite jargon that only a few understand, but rather to (1) recognize when rhetoric is being weaponized against covenant faith, (2) seek out direct communication of truth from prophetic sources, and (3) cultivate the discernment to hear false claims for what they are, even when they use the language and concepts of our own tradition.

text_kjv: But Rabshakeh said unto them, Hath my master sent me to thy master, and to thee, to speak these words? hath he not sent me to the men which sit on the wall, that they may eat their own dung, and drink their own piss with you?

commentary.narrative: The Rabshakeh refuses the request for Aramaic and instead escalates with brutal contempt. His rhetorical move is both defiant and psychologically sophisticated: he turns the question back on the officials, implying that their status is irrelevant. He was not sent to negotiate with them but to address the people directly—those on the wall who will suffer the consequences of resistance. The crude imagery of siege famine (eating excrement and drinking urine) is not merely an insult but a psychological weapon: it forces the soldiers on the wall to contemplate the specific, degrading reality of siege death. The Rabshakeh is saying: your commanders want to hide the truth from you, but I will speak it plainly. The people will starve so severely that the normal human repugnance toward consuming waste will be overcome by hunger.
commentary.narrative_continued: The escalation is also a power demonstration. By ignoring the request to use Aramaic, the Rabshakeh shows that he answers to no one's demands for civility or restraint. His master (the Assyrian king) has sent him to achieve a goal—the capitulation or destruction of Jerusalem—and he will pursue that goal by whatever means prove effective. The refusal to switch languages becomes a statement: I am not a subject to your diplomatic niceties; I am an agent of empire speaking on behalf of absolute power. The officials' failed diplomatic attempt is now public knowledge among the wall-defenders, and the people have witnessed that their leaders cannot even constrain the enemy's speech.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The verse also reveals the Rabshakeh's understanding of where real power lies in a siege. Commanders and officials can be managed through diplomacy, threats, and negotiation, but the soldiers and defenders are the ones who must endure starvation, wounds, disease, and death. The Rabshakeh's strategy is to bypass elite political structures entirely and speak directly to the people who bear the burden. In doing so, he grasps a profound truth about all power—ultimately it depends on the willingness of ordinary people to sustain it. By addressing the people directly with an image so visceral that it forces them to contemplate the cost of continued resistance, he is attempting to break their will where diplomatic or military pressure alone might fail.

word_study.meaning: The Hebrew term refers to excrement or feces. The Masoretic margin (Qere) suggests that this term was considered too crude for public reading and provided a less offensive substitution, indicating that even the scribal tradition recognized the deliberate vulgarity of the Rabshakeh's language. The term appears in warnings of siege famine in Deuteronomy 28:53-57, describing the horrors that will befall those who break covenant.
word_study.significance: The Rabshakeh is not inventing this imagery but drawing it from Israel's own covenant curses—words that Deuteronomic theology associates with divine judgment for covenant-breaking. By invoking this language, the Rabshakeh is ironically fulfilling Israel's own prophetic vocabulary about the consequences of disobedience. The crude vulgarity of the term serves a rhetorical purpose: it is meant to break through any emotional distance the listeners might maintain and force visceral, body-level confrontation with the reality of siege death.

word_study.meaning: The term refers to urine or liquid waste, also considered too crude for polite speech. The Qere (Masoretic margin) again suggests alternative, less vulgar readings were preferred in public recitation, though the original text retained the stronger language. The pairing of fecal matter with urine creates a comprehensive image of bodily degradation.
word_study.significance: The pairing of two forms of human waste emphasizes the completeness of the degradation. In the ancient Near Eastern context, contact with human waste was considered both physically dangerous (risking disease) and ritually defiling (creating impurity). The image thus attacks not only the comfort and dignity of the defenders but also their ritual purity—their status as a covenanted people set apart. For Judahites, to be rendered ritually impure through starvation was to be made unfit for worship and covenant participation, adding a spiritual dimension to the physical horror.

word_study.meaning: The phrase identifies the soldiers and defenders who man the city's defenses. 'Sitting on the wall' is a fortification posture—a place of visibility and vulnerability. The wall-sitters are those most exposed to enemy action and most likely to be killed in a siege assault or starved in a prolonged blockade.
word_study.significance: The Rabshakeh addresses his remarks precisely to those with the most to lose—not the royal officials sheltered in the palace but the ordinary soldiers who will die if resistance continues. This is a masterful rhetorical move: it bypasses leadership entirely and appeals directly to self-interest and fear. The 'men on the wall' are the ones whose consent and will to fight are essential to any defense, and the Rabshakeh is attempting to withdraw that consent through the force of a terrifying image.

cross_references.connection: The Deuteronomic covenant curses explicitly warn of siege famine so severe that people will eat their children and 'the fruit of thy body.' The Rabshakeh draws on Israel's own covenant language to depict the judgment that will follow resistance, though he does not acknowledge that the covenant also promises deliverance for faith.

The book of Lamentations, written after Jerusalem's fall, confirms that the horrors the Rabshakeh describes actually occurred: 'The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children: they were their meat in the destruction of the daughter of my people.' The Rabshakeh's crude threat becomes historical reality.

The parallel passage in Isaiah 36 contains the same verse with nearly identical language, confirming the historicity of the Rabshakeh's address and the shock value of his crude speech to the Judahite audience.

Nephi describes his own periods of despair using language of degradation and suffering, including bodily distress. The Rabshakeh's attempt to induce despair through vivid imagery of suffering mirrors the adversarial psychological assault that the righteous must resist through faith.

The Lord teaches that those who are 'chastened and tried' might 'know the sweetness of an eternal victory.' The Rabshakeh assumes that the prospect of physical suffering will break the people's will to resist, but the covenant tradition teaches that suffering borne in faith produces eternal fruit.

commentary.historical_context: Siege warfare in the ancient Near East was a prolonged affair, sometimes lasting months or years. Starvation was indeed the most common cause of death in besieged cities, and historical records confirm that extreme famine could lead to cannibalism and consumption of waste products. The Assyrian royal annals boast of cities besieged until inhabitants 'ate the (unclean) flesh of their brothers,' confirming that the Rabshakeh's threat was grounded in historical reality. The deliberate vulgarity of the language was a calculated rhetorical choice: refined speech might be dismissed as diplomatic exaggeration, but crude, specific, bodily language would penetrate the emotional defenses of the listeners. The Rabshakeh's refusal to accommodate the officials' request for Aramaic was also a power play recognizable in ancient Near Eastern courts—demonstrating that he answered to his master's will, not to the diplomatic niceties of the besieged city. Such contempt for conventional courtesy was itself a sign of absolute confidence in military superiority.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 11:23-24, Zeezrom attempts to tempt Amulek with wealth and earthly reward, appealing to base instincts rather than faith. Similarly, in Alma 30, Korihor seeks to persuade the people that their concerns about judgment and covenant are unfounded and that they should pursue material comfort. Like the Rabshakeh, Korihor and Zeezrom attempt to work through concrete, physical images and bodily concerns to break faith. The righteous characters respond not by refuting the physical reality of suffering but by placing it within the broader context of covenant and eternal judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-8 describes afflictions and trials that the Lord's people will endure: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment.' The Rabshakeh assumes that the prospect of affliction will break resistance, but the covenant tradition teaches that afflictions are 'but a small moment' when viewed against eternal perspective.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that the adversary will present images of suffering and degradation to test faith, but the covenant path leads through these trials to exaltation. The Rabshakeh's brutal imagery is a type of adversarial temptation—an appeal to abandon the covenant path in exchange for avoiding physical suffering. Temple participants learn to recognize and resist this appeal.

commentary.christological_typology: The Rabshakeh's appeal to fear and bodily suffering mirrors the tempter's approach in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11): turn stones to bread, throw yourself down, worship me and avoid suffering. Christ's refusal to prioritize bodily comfort over covenant faithfulness, and his later willing endurance of physical torture and death, establish the pattern for all covenant believers. The contrast is stark: the Rabshakeh seeks to induce surrender through fear of the body; Christ teaches that 'he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me' (Matthew 10:38). The salvation offered through Christ is not deliverance from physical suffering in this life but victory over it through resurrection and eternal exaltation.
commentary.application: Modern believers encounter sophisticated psychological appeals designed to erode faith through appeals to fear, comfort, and bodily security. Social media, entertainment, and public discourse often use visceral imagery of suffering and degradation to persuade people to abandon traditional values and religious commitment. The Rabshakeh's tactic—bypassing rational argument and appealing directly to survival instinct through crude, terrifying imagery—is replicated in modern persuasion. The lesson is not that suffering is unreal or unimportant, but that it must be viewed within the context of covenant and eternal perspective. Like the defenders of Jerusalem, we must learn to hear terrifying voices without allowing them to dictate our choices. The remedy is to maintain direct communication with God through prayer and scripture study, to seek counsel from living leaders, and to remember that faith in God's promises is the only secure foundation when the world around us is filled with voices of despair.

text_kjv: Then Rabshakeh stood and cried with a loud voice in the Jews' language, and spake, saying, Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria;

commentary.narrative: The Rabshakeh's response to the officials' request is to stand and shout even more loudly, in an even more defiant Hebrew, directly addressing the people on the wall. The physical posture of standing emphasizes authority and dignity. The 'loud voice' (qol gadol) is not merely volume but a rhetorical power—in Hebrew speech, a 'great voice' carries weight and authority, often associated with divine proclamation or authoritative instruction. The Rabshakeh's deliberate choice to speak in Judahite Hebrew, after the request to use Aramaic, is an act of contempt toward the officials. By speaking so that everyone can hear, he is demonstrating that he will not be constrained, that he answers to a higher authority (his king), and that the officials' attempt to control the narrative has failed.
commentary.narrative_continued: The formula 'Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria' directly parallels the prophetic call 'Hear the word of the Lord' (shim'u devar YHWH), which appears throughout the Hebrew prophets as the introduction to divine judgment or salvation. The Rabshakeh is structurally mimicking the prophetic word-event, presenting the Assyrian king's message as if it were a divine utterance. The repetition of 'great king' (melekh hagadol) emphasizes the superlative power of the Assyrian monarch. In doing so, the Rabshakeh elevates the Assyrian king to a level of authority that rivals or perhaps supersedes YHWH in the minds of the listening people. This is not merely political propaganda but theological subversion—an attempt to replace the people's ultimate loyalty to God with loyalty to the king of Assyria.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The verse marks a turning point in the siege narrative. Up to this point, the Rabshakeh has been making arguments and engaging with the officials. Now he abandons all pretense of negotiation and launches a full propaganda assault on the people themselves. His willingness to stand and proclaim openly, despite the officials' request for restraint, shows that the propaganda campaign has always been his true objective. The loud voice and Hebrew speech are deliberate choices designed to maximize emotional impact on a population facing siege, starvation, and the fear that even their God has turned against them.

word_study.meaning: The verb 'qara' (to call, to cry out, to proclaim) combined with 'beqol gadol' (in a loud voice) denotes not merely shouting but authoritative proclamation. The phrase appears in contexts of prophetic utterance (Isaiah 40:3-4), divine pronouncement, and official decree. To 'cry with a loud voice' is to claim the right to speak with authority that cannot be ignored or suppressed.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew, the 'voice' (qol) is the vehicle of power, covenant-making, and authority. God's qol is heard at Mount Sinai. The 'great voice' of the Lord establishes covenant. By adopting this formula, the Rabshakeh is claiming a spiritual and authoritative register that is reserved in Israelite tradition for the covenant God. The phrase suggests that the Rabshakeh understands Hebrew theological language deeply enough to weaponize it.

word_study.term_english: Hear the word of the great king
word_study.term_original: שִׁמְעוּ דְּבַר־הַמֶּלֶךְ הַגָּדוֹל (shim'u devar hammelekh hagadol)
word_study.meaning: The imperative 'shim'u' (hear!) is the foundational command of the Shema and of all Hebrew prophecy. The word 'devar' (word, saying, matter) in prophetic contexts refers to the authoritative utterance of God's will. 'Hammelekh hagadol' (the great king) emphasizes superlative power and authority. The phrase structure—imperative verb followed by the object 'word of the king'—mirrors covenant speech and prophetic utterance.
word_study.significance: In the Covenant Rendering, Aaron Blonquist notes that this formula directly mimics 'Hear the word of the Lord' (shim'u devar YHWH). By using this structure, the Rabshakeh is presenting Assyrian royal speech as functionally equivalent to divine speech. For the Judahite listener, this would be immediately recognizable as either blasphemy or a terrifying suggestion that God's authority has been transferred to the Assyrian king. The structural parallel is weaponized theology.

word_study.meaning: The Judahite dialect of Hebrew, the language specific to the southern kingdom and its inhabitants. The use of the term 'Yehudit' rather than simply 'Hebrew' emphasizes the ethnic and covenantal identity bound up in the language. To speak in 'Yehudit' is to address the Judahites as a people, invoking their shared identity and history.
word_study.significance: The Rabshakeh's insistence on speaking in Judahite Hebrew, after being asked to use Aramaic, shows his determination to bypass all diplomatic filters and speak directly to the people's ethnic and religious identity. He is saying: I will not be constrained; I will speak to you as you are, in your own language, and my words will reach you directly. This is why the officials wanted Aramaic—they understood that translation into the abstract language of diplomacy would diminish the psychological power of the message.

cross_references.connection: The formula 'Hear the word' appears in Isaiah's prophecy of comfort and restoration, where the prophet calls the people to listen to God's promise of redemption. The Rabshakeh's echo of this formula is a dark inversion—offering instead a message of despair and surrender.

The Shema ('Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one') is the foundational covenant statement. The Rabshakeh's use of 'Hear' (shim'u) invokes this most sacred formula, attempting to displace God with the Assyrian king as the object of ultimate loyalty.

The prophet Samuel addresses King Saul with 'Hear the word of the LORD,' a prophetic formula that establishes divine authority over earthly kingship. The Rabshakeh inverts this relationship, placing the Assyrian king above all prophetic authority.
The parallel account in Isaiah confirms the defiance of the Rabshakeh's public proclamation and the theological challenge inherent in his use of Hebrew and the prophetic formula.

The Lord teaches that his word 'shall not pass away, but all shall be fulfilled.' In contrast, the Rabshakeh's confident proclamation will be rendered void when God's protective hand saves Jerusalem. The survival of Judah despite the Rabshakeh's certain predictions becomes a vindication of God's word over the word of human power.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern siege warfare, psychological operations were as important as military operations. The sight of an enemy commander standing openly on a hill or elevated position, shouting at the defenders in their own language, would create visceral fear and demoralization. The fact that the Rabshakeh speaks Judahite Hebrew suggests either that he was a skilled linguist or that Assyria had invested in understanding the language and culture of conquered peoples. The use of the prophetic formula 'Hear the word' would be immediately recognizable to any Judahite with knowledge of scripture. For those on the wall who had heard prophetic proclamations, the formula would create cognitive dissonance: the words sound like a divine summons, but they come from an enemy commander. The public defiance of the officials' diplomatic request also served a tactical purpose—it showed that the Assyrian commander answered to no one and would not be bound by conventional courtesies. This display of arrogance and power was meant to convince the defenders that resistance was futile.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 12:27, Abinadi stands before King Noah and declares the word of the Lord with a power that mirrors the prophetic formula the Rabshakeh mimics. Like Abinadi, the Rabshakeh uses the authoritative speech pattern to proclaim judgment, but whereas Abinadi calls the people to repentance and covenant faithfulness, the Rabshakeh calls them to despair and surrender. The contrast reveals that the form of prophetic speech can be identical while the content and spirit are opposite.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:17 teaches that the Lord speaks his word 'whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The Rabshakeh's imitation of this principle—using the prophetic formula to deliver a non-divine message—shows how truth-telling forms can be corrupted when separated from actual divine authority. The test of true versus false prophecy is alignment with God's revealed character and purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, sacred speech and covenants are delivered in specific forms and with specific authority. The Rabshakeh's mimicry of prophetic speech without prophetic authority represents the adversary's attempt to corrupt sacred forms and usurp divine authority. Temple participants learn to recognize the voice of the true shepherd and to discern it from imitative or false authority.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ repeatedly claims the authority to speak the word of God with finality: 'Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away' (Matthew 24:35). In contrast to the Rabshakeh's usurped and ultimately powerless words, Christ's words carry divine authority that endures eternally. The Rabshakeh's use of the prophetic formula represents the ultimate temptation of earthly power—to claim divine authority while serving ultimately destructive ends. Christ's refusal to use his divine authority for self-aggrandizement or to coerce belief establishes the contrast: true divine authority is used for salvation and covenant establishment, not for conquest and psychological manipulation.
commentary.application: In the modern world, we encounter multiple voices claiming authority and speaking in the language and forms of truth while delivering messages of despair, fear, and surrender to ultimatums that serve the speaker's interests rather than the listener's. Media, political rhetoric, and even corrupted religious voices can adopt the forms of truth-telling while distorting the message. The lesson from the Rabshakeh's proclamation is that we must develop discernment not merely about the form of a message but about its actual content and spiritual character. A message delivered with authority and in our own language is not necessarily true or divine. The test is whether it aligns with God's revealed character and his covenants with his people. Hezekiah's later prayer and faith (2 Kings 19:14-19) will show the proper response: not to be swayed by confident human pronouncements, no matter how authoritative they sound, but to appeal directly to God in prayer and to trust his word over all human speech.

text_kjv: Thus saith the king, Let not Hezekiah deceive you: for he shall not be able to deliver you out of his hand:

commentary.narrative: The Rabshakeh shifts from grand proclamation to direct attack on Hezekiah's credibility and power. The phrase 'Thus saith the king' (ko amar hammelekh) is a formal speech formula delivering the Assyrian king's official judgment. The specific charge against Hezekiah is deception (nashshi—to mislead, to beguile). The Rabshakeh is claiming that Hezekiah is systematically deceiving his people, feeding them false hope that the king can deliver them from Assyrian power. By attacking Hezekiah's truthfulness, the Rabshakeh is severing the bond between a ruler and his people—the bond of trust that allows governance to function. If the people believe their king is lying to them, they will not follow his orders or endure siege hardship on his behalf.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'shall not be able to deliver you out of his hand' uses the verb natsal (to snatch away, to rescue, to deliver), which in Hebrew covenant theology is God's verb. God 'delivers' Israel from Egypt; God 'delivers' the righteous from judgment. By claiming that Hezekiah cannot 'deliver' his people and cannot prevent them from falling into the Assyrian king's 'hand' (yad), the Rabshakeh is arguing that kingship itself is impotent. The king's proper function—to protect his people—cannot be performed. Therefore, the Rabshakeh is saying, trust in the king is futile. What the Rabshakeh does not acknowledge is that Hezekiah's primary role in the covenant theology of Judah is not to be an independent deliverer but to lead his people in faith toward the God who is the true deliverer.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: This verse represents the first explicit attack on Hezekiah as a leader. Previous verses have attacked God's reliability; this verse attacks the king's reliability. The narrative is building a comprehensive assault on all sources of authority and hope: God has authorized the invasion (v. 25), the officials cannot control the message (v. 26), resistance leads to starvation (v. 27), and now even the king has no power to save his people (v. 29). The cumulative effect is to create a situation of utter hopelessness in which surrender appears to be the only rational choice. Yet the narrative itself will show that this apparent totality of despair is precisely the condition under which faith becomes possible—when all human power has been exhausted, trust in God alone remains.

word_study.meaning: The verb 'nasha' (he lifted up, caused to lift, exalted; also, seduced, beguiled, deceived) means to mislead by exaggeration of hope or false promises. The specific sense here is that Hezekiah is lifting up the people's hopes falsely—raising their expectations beyond what can actually be delivered. The verb can also mean 'to entice away' from a proper course.
word_study.significance: The term appears in contexts of seduction and false prophecy, where someone exploits another's trust by promising more than can be delivered. In Latter-day Saint context, the verb resonates with deception related to covenant breaking—Lucifer is the ultimate 'nasha,' offering false hope of exaltation apart from covenant obedience. The Rabshakeh's use of this term is meant to reframe Hezekiah's faith as manipulation rather than leadership.

word_study.meaning: The verb 'natsal' means to snatch away, to rescue, to deliver, to save from danger or death. In covenant theology, natsal is God's action toward his people: 'The LORD will natsal thee from the hand of thine enemies.' The verb appears repeatedly in the Psalms and prophetic books describing God's protective and salvific action. To 'natsal' requires power over circumstances and the ability to overcome opposition.
word_study.significance: By using natsal to describe what Hezekiah cannot do ('he shall not be able to natsal you'), the Rabshakeh is claiming that Hezekiah lacks the power that only God possesses. The irony is that Hezekiah would not claim such power for himself—his hope lies precisely in faith that God will natsal his people. But the Rabshakeh's language subtly shifts the meaning: Hezekiah claims his people will be saved, therefore Hezekiah should be able to deliver. The logical move creates cognitive dissonance in the listeners' minds.

word_study.meaning: The phrase 'from his hand' (mi-yad) is an idiom for power, authority, and control. To be 'in someone's hand' is to be subject to their power. To be delivered 'from the hand' is to escape subjection and regain freedom. The 'hand' of the Assyrian king represents absolute power and control.
word_study.significance: The image of the hand is one of the most powerful in covenant theology. God's 'mighty hand' delivers Israel from Egypt; God's 'hand' upholds the faithful. The Rabshakeh's use of this language—claiming that the Assyrian king's hand is absolute and inescapable—is an implicit claim that the Assyrian king's power is as total as God's. This is a theological claim masked as a political assertion.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist declares, 'Though my father and mother forsake me, yet will the LORD take me up.' Hezekiah's people are being told to doubt their king's ability to protect them, yet the covenant promises God will not abandon his people even when earthly protectors fail.

The parallel passage in Isaiah records Hezekiah's response: he sends his officials to seek the prophet Isaiah rather than rely on his own power or on negotiation. Hezekiah implicitly acknowledges that he cannot 'deliver' his people but that God can.

The book of Proverbs warns against false confidence in riches or power: 'The rich man is wise in his own conceit; but the poor that hath understanding searcheth him out.' The Rabshakeh's confidence in Assyrian military power mirrors the false confidence the wise reject.

The Lord teaches that 'no man can take this knowledge away from you.' In contrast, the Rabshakeh is attempting to take away the Judahites' knowledge of God's power and their faith in his promises through psychological assault and false reasoning.

Ammon testifies that the Lord is 'mighty in power and mighty in wisdom and mighty in judgment,' emphasizing God's power over all earthly powers. The Rabshakeh's claim that Assyrian power is supreme and inescapable directly contradicts this doctrine of God's supremacy.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern political theory, the primary function of a king was to protect his people and to maintain his authority through the demonstration of power. A king who could not protect his people from invasion was considered weak and could expect to lose his throne. The Rabshakeh's argument—that Hezekiah cannot deliver his people—would be immediately understood as a claim that Hezekiah is an ineffectual king and that the people should not expect survival if they continue to follow him. This was a sophisticated attack on the fundamental basis of Hezekiah's legitimacy. Interestingly, the Rabshakeh's argument would be convincing from a purely military standpoint: a small, wealthy city facing the greatest military empire of the age, with no obvious military allies, had virtually no chance of military victory. The only factor the Rabshakeh does not account for is divine intervention—precisely because the Rabshakeh's entire theology is one of material power and human capability, not covenant faith.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 5:35-40, Alma directly addresses the question of who can save the Zoramites. He teaches that it is not the king's power or earthly authority that saves, but rather the 'mighty change' that comes through faith in Christ. Similarly, Hezekiah's response will be to rely not on his own kingly power but on divine power accessed through prayer and faith. The lesson is that kingship means leading people toward God, not claiming to save them through independent power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 81:3 teaches that those who hold authority should 'magnify your calling,' and D&C 8:8 teaches that God will give the faithful the answer to their questions. Hezekiah's proper response to the Rabshakeh's attack on his credibility is not to defend his own power but to lead his people in prayer and faith toward God. The Restoration teaches that true leadership serves God's purposes, not independent human interests.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple covenant, the individual makes promises directly to God, not through intermediaries or earthly authorities alone. The Rabshakeh's attack on Hezekiah's reliability is an attempt to sever the connection between the king and his people, just as the adversary seeks to sever the connection between individual and God. The temple covenant teaches that no earthly power can separate a faithful person from God's care.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's kingship is radically different from earthly kingship: 'My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight' (John 18:36). Christ demonstrates a kind of power fundamentally different from the Rabshakeh's concept of power based on military might. When Christ is mocked as unable to 'deliver' himself from the cross (Matthew 27:40-43), his apparent powerlessness is precisely where his true power resides—in voluntary submission to God's will and in trust that God will vindicate him through resurrection. The Rabshakeh's argument is that power is the ability to coerce compliance; Christ shows that true power is the ability to remain faithful even unto death.
commentary.application: In modern life, we are constantly told that our leaders and institutions are weak, untrustworthy, and incapable of delivering on their promises. This message serves to undermine faith in leadership while promoting cynicism and despair. The lesson from Hezekiah is that a leader's true authority does not rest on claim to unlimited power or ability to deliver perfect outcomes, but on fidelity to God and willingness to lead people toward covenant faith. Modern covenant believers should be cautious about leaders who claim unlimited power to solve all problems or who present themselves as saviors. The appropriate response to the Rabshakeh's attack on Hezekiah is not to defend the king's absolute power but to affirm that the king's proper role is to lead the people toward God. When we understand this, attacks on leaders' credibility become opportunities for deepening our own direct relationship with God rather than crises of faith.

text_kjv: Neither let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD, saying, The LORD will surely deliver us, and this city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria.

commentary.narrative: The Rabshakeh now attacks not merely Hezekiah's power or credibility but the very foundation of Hezekiah's leadership: faith in God. He explicitly forbids the people to 'trust in the LORD' (batach el YHWH) and dismisses Hezekiah's message of divine protection as delusion. The Rabshakeh directly quotes—or paraphrases—what Hezekiah apparently says to his people: 'The LORD will surely deliver us, and this city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria.' By quoting this message, the Rabshakeh is demonstrating that he understands exactly what faith-claim Hezekiah is making, and he is attempting to preemptively delegitimize it. The structure of the statement is crucial: the Rabshakeh forbids trust while simultaneously claiming that divine protection is unnecessary because God has already authorized the Assyrian invasion (v. 25). He has created a false dilemma: either God has authorized this conquest, in which case trust in God is pointless, or God is unable to prevent it, in which case trust is futile.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb 'batach' (to trust, to confide, to rely upon) is the central covenant word for the Judahite relationship with God. The people are supposed to 'batach' in YHWH alone, not in horses, wealth, or military might. The Rabshakeh's use of the causative form—'do not let Hezekiah cause you to batach' (yavteach etkhem)—frames faith as something Hezekiah manipulates the people into, rather than as a genuine response to divine promises. This reframing is psychologically sophisticated: it transforms faith from a rational response to evidence of God's covenant faithfulness into irrational credulity induced by a dishonest king. The Rabshakeh is not merely attacking God's power; he is attacking the very category of faith itself, presenting it as a device of political manipulation.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The verse also contains a subtle logical move. The Rabshakeh says 'do not let Hezekiah make you trust... saying [that the city] shall not be delivered.' The specific claim being attacked is that 'this city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria.' By attacking this specific promise, the Rabshakeh is attempting to create cognitive dissonance: if the city is actually delivered into Assyrian hands, then Hezekiah's entire faith-message is exposed as false, and all faith in God is thereby discredited. The narrative is setting up a test: will the city be delivered or not? The answer to that question will determine whether Hezekiah's faith is rational or delusional, whether his message is true prophecy or false comfort. This is the climax of the Rabshakeh's psychological assault: he has attacked the king's power, the officials' credibility, and now the very possibility of faith. He has positioned himself as the voice of realism, clarity, and power, while positioning Hezekiah as a deceiver offering false comfort in the face of inevitable defeat.

word_study.meaning: The verb 'batach' means to trust, to rely upon, to have confidence in, to be at ease. In covenant theology, batach is the proper stance of the faithful toward God—a reliance and confidence rooted not in material circumstances but in covenantal promise. The noun 'bitachon' (trust, confidence) appears frequently in the Psalms as the foundation of spiritual security. To 'batach' is to place one's ultimate confidence in God rather than in human power, wealth, or military might.
word_study.significance: In The Covenant Rendering, Blonquist notes that the Rabshakeh uses the causative form 'yavteach' ('make to trust'), reframing what should be a genuine faith commitment as manipulation. This is the ultimate inversion: Hezekiah's call to faith is presented as a leader's tool for controlling the population. In Latter-day Saint theology, 'batach' resonates with the principle of 'trust in the Lord'—a reliance that is grounded in personal covenant experience and divine promise, not in emotional manipulation or false comfort.

word_study.meaning: The infinitive absolute construction 'hatsel yatssilenu' combines the infinitive absolute with the finite verb form of the same root, creating an emphatic statement: 'delivering, he will deliver,' or 'he will certainly/definitely deliver.' This construction expresses absolute certainty and totality of action. It emphasizes that the action is not merely hoped-for but assured, not partial but complete.
word_study.significance: The Rabshakeh quotes this emphatic form to highlight what he perceives as Hezekiah's overconfident claim. By emphasizing the absoluteness of the claim ('will certainly deliver'), the Rabshakeh makes it easier to dismiss as unrealistic if circumstances appear otherwise. The construction also echoes covenant language: when God makes a promise, it is often expressed with this emphatic form to indicate its certain fulfillment. Hezekiah's use of this construction claims for God's promise the same authority and certainty that characterizes all of God's covenantal commitments.

word_study.term_original: וְלֹא תִנָּתֵן אֶת־הָעִיר הַזֹּאת בְּיַד מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר (ve-lo tinnaten et-ha-ir hazot be-yad melekh Assur)
word_study.transliteration: ve-lo tinnaten et-ha-ir hazot be-yad melekh Assur
word_study.meaning: The phrase uses the negative particle 'lo' (not) with the passive verb form 'tinnaten' (will be handed over, will be delivered). The passive voice emphasizes that the city is the recipient of action from an outside agent. The phrase 'in/into the hand of' (be-yad) is an idiom for subjection to power and control. To say the city 'will not be delivered into the hand' of the Assyrian king is to assert that the city will remain outside his control despite his military power.
word_study.significance: The use of the passive voice is significant: Hezekiah's promise does not claim that the Judahites will actively defeat the Assyrians, but that God will prevent the city from being handed over. This is a promise not of human victory but of divine protection. The Rabshakeh's attack on this promise is an attack on the core Judahite belief that God's hand (yad) is stronger than any human hand and that God's will determines the outcome of events.

cross_references.connection: The psalm explicitly commands 'Trust in the LORD' (batach b'YHWH) and promises that those who do will be delivered from their enemies and established in the land. Hezekiah's call to faith directly reflects covenantal theology expressed in the Psalms.

The parallel passage in Isaiah shows that God's promise to protect Jerusalem is indeed fulfilled when the angel of the Lord destroys the Assyrian army, vindicating Hezekiah's faith and making clear that the Rabshakeh's dismissal of divine protection was premature.

The parallel account in Chronicles records Hezekiah's actual words to his people: 'With us is the LORD our God to help us and to fight our battles.' Hezekiah's faith is explicit and covenantal, not the false comfort the Rabshakeh claims.
The wisdom literature teaches, 'Be not afraid of sudden fear... for the LORD shall be thy confidence,' a teaching that directly contradicts the Rabshakeh's claim that trust in God is irrational.

Alma teaches his son, 'Trust in God; whither soever he leadeth thee, the Lord shall deliver thee in the end.' The Book of Mormon affirms the principle that trust in God, even in circumstances that appear impossible, leads to divine deliverance.

commentary.historical_context: From a military and historical standpoint, the Rabshakeh's dismissal of Hezekiah's faith as unrealistic would appear reasonable to most observers. Jerusalem was a small, wealthy city facing the greatest military power of the ancient world, with no military allies and no realistic hope of military victory. No rational military strategist would predict Jerusalem's survival based on military analysis. The Rabshakeh's position would appear to be the position of realism and clarity about power. However, the narrative of 2 Kings will show that history does not follow purely material logic. The Assyrian army is destroyed, Jerusalem is saved, and Hezekiah's faith is vindicated. This narrative pattern—apparent military impossibility followed by divine deliverance—becomes a foundational pattern in Jewish theology and appears repeatedly in later Jewish and Christian tradition. It establishes the principle that faith in God is not escape from reality but alignment with a deeper reality that human power cannot ultimately control.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 26:8, Nephi teaches that 'the righteous shall be preserved' and that the Lord will 'show forth his power.' This principle is tested repeatedly in the Book of Mormon: in the wilderness with Lehi, in the land of Nephi with the sons of Mosiah, and in the final destruction before Christ appears. In each case, faith in God's promise proves justified despite circumstances that appear to confirm the critics' predictions. The pattern established in Hezekiah's story is central to Book of Mormon theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 78:4 teaches that the faithful should 'be not afraid of the trials which shall come,' and D&C 6:36 promises, 'Look unto me in every thought; doubt not, fear not.' The Rabshakeh's entire argument is designed to produce doubt and fear; the Restoration teaching is to overcome these through unwavering trust in God's word.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, covenants made with God carry promises of divine protection and guidance. The Rabshakeh's dismissal of these promises mirrors the adversary's attempt to make covenants seem worthless and God's promises seem false. Temple participation teaches that divine covenants are real, binding, and efficacious, and that faith in them produces actual protection and blessing.

commentary.christological_typology: In Matthew 4:1-11, Satan tempts Christ to doubt God's protection by invoking Scripture: 'If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down; for it is written, He shall give his angels charge over thee.' Satan uses the form of God's promise to invite doubt about whether God will actually fulfill it. Hezekiah faces a similar test: a sophisticated argument that doubts God's promise of protection. Christ's response—'It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God'—establishes the principle that faith must be grounded in God's word, not in human reasoning about whether divine promises are likely. The Rabshakeh's attack on Hezekiah's faith prefigures Satan's attack on Christ's faith in the wilderness; in both cases, the temptation is to abandon trust in God's word in favor of accommodation to apparently irresistible earthly power.
commentary.application: Modern covenant believers face constant pressure to abandon faith because circumstances appear to contradict God's promises. Economic hardship makes the promise of prosperity seem false; social pressure makes moral covenants seem impossible to keep; intellectual challenges make the truth claims of the gospel seem naive or irrational. The Rabshakeh's argument—that faith is irrational delusion in the face of overwhelming material circumstances—is replicated in countless modern voices. The lesson from Hezekiah is that faith is not escape from reality but alignment with a reality deeper than material circumstances can access. When the Rabshakeh's army is destroyed, it becomes clear that he misunderstood the nature of reality: he thought military power determined outcomes; he did not understand that God's will ultimately determines outcomes.
