In ancient Near Eastern and Hebrew contexts, tearing one's garments was the physical expression of extreme distress, grief, shock, or response to catastrophe. The act was spontaneous and public, signaling both personal anguish and recognition of a crisis that transcended ordinary circumstances.
word_study.significance: Hezekiah's tearing of his garments is not theatrical but covenantal — it acknowledges that the blasphemy against God crosses a threshold that politics cannot address. The same verb appears when David tears his clothes upon learning of Saul's death (2 Samuel 1:11) and when Job tears his robe upon receiving news of disaster (Job 1:20).

word_study.meaning: A coarse, dark fabric woven from goat or camel hair, worn as a sign of mourning, repentance, or severe distress. Sackcloth was the garment of the penitent and the bereaved. Wearing sackcloth was an outward sign of inner transformation — a renunciation of status and comfort in the face of judgment or crisis.
word_study.significance: In the context of Judah's covenant with God, Hezekiah's donning of sackcloth is an act of repentance not for Hezekiah's personal sin but for the nation's vulnerability and need for divine mercy. It signals readiness to accept God's judgment and dependence on divine grace rather than national pride or military strength.

word_study.meaning: The Temple in Jerusalem, the central sanctuary where God's presence dwelt according to covenant theology, where sacrifices were offered and prayers were heard. The 'house' of God was the place where heaven and earth met, where human intercession could reach the divine ear.
word_study.significance: For Hezekiah, entering the Temple is not a retreat from the crisis but an engagement with it at the deepest level. The Rabshakeh has challenged whether God can save; Hezekiah's entry into the Temple affirms that God's presence and power are located there, and that prayer offered in that house will be heard. This also contrasts sharply with Ahaz, who during his crisis shut the Temple doors (2 Chronicles 28:24).

cross_references.connection: The Rabshakeh's taunt that no god has saved any nation from Assyria's hand, which immediately precedes Hezekiah's response and contextualizes why the king tears his garments and turns to the house of the LORD.
David's exhortation to 'Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him,' which describes the same posture of relinquishment and reliance that Hezekiah models through his actions in the Temple.
Ahaz shut up the doors of the house of the LORD during his crisis, contrasting sharply with Hezekiah's decision to enter the Temple and turn to God rather than to foreign alliances.
The parallel account in Isaiah 37, which uses nearly identical language, reinforcing that Hezekiah's response is theologically significant across both Kings and Isaiah narratives.
Alma's teaching that 'ye cannot dwell with God' except through prayer and supplication, which resonates with Hezekiah's movement to the Temple as the place where prayer reaches the divine presence.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern royal court, a king's response to military threat typically involved either rapid diplomacy, mobilization of forces, or capitulation to terms. The Assyrian Empire under Sennacherib had destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel and was now encircling Judah. Sackcloth and ashes were standard mourning practices across the Levant, not unique to Israel, but their religious significance — as acts of repentance before God — was distinctively part of Hebrew covenant theology. The Temple, completed under Solomon, was understood as the place where God's name dwelt and where the king could intercede on behalf of the nation. Hezekiah's public entry into the Temple in sackcloth was a statement of national covenant orientation: Judah's hope lay not in military or diplomatic strategy but in the covenant God who had made promises to David's line.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Enos 1:4-5, Enos similarly turns his distress into an act of faith: 'And I kneeled down before my Maker, and I cried unto him in mighty prayer and supplication for my own soul.' Like Hezekiah, Enos recognizes that human effort alone is insufficient and turns to God in personal prayer during crisis. Both men model the shift from reliance on worldly power to reliance on divine intervention.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-5 instructs that the president of the Church should 'be obedient unto the things which I shall give unto him, saith the Lord.' Hezekiah's immediate obedience to turn to God's house, rather than to military or political expedients, reflects the same principle of covenantal obedience before tactical calculation. The Lord values the heart that seeks Him first.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Hezekiah's entry into the Temple during crisis establishes a pattern reflected in modern temple worship: the Temple is the place where we take our burdens and sorrows before God, where we present ourselves in humility and covenant, and where we seek divine direction when earthly solutions fail. His movement into the house of the LORD prefigures the later covenant pattern where the faithful, when pressed by adversity, seek the presence of God in holy spaces.

commentary.christological_typology: Hezekiah's voluntary stripping away of royal garments and assumption of sackcloth prefigures the humiliation and suffering of the Christ. Just as Hezekiah laid aside the symbols of earthly power and authority to seek God's mercy on behalf of his people, Christ stripped Himself of divine privilege (Philippians 2:7) and took upon Himself human weakness and suffering to intercede for humanity before God. Hezekiah's entry into the Temple also foreshadows Christ as the ultimate High Priest who enters the heavenly sanctuary on behalf of all believers (Hebrews 4:14-16), bringing their cries and needs before the Father.
commentary.application: When we face crises that lie beyond human resolution — illness that medicine cannot cure, relational breach that apology alone cannot mend, adversity that our resources cannot overcome — we are invited to follow Hezekiah's example: to lay aside the pride that says we should handle this ourselves, to acknowledge our helplessness through genuine repentance and prayer, and to turn toward God's house with vulnerability and faith. The impulse to manage, strategize, and solve can be legitimate, but Hezekiah teaches us that the first act should be the act of turning toward God, not away from Him. Modern covenants teach the same principle: we covenant to take upon ourselves the name of Christ and to remember Him always, which means placing Him and His will before our own calculations. Hezekiah's sackcloth invites us to examine whether we, in our crises, wear the garments of trust or the garments of self-sufficiency.

text_kjv: And he sent Eliakim, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz.

commentary.narrative: Hezekiah's action in verse 1 — entering the Temple in sackcloth — was individual and liturgical; now in verse 2, he moves from personal prayer to official delegation. He dispatches three classes of leaders to the prophet Isaiah: Eliakim (palace administrator), Shebna (royal secretary), and the senior priests. The TCR rendering emphasizes that all three groups are 'wearing sackcloth,' indicating this is not merely a political embassy but a united national act of mourning and prayer. The delegation is sent to Isaiah, identified as 'the prophet son of Amoz' — a formal title that grants him official status as the voice of God for this moment. This is significant because the Rabshakeh, in his taunt, had claimed to speak for the Assyrian king; now Hezekiah summons the prophet to speak for God.
commentary.narrative_continued: The composition of the delegation reveals Hezekiah's theological sophistication. He does not send only civil officials or only priests; he sends both, united in sackcloth. Eliakim, 'over the household' (asher al-habayit), held one of the highest administrative positions in the Judean kingdom — essentially the palace manager or chief steward. Shebna, the scribe (hassopher), was the royal secretary and record-keeper, a position of considerable influence. These two represent the civil administration. The ziqnei hakkohanim — the 'elders of the priests' — represent the religious hierarchy. By including both civil and religious leaders, Hezekiah signals that this crisis transcends bureaucratic response; the entire fabric of Judean leadership, civil and religious combined, now stands in need of prophetic counsel. The unanimity of the delegation — all wearing sackcloth — demonstrates corporate repentance and corporate recognition that human wisdom alone cannot address the Assyrian threat.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The act of sending this delegation to Isaiah is itself an implicit prayer. In ancient Near Eastern culture, approaching a prophet during crisis was an act of piety and submission to the divine will. The prophet functioned as the boundary-crosser between human and divine realms, the one who could hear God's word and deliver it to kings and nations. By sending his three most senior leaders to Isaiah, Hezekiah is publicly affirming that the prophet's word carries more weight than the king's own authority — a remarkable act of humility in an ancient royal context. The prophet is not summoned as a courtier; rather, the king's representatives come as supplicants to hear what God will say through the prophet.

word_study.meaning: 'Over the house/household.' This phrase denotes the chief administrator of the royal palace, responsible for the day-to-day operations of the royal complex, supplies, personnel, and protocols. It was one of the highest administrative posts in the Judean monarchy.
word_study.significance: Eliakim's position underscores that Hezekiah is consulting the prophet at the highest levels of government. This is not a secondary or tertiary official but the chief palace administrator, indicating the gravity with which the king views the prophet's counsel.

word_study.meaning: Secretary, recorder, or scribe — a literate official responsible for royal correspondence, records, and documentation. In the Assyrian imperial system and among Levantine kingdoms, the scribe (or 'secretary') was a highly educated official who often held significant diplomatic authority.
word_study.significance: Shebna's presence in the delegation suggests that his role might include not only record-keeping but also diplomatic communication. However, in this moment, he comes not as a diplomat representing the king to foreign powers but as a supplicant bringing the king's request to the prophet.

word_study.meaning: The senior members of the priestly hierarchy, the oldest and most experienced priests who held leadership positions within the Temple and religious establishment. 'Elders' (ziqnim) in Hebrew denotes both age and authority — those whose experience and wisdom qualified them for leadership.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of priestly elders underscores that this is not merely a political crisis but a spiritual one. The priests represent the covenant relationship between God and Israel; their presence in the delegation affirms that the nation's survival depends on maintaining right standing with God through the priesthood and Temple.

word_study.meaning: One who speaks forth God's word; a divinely called messenger. The Hebrew navi is derived from a root meaning 'to call' or 'to announce,' indicating that a prophet is one called by God to announce His word to the people or nation.
word_study.significance: Isaiah is identified formally as hannavi — 'the prophet' — giving him the authoritative status as the designated voice of God in this crisis. The Rabshakeh had attempted to speak with divine authority for the Assyrian king; Isaiah's title asserts a higher divine mandate.

word_study.meaning: A patronymic designation, 'son of Amoz,' identifying Isaiah by his father's name. This is his formal genealogical identification, similar to how the Rabshakeh had been identified by his title and king. The name Amoz (אָמוֹץ) is of uncertain etymology but appears only in the Isaiah narrative, emphasizing the prophet's historical particularity.
word_study.significance: By naming Isaiah 'son of Amoz,' the text grounds the prophet in real genealogy and history. This is not a legendary or mythical figure but a specific historical prophet whose word could be documented and remembered. The naming also differentiates Isaiah from other prophets (Elijah, Elisha, etc.) active in Israel's history.

cross_references.connection: The parallel account in Isaiah confirms this verse, noting that Hezekiah sent the same delegation to Isaiah, establishing the consistency of this historical moment across multiple scriptural sources.

Earlier in the narrative, the same three officials — Eliakim, Shebna, and the high priest Joah — are sent to confront the Rabshakeh. Here they return to seek the prophet's counsel, showing the progression from failed negotiation to prayer and prophetic guidance.

Mentions 'Ahishar, over the household' (asher al-habayit), using identical terminology for the palace administrator position, confirming the historical reality of this administrative role in the Judean monarchy.

Moses' prophecy that God will raise up a prophet like him to whom the people must hearken, which provides the theological framework for why Hezekiah turns to Isaiah as the authoritative voice of God in crisis.

Mentions 'Hananiah, one of the king's captains, in charge of the mighty men,' using the same administrative structure (officials 'over' various domains) that characterizes Judean governance and appears in Eliakim's role.

commentary.historical_context: The delegation of palace and priestly officials to consult a prophet was not unique in the ancient Near East, but it was characteristic of Hebrew covenant theology. In Assyrian administrative records, kings consulted priests and diviners, but the Hebrew practice of the king submitting to a prophet's word was distinctive. Eliakim's role as 'over the household' is well-documented in Assyrian records — such officials (often called 'majordomo' in English) held considerable power in palace hierarchies. Shebna as 'scribe' reflects the scribal bureaucracy of the Levantine kingdoms, which required literacy and often diplomatic skill. The Temple priesthood in Jerusalem maintained genealogical records and served as custodians of covenant tradition; the 'elders of the priests' would have been senior figures with decades of experience in Temple ritual and covenant interpretation. The fact that all three groups donned sackcloth for this delegation indicates corporate recognition that this crisis exceeded normal administrative or diplomatic remedy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 22:16-18, King Lamoni's father, upon learning the truth about God, calls for his people to gather and 'cast away every sin' — a delegation of spiritual seeking parallel to Hezekiah's official journey toward the prophet. Both kings recognize that spiritual guidance from one who knows God's will is essential during national crisis.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:7-8 establishes that 'no commandment of the Lord is binding unless it is sealed by my Spirit and my voice,' affirming the principle that God's will comes through His designated spokesman — in Hezekiah's time, the prophet Isaiah; in the latter-day context, the President of the Church. Hezekiah's delegation to Isaiah reflects the same principle of seeking counsel from God's anointed.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The inclusion of 'elders of the priests' in the delegation emphasizes the Temple as the center of covenant connection. In modern temple practice, members approach the Lord through covenantal action and through leaders who stand in the priestly tradition. Hezekiah's sending of priestly elders to the prophet affirms that spiritual leaders have a role in helping the covenant people access God's will during crisis.

commentary.christological_typology: Hezekiah's three classes of leaders — civil administrators, scribes/educators, and priests — prefigure the threefold office of Christ as Prophet, Priest, and King. Just as these three groups unite to seek the word of God through Isaiah, all legitimate authority and wisdom flow through Christ, who combines in Himself prophetic authority (He speaks God's word), priestly mediation (He intercedes before God), and kingly rule (He governs all creation). The delegation seeking the prophet also foreshadows how all human authority is ultimately subordinate to God's word spoken through His chosen messenger — a principle fulfilled in Christ as the Word of God made flesh.
commentary.application: Hezekiah's dispatch of three groups of leaders to the prophet teaches modern covenant members about the proper use of authority during crisis. Rather than relying solely on administrative expertise (represented by Eliakim), documentation and communication (represented by Shebna), or institutional tradition (represented by the priestly elders), Hezekiah unified all three perspectives and brought them together in genuine seeking for God's word. This suggests that in our families, our callings, and our personal crises, we should not rely on a single lens — not only practicality, not only tradition, not only education — but should seek unified counsel from God through His appointed servants and through personal prayer. Furthermore, the fact that Hezekiah, as the supreme authority in the kingdom, sent his leaders to submit to the prophet rather than summoning the prophet as a servant, teaches us that true leadership means recognizing when we have reached the limit of our own wisdom and humbly placing ourselves under the guidance of those who speak for God.

text_kjv: And they said unto him, Thus saith Hezekiah, This day is a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and blasphemy: for the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth.

commentary.narrative: Hezekiah's message to Isaiah, delivered through his delegation, comprises two parts: a three-part diagnosis of the crisis and a one-part metaphor of futility. The diagnosis names the nature of the moment: tsarah (trouble, distress, anguish), tokhechah (rebuke, correction, punishment), and ne'atsah (disgrace, blasphemy, mockery). These are not abstract theological concepts but descriptions of what has happened to Judah. The Rabshakeh's taunt was not merely an insult to the king; it was, in Hezekiah's understanding, tokhechah — a divine rebuke delivered through the mouth of a foreign enemy — and ne'atsah — blasphemy against God's very character and power. Hezekiah reads the crisis not merely as a military or political failure but as a moment of divine correction and offense against God.
commentary.narrative_continued: The metaphor of childbirth near the breaking point is devastating in its desperation. 'Children have reached the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them.' The mashber (birth stool, or the breaking/opening moment of childbirth) represents the final, critical moment of labor. A woman who reaches this point has no choice but to push forward; to stop is to risk death to both mother and child. Yet Hezekiah says that Judah has reached this point with 'no strength to deliver.' The nation has arrived at the final crisis, the moment of no return, and yet possesses no resources, no military capacity, no strategic maneuver, no diplomatic gambit that will save it. The metaphor is not merely about danger; it is about utter dependency. A woman in advanced labor cannot will herself out of the crisis; she must rely entirely on her body's strength, the midwife's skill, and ultimately divine favor. Hezekiah is saying that Judah has reached the point where human effort and strategy are exhausted.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: This message is remarkable because Hezekiah, the king, is essentially confessing national helplessness to the prophet. He does not send a message saying, 'We are strong and will resist' or 'We are making diplomatic overtures.' Instead, he sends a message of utter admission: We are in distress, we are under God's rebuke, we are blasphemed against, and we have no strength left. This is not a confession of sin exactly — though it may imply that — but rather a confession of the reality that the nation has reached the end of its own resources and now depends entirely on God's intervention. In the ancient Near Eastern context, such an admission from a king would normally be political suicide; it would invite vassalization or conquest. But in the Hebrew theological framework, such admission opens the door for God to act, because it clears away the pretense that human power is sufficient.

word_study.meaning: Distress, anguish, trouble, straits. The root can mean 'to be narrow' or 'to be pressed,' conveying the sense of being hemmed in, compressed, unable to move or breathe freely. Tsarah describes the subjective experience of crisis — the feeling of being trapped and pressed from all sides.
word_study.significance: Hezekiah uses tsarah to describe the immediate experience of Judah under Assyrian siege. The word conveys both objective military danger and subjective psychological and spiritual distress. In covenantal language, tsarah often appears in contexts where the faithful cry out to God from constraint and danger (see Psalm 25:17).

word_study.meaning: Rebuke, correction, reproof, punishment. Related to the verb hokiach ('to reprove,' 'to correct,' 'to convict'), tokhechah describes the action by which someone in authority corrects or punishes a subordinate. In covenantal language, tokhechah is often God's corrective action toward His people.
word_study.significance: Hezekiah identifies the Assyrian threat not as mere military aggression but as tokhechah — a divine rebuke. This indicates that Hezekiah, despite his religious reforms, recognizes that the crisis may be understood as God's correction of the nation. However, tokhechah need not be final punishment; it can be corrective discipline that leads to repentance and restoration.

word_study.meaning: Blasphemy, contempt, scorn, mockery. The root ne'ats means 'to despise' or 'to treat with contempt.' Ne'atsah describes speech or action that is contemptuous, that treats someone or something as worthless and deserving of ridicule.
word_study.significance: Hezekiah characterizes the Rabshakeh's speech as ne'atsah — not merely an insult to the king but a blasphemous contempt for God Himself. The Rabshakeh has not only challenged Judah's military capacity; he has mocked the idea that God can save. This elevation of the Rabshakeh's speech to the category of blasphemy means that the crisis is ultimately a matter between God and the Assyrian court, not merely between human powers.

word_study.meaning: Children, sons, offspring. In this metaphorical context, 'children' refers to the nation's future — the next generation who would be born and who would inherit the land. The image is of a pregnancy brought to term, ready for birth.
word_study.significance: The use of 'children' (vanim) in the birth metaphor connects the crisis to futurity and covenant promise. The covenant with David promised an eternal dynasty; 'children' would be the heirs to that promise. Hezekiah is essentially asking: How can the covenant promise continue if we have no strength to bring forth the future generation?

word_study.term_original: בָאוּ בָנִים עַד־מַשְׁבֵּר (ba'u vanim ad mashber)
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'the children have come to the breaking point.' The mashber is the critical moment of childbirth — the cervical opening that dilates during labor, the 'breaking' of the waters, the moment of transition from pregnancy to delivery. Ba'u ('have come') uses the verb 'to come' to indicate arrival at a point of no return.
word_study.significance: This is the point in labor beyond which retreat is impossible. The metaphor captures Judah's existential moment: the nation has reached the critical juncture where the future either will be born or will be lost. There is no returning to the previous state; the only question is whether new life will emerge.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'there is no strength for bringing forth.' Koach means 'strength,' 'power,' 'capacity.' Ayin means 'there is not.' Leledah means 'to bear,' 'to give birth,' 'to bring forth.' The phrase describes the absence of the power necessary to complete the act of childbirth.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering captures the heart of Hezekiah's despair: at the moment when Judah most needs power — koach — it has none. This is not merely a statement about military weakness but about existential powerlessness. Judah cannot save itself, cannot force its own future, cannot rely on its own strength. The only possible salvation is external — a salvation that must come from beyond human capacity.

cross_references.connection: The parallel account in Isaiah preserves the exact same message, confirming Hezekiah's words to the prophet about distress, rebuke, blasphemy, and the birthpang metaphor.

David's reflection on God's role from the womb and from birth, contrasting with Hezekiah's cry that there is no strength to bring forth — David affirms God as the one who brings forth life, while Hezekiah acknowledges the nation's inability to birth its own future.

Jeremiah uses the same birth imagery to describe Jerusalem in crisis: 'a voice as of a woman in travail, and the anguish as of her that bringeth forth her first child,' showing that the metaphor of childbirth distress was a standard way to describe national crisis.
The parallel account in Chronicles records Sennacherib's message claiming that no god has been able to save any nation from Assyria, to which Hezekiah's message of utter helplessness is the response.

Paul's description of all creation 'groaning and travailing in pain together until now' uses the same birth imagery to describe a moment of crisis and waiting for deliverance, resonating with Hezekiah's desperation.

commentary.historical_context: The birth metaphor would have been immediately understood in the ancient Near Eastern context. Childbirth was one of the most dangerous moments in a woman's life, and the cry for a midwife or for help during difficult labor was a desperate plea. The image of a nation in the pangs of labor, unable to deliver, would have conveyed to listeners the absolute urgency and hopelessness of Judah's situation. The three terms — tsarah, tokhechah, ne'atsah — form a theological vocabulary for crisis that Hezekiah employs to reframe the Assyrian siege not as a merely political or military matter but as a covenant crisis. In Assyrian records, kings typically responded to siege situations with displays of strength, boasts of military power, or rapid diplomacy. Hezekiah's message does none of this; instead, it places Judah's situation directly before the prophet as a matter requiring divine intervention. The acknowledgment of weakness and helplessness, though counterintuitive in the ancient world, was the appropriate posture for seeking God's miraculous intervention.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26:35-36, Ammon speaks of being 'compassed about' and 'overpowered' yet rejoicing in God's deliverance. Similarly, in Helaman 12:1-3, the people 'began to remember God' during times of 'affliction' and 'hardness,' recognizing their dependence on Him. Hezekiah's admission of tsarah ('distress') parallels these moments when the covenant people recognize their utter dependence on God and cry out for His intervention.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:10 declares that the Lord will 'bring all things to light' and reveal 'things which have not been revealed,' while also indicating that mankind must come to Him in humility. Hezekiah's message to Isaiah reflects this principle — the nation has reached the end of its own understanding and power and must now depend on the revelation God will give through His prophet.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The birth imagery in Hezekiah's message connects to covenant themes of divine procreation and regeneration. In temple theology, the individual and the nation are 'born again' through covenant — a spiritual rebirth that depends entirely on God's creative power, not on human strength. Hezekiah's admission that there is 'no strength to bring forth' mirrors the requirement in temple experience that the natural self must be 'broken' in order to be 'born again' in the covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Hezekiah's description of Judah at the breaking point, with 'no strength to bring forth,' prefigures Christ in Gethsemane and on the cross, where He reaches the limit of human endurance and places Himself entirely in the Father's hands (Luke 22:42). Just as Hezekiah confesses that the nation has exhausted its own resources and must depend on God, Christ emptied Himself of independent will and became entirely dependent on the Father's sustaining power. The birth imagery also foreshadows Christ's resurrection as a 'bringing forth' of new life — the First-born from the dead (Colossians 1:18) — which is God's creative act, not dependent on human strength. Finally, the nation's desperate need to 'bring forth' its future echoes the promise of Christ as the one through whom all things are brought forth: 'all things are created by him, and for him' (Colossians 1:16).
commentary.application: Hezekiah's threefold naming of the crisis — distress, rebuke, blasphemy — invites us to examine the crises we face and to identify their true nature, not merely their surface appearance. When we face what seems to be a problem of resources, opportunity, relationships, or health, Hezekiah teaches us to ask: Is this distress a sign that I have relied too heavily on my own strength? Is it a rebuke that calls me to realign with God's will? Is there an element of blasphemy — a challenge to God's character or power — embedded in what I am facing? The birth metaphor teaches that there are moments in spiritual life when our own efforts are exhausted, when we have 'come to the breaking point' with 'no strength to bring forth.' In these moments, we are not meant to redouble our own efforts but to cry out to God and His prophets for the intervention that only God can provide. This is a profound teaching on the difference between human effort (which is good and necessary) and human dependence on God (which is ultimate and salvific). Hezekiah learned this distinction in a moment of national crisis; we can learn it through study of scripture and through honest recognition of our own limits.

text_kjv: It may be the LORD thy God will hear all the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of Assyria his master hath sent to reproach the living God; and will reprove the words which the LORD thy God hath heard: wherefore lift up thy prayer for the remnant that are left.

commentary.narrative: Hezekiah's message reaches its climax in verse 4, where the king explicitly requests that Isaiah pray for Judah. But before that request, Hezekiah frames the crisis in a way that elevates it from political to theological: the Rabshakeh has been sent 'to reproach the living God' (lecharef Elohim chai). This reframing is crucial. In verses 1-3, the focus was on Judah's military vulnerability and desperate straits. But in verse 4, Hezekiah identifies the true opponent: it is not Sennacherib or the Assyrian military machine, but the God of Israel who has been blasphemed. The Rabshakeh's words were not directed first at the king or the nation; they were directed at God's character and power. This theological reorientation transforms the entire crisis.
commentary.narrative_continued: Hezekiah's request itself is modest and honest: 'Perhaps' (ulai) the Lord will hear the Rabshakeh's words and 'reprove' (hokhiach) them. Hezekiah does not presume on God's action. The word ulai ('perhaps') is the language of hope without certainty, of petition without demand. He does not say, 'The Lord will definitely deliver us' but rather 'Perhaps the Lord will hear and respond.' This linguistic humility is important because it shows that Hezekiah, despite his faith, is not claiming special knowledge of God's will; he is asking the prophet to intercede and to learn what God will do. The request to 'lift up a prayer' (venasata tefillah) recognizes that Isaiah, as the prophet, has direct access to God's ear in a way that even the king does not. This is not weakness on Hezekiah's part; it is theological clarity. In the covenant system, the prophet is God's spokesman; the king must sometimes defer to the prophet's intercession.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The final phrase is weighted with theological significance: 'Lift up a prayer for the remnant that are left' (na'ar tefillah be'ad hashe'erit hannimtsa'ah). The word she'erit ('remnant') is the prophetic term for the survivor community, the small portion of Israel or Judah that God preserves despite judgment. Hezekiah is essentially acknowledging that most of the nation has already fallen — Israel to the north has been destroyed, most of Judah has been conquered — and what remains is only Jerusalem and its population. Judah is not the whole nation; it is the she'erit, the remnant of the original covenant people. This is a humbling admission: we are not the nation in its strength; we are what is left. But the theological importance is that she'erit carries covenant meaning — God has promised to preserve a remnant through whom the covenant promises will continue. The remnant theology suggests that even in Judah's near-total collapse, God's covenant purposes are not void; they continue in the small community that remains.

word_study.meaning: Perhaps, maybe, possibly. A particle expressing uncertainty, possibility, or hope without assurance. It indicates that what follows is not certain but is a possibility one hopes for.
word_study.significance: Hezekiah's use of ulai reveals spiritual humility and honesty. He does not presume to know God's will but rather hopes and prays for God's intervention. This is the language of faith seeking God's mind, not faith claiming to know it in advance.

word_study.meaning: To hear, listen, obey. In Hebrew, 'hearing' often implies not merely the physical reception of sound but attentive listening and responsive action. To say that God 'hears' a prayer means He receives it, attends to it, and will act in response.
word_study.significance: Hezekiah's petition hinges on the phrase yishmah YHWH ('the LORD will hear'). The assumption is that if God truly attends to the Rabshakeh's blasphemy, He will respond to it. God's hearing is the prerequisite for God's action — once God has heard the affront against His character, He will respond to defend His honor.

word_study.meaning: To reproach, taunt, insult, defy. Related to the noun cherpah ('reproach,' 'shame'), the verb chareph describes the action of insulting someone's honor or challenging their power.
word_study.significance: The Rabshakeh's words are characterized as chareph — he has not merely challenged Judah's military capacity but has insulted and taunted God's power. This is not a normal diplomatic exchange but a cosmic insult that demands a response from God Himself.

word_study.meaning: The living God; the God who lives and acts. This phrase contrasts with dead idols — gods that are merely stone or metal, that have no power to see, hear, speak, or act. The 'living God' is characterized by dynamism, agency, and responsiveness.
word_study.significance: Hezekiah invokes the title 'the living God' precisely because the Rabshakeh had mocked the idea that any god can act to save a nation. By emphasizing that God is 'living' — that is, active, powerful, capable of intervention — Hezekiah asserts that the God of Israel is fundamentally different from the dead idols of the nations. This title becomes the basis for hope: a living God can and will respond.

word_study.meaning: To reprove, correct, rebuke, convict. This verb indicates the action by which authority corrects wrongdoing or proves someone's words to be false.
word_study.significance: Hezekiah asks that God will 'reprove' (hokhiach) the Rabshakeh's words. He is asking not for mere retaliation but for a demonstration that will expose the falsity of the Assyrian claims — a proof, through divine action, that contradicts what has been said against God.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'and you shall lift up a prayer.' The verb nasa ('to lift up,' 'to bear,' 'to raise') when combined with 'prayer' (tefillah) creates an image of the prophet raising up supplication to God, bearing it upward to the divine ear.
word_study.significance: The image of 'lifting up' prayer suggests that Isaiah's intercession is an act of bringing Judah's need before God's presence. This is not a casual request but a solemn, deliberate act of intercession on behalf of the nation.

word_study.meaning: Remnant, remainder, what is left. In biblical prophecy, the 'remnant' (she'erit) refers to the small portion of the people of God who survive judgment and through whom God's covenant purposes continue.
word_study.significance: The term she'erit appears throughout the prophetic books, especially in Isaiah and Jeremiah, as a designation for the community that will be preserved and through whom God's promises will be fulfilled. Hezekiah's use of this term affirms that Jerusalem represents the she'erit — the survivor community through whom the Davidic covenant will continue.

cross_references.connection: The parallel account in Isaiah preserves this verse with nearly identical wording, including the distinctive phrase 'the living God' (Elohim chai) and the request to 'lift up a prayer for the remnant.'

Isaiah's own prophecy about the remnant (she'erit) of Israel that will return to God — directly relevant to Hezekiah's invocation of 'the remnant that are left' as the basis for continued covenant faith.

Paul's theological reflection on the remnant according to grace: 'Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace,' affirming the biblical principle that God always preserves a remnant.
David's testimony: 'I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry,' expressing the same confidence that God hears and will respond to the prayer of the faithful.

The parallel account in Chronicles notes that Hezekiah and Isaiah 'cried to heaven' and God 'sent an angel, which cut off all the mighty men of valour' — showing that Hezekiah's prayer through Isaiah results in divine deliverance.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern understanding of prayer and divine response, the prophet was understood as the mediator between human and divine realms. Hezekiah's request that Isaiah 'lift up a prayer' reflects the common ancient Near Eastern practice of seeking a religious intermediary during crisis. However, the Israelite understanding was distinctive: the prophet did not perform ritual magic but conveyed God's word and interceded on behalf of the people. The title 'the living God' (Elohim chai) is a polemical assertion against Assyrian theological concepts; the Assyrian gods were conceived as living but in a way analogous to powerful kings. The Israelite God was 'living' in the sense of being present, responsive, and capable of acting in history. The concept of the 'remnant' (she'erit) reflects the historical reality that northern Israel had been destroyed in 722 BCE, nearly a century before Hezekiah's time. Judah was already in a situation of being the 'remnant' — the small survivor community of what had once been a unified monarchy. Prophets like Isaiah and Jeremiah used remnant theology to explain both judgment (most of the nation will be destroyed) and hope (God will preserve a remnant through whom His purposes continue).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 10:18-22, Jacob speaks of the covenant being preserved among 'the remnant of the house of Israel,' and in 2 Nephi 30:3-6, Nephi prophesies about the remnant of his seed that will be brought back into the covenant. The she'erit concept in Hezekiah's prayer parallels the Book of Mormon's extended theology of the remnant of Israel being preserved and restored in the latter days.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 86:8-11 describes the 'field is white already to harvest' and God's gathering of His elect, reflecting the same remnant principle that Hezekiah invokes — that God has always a people, a community through whom His purposes continue. The D&C emphasizes that this remnant is gathered through covenant and priesthood, just as Hezekiah's remnant was preserved through the Temple and the covenant with David.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Hezekiah's prayer for 'the remnant that are left' is a prayer focused on covenant preservation — that the Temple, the covenant relationship with God, and the Davidic succession will be maintained through whatever crisis comes. The Temple is the physical embodiment of the covenant with the remnant; its preservation symbolizes the preservation of the covenant people.

commentary.christological_typology: Hezekiah's invocation of 'the living God' (Elohim chai) and the subsequent divine deliverance through Isaiah prefigure Christ as the Word of God made flesh — the ultimate manifestation of the living God acting in history. Just as God's living character was proven through the deliverance of Judah from Assyria, the Resurrection of Christ is the ultimate proof that God is 'the living God,' having power over death itself. Hezekiah's request that Isaiah intercede for the remnant also prefigures Christ's intercessory role: 'Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them' (Hebrews 7:25). The concept of the 'remnant' ultimately finds its fulfillment in the Church of Christ, the covenant community that inherits the promises made to Israel.
commentary.application: Hezekiah's careful framing of his request — using 'perhaps' rather than demanding certainty, asking Isaiah to intercede rather than presuming on God's immediate response, and identifying Jerusalem as the 'remnant' rather than as the full nation — teaches modern covenant members about appropriate spiritual humility and theological honesty. When we face crises, we are invited to recognize that our true opponent may not be the visible threat but the challenge to God's character and power that the crisis represents. We should also recognize the role of prophetic intercession: just as Hezekiah asked Isaiah to 'lift up a prayer,' we live in a dispensation where we have prophets and apostles whose role includes interceding for the Church and the world. Additionally, the remnant theology invites us to recognize that we, as members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, stand in the line of the covenant remnant — not because we are perfect or numerous, but because God has preserved a people through whom His purposes continue. This carries both blessing and responsibility: we are preserved for covenant purposes, and we have a duty to maintain faith and righteousness on behalf of those who will come after us.

text_kjv: So the servants of king Hezekiah came to Isaiah.

commentary.narrative: Verse 5 is a brief transitional verse that marks the completion of the delegation's journey to Isaiah the prophet. The servants who departed from Hezekiah in verse 2 have now arrived at Isaiah's location. The simplicity of this verse belies its narrative importance: it bridges the moment of Hezekiah's desperate petition and the moment when the prophet will deliver God's response. In terms of structure, this short verse creates a pause — a moment between Hezekiah's anguished message and Isaiah's word from the Lord. Theologically, it represents the threshold between human desperation and divine revelation, between the plea for intercession and the reception of God's word.
commentary.narrative_continued: The designation of the delegation members as 'servants of king Hezekiah' (avdei hammelekh Hezekiah) emphasizes that they act under royal authority and commission. They do not come as private individuals but as official representatives carrying the king's words and bearing his authority. Yet simultaneously, they come to a prophet, a figure who stands outside the royal administrative structure. The prophet's authority derives not from the king but from God; when Isaiah receives these servants and listens to their message, he does so as God's spokesman, not as a subordinate of the king. This verse, though brief, thus establishes the proper relationship in the covenant community: the king is important, the servants of the king are important, but they are all finally subject to the word of God spoken through His prophet.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The brevity of verse 5 also serves a literary function in the flow of 2 Kings 19. The narrative has been building in intensity: Hezekiah's distress and turning to the Temple (verse 1), the dispatch of a formal delegation carrying a message of national desperation (verses 2-4). Now, at verse 5, there is a momentary stillness — the servants have arrived. In verse 6, Isaiah will speak, and the word of God will begin to reshape the entire crisis. The one-verse interlude allows the reader a moment to anticipate what the prophet will say. Will Isaiah confirm Hezekiah's fears? Will he offer strategic advice? Or will he bring a word from God that transforms the understanding of the crisis itself? Verse 5 holds the breath before the answer comes.

word_study.meaning: Servants, officials, attendants, those who serve. The term can denote both literal servants and high-ranking officials who 'serve' the king in an administrative capacity. In the case of Eliakim, Shebna, and the priests, these are important officials who represent the king's authority.
word_study.significance: The use of avdei ('servants') for what were actually the highest officials in the kingdom emphasizes the principle that all human authority, even that of the king's most important ministers, stands in a service relationship to God. These men are servants of the king, but implicitly, they are also servants of God and come before His prophet to receive His word.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'and they came to Isaiah.' The verb bo'a ('to go,' 'to come') is used of the servants' physical arrival at the prophet's location. There is no elaborate description of where Isaiah is or how the servants found him; the focus is simply on the fact of arrival.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'came to Isaiah' echoes the same verb used in verse 1 when Hezekiah 'went into the house of the LORD' (vayyavo beit YHWH). Both movements — Hezekiah entering the Temple and the servants approaching the prophet — are movements toward God's presence, though through different channels. Hezekiah approaches God through the Temple; the servants approach God through the prophet. Both movements lead toward the divine word.

cross_references.connection: The parallel account in Isaiah 37 is nearly word-for-word identical, confirming the historical consistency of this moment across both the Kings and Isaiah narratives.
Verse 2 describes the departure of the servants to Isaiah; verse 5 completes that journey, showing the fulfillment of Hezekiah's sending.

When Jeroboam's wife came to the prophet Ahijah to inquire about her sick son, the text uses similar language of going to the prophet to receive God's word: 'Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam' — showing the pattern of seeking the prophet during crisis.

Saul's servants help him find a woman with a familiar spirit when ordinary prophetic channels are closed, illustrating the consistent ancient practice of seeking out those believed to have access to divine communication during crisis.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern context, consulting a prophet, priest, or diviner during military or political crisis was standard practice. The Assyrians consulted their priests and diviners; the Hittites had their oracular systems; Egypt had its priestly advisors. However, the Israelite pattern was distinctive because the prophet was understood as God's spokesman, not as someone performing divination or working magic. The prophet was authorized to speak directly for God and to declare His will. Seeking out the prophet during crisis was therefore an act of placing oneself under God's authority. The narrative rhythm of verses 1-5 — crisis, prayer, delegation, arrival — reflects actual historical processes by which such crises would have been addressed in ancient Judah.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 43:1, during military crisis, the Nephites consult their leaders and prophets to determine the will of God, reflecting the same principle that during times of crisis, the covenant people turn to those who can communicate God's will rather than relying solely on military or political strategy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:38 declares, 'What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken; and I excuse not myself.' The servants coming to Isaiah to receive the word of the Lord reflects the principle that God's word, spoken through His servants, is binding and trustworthy. Members of the Church are invited to similarly approach the prophets and apostles to understand God's will in our time.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Just as the servants came to Isaiah to receive God's word at a moment of crisis, in modern temple worship, members come to the Temple as a place where God's word can be received and understood. The temple, like Isaiah's presence in this verse, is understood as a place of access to divine guidance.

commentary.christological_typology: The servants coming to Isaiah to receive God's word prefigures believers coming to Christ, who is Himself the Word of God made flesh (John 1:1). Just as Isaiah stood as the mediator between God and the servants of Hezekiah, Christ stands as the ultimate mediator between God and humanity, the one through whom God's word is definitively communicated. The coming of the servants to Isaiah also foreshadows the role of the Apostles and disciples in the New Testament, who came to Jesus to receive His teaching and to understand God's will.
commentary.application: The brevity and simplicity of verse 5 contains an important teaching about the proper approach to seeking God's guidance. The servants did not come to Isaiah with arguments, negotiations, or alternative proposals; they came to receive the word. In modern life, when we face crises that exceed our capacity to solve, we, too, are invited to 'come' to those through whom God speaks — the prophets and apostles, the scriptures, and ultimately the Holy Ghost. The principle is one of receptiveness rather than insistence: we come not to convince God of our rightness but to hear and understand His will. This requires a particular posture — one of listening, openness, and willingness to receive whatever the Lord's word may be, even if it contradicts our expectations. The servants' arrival at Isaiah's presence marks a moment of vulnerability where the kingdom's fate will be determined not by human strategy but by God's word. We, too, reach such moments in our spiritual lives, and the invitation is to 'come' to God's spokespersons with genuine openness to hearing and obeying what God wishes to communicate.

text_kjv: And Isaiah said unto them, Thus saith the LORD, Be not afraid of the words which thou hast heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me.

commentary.narrative: With verse 6, Isaiah speaks, and the tone of the narrative shifts decisively. Where Hezekiah's message was characterized by distress, weakness, and desperation, Isaiah's message opens with the prophetic formula 'Thus saith the LORD' (koh amar YHWH) and follows immediately with the oracle of reassurance: 'Be not afraid' (al tira). This is the fundamental reassurance offered by God through His prophet. The oracle of reassurance is one of the most common forms of divine speech in the Hebrew Bible, appearing in contexts where the faithful face threat and uncertainty. But what Isaiah reassures Hezekiah about is specific: 'Be not afraid of the words which thou hast heard.' The 'words' (davarim) refer to the Rabshakeh's taunt. These words — the claims that God cannot save, that no god has ever saved a people from Assyria's hand, the mockery of God's power — are presented as the thing Hezekiah should not fear. Isaiah essentially says: The Rabshakeh's words have no power; they are merely speech, and God's speech is greater.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second crucial element in Isaiah's response is his identification of what the Rabshakeh has done: 'with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me' (asher giddefu na'arei melekh Ashshur oti). Note that the prophet says not, 'They have blasphemed God' or 'They have blasphemed the LORD' but rather 'They have blasphemed me' (oti, 'me'). This is the personal claim of the prophet — Isaiah identifies so completely with God's cause and God's word that an insult to God is an insult to him as God's spokesman. But more importantly, this phrase identifies the true nature of the crisis: the Rabshakeh has not merely engaged in political rhetoric or military threat; he has committed blasphemy against God. The word giddefu (from gadaph, 'to blaspheme,' 'to taunt,' 'to revile') describes speech that is contemptuous and insulting to the divine. God takes this personally and will respond to it.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: Notably, Isaiah diminishes the Rabshakeh's status. The Rabshakeh, who had presented himself as the official spokesman of the king of Assyria and who had addressed Hezekiah and Jerusalem with imperial authority, is now called 'servants' (na'arei — more literally, 'boys' or 'lads') of the king of Assyria. The same word na'ar appears earlier in the account (2 Kings 18:26) when the Rabshakeh is the one using it dismissively. Now Isaiah turns the language back: these 'boys' or 'servants' of Assyria are not as mighty as they claim. Their master, the king of Assyria, stands behind them, but they themselves are mere servants. The prophet's word is already reframing the entire crisis: the massive Assyrian military apparatus, which had seemed so overwhelming, is reduced in God's perspective to servants bearing their master's words. The true issue is not military might but blasphemy — and blasphemy is something God will not tolerate.

word_study.meaning: This is the prophetic messenger formula, the standard way a prophet introduces a direct utterance from God. It literally means 'Thus says the LORD,' and it functions as a formal certification that what follows is God's direct speech, not the prophet's own words or interpretation.
word_study.significance: The prophetic formula koh amar YHWH appears hundreds of times in the Hebrew Bible and serves to distinguish between the prophet's own thoughts and God's direct utterance. When Isaiah uses this formula, he claims divine authority for what he is about to say. This is precisely what Hezekiah needs to hear: not Isaiah's opinion but God's own word. Notably, the Rabshakeh had also used a messenger formula in 2 Kings 18:28, introducing Sennacherib's words: 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria.' Now Isaiah uses the same formal structure to introduce God's words, creating a rhetorical contest between the word of the Assyrian king and the word of the God of Israel. God's word, introduced by the prophetic formula, is implicitly asserted as superior.

word_study.meaning: Do not fear, do not be afraid. The phrase is an imperative command to cease or refrain from fear. 'Fear' in this context can mean both emotional anxiety and a deeper sense of dread or deferential submission to a more powerful force.
word_study.significance: The command 'al tira' is the opening word of reassurance, the fundamental consolation offered to someone in crisis. This phrase appears throughout the psalms, in the patriarchal narratives, and in the prophetic books. When God (or God's representative) says 'al tira,' He is asserting that despite appearances, He is in control and the fearful person should trust in Him. In this specific context, Hezekiah should not fear the Rabshakeh's words because God's word is greater. The command addresses the emotional and spiritual crisis directly: the inner terror that the Rabshakeh's taunt has created must be dispelled by the assurance that God stands against Assyria.

word_study.meaning: Words, utterances, matters, things. Can refer to anything from a single utterance to a body of speech or even to events and matters more broadly. In this context, it refers specifically to the Rabshakeh's taunt and threats.
word_study.significance: By calling the Rabshakeh's message merely 'words' (davarim), Isaiah subtly diminishes their power. Words are not reality; they are claims about reality. The Rabshakeh's words claim that God cannot save — but words do not determine reality. God's word, by contrast, carries creative and redemptive power. The contrast between the empty words of the Rabshakeh and the word (davar) of God spoken through Isaiah will be central to the outcome of this crisis.

word_study.transliteration: gadaph (giddefu is third person plural perfect)
word_study.meaning: To blaspheme, revile, taunt, reproach, treat with contempt. Describes speech that shows utter disrespect and contempt for someone or something held sacred. Blasphemy against God is one of the gravest offenses in biblical theology.
word_study.significance: The verb gadaph identifies the Rabshakeh's words as not merely political rhetoric or military threat but as blasphemy — an offense against God's character and majesty. This classification transforms the entire crisis: it is not a military or political problem primarily but a theological one — God's honor has been insulted. God will respond to the blasphemy not because of political calculations but because His very nature has been affronted. God cannot tolerate contempt for His character and power.

word_study.transliteration: na'ar (plural na'arim, na'arei in construct form)
word_study.meaning: Boys, young men, servants, attendants. Can denote actual youth or a subordinate status and role. When applied to high-ranking officials, it emphasizes their status as subordinates to the one who sent them.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering captures a crucial theological move: Isaiah dismisses the Rabshakeh's status by calling him and his companions 'servants/boys' (na'arei) of the king. While the Rabshakeh had presented himself as the authorized voice of the Assyrian king, Isaiah reduces his position to that of a mere servant or subordinate. This is both a rhetorical diminishment and a theological assertion: the true power does not lie with the servants but with the one who sent them, and above all earthly kings stands God.

word_study.meaning: The king of Assyria; in this historical context, Sennacherib, the reigning Assyrian monarch who had conquered most of the Near East and was now threatening Jerusalem.
word_study.significance: By referring to Sennacherib as 'the king of Assyria,' Isaiah formally names the human opponent while simultaneously placing that human power in a subordinate relationship to God. The Assyrian king, for all his might, remains 'the king of Assyria' — a powerful but finite human authority. God is infinitely greater.

cross_references.connection: The parallel account in Isaiah 37 provides the identical message from Isaiah to Hezekiah's servants, confirming the prophetic word across both scriptural narratives.
David's declaration, 'The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?' echoes the same confidence that Isaiah offers to Hezekiah — when God is with you, there is no reason for fear.

Moses establishes the standard for recognizing a true prophet: if his word comes to pass, he speaks for the LORD. Isaiah's prophecy of deliverance will be tested by this standard — and it will be fulfilled.
John's assertion that 'perfect love casteth out fear' resonates with Isaiah's command 'Be not afraid,' indicating that trust in God's power and character is the antidote to fear.

The immediate outcome of Isaiah's prophecy: 'And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the LORD went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians.' Isaiah's word of reassurance is immediately validated by God's action.

The king of the Lamanites, upon conversion, declares his trust in God despite his fears: 'Now if thou believest this we can come unto him' — expressing the same movement from fear to faith that Isaiah calls Hezekiah to make.

commentary.historical_context: The prophetic message formula 'Thus saith the LORD' was distinctive to Hebrew prophecy and set it apart from other forms of religious mediation in the ancient Near East. While Assyrian, Egyptian, and Hittite priests might perform divinations or read omens, the Hebrew prophet made an explicit claim to direct divine speech. This claim was either true or it was blasphemy — there was no middle ground. Isaiah's use of the formula at this critical moment affirms that God has not been silent and will not allow His name to be blasphemed without response. The reduction of the Rabshakeh to the status of 'servants' (na'arei) reflects actual hierarchical relationships in the ancient Near Eastern court: the Rabshakeh was indeed a high-ranking official, but he was still subordinate to Sennacherib and received his authority from the king. Isaiah's point is that even the most powerful human authority pales in comparison to God. The concept of blasphemy (gadaph) against God was serious in Near Eastern cultures, but particularly in Israel, where God's character and power were central to the covenant community's identity. An insult to God's power was understood as an insult to the very foundations of the covenant people's existence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Helaman 12:1-3, the people of Nephi 'remembered God' and were able to 'overcome their enemies' through faith, demonstrating the same principle Isaiah teaches: when fear is replaced by faith in God, the apparent strength of enemies is overcome. In 1 Nephi 15:11, Nephi encourages his brothers not to be 'hardhearted' but to 'believe in the Lord thy Redeemer, and in the redemption which is made for thee through his Son. Ye shall have joy and gladness instead of your sorrows.' This is the same message — replace fear with faith in God's power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 54:10 declares, 'Therefore, be faithful; stand in the office which I have appointed unto you; succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees,' teaching that faith and steadfastness in righteousness are the answer to fear and threat. Similarly, D&C 6:36 states, 'Fear not, for I am with thee,' echoing Isaiah's command and affirming that the presence of God through His servants dispels fear.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Isaiah's message that Hezekiah need not fear the Rabshakeh's words points toward the temple as the place where one stands in God's presence and receives reassurance from God. In temple covenants, members make promises to the Lord and receive promises from Him regarding protection and safety — promises that rest on God's character, not on earthly might. The temple becomes the place where fear of worldly powers is replaced by trust in God's covenant promises.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's word of reassurance — 'Be not afraid, for I am with you' — prefigures Christ's recurring message to His disciples, particularly in Matthew 28:20, where the Risen Christ promises, 'I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.' Just as Isaiah assures Hezekiah that God will respond to blasphemy against His character, Christ's resurrection is the ultimate vindication of God's power against those who would mock or deny it. Isaiah's identification of the Rabshakeh's words as blasphemy against God (oti, 'against me') foreshadows how the crucifixion of Christ is ultimately an offense against God, not merely against a human being, and how God's resurrection of Christ is His vindication and response to that offense. Additionally, Isaiah's role as prophet who speaks God's word directly prefigures Christ as the Word of God (logos) — the ultimate and final prophet through whom God speaks.

text_kjv: Behold, I will send a blast upon him, and he shall hear a rumour, and shall return to his own land; and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land.

commentary.narrative: This verse contains God's direct promise to Hezekiah through Isaiah, and it is remarkable for its precision and specificity. Rather than a dramatic military reversal on the battlefield, God announces a two-part strategy: first, He will place a spirit (disposition, impulse) in Sennacherib that will cause him to hear a report and withdraw to Assyria; second, He will orchestrate Sennacherib's assassination in his own homeland. The promise is not about Jerusalem's armies defeating the Assyrian forces—it is about God directly intervening in the heart and fate of the Assyrian king himself. This shifts the entire narrative away from military logistics and into the realm of divine providence working through seemingly natural events (rumors, internal politics, assassination).

word_study.meaning: Wind, breath, spirit, disposition, impulse. Here it refers not to a supernatural force but to an inner inclination or emotional state that God plants within Sennacherib. The Covenant Rendering clarifies this as God putting a disposition in him—an internal motivation he will experience as his own.
word_study.significance: The word ruach appears throughout scripture to describe both God's Spirit and human states of mind. In this context, God is not possessing Sennacherib but rather influencing his internal disposition in a way consistent with human agency and natural causation. This reflects the Old Testament's subtle theology of divine action working through human psychology.

word_study.meaning: Report, rumor, news. A word that emphasizes the act of hearing and the transmission of information rather than verified fact.
word_study.significance: The specific report Sennacherib hears (likely about Tirhakah's advance, mentioned in v. 9) becomes the vehicle for God's will. God uses natural political intelligence to redirect the Assyrian king's attention and priorities, demonstrating that divine action and natural causation are not mutually exclusive.

word_study.meaning: To cause to fall, to strike down, to defeat. The hiphil form makes clear that God is the active agent—He will cause Sennacherib to fall by the sword.
word_study.significance: This is not a passive death but one caused by God's direct intervention. The hiphil intensifies the promise: God Himself will bring about Sennacherib's downfall, fulfilling the word spoken here in verse 37 when Sennacherib is assassinated by his own sons.

cross_references.connection: The fulfillment of this promise: the Angel of the Lord destroys the Assyrian army, and Sennacherib returns to Nineveh where his own sons assassinate him by the sword.
Isaiah's parallel account of the same prophecy, showing the unity of the promise across both accounts of this event.
A thematic parallel on the futility of military might without God: 'No king is saved by the multitude of an host...our soul waiteth for the LORD.'
The principle underlying this verse: 'The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.'

commentary.historical_context: Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign against Judah is well documented in Assyrian records, though Assyrian sources describe a different outcome than the biblical account. The report Sennacherib hears is historically credible: Tirhakah's Cushite/Egyptian forces were indeed advancing northward, and this threat would have forced Sennacherib to reassess his campaign. Ancient Near Eastern military strategy often involved rapid reassessment when a second front opened. The specific assassination of Sennacherib by his sons occurred in 681 BCE, some twenty years later, but the theological point is that God had already announced this outcome. The mention of a 'spirit' reflects the ancient understanding that impulses and decisions came from both human agency and divine influence—not as competing explanations but as complementary layers of causation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 17, Nephi describes how God can soften hearts and redirect even hostile actors, much as God redirects Sennacherib's disposition here. The principle that God influences human hearts and circumstances is central to Book of Mormon theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:14 speaks of God's power to 'gather his own elect from his own.' The concept of God's direct intervention in human affairs and the certainty of His word being fulfilled underlies much of Doctrine and Covenants revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The principle of covenant protection—that those in covenant with God are ultimately safe despite external threats—is foundational to temple theology. Hezekiah's trust in God's word prefigures the faith required of covenant members.

commentary.christological_typology: Sennacherib's threatened destruction of God's people and their city prefigures the later threat of Satan and worldly powers against the covenant people of God. The manner of deliverance—through God's direct intervention and promise rather than human military might—points to Christ's ultimate triumph over death and sin, which comes not through worldly power but through divine authority. Hezekiah's trust in God's word in the face of overwhelming odds mirrors the faith required to believe in Christ's redemptive work.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that when we are in covenant relationship with God, we need not rely on our own resources or strength. The promise here is not that our circumstances will immediately reverse but that God has a plan we cannot yet see—and that plan will be fulfilled. For modern Latter-day Saints facing seemingly insurmountable challenges, the message is to trust in God's word as spoken through living prophets and to understand that divine intervention often works through apparently natural causes (a 'rumor' that causes a shift in perspective). Our responsibility is faith; God's responsibility is fulfillment.

text_kjv: So Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah: for he had heard that he was departed from Lachish.

commentary.narrative: While Isaiah is delivering God's promise of deliverance to Hezekiah, the narrative perspective shifts to show Sennacherib's military operations continuing in real time. The Rabshakeh (the Assyrian commander who had delivered the threats at Jerusalem's walls in chapter 18) returns from his propaganda mission at Jerusalem only to discover that the king has moved on to a new siege target: Libnah. This verse emphasizes the relentless, methodical nature of the Assyrian campaign. Sennacherib does not wait for Jerusalem's capitulation; he prosecutes multiple sieges simultaneously, moving his forces to maximize pressure on Judah's fortified cities. The verse thus provides a reality check: even as God is promising deliverance, the Assyrian war machine is still grinding forward, still demolishing Judah's cities.

word_study.meaning: And he returned, turned back, came back. The verb shiv/shuv indicates a change of location or direction.
word_study.significance: The Rabshakeh's return from Jerusalem marks his failure to secure the city's surrender through intimidation. He must report back to his king, only to find Sennacherib has not waited—the campaign continues without him.

word_study.meaning: To fight, to wage war, to battle. The participle form suggests ongoing, continuous action.
word_study.significance: The present tense emphasizes that Sennacherib's military operations are ongoing and relentless. There is no pause, no hesitation. Even as diplomatic pressure fails at Jerusalem, military pressure continues elsewhere.

word_study.meaning: Heard/learned and departed/moved away. The word nasa suggests not a forced retreat but a deliberate military redeployment.
word_study.significance: Sennacherib heard news of the situation at Lachish and made a strategic decision to move his forces. This parallels how Sennacherib himself will later 'hear' the report that causes him to withdraw (v. 7), showing a literary symmetry in how information drives decisions.

cross_references.connection: The earlier siege of Lachish, where Hezekiah initially paid tribute to try to appease Sennacherib, though the Assyrian king broke the agreement and continued the campaign.
The parallel account emphasizing Sennacherib's systematic siege campaign against the fortified cities of Judah while his forces surround Jerusalem.
Libnah appears in Joshua's conquest narrative, showing it was one of the major fortified cities of Judah that had long strategic importance.

commentary.historical_context: Libnah was located in the Judahite lowlands (the Shephelah) near Lachish, in a region of rolling hills and agricultural valleys. Sennacherib's inscription (the Taylor Prism) details his siege campaign against multiple Judahite cities. Archaeological evidence from this period shows systematic destruction of Judahite fortified cities. The movement from Lachish to Libnah represents standard Assyrian military doctrine: maintain pressure across multiple fronts, prevent the enemy from concentrating forces, and systematically reduce each fortified position. The Rabshakeh's return to find the king elsewhere underscores the efficiency of the Assyrian command structure and the scope of operations—there is no single point of decision but a coordinated, multi-pronged campaign.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 43-44, the Nephite general Moroni conducts defensive campaigns using strategic military positioning and coordination, showing that skillful military strategy (even when defensive) reflects divine principles of order and preparation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:37 counsels that those who refuse to hear God's word will face consequences. Sennacherib's refusal to hear God's message through Hezekiah sets the stage for his own downfall despite his military success.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant people of God are often surrounded by hostile forces (enemies of the covenant). The temple represents the safe haven—the place where God's presence is, even when external enemies are powerful.

commentary.christological_typology: Sennacherib's relentless siege against Judah's cities prefigures the ongoing spiritual warfare against God's people. Yet just as Sennacherib's military might does not ultimately prevail, neither do the powers of evil ultimately prevail against Christ and His Church. The verse shows the world's machinery operating at full capacity, yet that machinery will ultimately be overruled by God's purposes.
commentary.application: This verse reminds us that the world's opposition to God's people is systematic, coordinated, and relentless. We should not be surprised when challenges come from multiple directions or when opposition is persistent. However, the verse also shows that God is not ignoring these threats—He is actively directing history even as worldly powers pursue their goals. For us, this means maintaining faith in God's promises even while we see opposition intensify, understanding that God works through all circumstances to accomplish His purposes.

text_kjv: And when he heard say of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, Behold, he is come out to fight against thee: he sent messengers again unto Hezekiah, saying,

commentary.narrative: This verse marks the crucial turning point in the narrative. Sennacherib receives intelligence that Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia (Cush), has advanced northward with military forces. This is the external threat that causes Sennacherib to intensify his pressure on Jerusalem before he must turn south to meet this new challenge. Rather than withdraw immediately, Sennacherib makes a final diplomatic push to secure Jerusalem's surrender, sending messengers again to Hezekiah (the word 'again' recalls his previous emissary, the Rabshakeh). The timing is psychologically strategic: Sennacherib wants to present Hezekiah with a stark choice—surrender now, or face both the Assyrian army and be trapped between the Assyrians and the approaching Egyptian/Cushite forces. This verse reveals Sennacherib's underlying weakness: he cannot simultaneously prosecute the siege of Jerusalem and march south to confront Tirhakah. The approach of Tirhakah is the external catalyst that makes God's promise in verse 7 about to come true.

word_study.meaning: To hear, to receive information (yishma) and to say/report (lemor). The construction emphasizes the receiving of a report or intelligence.
word_study.significance: The same root shama (hear) that God will use to cause Sennacherib to hear a report (v. 7) here describes how Sennacherib learns of Tirhakah's advance. God's promise will work through the very natural process of military intelligence reaching the Assyrian king.

word_study.meaning: Tirhakah (Egyptian Taharka) was a ruler associated with Egypt's 25th Dynasty from the south (Cush/Nubia). Ethiopia/Cush referred to the region south of Egypt, in Nubia.
word_study.significance: Tirhakah became Pharaoh around 690 BCE, but this account dates to 701 BCE. Some scholars suggest either an anachronistic title in the text, a second campaign, or that Tirhakah held a military position before becoming pharaoh. Regardless, his advance represents a serious military threat from Egypt's southern ally.

word_study.meaning: To go forth, to come out, to engage in battle. Yatsa emphasizes taking an active military stance; hilcham means to wage war.
word_study.significance: Tirhakah is not merely approaching but actively preparing for battle. This is a military threat that demands Sennacherib's immediate strategic response.

cross_references.connection: The fulfillment of God's promise: Sennacherib hears a report (the news of Tirhakah's advance) and this becomes the catalyst for his withdrawal.
Isaiah's parallel account of the same report about Tirhakah, confirming the historical unity of these accounts.
An earlier example of Egyptian forces threatening Judah under Shishak, showing the recurring pattern of pressure from Egypt and the south.
A later prophecy about the fall of Nineveh (Assyria's capital) using the fate of No-Amon (Egyptian Thebes) as a comparison, showing Assyrian awareness of Egyptian military power.

commentary.historical_context: The advance of an Egyptian or Nubian force northward was a known pattern in ancient Near Eastern geopolitics. Egypt periodically reasserted influence in Syria-Palestine to counter Assyrian expansion.
