commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, a prophet was understood as a conduit for divine speech, not as an independent interpreter. Once a prophet had delivered a divine word, that word was considered binding—it would come to pass. The idea that a prophet might deliver one word and then, immediately, deliver a contradictory word would have been shocking to ancient audiences. Yet the Old Testament records such reversals, and they are understood not as a contradiction of prophecy but as a demonstration of God's sovereignty over prophecy itself. God's words are not merely predictions of inevitable futures but declarations of God's will in response to human and divine circumstances. The palace architecture referenced here (middle court, inner court) is attested in Iron Age palaces in the Levant and helps situate the narrative in a realistic historical setting. The protocol of a prophet approaching the king, delivering a message, and potentially receiving a new message before even leaving the premises reflects the understood relationship between prophets and royalty in the ancient Levantine kingdom.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 42, Alma teaches that mercy cannot rob justice—yet this passage illustrates that prayer and faithfulness can alter the conditions under which justice operates. In the Book of Mormon, prophets frequently receive new revelations that adjust or expand previous understandings (e.g., Nephi receiving new understanding about the vision of the tree of life, or Mormon's editorial comments that clarify or expand earlier accounts).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 56:4 declares that 'the rebellious shall be appointed to their own place'—suggesting that divine decrees take into account human response. D&C 82:10 teaches the principle 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise,' indicating that God's covenantal commitments are responsive to human obedience. D&C 93:31 teaches that 'all truth is independent in that sphere in which God has placed it,' suggesting that prophecy operates within the sphere of human agency and can adjust to human response within God's sovereign purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the concept of covenant is not merely one-directional (God dictates, human obeys) but dialogical (both parties respond to each other in binding relationship). God's immediate reversal of the death sentence in response to Hezekiah's prayer exemplifies the responsiveness of God to covenantal partners. The temple is the place where this covenantal dialogue is most fully enacted.

commentary.christological_typology: God's willingness to hear prayer and alter the course declared through a prophet anticipates Christ's intercessory prayer. Just as Isaiah's first word was a word of judgment that was then overturned through prayer, Christ's work as High Priest involves intercession that brings about outcomes different from what human judgment alone would determine. Hebrews 7:25 teaches that Christ 'ever liveth to make intercession' for those who 'come unto God by him.' In both cases—Hezekiah's prayer intercepting a death sentence, and Christ's intercession intercepting humanity's condemnation—prayer and faithfulness alter judgments that seemed final.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse teaches that prayer is not futile, even when circumstances seem final. The very fact that God responds to Hezekiah's prayer before Isaiah can even complete his departure from the palace suggests that God is attentive to sincere supplication and that divine decrees are not necessarily immutable when they pertain to responsive creatures. This does not mean that every prayer will receive the specific outcome requested, but it establishes that prayer is heard, that it matters, and that it can genuinely affect outcomes. The implication is that believers should persist in prayer even when circumstances seem dire, and should not assume that a difficult initial answer (in Hezekiah's case, the death sentence) is the final answer. God's willingness to speak a new word suggests that faithful, earnest prayer can prompt divine response. Additionally, the detail about Isaiah not yet departing the palace suggests that God acts with what we might call 'divine attentiveness'—God is not absent or negligent but present and responsive in the midst of human crisis.

text_kjv: Turn again, and tell Hezekiah the captain of my people, Thus saith the LORD, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will heal thee: on the third day thou shalt go up unto the house of the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
God's word to Isaiah contains four major elements, each theologically significant. First, God identifies Hezekiah not by his name alone but by his role: 'the captain of my people' (negid ammi)—a title that emphasizes Hezekiah's position as God's appointed leader and his relationship to God as His people's steward. This is not a title of distance but of intimacy; it is what a sovereign calls a trusted subordinate in a relationship of mutual regard. Second, God identifies Himself not merely as 'the LORD' but as 'the God of David thy father'—anchoring the promise in the Davidic covenant, reminding Hezekiah that his kingship, like David's, is grounded in God's covenantal commitment to his dynasty. Third, God makes a remarkable declaration: 'I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears.' These are not metaphorical phrases but a statement of God's attentiveness. The God who is beyond all creatures nonetheless perceives the details of a man's prayer and weeping. Fourth, God makes specific promises: healing, return to the Temple on the third day.

The 'third day' reference deserves attention. It is not merely a timeframe but a symbolic marker. In biblical symbolism, the third day often marks renewal, resurrection, and divine restoration (Hosea 6:2 speaks of rising 'in the third day'; the Gospels record Christ's resurrection 'on the third day'). Hezekiah will move from his deathbed to the Temple—from the isolation of private suffering to the public place of covenant renewal and thanksgiving. The healing is thus not merely physical restoration but a reintegration into the community of faith and the covenant relationship that his illness had temporarily severed. This is why the movement to the Temple is mentioned in the same breath as the healing promise—they are aspects of a single restoration. God is not merely curing Hezekiah's body but restoring his full life as a king, a father, a covenant partner, and a worshiper.

word_study.meaning: Return, turn back, go back. Shuv is a fundamental biblical word indicating reversal of direction, repentance, or renewed orientation.
word_study.significance: God commands Isaiah to return—to go back to Hezekiah with the new word. Structurally, this reverses Isaiah's outward movement toward the palace door, turning him back to the dying king's chamber. The word also echoes the idea of repentance/return (teshuva), suggesting that the entire interaction involves a turning or reversal of outcomes.

word_study.meaning: Leader, prince, or captain of my people. Negid is derived from a root meaning to lead, to go before, or to rule. It emphasizes the leader's responsibility to guide and protect those under their authority.
word_study.significance: This is a title of honor and relationship. God does not address Hezekiah as merely 'king' but as 'leader of my people,' emphasizing that the relationship between God and the king is mediated through the king's responsibility to God's people. Hezekiah is not a autonomous ruler but a steward accountable to God.

word_study.term_english: the God of David thy father
word_study.meaning: The God of David your father. This is an invocation of covenant continuity. The God who was with David is with Hezekiah. The phrase emphasizes that Hezekiah stands in the line of David and that the covenantal promises made to David extend to him.
word_study.significance: By invoking the Davidic covenant, God is signaling that Hezekiah's kingdom is not merely his personal rule but part of a larger divine plan centered on David's dynasty. The healing of Hezekiah is thus a confirmation of the Davidic covenant, not merely a private mercy.

word_study.meaning: I have heard your prayer. Shamati (I heard) is the perfective form, indicating completed action. Tefillatekha (your prayer) invokes the same root palal used of prayer as intercession.
word_study.significance: God testifies that he has heard Hezekiah's prayer. This is not a vague promise ('prayers are always heard') but a specific affirmation that this particular prayer has reached God and has been given divine attention. The use of 'heard' rather than 'granted' allows for a distinction: God heard the prayer and has responded with judgment based on what he perceived in that prayer.

word_study.meaning: I have seen your tears. Ra'iti (I saw) is the perfective form. Dim'atekha (your tears) is the plural form of dim'a (tear), indicating that God has observed Hezekiah's weeping.
word_study.significance: God's perception extends beyond words to emotional expression. The tears that accompanied Hezekiah's prayer are themselves 'seen' by God—they are part of the prayer, not incidental to it. This teaches that God perceives the whole person—mind, will, and emotion—in prayer.

word_study.meaning: Behold, I am healing you / I will heal you. Hinneni (behold me, I am here) is a self-presentation formula used when God announces divine action. Rofe (healer, I heal) is from the root rapa, to heal or restore.
word_study.significance: The use of 'hinneni' ('behold I am') marks this as a moment of divine presence and action. God is not merely promising future healing but announcing present engagement—'I am healing you.' The verb rofe, though translated as future, has the force of a present reality entering the world through God's declaration.

word_study.term_english: on the third day thou shalt go up unto the house of the LORD
word_study.term_original: בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי תַּעֲלֶה בֵּית יְהוָה (bayyom hashelishi ta'aleh beit YHWH)
word_study.meaning: On the third day you will go up to the house of the LORD. Bayyom hashelishi (on the third day) is a specific timeframe. Ta'aleh (you will go up) uses the verb 'alah (to ascend, to go up), which is the specific term for moving toward the Temple in Jerusalem. Beit YHWH (house of the LORD) is the Temple.
word_study.significance: The 'third day' motif appears elsewhere in Scripture as a marker of divine restoration (Hosea 6:2). For Hezekiah, movement to the Temple represents reintegration into covenant community and renewed worship. The verb 'alah (to ascend) has both physical and spiritual significance—it is the precise term used for pilgrimage and for movement toward God. This is not merely recovery of health but restoration of Hezekiah's entire role as a worshiping king.

cross_references.connection: The Davidic covenant, which God invokes here through Hezekiah, promises perpetual dynasty and God's steadfast love; God's healing of Hezekiah confirms this covenant is still operative.
A prayer expressing desire to 'dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life'; Hezekiah's promise to ascend to the Temple connects his healing to renewed covenant relationship and worship.

A prophecy stating 'After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight'; the 'third day' motif here carries connotations of resurrection and divine restoration.

God reminds Israel that he has 'borne you on eagles' wings and brought you unto myself'; God's declaration of being with Hezekiah and hearing his prayer echoes the intimate covenantal language God uses with all his covenant people.

A psalm expressing longing for the house of the LORD; Hezekiah's ascent to the Temple on the third day will fulfill this longing—restored physical and spiritual vitality bringing him back to the place of God's dwelling.

commentary.historical_context: The third-day motif in ancient Near Eastern religious thought often marked a turning point or moment of transformation. In Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts, the third day frequently appears as a significant marker (resurrection, restoration, or divine action). The Temple in Jerusalem, while not yet fully developed as the complex structure it would become in later periods, was the center of covenant relationship for Judah and the place where kings offered sacrifice and received divine blessing. The promise that Hezekiah would ascend to the Temple three days after receiving his death sentence would have been understood both as a physical healing (to be strong enough to travel) and as a spiritual restoration (to be acceptable before God in the Temple). The language of 'ascending' to the Temple uses a verb ('alah) that carries the sense of upward movement, connecting physical ascent to Jerusalem's higher elevation and spiritual ascent toward God's presence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of hearing and seeing on God's part appears in Book of Mormon accounts. In 1 Nephi 11:5-6, Nephi describes how 'the Spirit said unto me: What seekest thou?' and later, 'And I beheld that he looked upon the children of men, and he weepeth.' God's attentiveness to seeing and hearing is a recurring theme. Also, the Book of Mormon emphasizes that covenant members have direct access to God's presence and hearing—a principle illustrated here in Hezekiah's case.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:1 records the Lord saying 'Hearken, O ye people of my church... hear the voice of Jesus Christ.' The principle that God hears and sees those who call upon him is central to Doctrine and Covenants. D&C 88:63 teaches that 'prayer is the act by which the volition of the Father and the volition of the child are brought into correspondence with each other.' Hezekiah's prayer has brought his will and God's will into alignment, resulting in divine action. D&C 130:3 teaches that the Holy Ghost 'is not a personage of flesh and bones; but is a person, and is the Holy Ghost,' yet it can perceive and respond to human prayer—similar to how the God of Hezekiah perceives and responds.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The promise that Hezekiah will 'go up unto the house of the LORD' on the third day connects healing with temple worship and covenant renewal. In temple theology, going up to the Temple represents movement from the profane world to sacred space, from separation to communion with God. The healing itself prepares Hezekiah to make this ascent. The third day may also echo the three degrees of glory or three levels of temple endowment, suggesting that restoration is not merely physical but involves all levels of existence.

commentary.christological_typology: Hezekiah's restoration through prayer and divine healing, culminating in his ascent to the Temple on the third day, prefigures Christ's resurrection on the third day and his ascent to his Father's house. Both involve: (1) death approaching; (2) prayer and tears; (3) divine reversal through God's action; (4) restoration on the third day; (5) movement toward the Father's house. In Hezekiah's case, it is a temporary reprieve from mortality; in Christ's case, it is the definitive conquest of death. Yet the pattern is the same: prayer, divine response, third-day restoration, ascent to God's house. Additionally, God's statement 'I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears' will later be directed toward humanity through Christ, who intercedes for us and presents our prayers and tears before the Father.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse contains several applications. First, it teaches that God actively perceives both words and tears—both rational prayer and emotional expression are seen by God and matter in his response. Second, it affirms that God identifies covenant members by their role in His purposes, not merely by their personal status. Hezekiah is called 'the captain of my people,' reminding him (and us) that our callings and responsibilities are part of our identity before God. Third, the promise to 'go up unto the house of the LORD' suggests that true healing involves not merely physical recovery but return to covenant community and renewed worship. Fourth, the invocation of 'the God of David thy father' teaches that we are connected to the lineage of covenant—to those who have gone before us in faith. Our prayers are heard in continuity with the prayers of the faithful in all generations. Finally, the third-day timeframe suggests that divine restoration happens within a comprehensible human timeframe—not instant, but not indefinitely delayed. We are to trust that God acts, and acts with an eye toward our ultimate return to His presence.

text_kjv: And I will add unto thy days fifteen years; and I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria; and I will defend this city for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake.

commentary.narrative:
God's promise moves from Hezekiah's personal healing to a comprehensive guarantee involving three dimensions: personal longevity, personal and national deliverance, and corporate protection. The 'fifteen years' is a precise, generous extension of life—not merely a reprieve of a few days or months, but a substantial period that will allow Hezekiah to rule, father children (which will be important to the succession), and see the fulfillment of his reforms. The second promise—deliverance 'out of the hand of the king of Assyria'—addresses the existential threat to Judah. While the Assyrians have already been turned back from Jerusalem's walls (in chapter 19), the threat remains. Hezekiah faces not merely personal death but the possibility of national destruction or vassalage. God promises both. The third promise—'I will defend this city for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake'—moves from the immediate political threat to a permanent commitment to Jerusalem's protection.

The structure of God's promises is important. Personal healing and national deliverance are intertwined—Hezekiah's life is not merely his own, but it is bound up with Jerusalem's fate. A king who dies demoralized or in despair can lead a nation to collapse; a king restored to health and confidence can lead a people to renewed trust in God. Conversely, national deliverance serves Hezekiah's personal purposes—he will have a kingdom to rule, a people to shepherd, a future to build. The double motivation at the end—'for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake'—anchors the promise both in God's character (His own sake, His own purposes) and in the covenantal relationship (David's sake, the covenant made with David generations earlier). God is not protecting Jerusalem because Hezekiah deserves it, but because God has committed Himself to the David covenant. Hezekiah is the beneficiary of that covenant relationship, but he is not its founder or its sole grounds. This teaches a profound truth: covenant loyalty extends across generations; a nation benefits from the faithfulness of its ancestors; we are held in God's covenantal care because of the commitments He made long ago to our spiritual forebears.

word_study.meaning: I will add to your days. Hosafti is the perfective form ('I will add'), from the root yasaf (to add, to continue, to supplement). Yamekha (your days) is the plural of yom (day), used collectively to refer to the span of one's life.
word_study.significance: The verb 'to add' suggests that Hezekiah's life span is not merely extended but accumulated—the new years are added to what has already been lived. This is not a rewriting of history but a continuation of the narrative. Hezekiah's original lifespan was incomplete; now it is being completed.

word_study.meaning: Fifteen years. Chamesh (five) and esreh (ten) combine to form fifteen. Shanah (year) is the standard unit of temporal measurement.
word_study.significance: The number fifteen is specific and substantial. It is enough time for a king to bear children (important for succession), to govern, to see the effects of his policies, and to establish a legacy. Historically, fifteen years would place Hezekiah's death around 686 BCE, which aligns with external historical sources. The precision of the number suggests that God's promises are not vague but definite—this is not 'some more time' but exactly fifteen years.

word_study.term_original: אַצִּילְךָ וְאֵת הָעִיר הַזֹּאת (atzilkha ve-et ha-ir hazot)
word_study.meaning: I will deliver/rescue you and this city. Atzil (from the root tzul, to deliver or save) is a strong verb indicating rescue from danger. Ha-ir hazot (this city) is Jerusalem, identified by the demonstrative 'this' (implying immediate, intimate familiarity).
word_study.significance: The verb 'deliver' is used in Psalm 22 of God's deliverance of the righteous from death. Here it serves both literally (protection from Assyrian invasion) and typologically (rescue from mortality). The coupling of 'you' and 'this city' reminds us that the king's fate and the city's fate are bound together.

word_study.term_english: out of the hand of the king of Assyria
word_study.meaning: Out of the hand (palm) of the king of Assyria. Kaf (palm, hand) is a synecdoche for power and control—to be in someone's 'hand' is to be under their power. Melekh Ashshur (king of Assyria) is the historical Assyrian empire, the dominant power of the era.
word_study.significance: The language emphasizes that Assyrian power is real and threatening—the 'hand' of the king is strong and grasping. Yet God promises to snatch Hezekiah and Jerusalem from that grasp. This is not a promise of weakness from Assyria but of God's superior power.

word_study.term_original: וְגַנּוֹתִי עַל־הָעִיר הַזֹּאת (veganoti al ha-ir hazot)
word_study.meaning: I will shield / defend this city. Ganiti (from the root gan, to shield or protect) conveys the image of a protective covering, like a shield covering a soldier. Al (over, upon) suggests the shield is placed over the city.
word_study.significance: The verb 'to shield' is more comprehensive and ongoing than 'to deliver.' Deliverance is a rescue from a specific threat; shielding is a continuous protection. God promises not merely to rescue Jerusalem from the current Assyrian threat but to maintain protective cover over the city going forward.

word_study.term_english: for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake
word_study.term_original: לְמַעֲנִי וּלְמַעַן דָּוִד עַבְדִּי (lema'ani ulma'an David avdi)
word_study.meaning: For my sake and for the sake of David my servant. Lema'ani (for my sake, for the sake of my purposes) invokes God's own character and purposes. Lama'an David avdi (for the sake of David my servant) invokes the covenantal relationship established with David and his line. Avdi (my servant) emphasizes David's role as God's chosen and loyal one.
word_study.significance: The double motivation teaches that God acts both for His own sake (consistency with His character and purposes) and for the covenant's sake (loyalty to His commitments made long before Hezekiah's time). This is a profound theological principle: we are beneficiaries of covenants we did not negotiate and promises made to our ancestors. God's commitment to David carries forward to David's descendants.

cross_references.connection: God's covenant with David, promising perpetual dynasty and God's protection of his line; verse 6 explicitly invokes 'my servant David's sake,' anchoring Hezekiah's deliverance in the Davidic covenant.

An earlier promise to Hezekiah regarding Assyrian deliverance: 'I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake.' Verse 6 repeats this promise verbatim, confirming its constancy.
The parallel account in Isaiah of the same Assyrian deliverance promise, with identical language about God defending the city 'for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake.'

A meditation on the Davidic covenant, emphasizing God's oath to David and the perpetual nature of His commitment to David's house; Hezekiah's fifteen-year reprieve is part of the fulfillment of that oath.

God's covenant with Abraham, the foundational covenant of Israel, in which God promises blessing to Abraham and his descendants; the principle that later generations benefit from ancestral covenants is established in Genesis and exemplified in Hezekiah's case.

commentary.historical_context: Hezekiah's reign (715-686 BCE approximately) did extend roughly fifteen years after his illness, according to both biblical and external historical sources. The Assyrian threat under Sennacherib is well-documented in Assyrian records and in the biblical account (2 Kings 18-19, Isaiah 36-37). The promise of protection for Jerusalem proved historically accurate—Jerusalem was not captured by Assyria during Hezekiah's reign or immediately after, though other Judean cities were devastated. The theological interpretation of this historical event—that it represented God's specific intervention on behalf of His covenant city—was the understanding shared by Isaiah, Hezekiah, and the Judean leadership. The doubling of the promise ('for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake') reflects ancient Near Eastern political practice, where a suzerain (powerful overlord) would justify protection of a vassal state both on grounds of the suzerain's own interests and on grounds of prior covenantal commitment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon teaches that God protects His covenant people based on their faithfulness and on covenants made with their ancestors. In 2 Nephi 10:10-15, Jacob teaches how the Nephites will be protected 'inasmuch as they shall keep my commandments,' echoing the principle that protection is covenantal and conditional. Yet the phrase 'for my servant David's sake' teaches that benefits accrue to later generations because of the faithfulness of their ancestors—a principle explored in Mosiah 7:18-19 regarding the blessings on the people of Limhi based on the righteousness of their fathers.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 82:10 teaches the principle 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' Yet D&C also emphasizes that God's covenants with previous generations create a protective framework for later generations (D&C 45:9-14 regarding the gathering of Israel). The fifteen-year extension is specific—not indefinite, not magical, but a precise span in which Hezekiah can fulfill his purposes. D&C 132:7 teaches that 'All covenants, contracts, bonds, obligations, oaths, vows... must be done in his name' and under his authority—and God's commitment to David's covenant is being re-activated through Hezekiah.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the relationship between king and God is covenantal and is renewed through temple worship and sacrifice. Hezekiah's reign saw significant temple restoration and worship renewal (see 2 Chronicles 29-31). The promise in verse 6 to defend the city is tied to the promise in verse 5 that Hezekiah will 'go up unto the house of the LORD'—worship and deliverance are connected. The temple is the place where the covenant relationship is performed and renewed. The Davidic covenant, invoked here, is the foundation for the temple itself—it is because of the covenant with David that the temple becomes the center of Israel's worship and covenant renewal.

commentary.christological_typology: The promise of fifteen years of additional life, coupled with deliverance from national enemies, prefigures Christ's redemptive work. While Hezekiah receives a temporary reprieve from death through God's specific intervention, Christ's resurrection represents the definitive defeat of death and the promise of eternal life to all covenant believers. The language of 'deliverance out of the hand' of enemies connects to Christ's deliverance of humanity from the dominion of Satan and death. The twofold motivation—'for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake'—reflects Christ's work as both the fulfillment of God's own purposes (the redemption of humanity, the glory of God) and the fulfillment of the Davidic covenant (Christ as the ultimate son of David, the king eternal). God's shielding of Jerusalem 'for David's sake' becomes, in the New Testament, God's protection of the Church 'for Christ's sake' (Ephesians 1:7: 'redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace').
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 6 contains several crucial principles. First, it teaches that God's promises are specific and time-bounded—Hezekiah does not receive eternal life, but fifteen years. This reflects the reality of mortality: even those who receive healing and divine favor eventually face death. The fifteen years are a gift, not a reversal of the human condition. Second, it teaches that personal deliverance and community deliverance are interconnected. Hezekiah's healing matters because he is a leader responsible for a people; his continued life will benefit the nation. Conversely, national stability is necessary for personal flourishing. This suggests that our personal concerns and our community's welfare are not separate—we pray for both, and God's purposes encompass both. Third, the invocation of 'David's sake' teaches that we benefit from covenants made before we were born. Our parents, ancestors, and spiritual forebears made covenants with God; we inherit both the benefits and the obligations of those covenants. We are not spiritual orphans but heirs of a covenant lineage. Finally, the promise that God will 'defend this city' teaches that God's protection is ongoing and comprehensive. God is not merely a responder to crisis but a consistent guardian. Trust in God means believing that we are continuously shielded by God's purposeful care, both for God's own sake (out of God's character) and for the sake of the covenants God has made with our spiritual lineage.

text_kjv: And Hezekiah hearkened unto them, and shewed them all the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a pivot point in Hezekiah's life that will reverberate across generations. The Babylonian envoys have arrived ostensibly to congratulate him on his recovery from illness (2 Kings 20:12), and Hezekiah, perhaps flattered or seeking to demonstrate Judah's strength and divine blessing, grants them unfettered access to his treasury. The narrator's emphasis on totality—nothing was hidden, everything was displayed—is not incidental. By using the phrase 'there was nothing...that Hezekiah shewed them not,' the text constructs this moment as an exhaustive inventory of what will later become plunder.

The Covenant Rendering clarifies that Hezekiah 'welcomed' the envoys (vayyishma 'aleihem), suggesting genuine hospitality and receptivity rather than suspicion or caution. We are not told his motivation. Was this diplomatic savvy—building an alliance against Assyria? Was it vanity—displaying the wealth that God's blessing had granted? Was it naiveté—failing to recognize the threat posed by a rising eastern power? The narrator's silence on motive is devastating because it forces readers to reckon with the ambiguity that defines much of Hezekiah's reign: a king of genuine faith whose political choices would have consequences extending far beyond his lifetime.

Each item Hezekiah displays—silver, gold, spices, fine oil, weapons, stores—will reappear by name in Isaiah's judgment prophecy (verse 17). The display is not merely hospitality; it is a prophetic catalog of future loss. The double negation ('nothing...that he did not show') emphasizes that the loss, when it comes, will be equally comprehensive.

word_study.meaning: To hear, listen, obey, or receive. The term carries the sense of receptive attention and willingness to comply. In this context, vayyishma 'aleihem means he listened favorably to them and gave them what they asked.
word_study.significance: The verb positions Hezekiah not as cautious or discerning, but as open and accommodating. This receptiveness will be exposed by Isaiah as the vulnerability through which judgment enters.

word_study.meaning: House of his precious things; the word nekhot derives from the root meaning 'precious' or 'valuable.' The TCR renders this as 'treasure house,' emphasizing its function as a repository of wealth accumulated across generations.
word_study.significance: The treasure house represents not just current wealth but dynastic accumulation—the security and splendor of the Judahite monarchy itself. Its display and subsequent loss carries both political and spiritual weight.

word_study.meaning: Aromatic spices and fine/good oil. These were luxuries of immense value in the ancient Near East, used in religious rites, burial practices, and elite cosmetic preparation. Their inclusion signals not military power but commercial wealth and cultural refinement.
word_study.significance: The catalog moves from precious metals to luxuries that signify both international trade connections and participation in practices of high civilization. Their loss to Babylon will represent the stripping away of Judah's cultural identity.

word_study.term_original: לֹא־הָיָה דָבָר אֲשֶׁר לֹא־הֶרְאָם (lo hayah davar asher lo her'am)
word_study.transliteration: lo hayah davar asher lo her'am
word_study.meaning: A double negative construction in Hebrew ('there was not a thing that he did not show them') that is emphatic. It does not mean there might have been something hidden; it means emphatically that everything was revealed. The TCR calls this 'a double totality formula.'
word_study.significance: This emphatic negation will echo in verse 17 when Isaiah pronounces that nothing will remain (lo yivvater davar). The parallel structure makes Hezekiah's exhaustive display the basis of his exhaustive loss. The reader hears both statements together: all shown...all taken.

cross_references.connection: The context: Babylonian envoys arrive to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery from illness. Hezekiah's welcoming response in verse 13 flows directly from this diplomatic overture.
Isaiah's prophecy directly invokes the same catalog of treasures Hezekiah displays here, making verse 13 the narrative setup for the judgment to follow.
The prudent see danger and take refuge; the simple proceed and suffer. Hezekiah's lack of discernment in displaying all treasures contrasts with wisdom literature's call for caution before strangers.

This passage records how Nebuchadnezzar took temple vessels to Babylon and some of Judah's royal descendants (including Daniel) as captives—the literal fulfillment of what Hezekiah's display foreshadowed.
The parallel account in Isaiah 39 provides the same narrative with Isaiah's presence already implied, showing this event from the prophetic perspective.

commentary.historical_context:
Babylon under Merodach-baladan was rising as a regional power in the late 8th century BCE, seeking to build anti-Assyrian coalitions. The envoys' arrival coincided with Hezekiah's recovery and likely reflected geopolitical interest in allying with Judah. Hezekiah's display of wealth would have been both a diplomatic signal (showing Judah's capacity to be a valuable ally) and a demonstration of divine favor (the prosperity that marked a blessed reign).

In the ancient Near East, such treasury displays served multiple functions: diplomatic signaling, assertion of power, and religious proclamation. However, the historical record shows that such displays could also invite predatory attention. The fate Hezekiah's show of wealth foreshadowed—Babylonian conquest and looting—became historical reality under Nebuchadnezzar II (606-562 BCE), when Jerusalem fell and its treasures were carried to Babylon. The specificity with which verse 13 catalogs treasures, and verse 17 promises their removal, suggests the narrator is writing with historical hindsight, aware of what actually occurred.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The display of possessions as a prelude to loss parallels episodes in the Book of Mormon where pride in wealth leads to vulnerability. See Alma 4:6-8, where the worldly prosperity of the Church leads to pride and spiritual decline. The principle that displaying one's treasures without spiritual discernment invites judgment appears throughout the Book of Mormon narrative.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 56:16-17 warns: 'Wo unto you rich men, that will not give your substance to the poor, for your riches will canker your souls.' Hezekiah's display represents a form of pride in possessions that, while not explicitly sinful in itself, reveals a heart not fully grounded in reliance on God rather than on displays of strength.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The treasure house (beit nekhoto) echoes the treasury of the temple in Jerusalem. In temple theology, the holy place and its furnishings represent God's presence and blessing. The loss of these treasures to Babylon foreshadows the later loss of the temple itself—a rupture in the covenant relationship that demands repentance and restoration. This prefigures the covenant restoration brought through Jesus Christ, by which a new and everlasting covenant replaces what was lost.

commentary.christological_typology: Hezekiah's display of treasures and their subsequent loss typologically prefigure the stripping away of earthly glory that Christ experienced. Just as Hezekiah's wealth and power were emptied before Babylon, Christ emptied himself of heavenly glory and submitted to humiliation, loss, and death. Yet where Hezekiah's treasures departed never to return, Christ's emptying was followed by exaltation and the restoration of all things. The typology speaks to how judgment and loss can be reversed through covenant faithfulness.
commentary.application: The passage warns modern covenant members against what might be called 'transparent pride'—displaying or relying upon visible markers of blessing (wealth, status, accomplishment) without recognizing that all such things are held by permission and are vulnerable to loss. The double-negative construction ('nothing he did not show') invites self-examination: What do we display or rely upon that signals our identity? Are we trusting in the arm of flesh or in God? The deeper lesson is that hospitality and openness to visitors must be paired with spiritual discernment. Hezekiah's failure was not in showing kindness but in failing to ask the prophetic question: 'Who are these people, and what do they truly seek?' In our own lives, this means cultivating the discernment to distinguish between genuine fellowship and exploitative relationships, and remembering that no display of temporal blessing can substitute for covenant fidelity.

text_kjv: Then came Isaiah the prophet unto king Hezekiah, and said unto him, What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee? And Hezekiah said, They are come from a far country, even from Babylon.

commentary.narrative:
The prophet Isaiah appears suddenly, and his entrance is marked not by greeting but by interrogation. His questions—'What did these men say? Where did they come from?'—are pointed and probing, not requests for information Isaiah lacks. This is prophetic cross-examination. The prophet's arrival after Hezekiah's display suggests either immediate divine prompting or knowledge obtained through spiritual means. Hezekiah answers straightforwardly: the men came from 'a far country, even from Babylon.'

Hezekiah's response carries an undertone of pride. The Covenant Rendering notes that the phrase 'from a distant land' (me-erets rechoqah) seems to emphasize the distance itself—Babylon is far away, yet Babylon sought out Hezekiah. This reverses the normal flow of diplomatic attention: ordinarily, a powerful king sends envoys to distant lands. That a distant power sent envoys to him signals Hezekiah's importance on the international stage. Yet the narrator immediately begins to load 'distant' with ominous weight. What seemed like flattering attention from afar will bring judgment from afar.

The brevity of this exchange masks its significance. Hezekiah makes no mention of what he showed the envoys. He answers only where they came from. This silence is crucial because it allows Isaiah's next question (verse 15) to extract the confession from Hezekiah himself. The prophet does not accuse; he interrogates. The king indicts himself.

word_study.meaning: To come, enter, arrive. The simple form conceals movement toward a destination with intentional purpose. In diplomatic contexts, it signals arrival on a mission.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes arrival and intent. Later, when Isaiah promises that all treasures 'will be carried away' (venissa), the same sense of deliberate movement applies—Babylon will come to take what its envoys came to see.

word_study.meaning: A far or distant land. The adjective rechoqah (distant) appears only here in this context. It emphasizes geographic separation and, by implication, the remarkable nature of contact across such distance.
word_study.significance: The word will gain prophetic weight in Isaiah's promise that all treasures will be taken. Distance, which seemed to provide safety and independence, becomes the source of judgment. A far-off power will reach in and take all Hezekiah displays.

word_study.term_original: מָה אָמְרוּ הַאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה (mah ameru ha-anashim ha-elleh)
word_study.meaning: What did these men say? The question seeks to determine what the envoys communicated or requested. Ameru (they said) can mean both what they spoke and what they effectively asked for.
word_study.significance: Isaiah's question pivots from identity (who they are) to intention (what they want). The prophet is probing whether Hezekiah recognizes the envoys' true purpose. By asking what they said, Isaiah invites Hezekiah to think about their mission beyond mere social courtesy.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah's follow-up question shifts from where the envoys came to what they saw, building the interrogation that will extract Hezekiah's confession of complete disclosure.
The parallel account in Isaiah 39 preserves Isaiah's identical questions, confirming the prophetic interrogation and Hezekiah's response.

Solomon similarly received distant visitors (the Queen of Sheba) and displayed his wealth and wisdom. Unlike Hezekiah, Solomon's display is not followed by prophetic judgment, suggesting different contexts and outcomes.

Counsel in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out. Isaiah draws out truth from Hezekiah through careful questioning, embodying the wisdom of extracting what is hidden.
Jeremiah later prophesies the same Babylonian captivity that Isaiah foreshadows here, providing the broader historical and prophetic context for Babylon's eventual dominion.

commentary.historical_context:
The reign of Merodach-baladan II (Marduk-apla-iddina II, r. 721-710 and 703-702 BCE) was marked by constant resistance to Assyrian domination. His envoys to distant lands like Judah were part of a deliberate strategy to build anti-Assyrian coalitions. Hezekiah himself had recently resisted Assyrian pressure (2 Kings 18-19), so from a diplomatic standpoint, contact with Babylon made strategic sense.

However, the historical irony is profound: Babylon, which sent envoys to Hezekiah seeking alliance against Assyria, would itself become the instrument of Judah's destruction. By the time of Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 BCE), Babylon was the dominant regional power, and Jerusalem fell to Babylonian siege. The narrative captures this tragic foresight: what seemed like promising diplomatic contact would result, generations later, in exactly the kind of exile and looting the text predicts.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:21-32 describes how the prophet Alma interrogates his son Helaman, drawing out truth about his wandering in darkness and bringing him to repentance. Similarly, Isaiah's probing questions function not to condemn but to awaken Hezekiah to the reality of his choices. The Restoration pattern shows that prophetic interrogation, though challenging, is an act of covenant love.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:39 teaches that 'power or influence can or may be maintained by virtue of the priesthood alone.' Hezekiah's attempt to maintain Judah's security by displaying material power and diplomatic achievement is implicitly contrasted with reliance on priesthood and covenant. Isaiah's questioning redirects toward spiritual reality.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Isaiah's role as priest and prophet in Jerusalem (he is called 'the prophet' without qualification, as if his identity as God's spokesman is complete) stands in contrast to Hezekiah's kingship. The temple covenant required that earthly kings submit to prophetic authority. Isaiah's interrogation reasserts that prophetic voice takes precedence over royal will.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's prophetic interrogation of Hezekiah anticipates Christ's own prophetic function. Just as Isaiah questions Hezekiah to draw out truth and expose hidden reliance on earthly power, Christ questioned those who trusted in outward displays of righteousness (Matthew 23). The prophet's role is to pierce through surface to reality, calling God's people back to covenant fidelity.
commentary.application: The passage invites reflection on what prophetic scrutiny means in modern covenant life. When church leaders or the Holy Spirit raises questions about our choices—our spending, our ambitions, our displays of status—the initial instinct may be defensive. Yet Isaiah's questions are not accusations; they are invitations to honesty. Hezekiah could have refused to answer, or could have become defensive. Instead, he answers directly. This openness to prophetic questioning is itself a form of covenant faithfulness. The application is to cultivate willingness to be questioned by authorized voices, and to recognize that prophetic interrogation, though uncomfortable, is an expression of the Lord's concern for our spiritual welfare. Do we hide our real choices from those set over us in the Lord? Or do we answer honestly when asked difficult questions?

text_kjv: And he said, What have they seen in thine house? And Hezekiah answered, All the things that are in mine house have they seen: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah's follow-up question directly targets what Hezekiah allowed the envoys to see. 'What have they seen in thine house?' is not a request for inventory; it is a probe designed to make Hezekiah articulate the scope of his disclosure. And Hezekiah does so—with full clarity and seemingly without hesitation. He confesses that 'all the things...they have seen' and repeats the totality formula: 'nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them.'

The TCR notes that Hezekiah's repetition of the totality language from verse 13 makes him 'the witness against himself.' In verse 13, the narrator reports exhaustively what was shown. In verse 15, Hezekiah confirms it in his own voice. This doubling is significant: the reader hears the fact stated objectively (verse 13) and then hears Hezekiah own it personally (verse 15). There is no ambiguity, no claim of misunderstanding, no excuse. Hezekiah is fully aware of what he did. And the TCR adds the crucial observation: 'He is not yet aware that this display has prophetic consequences.'

This is the moment of maximum vulnerability. Hezekiah has confessed the complete disclosure of all treasures. Isaiah now has what he needs to deliver the divine judgment. The prophet has not accused; he has questioned. The king has not been condemned; he has confessed. The narrative structure creates the conditions for prophecy to land with full weight because Hezekiah, in his own words, has confirmed the facts upon which Isaiah's judgment rests.

word_study.term_english: All the things that are in mine house
word_study.term_original: אֵת כׇּל־אֲשֶׁר בְּבֵיתִי (et kol asher beveiti)
word_study.meaning: Everything that is in my house. The phrase uses the word kol (all, everything) with emphatic definiteness. It is not 'some things' or 'many things' but comprehensively 'all things.'
word_study.significance: The repetition of kol from verse 13 creates a verbal echo that hammers the totality. When Isaiah later says 'all that is in your house will be carried away,' the same word kol will echo back. The display and the loss are structurally parallel through repeated vocabulary.

word_study.term_original: לֹא־הָיָה דָבָר אֲשֶׁר לֹא־הִרְאִיתִם (lo hayah davar asher lo hir'itim)
word_study.transliteration: lo hayah davar asher lo hir'itim
word_study.meaning: The same emphatic double negative as verse 13, but now in Hezekiah's mouth rather than the narrator's. The king is testifying to the completeness of the disclosure.
word_study.significance: This repetition from verse 13 in Hezekiah's own voice makes him a co-narrator of his vulnerability. He is not claiming to have been forced or misled; he is acknowledging his own choice to show everything. This self-witness will make the prophecy of loss feel more like consequence than arbitrary judgment.

cross_references.connection: Immediately following this confession, Isaiah delivers the judgment prophecy, using the same vocabulary of 'all' and 'nothing' to promise complete loss of what Hezekiah completely revealed.
The parallel in Isaiah 39 preserves Hezekiah's identical response, confirming the prophetic record across both books.
The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool brings ruin near. Hezekiah's unguarded disclosure of all treasures is the inverse of wisdom's reserve.

Out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks. Hezekiah's ready confession of showing all treasures reveals a heart oriented toward display and external power rather than hidden covenant loyalty.

Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth. Hezekiah's display of wealth and power constitutes a form of boasting about future security, which the passage immediately undercuts.

commentary.historical_context: The interrogation format—question followed by confession—is common in both ancient Near Eastern legal and prophetic contexts. A person questioned in the presence of witnesses would be expected to answer honestly. The prophet's role included functions analogous to a judge: investigating, questioning, and then pronouncing judgment. Hezekiah's straightforward answers suggest either his confidence in his own position or his willingness to submit to prophetic authority (or both). The historical reality is that such displays of wealth to foreign powers were indeed diplomatic gambles with unpredictable outcomes.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:1-3 records how Alma questions Zeezrom with careful, probing questions designed to expose contradiction and draw out truth. The method is prophetic: ask, listen, draw conclusions from the other's own words. Hezekiah, like Zeezrom, is caught in his own testimony.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:1-2 portrays the prophet Samuel the Lamanite standing on the wall and crying repentance, holding the people accountable through prophetic speech. Isaiah similarly stands as the voice of divine accountability, not accusing but questioning until truth emerges.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple treasury (which Hezekiah's display likely included or referenced) was held in trust for the Lord, not as personal property of the king. Showing these sacred treasures to foreign powers violated the boundary between covenant stewardship and private display. The loss that follows is, in part, the restoration of proper boundaries.

commentary.christological_typology: Hezekiah's confession in verse 15 parallels the confessional moments in Christ's ministry where people acknowledge truth about themselves before the judgment of God becomes active. The pattern is: awareness → confession → judgment → redemption (when repentance follows). Hezekiah's honest answer sets the stage for gracious judgment that, while involving loss, will not be annihilation.
commentary.application: The passage teaches the spiritual power of honest self-awareness. Hezekiah could have minimized what he showed, or claimed the envoys pressed him, or offered excuses. Instead, he owns his choice. This honesty, while making him vulnerable to judgment, also positions him to receive God's mercy more fully. In modern covenantal life, the application is that confession and self-awareness—acknowledging what we have revealed, what we have compromised, what choices we have made—is the prerequisite for both divine judgment and divine mercy. We cannot receive grace if we will not acknowledge the reality of our choices. The covenant path requires both honesty about ourselves and openness to prophetic voice.

text_kjv: And Isaiah said unto Hezekiah, Hear the word of the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
This single sentence is a threshold moment. The interrogation ends. The confession is complete. Now comes the shift from dialogue to divine speech. The formula 'Hear the word of the LORD' is one of the most solemn and consequential utterances in Hebrew prophecy. It signals that what follows is not Isaiah's opinion, interpretation, or counsel, but the direct transmission of God's word. The shift in register is immediate and unmistakable.

In the ancient Israelite context, this formula announces a binding pronouncement. It is not advisory; it is declarative. When a prophet says 'Thus says the Lord' or 'Hear the word of the Lord,' the people are confronted with divine speech that cannot be negotiated, appealed, or softened. Hezekiah has answered the prophet's questions. Now he must hear what God has to say about those answers. The verse is short precisely because its weight needs no elaboration. The simple summons—'Hear'—carries the full authority of the covenant God.

word_study.meaning: To hear, listen, obey. In prophetic contexts, shema implies more than auditory reception; it means to heed, to receive with obedience, to accept the authority of what is being heard.
word_study.significance: The same verb appeared in verse 13 when 'Hezekiah hearkened unto' the envoys. Now the verb is inverted: Hezekiah must hear the Lord's word. The parallelism is instructive—Hezekiah listened to foreign envoys; now he must listen to God. The contrast implies a hierarchy of allegiance.

word_study.meaning: The word (utterance, proclamation, decree) of the Lord (YHWH). This formula appears hundreds of times in the prophetic literature and marks the transition from human speech to divine speech.
word_study.significance: The phrase devar YHWH is the standard technical term for prophetic proclamation in Israel. It is not merely speech about God; it is God's own speech transmitted through the prophet. The Covenant Rendering notes this as 'a formal prophetic oracle,' marking the moment when human question-and-answer becomes divine judgment.

cross_references.connection: Verse 16 introduces the prophecy that follows immediately—the judgment about the removal of treasures to Babylon and the captivity of Hezekiah's descendants.
Jeremiah is similarly commissioned to hear and proclaim the word of the Lord, establishing the prophetic pattern of divine speech transmission.
Moses calls Israel to 'hear' the statutes and judgments of the Lord, establishing shema as the fundamental response to divine covenant speech.
Isaiah himself uses this same summons, calling Israel to 'hear the word of the Lord,' establishing his own authority as God's spokesman.

Nephi records moments where the Lord's word comes through prophetic means, requiring the family to 'hear' and obey. The pattern of hearing divine speech through chosen messengers is central to the Book of Mormon.

commentary.historical_context: The prophetic formula 'Hear the word of the Lord' appears in the official records of ancient Near Eastern prophets and is particularly common in the Hebrew Bible. It was the recognized way a prophet announced the shift from personal discourse to divine proclamation. In the context of the Judahite court, this formula carried weight because the king was obligated by covenant to heed the Lord's word spoken through authorized prophets. Hezekiah's position as king did not exempt him from this obligation; if anything, it intensified it, since he was accountable for leading the nation in covenant fidelity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 29:11-12 describes how Alma desires to be 'an angel' sent to cry repentance, embodying the prophetic desire to transmit God's word faithfully. The Book of Mormon consistently portrays the transmission of divine speech as the essential function of priesthood leadership.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-5 teaches that 'the word which I give him he shall give unto you; and whatsoever he shall give you, I will judge to be right.' The Lord's word comes through prophetic channels, and obedience to that transmitted word is obedience to the Lord. Isaiah's pronouncement in verse 16 establishes this pattern in historical type.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple was the place where God's word was heard most directly. Prophets were often connected to temple worship and sacrifice. Isaiah's proclamation of the Lord's word would have carried the authority of temple priesthood, though here it is delivered in the royal court. The shift of location (from temple to palace) signals the urgency of the divine message.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is himself the 'Word of the Lord' (John 1:1), the final and most complete transmission of divine speech. What Isaiah mediates here—God's word through a prophet—is fulfilled ultimately in Christ, who is God's word made flesh. The pattern of 'hear the word' reaches its culmination in 'Hear him' (Mark 9:7), referring to Christ as the ultimate authority.
commentary.application: The verse invites reflection on how we respond to divine word in our own lives. Modern members of the Church encounter God's word through living prophets, scriptures, and the Holy Ghost. The formula 'Hear the word of the Lord' calls us to recognize moments when authority is being transmitted, and to shift from casual listening to serious heed. In an age of constant information, the capacity to recognize and respond to divine speech with full attention is spiritually critical. The application is to cultivate both the ability to recognize authentic divine communication and the willingness to hear it fully, even when—especially when—it challenges our preferred course.

text_kjv: Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store unto this day, shall be carried into Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
This is the judgment itself—swift, comprehensive, and framed with the precision of fulfilled prophecy. Isaiah pronounces what will come in 'days...to come' (yamim ba'im), an indefinite but certain future. The judgment has three components: (1) everything in Hezekiah's house will be taken, (2) everything his ancestors accumulated will be taken, and (3) nothing will be left. The TCR rendering shows the structure clearly: 'everything in your palace—everything your ancestors stored up until this day—will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left.'

The word 'carried' (venissa, from the verb nasa, 'to lift, bear, take away') reverses the active role Hezekiah played in verse 13. Then, Hezekiah showed the treasures; now, others will take them. The destination is named explicitly: Babylon. The distant power that sent envoys to Hezekiah will itself come, or will send its forces, to carry away what Hezekiah displayed.

Crucially, the prophecy extends beyond Hezekiah's personal possessions to dynastic accumulation: 'that which thy fathers have laid up in store unto this day.' This means the loss encompasses not just contemporary wealth but centuries of accumulation by Judahite kings before him. The judgment reaches backward in time (stripping ancestral wealth) and forward into Hezekiah's own future. The use of 'thy fathers' also reminds Hezekiah that he is the steward of dynastic inheritance, not its private owner. To display it and lose it is to betray a trust held across generations.

word_study.meaning: It will be lifted up/carried away...to Babylon. The verb nasa means to lift, bear, take. The passive form (with the vav-prefix) indicates the treasures will be the objects of this action. Babylon is the destination, named with finality.
word_study.significance: The verb creates a stark image: the treasures Hezekiah chose to display will be lifted up and borne away. The action is not a gradual loss but a decisive removal. That the destination is Babylon specifically (not a generic foreign power) ties the prophecy to geopolitical reality and emphasizes that what seemed like promising diplomatic contact would become the source of conquest.

word_study.meaning: Not a thing will remain. The verb yatar means to remain, be left over, survive. The negation makes the loss total. The noun davar (thing) echoes the same word used in verses 13 and 15 ('there was nothing...that'). The echo creates a verbal link between the display and the loss.
word_study.significance: The double negative construction (lo + yivvater) creates emphasis through negation. Combined with the earlier double negatives about what Hezekiah 'did not' show, the repetition of vocabulary makes the loss an inverse mirror of the display. All shown becomes all taken. The TCR notes: 'The totality of the display predicts the totality of the loss.'

word_study.meaning: Says the Lord. A formula that closes prophetic utterance and emphasizes its divine source and binding authority. It is the seal of divine speech.
word_study.significance: The closing formula marks this as binding divine decree. It is not a conditional warning ('if you do this, beware') but an absolute statement of what will occur. The use of amar (he says, he spoke) presents the prophecy in God's voice, transmitted through Isaiah.

cross_references.connection: The judgment continues immediately: not only treasures but Hezekiah's own descendants will be taken into Babylonian captivity, making the loss personal and dynastic.
The historical fulfillment: Nebuchadnezzar's forces carried off 'all the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king's house' to Babylon, exactly as Isaiah prophesied.
Further historical detail of Babylonian removal of temple and palace treasures, confirming the comprehensive nature of the loss Isaiah predicted.
Nebuchadnezzar carried vessels from the temple to Babylon and took some of Judah's royal seed as captives, fulfilling both aspects of Isaiah's prophecy in verses 17-18.
Jeremiah later prophesies the same removal of temple and palace vessels to Babylon, reinforcing Isaiah's earlier prophecy and showing its certainty across multiple prophetic witnesses.

commentary.historical_context:
The prophecy was given in Hezekiah's reign (late 8th century BCE), but its fulfillment occurred under Nebuchadnezzar II more than a century later, in 605-586 BCE. This vast gap between prophecy and fulfillment—spanning multiple generations—is characteristic of biblical prophecy. The specificity of the prophecy is remarkable: not just 'there will be invasion' or 'treasures will be lost,' but 'Babylon specifically will carry them away.' Historically, we know that Nebuchadnezzar's forces conducted multiple sieges of Jerusalem (605, 597, 586 BCE) and progressively stripped its treasures. The 2 Kings narrative, written after these events, records the prophecy with full knowledge of its fulfillment, adding to its prophetic weight.

The role of Babylon in the ancient Near East shifted dramatically during this period. In Hezekiah's time (late 700s BCE), Babylon was one power among several, resisting Assyrian domination. By Nebuchadnezzar's time (early 600s BCE), Babylon had become the dominant superpower. The prophecy thus captures a geopolitical transformation that would have been unimaginable in Hezekiah's day.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly records how God warns His people of coming judgment if they do not repent. See 1 Nephi 2:24, where Nephi prophesies that his rebellious brothers' descendants will be brought into bondage by the Lamanites—a prophecy fulfilled across generations. The pattern of prophecy spanning generations, with the prophet himself never seeing fulfillment, appears in both the Hebrew Bible and the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 5:19 teaches that God's 'word shall not pass away, but all shall be fulfilled.' The binding nature of divine prophecy, once spoken, is doctrine. Isaiah's word 'shall be carried into Babylon' is not a threat meant to motivate change but a bound decree.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The treasures carried away included temple vessels (as detailed in 2 Kings 24-25 and Jeremiah 27). In temple theology, these vessels represented God's presence dwelling in the holy place. Their removal to Babylon symbolizes the rupture of covenant relationship, the 'going down' that must precede any future restoration. This pattern prefigures how Christ's humiliation and apparent loss (his death and descent) precedes exaltation and restoration.

commentary.christological_typology: The removal of treasures and the loss of the temple anticipate Christ's passion, where the glory of God (represented in temple vessels and treasure) appears to be stripped away and defeated by pagan power. Yet as with the exile, apparent loss becomes the condition for restoration. The temple that Babylon destroys is eventually rebuilt; the covenant that is broken is renewed through Christ. The pattern of judgment-loss-restoration-redemption runs through both the historical narrative and the Gospel narrative.
commentary.application: The verse teaches that choices have consequences extending far beyond the chooser's lifetime. Hezekiah's display of treasures to Babylonian envoys set in motion a chain of events whose full weight would fall on his descendants, not on him. This is sobering for modern covenant members because it means our choices have stakes beyond ourselves. Parental choices shape children's futures. Institutional decisions carry long-term consequences. Displays of wealth or power, if they reflect misplaced trust, can invite judgment that affects those who come after us. The application is to think generationally: Are we making choices that honor the trust of those who came before (the 'fathers' whose accumulation we steward) and that will bless those who come after? Are we displaying possessions and power in ways that reflect reliance on God, or are we inviting future judgment through pride?

text_kjv: And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.

commentary.narrative:
The judgment reaches its deepest point: it is not merely property that will be lost, but people—Hezekiah's own descendants. The prophecy extends from treasure (verses 17) to family (verse 18). What began with the display of material wealth culminates in the loss of personal dignity and freedom for Hezekiah's biological descendants. The language is careful: 'thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget'—the emphasis is on direct biological descendants of Hezekiah himself, not distant heirs.

The TCR rendering clarifies: 'Some of your own descendants—your own offspring—will be taken away and will serve as officials in the palace of the king of Babylon.' The word sarisim can mean either 'eunuchs' (castrated court officials) or 'officials' more broadly. The historical record suggests castration was not always involved in Babylonian court service, but the term's possible meaning here conveys the ultimate humiliation: Hezekiah's sons, who should inherit his throne, will instead be stripped of normal masculine dignity and power, serving in a foreign king's court. Whether literally castrated or figuratively rendered impotent by servitude, the meaning is clear: the royal line is broken, and Hezekiah's posterity will be subject to foreign masters.

This is the inverse of Hezekiah's own father (Ahaz) and grandfather (Jotham). Each generation of kings faced choices about trust, display, and covenant. Hezekiah's choice to display treasures to Babylon did not result in immediate punishment to him, but it resulted in permanent displacement of his line. The prophecy was fulfilled historically when Daniel and his companions (among Judah's royal or noble seed) were taken into Babylonian captivity and trained for service in the Babylonian court (Daniel 1:1-7).

word_study.term_english: thy sons that shall issue from thee
word_study.term_original: מִבָּנֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר־יֵצְאוּ מִמְּךָ (mibanekha asher yets'u mimekha)
word_study.meaning: From your sons who will come from you. The phrase 'issue from thee' (yets'u mimekha) emphasizes biological descent. The verb yatsa (to go out, come forth) suggests generational succession.
word_study.significance: The language personalizes the judgment. It is not abstract punishment but the taking of Hezekiah's own biological sons. The double reference to descent (sons from thee, which thou shalt beget) hammers the personal nature of the loss.

word_study.meaning: They will take. The verb laqach (to take, seize, capture) is straightforward and active. The Babylonians will actively seize Hezekiah's sons.
word_study.significance: The same verb used for taking treasures (verse 17) applies to taking people. The parallelism makes clear: as treasures are taken, so too will sons be taken. Both are forms of loss of what Hezekiah thought secure.

word_study.meaning: Eunuchs or court officials. The term can refer to castrated men serving in royal courts (a common practice in ancient Near Eastern kingdoms) or more broadly to officials and administrators. The ambiguity is intentional—the loss of normal manhood and power is the point, whether by literal castration or by enforced servitude.
word_study.significance: The use of sarisim rather than a simple word for 'servant' or 'slave' conveys deep humiliation. In a patriarchal society, the loss of masculine power—literal or figurative—was profound shame. Hezekiah's sons, born to inherit a throne, will be rendered powerless in a foreign court.

word_study.term_english: palace of the king of Babylon
word_study.meaning: In the palace of the king of Babylon. The word heikhal (palace, temple, great house) is the same word used for the temple in Jerusalem. The irony is sharp: instead of serving in the Jerusalem temple or palace, Judah's sons will serve in Babylon's palace.
word_study.significance: The specificity of location—not just 'in Babylon' but 'in the palace of the king'—means Hezekiah's descendants will be visible, daily reminders of Judah's subjugation. They will serve the very power that sent envoys to Hezekiah.

cross_references.connection: The direct historical fulfillment: Nebuchadnezzar took Judahite captives, including members of the royal family, and trained them for service in his palace. Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah are named examples.
Shows the eventual fate of Jehoiachin (Hezekiah's descendant) taken captive to Babylon, who eventually receives favor from the Babylonian king but remains in captivity.
Records multiple deportations of Judahites to Babylon, including nobility and royal personnel, confirming the historical reality underlying Isaiah's prophecy.
The book of Lamentations mourns Jerusalem's fall and the exile of her people, providing the emotional context for understanding what Hezekiah's display initiated.
The parallel account explicitly interprets Hezekiah's display as a test: 'the Lord left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart.' The test revealed pride that needed humbling.

commentary.historical_context:
The prophecy was fulfilled historically when Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 605-562 BCE) conquered Judah and deported its nobility and skilled workers, including members of the royal family. The practice of taking royal captives and training them for service in the conquering king's court was standard ancient Near Eastern policy. It served multiple purposes: it prevented these potential rivals from leading rebellions, it provided educated administrators for the empire, and it symbolically demonstrated the subjugation of the conquered kingdom.

Daniel and his companions are the most famous examples, but they were not alone. The historical record and biblical accounts (2 Kings 25, Jeremiah 52) show multiple waves of deportation. The detail that Hezekiah's descendants specifically would be taken suggests the narrator knew of the historical deportation of Judahite royals and nobility. That it occurred generations after Hezekiah's display adds weight to the prophecy: the consequence of a choice made in Hezekiah's youth reached fruition in his descendants' captivity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's prophecy that his rebellious brothers' descendants will become servants to the Lamanites (1 Nephi 2:23-24) parallels Isaiah's prophecy. Both are generational judgments: a choice made by one generation shapes the captivity and servitude of descendants. The Book of Mormon pattern shows that such prophecies are vehicles of mercy as well as judgment—they warn, they humble, and they eventually lead to repentance and restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:15 teaches that 'the arm of the Lord shall not be shortened.' The inexorable progress of God's judgment, once declared, will be fulfilled. Yet the Restoration also reveals that judgments can be reversed through repentance and renewed covenant. The captivity Hezekiah's display initiated was not final; a remnant returned and rebuilt the temple.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Hezekiah's sons, who should have become priests in the Jerusalem temple, instead become officials in Babylon. This represents the fracturing of the covenant priesthood order. Yet the Restoration reveals that through Christ, the priesthood is restored and renewed. The exile of Judah's priesthood from the temple foreshadows the restoration of 'a kingdom of priests' through the Gospel.

commentary.christological_typology: The captivity of Hezekiah's descendants into Babylon typologically prefigures Christ's descent and apparent defeat. Like Judah's sons taken captive to a foreign king's palace, Christ descended below all things, became subject to the power of death and Satan, and served in the 'palace' of the enemy. Yet like the eventual return of the exiles, Christ rose and restored the covenant, bringing His own 'captives' back to the Father's house. The pattern is: descent, servitude, humiliation, then restoration and exaltation.
commentary.application: The passage teaches a sobering principle: our choices shape not just our own destinies but the futures of those we love. Hezekiah's display to the Babylonian envoys did not result in his own exile—he lived and died in Jerusalem—but it set in motion the captivity of his descendants. This is a call to think carefully about what we expose, what we trust in, and what kind of example and precedent we set. Are we displaying wealth, status, or power in ways that teach our children and posterity to trust in the arm of flesh? Or are we teaching reliance on God's power and covenant protection? The application is to recognize that parental choices, institutional decisions, and leadership examples have long-term consequences for those who come after. What we sow in terms of values, trust, and covenant commitment will be reaped by our descendants.

text_kjv: Then said Hezekiah unto Isaiah, Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken. And he said, Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?

commentary.narrative:
This verse captures one of the most theologically ambiguous moments in the entire Book of Kings. Hezekiah has just been told by Isaiah that within a few generations, his descendants will be stripped, castrated, and carried into exile in Babylon—a judgment on the kingdom for its sins. His response—'Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken'—can be read in at least two contradictory ways. The charitable reading sees a man of profound faith accepting God's sovereignty: the word of the LORD is always good, even when it brings hard news. The critical reading sees a man of profound self-interest: his word is good because it doesn't affect him personally. The follow-up—'Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?'—deepens rather than resolves this ambiguity. Is Hezekiah expressing humble acceptance of God's timing? Grateful relief that his own generation will be spared? Or something closer to indifference toward the suffering of his descendants, so long as his own reign remains secure?

The Hebrew allows all three interpretations with equal linguistic force. The phrase *shalom ve-emet* ('peace and stability') echoes covenant language—the very words used to describe faithfulness to God—yet here Hezekiah uses them to describe the condition of his remaining years. The narrator, who has praised Hezekiah above every other king for his trust in the LORD (18:5), refuses to comment on this moment. That silence is itself a verdict: even the greatest king is complicated, even the most faithful prayer-warrior can meet devastating prophecy with something less than prophetic grief for the future. The Covenant Rendering captures the tension perfectly—Hezekiah's statement 'The word of the LORD is good' sits alongside his unspoken calculation that at least the exile will not happen to him.

This moment is a hinge in the theological narrative of 2 Kings. It shows that righteousness is not the same as moral perfection, and that even a king who walks humbly before God can succumb to the deeply human temptation to be grateful for clemency at the cost of others' suffering. The silence of the narrator here is more honest than reassurance would have been. Hezekiah receives the last word—and we are left to judge whether his peace is the peace that passes understanding, or the peace of one who has arranged to not understand.

word_study.meaning: Good, pleasant, favorable, beneficial. The root carries the sense of that which is pleasing, right, or advantageous. In ethical contexts, it means righteous or morally sound; in circumstantial contexts, it means what works out well for the hearer.
word_study.significance: Hezekiah's use of *tov* ('good') to describe the LORD's word is ambiguous precisely because the Hebrew term spans both ethical and personal registers. When he says 'Good is the word of the LORD,' he may mean 'God's word is always righteous' (theological claim) or 'This word is favorable for me' (personal relief). The narrator does not clarify which sense Hezekiah intends.
