restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of institutional corruption through accumulation of unauthorized practices appears in the Book of Mormon when false priests and leaders introduce competing systems of authority and doctrine (Alma 1-2, 4). The creation of multiple 'altars' (metaphorically) to competing authorities mirrors the spiritual disorder of Manasseh's multiple astral altars. When institutional leadership permits competing sources of authority to flourish, the unity and clarity of covenant practice deteriorates.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The principle in D&C 76:100-109 describes the spirit prison prepared for those who reject the light and testimony of Jesus Christ. Manasseh's filling of the Temple with astral altars suggests a similar principle: the more fully one fills sacred spaces with competing authorities and false doctrines, the more completely one cuts oneself off from the true covenant. D&C 133:2 warns that God's voice 'shall shake the heavens, and the earth shall tremble'—suggesting that cosmic disorder (symbolized by the worship of celestial bodies) provokes divine judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Latter-day Saint temple theology, the temple is a unified space where a single system of covenants is made and a single authority presides. Any introduction of competing authorities, doctrines, or practices within the temple represents spiritual desecration. The specification of 'both courts' suggests that no space within the temple is exempt from the requirement of sanctity and unity. Modern temple standards emphasize that the temple must be maintained as a place of purity and holiness, free from worldly influence—a direct response to the principle Manasseh violates.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's action in the Temple—cleansing it of moneychangers and declaring its purpose ('My house shall be called the house of prayer')—stands as a direct repudiation of Manasseh's desecration. Where Manasseh filled the Temple courtyards with competing altars to false gods, Christ reasserted the Temple's singular purpose and alignment with covenant. Yet Christ's ultimate significance is that he transcends the Temple: the resurrection narrative shows that the physical Temple building becomes temporary and is superseded by the living body of Christ, which becomes the true temple 'not made with hands.' This suggests that while the desecration of physical spaces is serious, the desecration of human hearts and spirits is ultimately more significant. Manasseh's sin was not merely architectural contamination but spiritual confusion—replacing the knowledge of the true God with astral mythology. Christ's purification extends to both: he cleanses physical spaces and transforms human hearts.
commentary.application: For modern members, verse 5 suggests that spiritual desecration often occurs through accumulation rather than dramatic rupture. One altar to a false god might be challenged; but when multiple altars are constructed systematically throughout a sacred space, they become normalized and difficult to challenge without organizational disruption. The application is to examine what competing 'altars' exist within personal or communal spaces designated as sacred: competing sources of authority (media influence, worldly philosophies, false doctrines), competing claims on time and energy (entertainment, material pursuits, social status), and competing definitions of what is holy. The verse emphasizes that both courts are affected—meaning that no level of participation (leadership and laity, priest and people) is exempt from the need to maintain covenantal focus. The question is not only what leaders permit but what individual members allow within their personal spiritual spaces. Are we, through small compromises, gradually filling our spiritual courtyards with 'altars' to competing gods—materialism, ambition, sensuality, intellectual pride? The restoration principle is that God's house remains distinct, unified, and free from worldly intrusion; maintaining that distinction requires vigilance against incremental desecration.

text_kjv: And he made his son pass through the fire, and observed times, and used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 catalogs the most serious charges against Manasseh: practices explicitly prohibited in Deuteronomic law and associated with the most heinous violations of covenant. Each practice listed represents a violation of the law in Deuteronomy 18:10-12, where Moses declares these practices 'abominable' (to'evah) and grounds for divine judgment. The verse opens with the gravest charge: 'he made his son pass through the fire.' This phrase (he'evir et beno ba-esh) describes either child sacrifice to Molech (the Canaanite underworld deity) or a dedicatory fire ritual associated with that deity. Ancient Near Eastern texts and archaeology provide evidence of child sacrifice in Iron Age religious practice, particularly in Phoenician contexts. Whether Manasseh engaged in literal child sacrifice or in a related ritual practice that involved passing children through fire as a dedication or ordeal, the fact that biblical narrators condemn it in the same terms suggests extreme gravity. The loss of an heir to fire would have been a cosmic transgression in biblical thought—the denial of future continuity, the literal destruction of covenant succession.

The next four practices—observing times (onen, soothsayer), using enchantments (nichesh, diviner), dealing with familiar spirits (ov, medium), and consulting wizards (yid'onim, spiritists)—constitute the full repertoire of forbidden mantic practices. Together, they represent an entire alternative system of accessing divine knowledge and power. Instead of relying on the prophets whom God sends (and Manasseh had access to Isaiah and other authentic prophets), Manasseh systematically consulted forbidden sources of guidance: astrologers, diviners, mediums, and spiritists. This was not merely unorthodox religion; it was a deliberate substitution of pagan epistemology (knowledge systems) for covenantal revelation. The phrase 'he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD' (ha-rav la'asot ha-ra be-einei YHWH) uses the comparative ra'ab ('much, abundant'), suggesting not isolated incidents but systematic practice. The final phrase, 'to provoke him to anger' (le-hakh'is), attributes intentionality: Manasseh's actions are not careless but provocative. This is crucial: the text suggests that Manasseh knew his actions violated covenant and did them anyway—not out of ignorance but out of defiance.

The theological significance of this verse is that it moves beyond religious error (worshipping wrong gods) to cosmic rebellion (accessing knowledge and power through forbidden means, practicing child sacrifice, systematically provoking divine judgment). The accumulation of these charges—high places, Baal worship, Asherah poles, astral worship, pagan altars in the Temple, child sacrifice, divination, mediumship, spiritism—constructs a portrait not of a confused or syncretic king but of one who has comprehensively inverted the covenantal order. Every element of his religious practice contradicts core Deuteronomic law. That he maintained this for fifty-five years and apparently faced no serious prophetic or priestly resistance until near the end of his reign (2 Chronicles 33 mentions a period of captivity and repentance, though 2 Kings omits this) suggests that institutional resistance to systematic apostasy can be rendered ineffective through long-term power, wealth, and the normalization of deviation over time.

word_study.term_english: made his son pass through the fire
word_study.meaning: and he passed his son through fire; he'evir ('caused to pass, made pass') with direct object beno ('his son') and prepositional phrase ba-esh ('through fire' or 'in fire')
word_study.significance: The verb he'evir ('cause to pass') suggests deliberate action, not accident. The phrase ba-esh ('through fire' or 'in fire') indicates either child sacrifice (the child dies in fire) or a dedicatory ritual (the child is passed through fire but survives, consecrated to the deity). The Covenant Rendering specifies 'passed his son through fire,' leaving the exact nature ambiguous but clear in its reference to practices 'associated with Molech.' In biblical thought, this was the ultimate violation: the destruction or dedication to foreign gods of one's own heir, the denial of future covenant continuity. The specificity 'his son' (not 'a son') suggests this may have been Manasseh's heir, making the violation even more profound—the sacrifice of the very person through whom the Davidic covenant was supposed to continue.

word_study.meaning: and he observed times/practiced soothsaying; onen refers to reading omens from clouds, weather, or celestial signs
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'practiced cloud-reading' clarifies the original sense: onen (עוֹנֵן) refers to a specific form of divination—reading signs in clouds or observing celestial phenomena to predict future events or divine will. This was a Mesopotamian practice (particularly Babylonian astrology) and was explicitly forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10. The prohibition appears in Israel's law precisely because such practices were common in surrounding cultures and posed a spiritual temptation. By engaging in onen, Manasseh is accepting a Mesopotamian epistemology—the belief that the future and divine will can be accessed through observation of natural phenomena rather than through covenant relationship with YHWH.

word_study.meaning: and he practiced divination; nichesh refers to reading omens from behavior, movement, or entrails
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering uses 'divination,' a broader category encompassing various mantic practices. Nichesh (נִחֵשׁ) from the root nichasch means to observe signs or omens. Ancient diviners read omens from animal entrails (haruspicy), from the flight of birds, from patterns in water or oil, or from other natural phenomena. Like onen, nichesh was common in Mesopotamian and Canaanite practice and explicitly forbidden in Deuteronomic law. By practicing nichesh, Manasseh is turning to the same forms of divination used by surrounding nations, rejecting the Deuteronomic principle that Israel should rely on God's prophets, not on pagan mantic specialists.

word_study.meaning: with familiar spirits/mediums; ov refers to a spirit (possibly a spirit of the dead) or a person who consults such spirits
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering specifies 'mediums'—persons who claimed to contact and consult spirits of the dead or other supernatural entities. Ov (אוֹב) appears to derive from a root related to bottles or containers, possibly suggesting spirits 'contained' in human mediums. The practice of consulting mediums (necromancy) was widespread in ancient cultures but was strictly forbidden in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:11, Leviticus 19:31). The prohibition reflects a biblical conviction that the dead should not be contacted and that divine knowledge comes through God's living prophets, not through communication with the dead. Manasseh's consultation of mediums represents a rejection of this covenantal restriction and acceptance of pagan epistemology.

word_study.meaning: and spiritists/knowing ones; yid'onim (plural of yid'oni) possibly from a root meaning 'to know,' suggesting persons who claim special supernatural knowledge
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'spiritists' clarifies that yid'onim refers to specialists in accessing supernatural knowledge, possibly through possession or altered consciousness. The term may derive from a root meaning 'to know' (yada), suggesting persons who claim to 'know' things through supernatural means. Like mediums, spiritists were common in ancient cultures but explicitly forbidden in Israel. Yid'onim appear in lists with ov (mediums) and nichesh (diviners), suggesting a range of mantic practices united by their claim to access knowledge outside the covenant framework.

word_study.meaning: he greatly multiplied/increased doing evil; hirbah ('he multiplied, he made abundant') with infinitive la'asot ('to do') and direct object ha-ra ('the evil')
word_study.significance: The verb hirbah ('to multiply, to make abundant') suggests not isolated incidents but systemic, ongoing practice. The combination hirbah + la'asot ('to multiply doing') emphasizes that Manasseh's evil was not a single act but a sustained pattern. The phrase 'much wickedness' (har-rab) combined with the comparative hirbah suggests an abundance and escalation of sin. This is not a king who stumbled into error but one who systematically and repeatedly violated covenant.

word_study.meaning: to provoke, to anger; hakh'is (causative form of ka'as, 'to anger') with le ('in order to, so as to')
word_study.significance: The infinitive le-hakh'is ('in order to provoke') attributes intentionality to Manasseh's actions. This is not a suggestion that Manasseh's evil inadvertently angered God; rather, the text asserts that provoking God's anger was the goal or at least a known result that Manasseh persisted in anyway. This attribution of intent is theologically crucial: it transforms Manasseh from a confused or misguided king into one who actively rebels against known covenant. He is not ignorant of the law; he is defiant toward it. This intentionality makes his guilt more severe and his judgment more justified.

cross_references.connection: The law explicitly prohibits all practices Manasseh engages in: 'There shall not be found among you...one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer.'—establishing that Manasseh's practices are comprehensively contrary to Deuteronomic law.

The law warns: 'Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them'—forbidding the exact practices Manasseh engages in, with emphasis on the defiling effect of such consultation.

The law prescribes capital punishment for mediums and spiritists: 'A man also or woman that hath a familiar spirit, or that is a wizard, shall surely be put to death'—establishing that these practices warranted the highest penalty in Israel's law.

The prophet warns against false prophets, diviners, dreamers, enchanters, and sorcerers, condemning the same mantic practices Manasseh engages in, and warning that they will 'remove you far from your land.'

Isaiah (who prophesied during Manasseh's reign) criticizes those who consult 'familiar spirits and the wizards that peep and mutter,' contrasting pagan divination with reliance on 'the law and to the testimony' of God—a direct critique of the religious practices Manasseh engaged in.

The parallel account adds detail: 'he wrought much evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger,' and then specifies his later repentance while in captivity—suggesting that the text's attribution of intentional provocation led to divine judgment that included a period of captivity and opportunity for repentance.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Levant confirms that the practices Manasseh engaged in were indeed widespread in contemporary cultures. Child sacrifice is evidenced in Phoenician contexts (notably at Carthage, though not conclusively in Iron Age Judah proper, though the practice existed in the region). Divination, mediumship, and spiritism are well-attested in Mesopotamian, Egyptian, and Levantine cultures. The consultation of mediums and spiritists was formalized in many ancient cultures; specialized practitioners (like the 'witch' of Endor in 1 Samuel 28) claimed authority through supernatural experiences. The prohibition of these practices in Deuteronomic law reflects the legal and theological framework that distinguished Israel from surrounding nations: Israel was to rely on God's prophets, not on mantic specialists. The fact that Manasseh engaged in all these practices suggests either genuine belief in their efficacy (and thus an epistemological rejection of covenantal reliance on YHWH) or a deliberate statement of defiance against Deuteronomic restriction. The reference to consulting mediums and spiritists is particularly interesting given the later narrative in 1 Samuel 28, where Saul (also a failed king) consults the medium of Endor in desperation—suggesting that resort to such practices was associated with spiritual desperation and isolation from God's true prophets. Manasseh's comprehensive engagement in forbidden practices suggests a king who had cut himself off from prophetic guidance (Isaiah and other contemporary prophets would have been available to him) and turned instead to alternative sources of knowledge and power.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of seeking knowledge and guidance from sources contrary to covenant appears in the Book of Mormon when people 'hearken unto the voice of the devil' (Alma 5:37-41) rather than to God's prophets. The Gadianton robbers, described as engaging in secret combinations and claiming supernatural knowledge (Helaman 2, 6), parallel Manasseh's reliance on forbidden mantic practices. King Amalickiah's resort to false counsel and rejection of prophetic guidance (Alma 46-47) shows a similar pattern: leaders who reject God's living prophets in favor of alternative sources of authority and knowledge ultimately bring judgment on themselves and their people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 establishes the principle that members should 'hearken to the voice of him who speaketh' (the prophet, who receives revelation from the Holy Ghost), with a warning against those who 'speak that which they have not heard from the Holy Ghost.' This directly addresses the error Manasseh commits: he rejects God's true prophets in favor of false sources of knowledge (mediums, diviners, spiritists). The principle in D&C 9:8-9 establishes that divine guidance comes through the Holy Ghost, not through human manipulation (divination, spiritism, enchantment) or contact with non-human spirits.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In restored temple theology, the temple is the place where God speaks directly to his people through prophetic ordinances and revelation. The prohibition on consulting mediums and spiritists is understood as part of the temple covenant: those bound by temple covenants commit themselves to seeking guidance through God's appointed channels (prophets, personal revelation through the Holy Ghost), not through unauthorized spiritual sources. Manasseh's engagement with mediums and spiritists represents a violation of this principle—seeking guidance outside the covenant framework.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is presented in the New Testament as the supreme prophet who speaks God's word authoritatively (Hebrews 1:1-2, 'God...hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son'). Where Manasseh rejected God's prophets (Isaiah, etc.) and consulted forbidden mantic specialists, Christ offers an unmediated path to divine knowledge and grace. The Incarnation itself represents God's ultimate answer to the human longing for divine guidance: not through divination, mediumship, or spiritism, but through direct presence and relationship. In Matthew 12:43-45, Christ addresses the problem of demonic spirits and unclean spirits, warning against the spiritual emptiness that results from expelling evil spirits without filling the space with God's presence—a principle that applies to Manasseh's reliance on contact with spirits rather than on covenant relationship with God. Christ's resurrection establishes that the dead are not consulted (contrary to necromancy) but are part of God's plan of salvation accessed through Christ, not through mediums.
commentary.application: For modern members, verse 6 warns against substituting convenient or seductive alternative sources of guidance and power for reliance on God's covenantal framework and living prophets. In contemporary context, this applies to: (1) Seeking spiritual guidance from sources outside the Church (false teachers, internet influencers, worldly philosophies presented as spiritual wisdom), (2) Relying on 'signs' and 'omens' (numerology, astrology, synchronicity interpreted as cosmic guidance) rather than on the Holy Ghost, (3) Consulting with sources of knowledge that promise power and understanding outside covenant (meditation practices divorced from covenantal context, dabbling in occultism or fortune-telling, seeking knowledge through LSD or other consciousness-altering substances presented as spiritual tools). The phrase 'to provoke him to anger' suggests that persistent choice of unauthorized sources of spiritual guidance is not merely personal error but a deliberate rejection of God's authority. The application is honest assessment: What unauthorized sources of spiritual guidance am I consulting? Am I seeking 'signs' from sources other than God's prophets and the Holy Ghost? Am I tempted to knowledge or power offered outside covenant boundaries? The antidote is renewed commitment to relying on living prophetic guidance and personal revelation through the Holy Ghost—the authorized and covenant-aligned sources of spiritual knowledge. Modern members have advantages Manasseh did not: direct access to living prophets (through conference and publications), a structured system of revelation and guidance (the temple), and personal access to the Holy Ghost. The question is whether we, like Manasseh, will neglect these authorized sources in favor of seductive alternatives.

text_kjv: And he set a graven image of the grove that he had made in the house, of which the LORD said to David, and to Solomon his son, In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all tribes of Israel, will I put my name for ever:

commentary.narrative:
This verse depicts one of the most spiritually catastrophic moments in Judah's history: King Manasseh placing a carved image of Asherah inside the temple of Solomon. The narrator deliberately quotes the divine promise to David and Solomon at length—emphasizing the covenant God made about this very building—in order to maximize the theological contrast. Manasseh does not merely commit idolatry; he violates the sanctity of the house where God promised to establish His name forever. The word 'forever' (le-olam) at the end of the divine promise echoes painfully through the verse: the permanence God pledged is now confronted directly by Manasseh's idol.

The Asherah image was not a minor religious accommodation. Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess figure, and her cultic representation was among the most abhorrent practices in the eyes of the Deuteronomistic covenant tradition. That Manasseh places this 'carved image of Asherah' (pesel ha-Asherah) inside the temple—not in some peripheral shrine but in the very house about which God made covenant promises—represents a deliberate inversion of the temple's sanctity. This is not syncretism or religious compromise; it is a calculated profanation of the covenant itself.

word_study.meaning: A carved or hewn image, typically of wood or stone. The root suggests cutting or fashioning. In biblical usage, pesel consistently refers to idols or cult objects forbidden under the Mosaic law.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'carved image' preserves the sense of deliberate human craftsmanship—Manasseh 'had made.' This is not an inherited practice but a newly fashioned violation, making his sin one of intentional creation rather than passive acceptance.

word_study.meaning: A Canaanite goddess figure, or more precisely here, the cultic image/pole representing the goddess. The term can refer either to the deity herself or to the wooden pole/image used in her worship. The 'grove' in KJV is a misleading translation; TCR's 'Asherah' preserves the proper noun, making clear this is a specific goddess cult object.
word_study.significance: This is the worship of a foreign goddess within God's house. The precision of the term matters: Manasseh is not introducing an abstract 'false god' but specifically the Canaanite fertility goddess Asherah, whose worship was explicitly condemned in Deuteronomic law (Deuteronomy 16:21). The cultural context intensifies the violation.

word_study.meaning: Forever, perpetually, eternally. The temporal scope extends beyond human time into the infinite future. This is the strongest statement of permanence available in Hebrew.
word_study.significance: The covenant promise uses le-olam to guarantee Israel's permanence in the land through David's line. The tragic irony is that this very promise—made about this very house—is being violated in the place where it was sworn. The 'forever' of covenant is being contradicted by the 'forever' of idolatry.

cross_references.connection: The foundational covenant promise to David that his son would build a house for God's name and establish it forever—the very promise Manasseh now violates by desecrating that house.
Solomon's prayer at the temple dedication, invoking the same promise that God's name would be established in this house—the promise now breached by Manasseh's idolatry.
Moses explicitly forbids planting an Asherah pole next to the altar of the LORD—making Manasseh's placement of an Asherah image inside the temple a direct, knowing violation of Mosaic law.
The immediate narrative context describing Manasseh's ascension to the throne and his early turn toward evil, providing the setting for this act of temple desecration.
Jeremiah's condemnation of those who 'set their abominations in the house which is called by my name, to pollute it'—a direct parallel to Manasseh's act and its theological enormity.

commentary.historical_context:
Manasseh's reign (687–642 BCE) occurred during a period of Assyrian dominance. Some scholars note that Manasseh was a vassal of Assyria, and the introduction of Canaanite and foreign cult practices may have had a political dimension—demonstrating allegiance to broader Near Eastern religious syncretism under Assyrian hegemony. However, the Deuteronomistic History presents this strictly as a covenant violation regardless of political context.

The cult of Asherah was widespread in the Levant during the Iron Age, with archaeological evidence (stone figurines, votive offerings) confirming her worship across the region. That Manasseh introduces her worship into the Jerusalem temple represents a dramatic shift from the reform efforts of his grandfather Hezekiah, who had worked to centralize worship and remove high places. The temple had been the symbol of Judah's covenant uniqueness; Manasseh's action transformed it into a site of pagan worship indistinguishable from Canaanite shrines.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 36, Alma describes his own spiritual rebellion in terms remarkably similar to Manasseh's trajectory—leading others into sin and away from true worship. The pattern of a leader's personal apostasy corrupting an entire people recurs in Nephite history (Mosiah 11-12), where King Noah leads the people into iniquity and the desecration of sacred things.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 5:7 emphasizes that God's judgments come not from caprice but as inevitable consequence of covenant violation—'my word shall be verified.' Manasseh's placement of Asherah in the temple is the ultimate verification: God's promise is being tested by the people's rebellion.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple was meant to be God's earthly house, the place where His name would dwell and where His people could commune with Him. Manasseh's desecration represents the deepest possible violation of temple sanctity—introducing the worship of another god into the covenant house itself. This foreshadows the exile, which will result in the temple's destruction and the loss of the visible place of God's dwelling until the Restoration.

commentary.christological_typology: The desecration of the temple by Manasseh foreshadows the rejection of Jesus Christ, who is the true Temple—the fulfillment of the promise that God would establish His name forever. As Manasseh violates the physical temple through idolatry, the Jewish leadership would reject the true Temple incarnate. Yet Christ's resurrection reverses this pattern: where Manasseh's desecration led to exile and destruction, Christ's vindication leads to redemption.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members live in a restored temple tradition. This verse warns against the subtle desecration of sacred spaces and practices through syncretism—blending worldly values into our worship and family life. Just as Manasseh brought 'carved images' into God's house, we face pressure to introduce the 'idols' of this age (ambition, wealth, status, ideology) into our homes and personal worship. The lesson is not primarily about spectacular idolatry but about the erosion of spiritual distinctiveness—allowing our covenant community to become indistinguishable from the world around us. The question for each member is: what 'Asherah images' am I allowing into my personal temple (1 Corinthians 3:16)?

text_kjv: Neither will I make the feet of Israel move any more out of the land which I gave their fathers; only if they will observe to do according to all that I have commanded them, and according to all the law that my servant Moses commanded them.

commentary.narrative:
This verse continues the divine speech quoted in verse 7, now shifting from the promise of permanence to its devastating conditional clause. The narrator uses direct quotation of God's covenant word to amplify the tragedy: God did promise Israel permanent possession of the land—but never unconditionally. The key phrase 'raq im' ('only if') introduces the critical condition: the land promise was always dependent on Israel's obedience to the entire Mosaic covenant, not merely to a few commandments.

The verse draws a sharp distinction between the divine promise (permanence in the land) and the human responsibility (comprehensive obedience). God's commitment to Israel's inheritance is absolute; Israel's retention of that inheritance is contingent on covenant faithfulness. By invoking 'all that I have commanded them, and according to all the law that my servant Moses commanded them,' the text makes clear that Manasseh has not violated one or two isolated laws but has systematically rejected the entire covenantal framework. The word 'torah' (instruction) encompasses not scattered commands but the comprehensive body of Mosaic teaching—the totality of covenant obligation.

word_study.meaning: To shake, wander, move away. In the causative form (hiph'il), 'to cause to wander' or 'to make move.' The root suggests unsettledness and displacement.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'cause Israel's feet to wander' preserves the sense of forced displacement. God is saying: 'I will not remove you from the land'—but the conditional implies that continued violation will result in exactly that wandering and displacement that God promises not to inflict if obedience is maintained.

word_study.meaning: Shamar: to guard, keep, observe, watch over. Asah: to do, make, perform. The combination 'observe to do' means to carefully guard and maintain the practice of commandments—not mere passive belief but active, careful obedience.
word_study.significance: The phrase is not 'if they remember' or 'if they believe,' but 'if they observe to do'—action-oriented language. Covenant faithfulness in the Deuteronomistic framework is fundamentally about behavioral compliance, not internal sentiment.

word_study.meaning: The entire instruction/teaching. Torah refers not to a single law but to the comprehensive body of Mosaic teaching—the complete covenantal curriculum. The word derives from a root meaning 'to teach' or 'to direct.'
word_study.significance: The TCR note emphasizes that torah here is not reducible to scattered commandments but represents the 'comprehensive covenantal instruction.' This is the entire Deuteronomic framework. Manasseh's violation is not a breach of one law but a systematic rejection of the whole covenantal system. The condition for remaining in the land is total, not partial, obedience.

cross_references.connection: Moses sets before Israel the choice between blessing (obedience) and curse (disobedience), with possession of the land contingent on keeping the covenant—the foundational conditional promise that verse 8 echoes.
Joshua's farewell address warns Israel that God's good promises will become curses if the people abandon the covenant and serve other gods—foreshadowing exactly what Manasseh does.

God appears to Solomon after the temple's dedication and restates the conditional covenant: if Solomon walks before God in integrity, the dynasty will endure; if not, Israel will be cast out of the land.

The covenant curses in Leviticus spell out the progression of judgment for covenant violation—from plague to famine to exile—setting the theological framework for understanding Manasseh's imminent judgment.

Moses warns that if Israel turns to idolatry in the land, they will be scattered among the nations—a prophecy that will be fulfilled during the Babylonian exile under the judgment triggered by Manasseh's apostasy.

commentary.historical_context:
The theological framework of verse 8 is Deuteronomic—rooted in the covenant theology of Deuteronomy and developed through the Deuteronomistic History (Joshua through 2 Kings). This historical school of thought interprets Israel's political fortunes through the lens of covenant faithfulness: blessing follows obedience, curse follows disobedience. The 'all the law that my servant Moses commanded' refers to the comprehensive Mosaic covenant as understood in Deuteronomic terms—not scattered rules but an integrated system of obligation, blessing, and curse.

The invocation of Moses as 'my servant' (avdi Mosheh) elevates the Mosaic law to the status of a divine mandate that cannot be negotiated or partially observed. In the ancient Near Eastern context, covenants (particularly vassal treaties) often contained conditional clauses binding the subordinate party to obedience; failure to observe all terms resulted in specified penalties. The biblical covenant framework functions similarly: the land grant to Israel is a gift from God, but retention of the gift depends on the vassal's (Israel's) faithful performance of covenant obligations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes the conditional nature of divine promises. In 2 Nephi 4:4, Lehi teaches that 'inasmuch as ye shall keep the commandments of my son, or the commandments of God, ye shall prosper in the land.' The Nephite civilization rises and falls on precisely this conditional promise—obedience brings blessing, disobedience brings destruction. Manasseh's violation of the 'whole torah' parallels Nephite apostasy under wicked kings.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 82:10 restates the same principle in the Restoration: 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' Covenant blessings in the Restoration, as in ancient Israel, are conditional on obedience to the 'whole' revealed word, not partial compliance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple was meant to be the place where Israel's covenant with God was renewed and symbolized. The condition stated in verse 8—obedience to all the law—was the prerequisite for accessing God's presence in the temple. Manasseh's violation of the temple (verse 7) is thus a violation of the very place where these conditions were meant to be honored. In the Restoration, temple covenants similarly bind members to comprehensive obedience to God's law.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the fulfillment of the conditional covenant. Where Israel failed to keep 'all the law,' Christ perfectly fulfilled all righteousness (Matthew 3:15). He alone merited permanent possession of the covenant promises through complete obedience. Yet His obedience is vicarious: through faith in Christ, believers are grafted into the covenant promises despite their failure to keep the law perfectly. The condition remains, but Christ provides the righteousness that satisfies it.
commentary.application: This verse teaches a critical distinction: God's promises are trustworthy and generous, but they are not unconditional grace divorced from moral responsibility. Modern covenant members often struggle with this balance—sometimes emphasizing God's mercy to the point of minimizing obedience, sometimes emphasizing works-righteousness. Verse 8 holds both: God's promise to sustain us spiritually and eternally is real and reliable ('I will not make the feet of Israel move'), but it operates only 'if' we are 'careful to do' covenant law comprehensively, not partially. This applies to temple covenants, family responsibilities, and personal integrity. The question is not whether we keep one commandment well, but whether we are maintaining comprehensive faithfulness across all areas of covenant life.

text_kjv: But they hearkened not: and Manasseh seduced them to do more evil than did the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the children of Israel.

commentary.narrative:
With verse 9, the narrative shifts from the covenant promise and its condition (verses 7-8) to Israel's actual response: they 'hearkened not.' The people ignored the covenant obligation. But the verse goes further: Manasseh did not merely commit idolatry himself; he 'seduced' (va-yat'em) the entire nation into apostasy. The verb suggests leading astray, causing to wander—it makes Manasseh active in corrupting the whole people, not merely a passive violator of the law himself.

The comparative clause 'more evil than did the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the children of Israel' is the most extreme condemnation possible in the Deuteronomistic framework. The 'nations' (goyim) refers to the Canaanites and other pre-Israelite inhabitants whose abominations had forfeited them the land. God destroyed the Canaanites precisely because of their wickedness and gave the land to Israel. Now, under Manasseh's leadership, Judah has surpassed even the wickedness of those destroyed nations. The logic is inevitable and terrifying: if the Canaanites lost the land for their sins, and Judah has exceeded those sins, then Judah too forfeits the land. The verse contains an implicit judgment that does not yet need to be stated—it follows from the premises already established.

word_study.meaning: To hear, listen, obey. In biblical usage, shama is not merely auditory but relational—to 'hear' is to 'obey.' Negative form: to refuse to hear, to disobey, to reject.
word_study.significance: The people are not deaf; they are defiant. They heard the covenant demand and chose to ignore it. This is willful rejection, not ignorance. The entire people's failure to 'shama' makes them accomplices to Manasseh's apostasy.

word_study.meaning: To lead astray, cause to wander, seduce into error. The root suggests wandering or straying from the correct path. In the causative form, it means to cause someone else to wander—to be a seducer or misleader.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'led them astray' is precise. Manasseh is not merely an individual apostate; he is a leader who actively corrupts the people. He causes them to 'wander' away from the covenant path. This is a leadership failure of the most severe kind—a king using his authority to seduce the nation into covenant violation.

word_study.meaning: Evil, wickedness. The comparative construction 'more evil than' (min is the Hebrew comparative preposition) establishes a ranking of moral transgression. Judah's evil exceeds even the evil of the Canaanites.
word_study.significance: This comparative is not incidental. It invokes the entire theodicy of the conquest: God destroyed the Canaanites because of their wickedness. If Judah now exceeds the Canaanites in wickedness, they too have forfeited God's protection. The comparison is both theological judgment and foreshadowing of exile.

cross_references.connection: Moses warns Israel not to inquire after the gods of the nations whom the LORD destroyed, explicitly forbidding the very practices Manasseh introduces—making his violation a conscious, knowable breach of explicit law.
The Torah warns that the nations were defiled by their abominations and were vomited out of the land—the exact framework that makes Judah's surpassing their wickedness grounds for exile.
Ahijah prophesies against Jeroboam that God will uproot Israel 'because they have made Asherah poles, provoking the LORD to anger'—a parallel apostasy that leads to national division and judgment.
Jeremiah compares Judah's apostasy to the unfaithfulness that characterizes gentile nations, highlighting the shame of Israel exchanging the living God for 'broken cisterns.'

The parallel account states that Manasseh 'made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, to do more evil than the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the children of Israel'—a direct confirmation of this verse's judgment.

commentary.historical_context:
The comparison to the Canaanites invokes the conquest narrative (Joshua) and its theological justification. In Deuteronomistic history, the conquest was not presented as unprovoked aggression but as divine judgment on Canaanite wickedness. Leviticus 18:24-30 explicitly states that the land 'vomited out' the nations because of their abominations. Now, under Manasseh, Judah has become morally equivalent—or worse—than the very peoples God destroyed.

Historically, Manasseh reigned during Assyrian dominance (687–642 BCE). Some scholars note that cultic pluralism and syncretism may have been politically expedient under Assyrian vassal status. However, the Deuteronomistic History judges Manasseh's actions by covenant criteria, not political pragmatism. From the narrator's perspective, political survival at the cost of covenant fidelity is spiritual death. The verse thus encodes a fundamental critique: a king who leads his people into idolatry to secure political advantage has actually guaranteed their destruction, because he has violated the only covenant that provides true security.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Noah in Mosiah 11 parallels Manasseh almost exactly: he establishes idolatrous practices, leads his people into iniquity, and seduces the priesthood and people into wickedness. Like Manasseh, Noah's leadership corruption affects the entire nation. Alma's description of Noah's reign—'the people did wax more hardened, being led on in idolatry and all manner of iniquity' (Mosiah 11:15)—mirrors verse 9's condemnation of Manasseh leading Israel astray.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 90:36-37 warns Church leaders: 'Be ye not deceived in me...All honor, power, and glory, be unto the Father, always.' The warning against leaders who seduce followers into apostasy applies to Restoration context as much as to Manasseh. A leader's apostasy inevitably seduces others; leadership magnifies both righteousness and wickedness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Manasseh's seduction of the people into Asherah worship inside the temple represents a complete inversion of the temple's purpose as a place of covenant learning and renewal. Instead of the temple being a place where people are taught to 'shama' (obey) the covenant, it becomes a place where they are seduced into covenant violation. This parallels apostasy within Restoration temples themselves—when the place meant to teach covenant fidelity becomes a site of hypocrisy and false doctrine.

commentary.christological_typology: Where Manasseh seduces Israel into apostasy, Christ calls Israel (and all people) into repentance and faithfulness. The contrast is not merely moral but redemptive: Christ's influence leads toward covenant restoration and healing; Manasseh's leads toward judgment and exile. Yet even Manasseh experiences repentance in 2 Chronicles 33:11-13—he is afflicted, cries out to God, and is restored. This foreshadows the redemptive work of Christ, who can reverse even the most destructive leadership and restore covenant relationship.
commentary.application: Verse 9 teaches the immense power and responsibility of leadership in shaping not merely individual righteousness but collective spiritual trajectory. A leader who violates covenant—whether a parent, bishop, educator, or public figure—inevitably affects those under their influence. The verse warns against a subtle spiritual danger: assuming that personal disobedience harms only the individual. In reality, those we influence are 'seduced' by our example and teaching. This applies to parents who teach children through word and example to compromise covenant values for worldly gain, to bishops who use authority to suppress truth, to friends who normalize drift from covenant practice. The verse demands that every covenanted member understand themselves as a leader in some sphere—a parent in a family, a teacher in a classroom, a friend in a peer group—and ask: Am I 'seducing' others toward obedience or away from it?

text_kjv: And the LORD spake by his servants the prophets, saying,

commentary.narrative:
Verse 10 is a transitional formula introducing the prophetic oracle of judgment that follows in verses 11-15. The phrase 'the LORD spake by his servants the prophets' (va-ydaber YHWH be-yad avadav ha-nevi'im) is a standard Deuteronomistic formula for prophetic mediation. The specific prophets are unnamed; the narrative presents this as a collective prophetic witness rather than attribution to a single named figure. This anonymity is theologically significant: the judgment is not personal opinion but the corporate witness of the entire prophetic office to God's will.

The use of 'be-yad' ('by the hand of') emphasizes that the prophets are instruments through whom God speaks directly. They are God's 'servants' (avadim), a term of honor but also subordination—they serve God's purposes, not their own. The phrase 'saying' (lemmor) introduces direct quotation of God's words, making what follows the direct speech of God Himself, mediated through the prophetic office. This is the moment when God responds to Manasseh's covenant violation: not with immediate punishment, but with a formal prophetic indictment that explains and justifies the coming judgment.

word_study.meaning: To speak, say. In the causative form (piel) or with 'by the hand of' construction, it emphasizes active, authoritative speech—not mere utterance but performative word that accomplishes its purpose.
word_study.significance: God's speech is not idle; it is covenantally binding. When God 'speaks by the hand of his prophets,' those words carry the full weight of divine authority. The judgment about to be announced is not a threat but a determination.

word_study.meaning: Servant, slave, one who serves. In the context of prophets, it emphasizes their fundamental role as those who serve God's purposes and speak His will. It is a title of respect (e.g., 'my servant Moses') but also indicates subordination to God's authority.
word_study.significance: The prophets are characterized as 'servants' (avadim), not independent authorities or politicians. They exist to serve God's covenantal purposes. Their judgment is authoritative precisely because it is not their own opinion but God's will expressed through their mouths.

word_study.meaning: Prophet, one who speaks God's word. The root is debated but likely relates to 'to call' or 'to proclaim.' A navi is someone called by God to proclaim His will and interpret His purposes to the people.
word_study.significance: The plural form 'prophets' suggests a collective institutional witness. This is not the private opinion of one charismatic figure but the sustained prophetic testimony of the office itself. The Deuteronomistic History understands prophecy as an institution through which God holds Israel accountable to covenant.

cross_references.connection: Moses promises that God will raise up prophets to speak God's words—establishing the institutional basis for prophetic authority that verse 10 invokes in bringing judgment on Manasseh.
Jeremiah is commissioned as a prophet 'to pluck up and to pull down, to destroy and to overthrow,' describing the prophetic role in announcing judgment—the very function being performed in verse 10.
'The Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets'—establishing that prophetic announcement precedes and explains divine judgment.

The narrator summarizes Israel's judgment: God 'testified against Israel, and against Judah, by all the prophets,' but 'they would not hear'—the same pattern of prophetic warning followed by judgment being initiated here.

In the Restoration, the Lord promises that His prophets will deliver His word: 'his word ye shall receive, as if from mine own mouth.' The principle of prophetic mediation established in verse 10 continues into Restoration theology.

commentary.historical_context:
The Deuteronomistic History (Joshua through 2 Kings) is structured as a sustained theological narrative explaining Israel's political fate through the lens of prophetic judgment. Prophets appear throughout this history as the institutional mechanism through which God holds kings and people accountable to covenant. The formula in verse 10 appears repeatedly: God speaks through prophets to warn the people before judgment falls.

Historically, the prophetic office in Israel evolved from charismatic figures (Samuel, Elijah, Elisha) to a more institutionalized role (the 'schools' of prophets), and eventually to the compilation and interpretation of prophetic oracles in written texts. By the time of Manasseh's reign (687–642 BCE), prophecy was an established institution. The unnamed 'servants the prophets' of verse 10 likely represents the collective witness of this institution, not attribution to a specific named figure. The anonymity may reflect the theological principle that the message matters more than the messenger.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly employs this same formula of prophetic warning preceding judgment. Nephi, Abinadi, Samuel the Lamanite, and Moroni all function as the 'servants the prophets' through whom God speaks judgment and calls to repentance. In Mosiah 13:33-34, Abinadi declares: 'Thus God executes vengeance upon those that destroy his people. O God, have mercy upon this people!' The pattern is constant: prophecy mediates divine judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:38 establishes the principle in the Restoration: 'What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken, and I excuse not myself...whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' Verse 10's formula—God speaking through prophets—is reinstated as a fundamental principle of the Restoration. The voice of the prophet is God's voice.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, endowed members covenant to receive and follow God's word through His authorized servants. Verse 10's principle—that God speaks through an authorized channel (the prophets)—is a core temple principle. The endowment teaches that covenant members sustain prophets and apostles as mediators of God's will.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of the prophetic office foretold in Deuteronomy 18:15. Where Old Testament prophets mediated God's word to prepare for judgment or call to repentance, Christ embodies the fullness of prophetic revelation—He is not merely a spokesman for God but God's very word made flesh (John 1:1). Yet Christ's function parallels the prophets of verse 10: He announces judgment on covenant violation (Matthew 23) and calls Israel to repentance (Mark 1:14-15). The prophetic pattern continues in Christ and is fulfilled in His redemptive work.
commentary.application: Verse 10 teaches that God does not execute judgment without warning. He establishes prophetic voices to explain the covenant stakes and call people to repentance before judgment falls. For modern covenant members, this principle means two things: (1) We should listen to and sustain living prophets as God's authorized voice, recognizing that their teaching carries divine weight; (2) We should understand ourselves as living under prophetic covenant—if we drift from covenant fidelity, we do so with full knowledge of the prophetic voice calling us back. Ignoring prophetic counsel is not a victimless private choice; it is covenant violation with communal consequences, as Manasseh's apostasy will affect the entire nation in the coming exile.

text_kjv: Because Manasseh king of Judah hath done these abominations, and hath done wickedly above all that the Amorites did, which were before him, and hath made Judah also to sin with his idols:

commentary.narrative:
With verse 11, the prophetic oracle of judgment formally begins. The charge is introduced with 'ya'an asher' ('Because'), a formal juridical formula marking the transition from narrative to indictment. The oracle consists of a protasis (the charge: verses 11-12a) and an apodosis (the sentence: verses 12b-15). This verse is the charge: God catalogs Manasseh's specific violations and their extent. The language is carefully constructed to show escalating guilt: (1) he has done 'abominations' (toebot—religious violations), (2) he has done wickedly 'above all' that the Amorites did, and (3) he has caused Judah to sin through his idols.

The phrase 'hath made Judah also to sin with his idols' is crucial. Manasseh is not merely guilty of personal idolatry; he is culpable for the nation's apostasy. His leadership has corrupted the entire people. The use of 'also' (gam) emphasizes that Judah's sin compounds Manasseh's sin—he has seduced (as verse 9 stated) the nation into covenant violation. The oracle thus indicts not only individual rebellion but institutional corruption: a king using his authority to seduce a people.

word_study.meaning: Abomination, something detestable or morally repugnant. The term is particularly used in Deuteronomic literature for idolatrous practices. It suggests moral revulsion and ritual uncleanness.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'detestable acts' preserves the moral and religious intensity of toebah. These are not merely 'mistakes' or 'lapses' but acts of fundamental spiritual offense. The term appears frequently in Leviticus and Deuteronomy to describe pagan religious practices.

word_study.meaning: To be wicked, act wickedly; wickedness. The root suggests moral distortion or perversion. A rasha is one who deliberately violates covenant and moral law.
word_study.significance: The adverbial form emphasizes willful moral corruption, not accidental error. Manasseh's apostasy is not naive but deliberate—a conscious choice to act wickedly. The escalating language ('abominations'... 'wickedly'... 'above all') shows intensifying moral depravity.

word_study.meaning: The Amorites, a generic term for pre-Israelite inhabitants of Canaan. Used sometimes to refer to the conquered population generically, sometimes to specific hill-dwelling peoples.
word_study.significance: The Amorites represent the pagan nations whose wickedness God judged through the conquest. That Manasseh exceeds their wickedness in the very land given because of their judgment is the ultimate condemnation. If the Amorites deserved destruction for their sins, Judah has forfeited any claim to continue in the land.

word_study.meaning: To sin, miss the mark, violate covenant. In the causative (hiph'il) form, 'to cause to sin,' 'to lead into sin.' This makes Manasseh an active seducer of the people's righteousness.
word_study.significance: The hiph'il form emphasizes Manasseh's agency in corrupting the people. He is not merely failing to prevent their apostasy; he is actively causing them to sin. His guilt is compounded by his leadership role—he seduces those under his authority.

word_study.meaning: Idols, cult objects. The term is likely derogatory, possibly derived from a root meaning 'dung pellets' or 'fecal matter,' expressing contempt for idol worship.
word_study.significance: The TCR translator notes suggest gillulim is 'deliberately derogatory.' The term does not neutrally describe cult objects but expresses moral repugnance. God is not merely saying 'idols' but 'contemptible dung-idols'—a deliberate intensification of the judgment.

cross_references.connection: The land 'vomited out' the nations before Israel because of their abominations—the same framework that now applies to Judah's abominations, suggesting they too will be vomited out through exile.
Moses clarifies that Israel entered the land not because of righteousness but because of the Amorites' wickedness—making Judah's surpassing their wickedness grounds for dispossession.

The narrator condemns Israel under Jeroboam for establishing high places and Asherah poles 'like the abominations of the nations which the LORD cast out before the children of Israel'—the same comparison applied to Manasseh.
Jeremiah condemns those who 'set their abominations in the house which is called by my name, to pollute it' and 'built the high places of Topheth'—mirroring Manasseh's desecration of the temple.

God condemns Jerusalem: 'She hath changed my judgments into wickedness more than the nations, and my statutes more than the countries that are round about her'—the same accusation of exceeding pagan wickedness.

commentary.historical_context:
The comparison to the Amorites invokes Israel's foundational narrative: the conquest of Canaan. Deuteronomic theology justified the conquest by appealing to Canaanite wickedness (Leviticus 18:24-30, Deuteronomy 9:4-5). The implication was that if Israel maintained covenant fidelity, it would retain the land; if it matched or exceeded Canaanite wickedness, it would forfeit it. Now, under Manasseh, Judah has exceeded the Amorites' abominations.

Historically, Manasseh's reign (687–642 BCE) was marked by significant religious pluralism and syncretism. While the exact nature of the Asherah cult and other religious practices remains debated by scholars, the Deuteronomistic History presents them as fundamentally violating Mosaic law. The theological argument of verse 11 is not historically neutral; it is a covenant-based indictment of religious pluralism as covenantal betrayal. From the Deuteronomistic perspective, there is no middle ground: serving other gods is not 'cultural accommodation' but 'abomination.'

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:13-15 describes Alma's own realization of his wickedness in terms similar to verse 11's indictment: 'Oh, how did I blaspheme, that I did not believe in the doctrine of Christ! But behold, I say unto you that the Lord in his mercy made known unto me the truth of his gospel.' Similarly, King Noah and his priests in Mosiah 11 are indicted for leading the people into abominations. The pattern of leadership-induced apostasy recurs throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:45-47 establishes judgment against those who lead people into apostasy: 'I will deliver those whom I send unto you, if they obey my voice; and all others shall be delivered into the hands of their enemies.' Leadership seduction into apostasy (as Manasseh engages in) invokes God's judgment on both leaders and followers.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple was meant to be a place where God's standards of holiness and covenant fidelity were taught and practiced. Manasseh's desecration of the temple with Asherah poles represents the inversion of the temple's purpose: instead of a place sanctifying the people to God's standard, it becomes a place teaching them pagan abominations. This mirrors any corruption of the restored temples through hypocrisy or false doctrine.

commentary.christological_typology: Where Manasseh causes Judah to sin, Christ calls sinners to repentance and righteousness. Christ does not use His authority to seduce people away from covenant but to restore them to it. In Matthew 23, Christ pronounces judgment on those who 'cause the least of these to stumble' (skandalon)—a direct reversal of Manasseh's seduction. Christ is the antithesis of the seducing king: He is the king who leads His people toward holiness, not away from it.
commentary.application: Verse 11 teaches that in covenant community, leadership carries amplified moral weight. A leader's apostasy is not merely personal failure; it inevitably corrupts those under their influence. This applies to parents, bishops, educators, and any person in a position of spiritual trust. The verse also teaches that we cannot excuse our own apostasy by claiming we were 'following leadership.' Manasseh seduced the people, but they also 'hearkened not' to the covenant. Both the leader and followers bear responsibility. For modern covenant members, this means: (1) If you are in a position of influence, understand that your choices about covenant fidelity directly affect those you teach or lead; (2) If you are following a leader who is leading you toward apostasy, do not absolve yourself of responsibility by claiming to be merely obedient. Covenant demands personal discernment and fidelity.

text_kjv: Therefore thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Behold, I am bringing such evil upon Jerusalem and Judah, that whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 12 transitions from the charge (verse 11) to the sentence of the oracle. The formula 'Thus saith the LORD God of Israel' (Koh amar YHWH Elohei Yisrael) marks the pronouncement of judgment. The specific judgment is stated with striking imagery: God is bringing 'such evil' upon Jerusalem and Judah that 'whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle.' The tingle or ringing of ears (tittsalnah shtei oznav) is not a figure for pleasant news but for shocking, devastating news so terrible that the physical body reacts to hearing it.

This particular expression appears elsewhere in the Deuteronomistic History as a marker of extreme judgment: in 1 Samuel 3:11, the LORD tells Samuel that He will do 'a thing in Israel, at which both the ears of every one that heareth it shall tingle'—referring to the judgment on Eli's house. Here, that same formula is applied to the judgment on Jerusalem and Judah under Manasseh. The phrase is carefully chosen to indicate that the judgment is not a minor correction but a catastrophic reversal of fortune so severe that all who hear of it will be shocked into a visceral response. The judgment is not yet specified (that comes in verses 13-15), but its enormity is telegraphed through this language of universal shock.

word_study.meaning: To bring evil/disaster. Ra'ah (evil, harm, disaster) is the object brought by God's active agency. Meviah is the hiph'il participle of 'to come/bring,' emphasizing God's direct causation of the calamity.
word_study.significance: God is not passively allowing disaster; He is actively bringing judgment. This distinguishes divine judgment from mere consequence. Manasseh's apostasy does not accidentally lead to ruin; God actively executes justice through bringing calamity on Jerusalem and Judah.

word_study.meaning: 'Evil such as this' or 'disaster of this kind.' The demonstrative phrase 'such as this' signals something unprecedented or extreme in scale or severity.
word_study.significance: The judgment is not ordinary; it is a specific, intense form of calamity. The vagueness of 'such evil' makes it more terrifying—the hearers do not know its exact form, only that it is catastrophic.

word_study.term_original: צַלַל (tsal-al) → תִּצַּלְנָה שְׁתֵּי אׇזְנָֽיו (tittsalnah shtei oznav)
word_study.meaning: To ring, buzz, tingle. The hiph'il form with 'ears' (oznav) as subject creates the vivid image of ears literally ringing from shock. The TCR rendering 'ears will ring' is more precise than KJV's 'tingle.'
word_study.significance: This is the physical manifestation of psychological and spiritual shock. The expression is not metaphorical but physiological: the news is so devastating that the body reacts involuntarily. It suggests a judgment so severe that it overwhelms normal emotional capacity and produces a visceral, almost neurological response.

cross_references.connection: Samuel hears the Lord say, 'I will do a thing in Israel, at which both the ears of every one that heareth it shall tingle'—the exact same formula, applied to the judgment on Eli's house, establishing this as a marker of catastrophic divine judgment.

Jeremiah announces judgment on Jerusalem with nearly identical language: 'Hear ye the word of the LORD...Thus saith the LORD...which when one heareth, his ears shall tingle'—confirming the formula as a standard announcement of city-level judgment.
The verses immediately following specify the exact nature of the 'evil' announced in verse 12: God will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish, measuring out judgment as He did to Israel under Jeroboam.
The covenant curses warn of progressive judgment for covenant violation, culminating in exile—the general framework that the specific judgment announced in verse 12 will exemplify.

In the Restoration, God announces judgment with urgency: 'I will come forth and show myself' in judgment to those who harden their hearts—mirroring the urgent, inescapable judgment formula of verse 12.

commentary.historical_context:
The formula 'ears shall tingle' (littsalnah oznayim) appears in 1 Samuel 3:11 and Jeremiah 19:3, suggesting it was a recognized idiom in prophetic speech for announcing extreme judgments. The judgment in view is not mere political defeat but theological catastrophe. From a historical perspective, Manasseh's reign was followed by his son Amon's reign (642–640 BCE) and then Josiah's reform (640–609 BCE). However, the oracle in verses 11-15 frames the judgment as inevitable and inescapable—though 2 Chronicles 33:11-13 records Manasseh's own repentance and restoration, the 2 Kings account treats the judgment as consequential.

Historically, the judgment referred to came through the Babylonian exile (586 BCE), which occurred roughly a century after Manasseh's reign. From the Deuteronomistic perspective, the judgment was 'set in motion' by Manasseh's apostasy—even though multiple generations elapsed before its execution. This reflects a theology in which covenant violation inevitably accumulates judgment that, once initiated, cannot be stayed (2 Chronicles 36:14-20 confirms this cumulative judgment trajectory).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly employs language of cosmic shock at coming judgment. In Alma 14:26-27, Amulek preaches: 'Ye shall be brought before the judgment seat of Christ'—a ringing summons to repentance before inescapable judgment falls. The 'ears shall tingle' formula is replaced in the Book of Mormon with language of trembling and fear before God's justice.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:3 records Joseph Smith's vision language: 'I heard a voice saying: John, my beloved, what art thou hearing?' The Restoration employs similar auditory imagery for divine communication of solemn consequence. D&C 87:6 announces judgment with urgency: 'In that day... they who have eyes to see, let them see; and they who have ears to hear, let them hear.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, covenantal curses and blessings are presented. The language of verse 12—that judgment will come with inescapable force—echoes the temple understanding that covenant violation is not a minor matter but a fundamental breaking of sacred obligation with inevitable consequences. Temple covenants place one in a position where violation leads to specific, serious consequences.

commentary.christological_typology: Where verse 12 announces judgment so severe that ears tingle at the report, Christ in His ministry announces coming judgment on Jerusalem with similar urgency (Matthew 24, Mark 13, Luke 21). Yet Christ also announces the possibility of repentance and redemption (Luke 13:1-5: 'Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish' offers the pathway to escape judgment). In Christ's ministry and in His Atonement, the pattern established by Manasseh's judgment is redeemed: judgment becomes not merely retribution but an opportunity for repentance and restoration.
commentary.application: Verse 12 teaches that judgment for covenant violation is not a private or hidden matter. The judgment comes with such force and consequence that all who hear of it are shaken. This has multiple implications: (1) Consequences for spiritual violation are not merely personal but communal—when a leader or influential person falls into apostasy, the entire community feels the shock; (2) Ignoring prophetic warnings about apostasy does not make judgment disappear; it makes it inevitable and more severe; (3) The fact that even the 'report' of judgment shocks people suggests that the actual judgment is even more devastating. For modern covenant members, this means taking seriously the prophetic warnings about the consequences of covenant violation. The language of verse 12 is designed to awaken urgency: this is not a distant, theoretical threat but a pressing moral reality that should cause ears to 'ring' with the seriousness of covenant fidelity.

text_kjv: And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down.

commentary.narrative:
This verse contains God's decree of judgment against Jerusalem, delivered through the prophet (likely Jeremiah, though the text does not explicitly name the speaker). The language draws from two distinct domains: construction and domestic labor. The measuring line (qav) and plumb line (mishqolet) were instruments used by builders to ensure structural integrity, but here they become instruments of measurement for destruction. The reference to Samaria invokes the fall of the northern kingdom in 722 BCE — a catastrophe Judah had witnessed roughly a century earlier. By applying the "line of Samaria" and the "plumb line of the house of Ahab" to Jerusalem, the prophecy establishes an exact parallel: what happened to Israel's capital and Ahab's dynasty will now happen to Judah's capital and Manasseh's kingdom.

The second image — wiping a dish clean — is deceptively simple. The verb machah (to wipe) also carries the meaning of complete erasure or blotting out (as in Genesis 6:7, where God blots out humanity in the flood). A woman wiping a dish after a meal is a routine, effortless act requiring no special strength or preparation. By comparing the destruction of Jerusalem to this domestic cleanup, the text emphasizes God's complete authority and the ease with which divine judgment will be executed. The city's fall will be as natural and inevitable as washing dishes; the effort required is negligible because God's power is absolute. The phrase "turning it upside down" (ve-hafakh al paneha) suggests thorough, methodical destruction — nothing will be left standing or salvageable.

Historically, this prophecy echoes warnings issued by earlier prophets like Isaiah and Micah, but the context of Manasseh's reign gives it terrible urgency. Manasseh has reversed the religious reforms of his father Hezekiah, rebuilt pagan altars, shed innocent blood, and led Judah into apostasy. The measuring lines applied to Samaria and the Ahab dynasty — both destroyed for their idolatry and rebellion — now measure Judah's fate. The domesticity of the image makes it more devastating, not less, because it removes any sense of struggle or dramatic resistance. Jerusalem's end will be as inevitable and unresisting as dirty dishes.

word_study.meaning: A measuring line or string used in construction to establish straight boundaries and alignment. The root carries the sense of direction, order, and measurement. In this context, the qav establishes exact parallel judgment: the measuring standard applied to Samaria (northern kingdom's destruction) is now stretched over Jerusalem.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this term is drawn from the technical language of builders but repurposed for judgment. It establishes a precise, measured equivalence between Israel's fall and Judah's coming fate — not random destruction but divinely ordered judgment applied with exact standards.

word_study.meaning: A plumb line or plumb bob used by builders to ensure vertical alignment and level construction. From the root shaqal ('to weigh'), it literally means 'a thing for weighing' and figuratively measures whether something is true, just, or aligned with divine standards.
word_study.significance: Applied to the house of Ahab, the plumb line of judgment that found Ahab's dynasty crooked and out of alignment with God's law will now be applied to Manasseh's Judah. The image suggests that spiritual and moral corruption have made Jerusalem spiritually unstable and out of alignment with God's covenant.

word_study.meaning: To wipe, sweep clean, or erase completely. The term carries connotations of total removal and obliteration. It appears in Genesis 6:7 (wiping out humanity in the flood) and Exodus 32:32 (blotting a name from the book of life), both indicating absolute, irreversible erasure.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that machah moves beyond simple cleaning to complete obliteration. Jerusalem will not merely be damaged or diminished but wholly erased from its former glory — its religious function, its role as God's chosen capital, its continuity as a living political center, all removed as thoroughly as a dish cleaned after a meal.

word_study.meaning: A shallow dish or plate used for serving or eating. The term appears only here and in Leviticus 6:28 (a cooking vessel). It represents the most ordinary, domestic object — the kind of item a household worker would handle dozens of times daily without thought.
word_study.significance: The juxtaposition of Jerusalem — the city of the great Temple, the seat of David's throne, the center of covenant worship — with a common eating dish creates shocking theological irony. The once-sacred city will be treated with the same indifference as tableware. This domesticity makes the judgment more, not less, terrible: God will erase Jerusalem as effortlessly as one wipes a plate.

cross_references.connection: Records the fall of Samaria and the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE, the historical precedent that now threatens Jerusalem and Judah under Manasseh's rule.
Describes Jehu's complete eradication of the house of Ahab, the violent end of a dynasty that becomes the measuring standard for Judah's coming judgment.
Uses the same metaphor of the measuring line and plumb line as instruments of divine justice, suggesting a widespread prophetic use of construction imagery for judgment.
God calls Jeremiah to pluck up and tear down kingdoms, paralleling the total destruction prophesied for Jerusalem in this verse.
Later reflects the desolation of Jerusalem after its destruction, the fulfillment of this prophecy spoken during Manasseh's reign.

commentary.historical_context: The imagery of measuring lines and plumb lines reflects practical construction techniques known throughout the ancient Near East. Assyrian and Babylonian building inscriptions describe similar tools for laying out cities and temples. The fall of Samaria in 722 BCE was a living memory for Judah — a warning about what happened to a kingdom that abandoned covenant loyalty. Manasseh's reign (c. 687–642 BCE) occurred during the height of Assyrian power under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal. Judah was a vassal state, and Manasseh's adoption of Assyrian religious practices (pagan altars, child sacrifice) was partly a political accommodation to Assyrian overlordship. However, from the biblical perspective, this accommodation represented covenant apostasy. The prophecy of Jerusalem's total destruction would come to pass nearly a century later when Babylon conquered the city in 586 BCE — a timeframe that fits the pattern of delayed judgment but inevitable fulfillment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently applies the language of measuring and judgment to covenant communities. In Alma 11:37, the people are warned that God's justice will measure out consequences according to their deeds. The principle of God applying one nation's judgment as a standard for another appears in Mormon 4:11-12, where Mormon observes that the Nephites' destruction mirrors patterns of judgment seen in earlier civilizations.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:14 contains similar language: "But the day soon cometh; the hour is nigh at hand, when the Lord shall come down in his vengeance, and the stubborn shall be destroyed." The precision of divine judgment — measured, inevitable, absolute — appears throughout the Doctrine and Covenants as a core principle of God's governance of covenant communities.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The destruction of Jerusalem meant the destruction of the temple — the house of God where Israel met with the divine, where sacrifices were offered, where God's name dwelt. The wiping clean of Jerusalem is thus the defiling and destruction of the holiest place on earth. In LDS theology, covenant violation leads to the withdrawal of divine presence from temples and sanctuaries. The prophecy here foreshadows a cosmic reversal: the place made holy becomes the site of desolation.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse, though not explicitly messianic, points to the pattern of judgment and redemption central to Christ's role. The measuring line and plumb line are instruments of justice that find Jerusalem wanting — out of alignment with God's law. Christ, when he comes, will be the "stone which the builders rejected" (Psalm 118:22, quoted of Christ in the New Testament), the one who redefines the standards of righteousness. Additionally, the complete wiping away of Jerusalem's defilement prefigures the work of atonement: Christ's blood will cleanse what judgment cannot merely destroy. The dish being wiped clean becomes, in resurrection theology, a type of the cleansing that makes all things new.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse presents a stark warning about the consequences of sustained apostasy. Manasseh did not commit a single terrible sin; his was a sustained, systemic rebellion lasting decades — the reversal of his father's reforms, the introduction of Assyrian pagan practices into the temple, the shedding of innocent blood. The measuring line applied to Samaria and the plumb line of Ahab's dynasty suggest that God's standards of judgment do not change; what destroyed one covenant nation will destroy another. The implication is that covenant communities cannot presume upon divine patience indefinitely. At the same time, the very clarity and specificity of the judgment — measured, not random; methodical, not vengeful — suggests that God's justice operates by clear, knowable standards. For individual members, the invitation is to align one's life with those standards before the measuring line reveals profound misalignment.
