word_study.meaning: sefer ('scroll, written document') + torah ('instruction, teaching, law'). This is the written text of the covenant—the document that defines Israel's legal, moral, and spiritual obligations to God and the blessings or curses that follow obedience or disobedience. Scholars identify this scroll with some form of Deuteronomy based on the reforms that follow.
word_study.significance: Torah is not merely 'law' but divine instruction—the revealed will of God for His covenant people. The recovery of this document represents the recovery of Israel's identity as a covenant community. In The Covenant Rendering, the term carries the full weight of 'the Book of the Law/Instruction'—the definitive statement of what God requires.

word_study.meaning: The Temple—God's dwelling place and the center of Israel's religious and national life. The phrase emphasizes that the scroll was discovered in the most sacred location in the nation.
word_study.significance: The irony is central to the verse's theological impact: the very place built to honor God and preserve His word had allowed His written word to become lost. This speaks to institutional religion becoming hollow—the building remains, the rituals continue, but the foundational text that gives meaning to those practices has been misplaced.

word_study.meaning: to read, call out, proclaim; can mean both the act of reading silently and the act of calling out or proclaiming publicly. When used with the scroll, it often implies public or formal reading.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests that Shaphan's reading is not private study but a proclamation—the scroll's words are being voiced aloud, transforming the silent text into living speech. This is the same verb used for prophetic utterance, indicating that the scroll speaks with prophetic authority.

cross_references.connection: Moses commanded the Levites to place the Book of the Law beside the Ark of the Covenant as a witness. The scroll discovered by Hilkiah may have been removed from its proper location, accounting for why it was 'lost' in the Temple.

Manasseh's long reign (697–642 BCE) introduced pagan practices into the Temple and reversed the religious reforms of his father Hezekiah. The scroll's burial or loss likely occurred during this period of spiritual apostasy.

Jeremiah, a contemporary of Josiah, describes the prophet's call to proclaim God's word when the nation has turned away. The discovery of the scroll parallels the prophetic effort to recover God's word in a rebellious nation.

Alma compares precious records kept by Nephi to God's word preserved for His people. Like the Book of Mormon, the discovered scroll represents God's enduring word meant to guide and redeem His covenant people.

The Lord declares that His word 'shall all be fulfilled, whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants.' The scroll's rediscovery represents the Lord speaking through His written word to the nation.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeological and textual evidence suggests the scroll discovered was a form of Deuteronomy or Deuteronomic teaching. Deuteronomy emphasizes covenant theology—the binding agreement between God and Israel with specific blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. The discovery occurred during the reign of Josiah (640–609 BCE), a period of Judean revival and attempted independence from Assyrian domination. The reforms that followed (described in 2 Kings 23) included the removal of pagan altars and idolatrous practices, the centralization of worship in Jerusalem, and the restoration of Passover observance. Ancient Near Eastern parallels suggest that religious reforms often involved the 'rediscovery' or reaffirmation of foundational legal and religious texts. The physical placement of the scroll during renovation work suggests that during Manasseh's reign, religious institutions had become so corrupted that even the foundational written text had been displaced or deliberately hidden by those opposed to covenant-based religion.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 3:3-4 describes Nephi's mission to retrieve the brass plates containing 'the record of the Jews and the genealogy of my fathers,' essential to preserving God's word and covenant. Like Hilkiah's discovery, the recovery of the plates represents the recovery of God's written word essential to covenant identity. 2 Nephi 4:15 emphasizes the spiritual power of searching and preserving God's word.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:59 addresses the importance of written records: 'And all this ye shall observe to do as I have commanded concerning your conduct and affairs.' The discovery of the scroll emphasizes that God's written instructions, not mere human tradition, must guide the people. D&C 21:4-5 emphasizes that the Lord's word comes through His established servants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is meant to be a repository of sacred knowledge and covenant understanding. The scroll's discovery within the Temple—yet lost to the nation's consciousness—illustrates how institutional religion can become separated from its foundational principles. The Restoration teaches that temples are places where God's word is remembered and reaffirmed (D&C 109).

commentary.christological_typology: The scroll represents Christ as 'the Word made flesh' (John 1:1, 14). Just as the scroll had been lost yet was recovered in the Temple, Christ—the living Word—was rejected by Israel yet remains the foundation of God's covenant. The reading of the scroll that brings immediate, convicting response prefigures Christ's ministry, where His words pierce hearts and demand response. Hebrews 1:1-2 teaches that God spoke through the prophets and finally through His Son—Christ is the ultimate 'Book of the Law,' the final revelation of God's will.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to consider whether God's word—both written and revealed through modern prophets—has become 'lost' in our personal practice. The Temple and Church exist to preserve God's word, but those institutions can become routine or merely cultural unless we deliberately seek out and engage with foundational teachings. The question is direct: Where are the 'lost scrolls' of your own spiritual life? What divine instructions or covenantal principles have been buried under the routines of institutional participation? Modern members are invited to rediscover the living power of God's word—in scripture, in temple worship, in prophetic counsel—as a transformative force rather than background decoration to faith.

text_kjv: And Shaphan the scribe came to the king, and brought the king word again, and said, Thy servants have gathered the money that was found in the house, and have delivered it into the hand of them that do the work, that have the oversight of the house of the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
Shaphan approaches King Josiah with what appears to be a routine administrative report regarding the Temple repair project's finances. He reports that his servants have 'gathered the money that was found' (hittikhu et ha-kesef—literally 'melted down the silver') in the Temple and have properly distributed it to the work supervisors appointed to oversee the Temple repairs. The verb 'gathered' or 'melted down' (hittikhu, from natakh) suggests the silver was processed into usable form for payments. This is a normal bureaucratic briefing—exactly what the king would expect when funds are collected during Temple renovation.

The narrative structure here is deliberately constructed to create anticipation. Shaphan begins with the financial routine, the expected matters of administration and accountability. His opening words create a frame of normalcy: funds are properly accounted for, distributed to qualified supervisors, and put to their intended sacred use. The audience (both ancient and modern) hears a straightforward administrative report and anticipates the conclusion will be similarly mundane. But this verse functions as a prologue—the ordinary administrative detail that precedes the extraordinary announcement. The king and reader are being positioned in a mental state of routine business, making the shock of the next verse—the discovery of the lost scroll—more explosive by contrast.

word_study.meaning: from the root natakh, 'to pour, melt'; the causative form suggests the servants actively caused the silver to be melted or collected in liquid form. The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'melted down,' indicating the silver was processed into usable form for dispersal to workers.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests professional handling of precious metal—the silver was not merely collected but refined and prepared for use, reflecting the careful stewardship described in verse 7.

word_study.meaning: kesef ('silver, money') + nimtsa ('was found, discovered'). This refers to the silver collected as donations or discovered during the Temple cleaning and renovation work.
word_study.significance: The silver itself represents the people's devotion to the Temple restoration—resources given willingly for God's house. The careful handling of this money reflects the principle established in verse 7.

word_study.meaning: from the root natan, 'to give, place, entrust'; the prefix va- indicates 'and they gave/delivered,' indicating proper distribution of the funds.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes proper transfer of authority and resources from the royal administration to the Temple workers. This reflects the chain of accountability established in verse 7.

word_study.meaning: literally 'doers of the work'; melakhah encompasses work, labor, and the skilled tasks required for construction and maintenance.
word_study.significance: These are the craftspeople and laborers executing the Temple repairs—the same workers described in verse 7 as acting 'with complete integrity.'

cross_references.connection: Verses 3-7 describe the initial authorization by King Josiah of the Temple repair project and the establishment of financial accountability measures. Verse 9 reports the progress and proper distribution of collected funds.

A parallel account of Temple repairs under Joash describes similar financial collection and distribution: 'And it was so, that at what time the chest was brought unto the king's office...then the Levites and the king's scribes came and emptied the chest...and gave the money...to such as did the work.'

The principle of the 'storehouse' and proper use of sacred resources: 'Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse...and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven.'

The Lord establishes principles of stewardship and proper accounting: 'The properties of the church...belong to the church...nevertheless, by the order of the church it was appointed unto this end' to care for God's house and institutions.

commentary.historical_context: Temple renovation projects in ancient Judah required extensive financial organization. The discovery of silver 'in the house' likely refers to accumulated donations, tax revenues devoted to the Temple, or precious metals displaced during the chaos of earlier religious neglect under Manasseh. The Covenant Rendering notes that the verb hittikhu ('melted down') indicates professional metalworking—the silver was being refined and cast into usable forms for payment or use in Temple work. The administrative structure described here (royal secretary, supervisors, appointed workers, careful financial tracking) reflects the bureaucratic sophistication of the Judean monarchy during Josiah's reign. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Levantine sites shows that major building projects involved hierarchical management with clear lines of authority and responsibility.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 29:38-40 describes King Mosiah's establishment of judges and proper administrative structures for the care of the people and the Lord's work. Like Shaphan's report here, it emphasizes accountability and proper stewardship of resources devoted to sacred purposes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 51:13-14 addresses proper accounting for Church resources: 'And let my servant Aaron have appointed unto him...to keep the Lord's storehouse...that every man...may receive according to his labor.' The financial report in this verse reflects the principle that sacred resources require careful stewardship and accountability.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple renovation itself is an act of covenant renewal and physical restoration of the Lord's house. The financial stewardship described here is part of the broader pattern of the people demonstrating fidelity to the covenant through devoted care of the Temple.

commentary.christological_typology: Just as Shaphan reports the proper care and restoration of the physical Temple, Christ is described as the true Temple (John 2:19-21). His body is the sanctuary where God's presence dwells. The faithful stewardship of resources for the Temple prefigures Christ's absolute dedication to His Father's work. 1 Peter 2:5 describes believers as 'living stones' built into a 'spiritual house'—the new Temple.
commentary.application: This verse teaches the importance of proper stewardship and transparent reporting in sacred work. Whether in Church callings, family finances, or personal commitments, members are invited to emulate the integrity described here—careful handling of resources, proper distribution to those doing the work, and willingness to report honestly on progress. The routine nature of this administrative report should not diminish its significance: faithful attention to the details of stewardship is itself a form of devotion. Modern members might ask: How carefully do I steward the resources (time, money, talents) devoted to God's work? Am I willing to give an honest account of how I've used them?

text_kjv: And Shaphan the scribe shewed the king, saying, Hilkiah the priest hath delivered me a book. And Shaphan read it before the king.

commentary.narrative:
After presenting the routine financial report, Shaphan shifts abruptly to deliver the extraordinary news: Hilkiah the priest has given him a book. The understated announcement—'Hilkiah the priest hath delivered me a book'—uses the indefinite article 'a book' rather than 'the Book of the Law,' suggesting that Shaphan may not yet fully grasp the scroll's significance or divine authority. The shift from financial accounting to the scroll's discovery creates a narrative rupture. What began as mundane business suddenly pivots to world-changing news.

Shaphan then reads the scroll aloud before the king (va-yiqra'ehu Shaphan lifnei ha-melekh). This formal public reading transforms the silent text into living speech. The verb 'read' (qara) can mean both to read privately and to proclaim publicly; in this context, with the king as audience and the formal setting, it clearly implies oral proclamation. The king is hearing words that define Israel's covenant with God—words that have been silent and absent from the nation's consciousness for decades. The text does not tell us how much of the scroll Shaphan reads, or precisely which portions create the shock that leads to Josiah's response in the next verse. But the very act of reading aloud breaks the silence and allows the scroll's prophetic voice to speak into the present moment.

The narrative structure is masterful: routine → extraordinary discovery → formal proclamation. The king moves from hearing about finances to hearing God's covenant requirements read aloud. The effect would be jarring and transformative.

word_study.meaning: from the root nagad, 'to tell, inform, report, declare'; suggests the communication of news or significant information. The prefix va- indicates past action ('and he informed/reported').
word_study.significance: The verb introduces the announcement as formal reporting to the king. This is not casual conversation but official communication of information the king needs to know.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'a scroll gave to me Hilkiah the priest'; the word order (scroll first, then the priest) emphasizes the object given. The verb natan ('give, deliver') indicates formal transfer of the scroll to Shaphan's care.
word_study.significance: The indefinite 'a book' rather than 'the Book of the Law' (which will be used in v. 11) suggests Shaphan has not yet identified its significance. Shaphan is reporting the fact of the scroll without yet understanding its covenant authority.

word_study.meaning: from the root qara, 'to read, call out, proclaim'; the prefix va- indicates past action. In the context of a scroll before a king, this clearly implies formal reading aloud, not silent study.
word_study.significance: The verb transforms the silent text into prophetic utterance. The scroll, which had been lost and silent, now 'speaks' through Shaphan's voice to the king. This is the same verb used for prophetic proclamation, elevating the reading to the level of divine speech.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'before the face of the king'; the phrase indicates direct audience with royal authority and implies formal, public proclamation in the king's presence.
word_study.significance: The reading is not private but official and formal. The king hears God's covenant word through his secretary's voice, making the scroll's message an immediate matter of state and spiritual concern.

cross_references.connection: Moses commanded: 'When all Israel is come to appear before the LORD thy God...thou shalt read this law before all Israel in their hearing.' Shaphan's reading echoes the covenant practice of publicly proclaiming God's law.

A similar scene after the Babylonian exile: Ezra 'read in the book of the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.' Public reading of God's law transforms and reforms the covenant people.
Jeremiah commands Baruch to read the scroll of God's words before the people and king. Like Shaphan, Baruch reads God's written word before authority figures, with profound consequences.

Nephi describes his father Lehi's vision in which an angel shows him God's word written in a book. The scroll becomes a vehicle for God's covenant voice—written, then spoken, then received by those who will hear.

The Lord declares: 'Wherefore, the voice of the Lord is unto all men...Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants.' The scroll's proclamation represents God's voice speaking to the king through Shaphan's faithful service.

commentary.historical_context: The practice of formal, public reading of significant texts was central to ancient Near Eastern political and religious life. Royal scribes (like Shaphan) were educated in reading, writing, and interpretation—they were not merely record-keepers but interpreters of official documents and, in this case, sacred texts. The king's audience with his scribe would have been a formal setting, likely involving witnesses. The identification of the scroll as 'the Book of the Law' in verse 11 (rather than the indefinite 'a book' here) suggests that as the reading progressed, its legal and covenantal significance became apparent. The scroll format itself—rolled papyrus or leather—would have been recognizable to someone of Shaphan's training. The speed with which Josiah recognizes the scroll's authority (evident in v. 11, where he tears his robes upon hearing its words) suggests that certain portions of the text contained specific prophecies or divine judgments that resonated with the king's spiritual consciousness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 5:11-14 describes Lehi reading from the brass plates before his family: the written word is made living speech for a specific audience at a specific moment. The result transforms understanding and commitment. Similarly, Shapan's reading makes the ancient text alive and present.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 describes the role of the prophet receiving and declaring God's word: 'He shall receive instruction from one who is mighty and strong...Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words.' Shaphan, though not a prophet, serves as a conduit for God's written word to reach the king.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The scroll discovered in the Temple represents the Temple as a repository of God's covenant word. In LDS theology, temples are places where God's word is taught and received. The formal reading here prefigures the formal declaration and covenant-making that occurs in the Temple.

commentary.christological_typology: Shaphan reading the scroll prefigures the role of apostles and prophets who proclaim Christ's words. Luke 24:27 describes the Risen Christ reading from the scriptures to the disciples: 'beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.' The scroll's proclamation, transforming the king's understanding, anticipates the power of God's word when truly heard. Revelation 1:3 promises a blessing on those who 'read, and they that hear the words of this prophecy'—the act of reading God's word aloud carries transformative power.
commentary.application: This verse emphasizes the transformative power of hearing God's word proclaimed aloud. Modern members often encounter scripture privately through reading. Yet this verse invites us to consider the power of hearing God's word formally proclaimed—in sacrament meetings, in priesthood blessings, in family home evening, in formal study groups. Sharing and proclaiming God's word is not merely intellectual transmission but a spiritual act that allows the text to speak into our present moment with new power. For families and individuals: How often do we formally read and discuss God's word together aloud? What would change if we treated our scripture study, prayer, and discussion more like the formal proclamation Shaphan offered the king—not casual background, but deliberate, focused, prophetic communication?

text_kjv: And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes.

commentary.narrative:
The king's response is immediate and visceral: upon hearing the words of the Book of the Law, Josiah tears his garments (va-yiqra et begadav). This action is not mere theater; it is the recognized gesture of profound anguish, mourning, and repentance in ancient Levantine culture. The action signals a complete rupture in the king's understanding. What had been hidden or unknown is now revealed with devastating clarity.

What specifically triggers Josiah's response is not stated, but scholars generally recognize that portions of Deuteronomy contain extensive blessings for obedience and severe curses for disobedience. The king, hearing these words for the first time (or the first time in his conscious political awareness), suddenly recognizes the gap between what God demands and what the nation has been practicing. Manasseh's reign had introduced pagan practices into the Temple; the people have been forsaking the covenant; and the scroll now articulates the divine judgment that must follow such abandonment. Josiah's tearing of his clothes is not grief for the dead but terror before the living word of God—recognition of imminent divine judgment.

The shift from verse 10 to verse 11 is dramatic: 'And Shaphan read it before the king' (v. 10) → 'And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words...that he rent his clothes' (v. 11). The transition from the act of reading to the consequence of hearing illustrates the power of God's word. The scroll had been silent for decades; now, proclaimed aloud, it penetrates the king's consciousness and produces immediate, involuntary response. Josiah cannot remain unmoved. The covenant word carries authority and demands response.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'when the king heard the words'; the verb shama ('to hear, listen, obey') in Hebrew encompasses not just acoustic reception but understanding and obedience. To hear God's word is to receive it with the expectation of response.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests that Josiah does not merely hear sounds but truly hears/understands the import of the words. In Hebrew thought, to hear God's word implies the obligation to obey.

word_study.term_english: words of the book of the law
word_study.meaning: Literally 'the words of the scroll of the law/instruction'; divre ('words, matters, things') emphasizes that the scroll contains concrete stipulations, not abstract philosophy. The Torah is presented as divinely-authored speech.
word_study.significance: These are not mere historical documents or wise sayings but covenantal utterances—God's direct speech establishing requirements and consequences. Josiah hears them as such.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'and he tore his garments'; from the root qara, 'to tear, rend'; begadim ('garments') refers to clothing. The action is the conventional physical manifestation of profound grief, shock, or repentance.
word_study.significance: This gesture is used throughout scripture to express anguish before God (2 Samuel 3:31, Isaiah 36:22, Job 1:20). For a king to tear his clothes in the presence of his servants is to make a public declaration of his inner state—his acceptance that divine judgment is warranted and his admission of the nation's corporate failure.

cross_references.connection: The curse passages in Deuteronomy, likely part of the scroll Josiah heard, detail devastating consequences for covenant disobedience. Josiah's anguished response likely reflects his recognition of these curses as descriptive of Judah's actual condition.

The prophet describes God's judgment on Manasseh and the house of Judah: 'I am bringing such evil upon Jerusalem...that whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle.' The covenant curses Josiah now hears were preceded by prophetic warnings.

King Hezekiah, hearing a threatening message, tears his clothes and enters the Temple—a similar response to crisis and the need for divine intervention. Like Hezekiah, Josiah's next action is to seek prophetic counsel.

Alma the Younger's conversion involves a sudden, wrenching recognition of his sins and God's judgment: 'And I was tormented with fear of the awful judgments of God.' Josiah experiences a similar rupture—conviction of covenant failure and fear of judgment.

The prophet Joseph Smith describes receiving God's word: 'And while we meditated...the veil was taken from our minds.' The scroll's words remove a veil from Josiah's understanding of Judah's condition.

commentary.historical_context: Tearing of garments was a culturally recognized gesture across the ancient Near East, serving as a visible, public sign of inner emotional state. Archaeological and textual evidence from Egypt and Mesopotamia show similar practices. The gesture was particularly significant when performed by a king—monarchy in the ancient world was partly a performance of divine approval and stability. A king tearing his clothes publicly admitted that something had gone profoundly wrong. For Josiah specifically, the scroll's words about covenant blessings and curses would have resonated with the religious and political crisis Judah faced: the kingdom was smaller, economically stressed, and dependent on its loyalty to the Assyrian Empire (a status that would shift during Josiah's later reign). The scroll articulates a theological explanation for Judah's weakness: covenant unfaithfulness brings divine judgment. Josiah's immediate response—tearing his clothes—indicates he accepts this theological interpretation and recognizes the urgency of response.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin's discourse in Mosiah 2-5 produces a similar response: 'And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying: Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us' (Mosiah 5:2). The words of God's covenant spoken aloud produce conversion and commitment. Later, 'when they heard these sayings they were filled with joy' and 'they took upon them the name of Christ' (Mosiah 5:5-8). The reading of God's word causes transformation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:1-2 describes the word of the Lord 'crying unto all men to repent...and prepare themselves for the judgment which is to come.' The scroll does the same—its words cry out judgment and call to repentance. Josiah's response—anguish followed by action—prefigures the response expected to divine proclamation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Josiah will take his anguish and the scroll's message to the Temple through the prophet Huldah (v. 14). The Temple becomes the setting where divine word and human repentance meet. In LDS theology, the Temple is where covenant people encounter God's word and renew their commitments.

commentary.christological_typology:
Josiah's anguished response to God's covenant word prefigures the response demanded by the Gospel of Christ. Romans 7:9 describes Paul's recognition of sin when confronted with God's law: 'When the commandment came, sin revived, and I died.' Christ's message, like the scroll's words, produces conviction and the choice to repent or resist. The tearing of clothes anticipates the 'rending of the veil' (Matthew 27:51) when Christ's death opens access to God's presence. Hebrews 10:19-22 invites believers to enter God's presence with 'a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience.'

More directly, Christ in Luke 24:25-27 responds to disciples' spiritual blindness with a question: 'O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Ought not Christ to have suffered these things?' The text, proclaimed, produces understanding and response—as the scroll does for Josiah.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern readers with a question: When do we truly hear God's word? Josiah's immediate, involuntary response—tearing his clothes—suggests that authentic encounter with God's word produces observable change. The action is public, costly, and irreversible (torn clothes cannot be restored). This raises uncomfortable questions for contemporary covenant members: When last did scripture strike us with similar force? When did God's word produce not mere intellectual assent but genuine transformation? The verse suggests that such encounters are possible when we approach scripture not with casual familiarity but with the expectation of meeting God. Modern members might ask: Do I treat scripture as living word capable of piercing my self-deception, or as familiar text I can domesticate? What would change if I approached scripture the way Josiah approached the scroll—as a message that demands everything, that reveals my condition before God, and that calls me to immediate repentance?

text_kjv: And the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Achbor the son of Michaiah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asahiah a servant of the king, saying,

commentary.narrative:
Immediately following his anguished response to the scroll, Josiah takes decisive action. He commands five delegates to form a delegation, establishing a formal commission to seek divine guidance about the scroll's implications and his nation's standing before God. The composition of this delegation is highly significant and tells a story about Judean governance and the integration of religious and civil authority.

The delegation includes: (1) Hilkiah, the high priest—the chief religious authority who discovered the scroll; (2) Ahikam son of Shaphan—a court official who will later protect the prophet Jeremiah from execution (Jeremiah 26:24), indicating he was sympathetic to God's word; (3) Achbor son of Micaiah—another senior administrator; (4) Shaphan—the royal scribe who read the scroll aloud; and (5) Asaiah—the king's personal attendant (eved ha-melekh, literally 'servant of the king'). This is not a random collection but a carefully balanced group representing both religious and civil authority, bureaucratic expertise, and personal trust.

The sequence of names suggests a hierarchy: the high priest is named first, emphasizing that this is fundamentally a theological and religious crisis, not merely political. Yet the civil authorities are equally represented, indicating that the king understands this as a matter requiring integrated response from both spheres. Notably absent from the delegation are military officials or prophets (though the delegation will consult with a prophetess, Huldah, in the following verse). The choice to send bureaucrats and religious officials rather than warriors suggests Josiah's understanding that this crisis requires wisdom and divine guidance, not military response.

The phrase 'and saying' (le-amor) indicates that what follows (in v. 13) will be Josiah's instructions to this delegation. The king has already determined the path: he must understand what the scroll means and what God requires of him and his nation. The urgency and specificity of his command—naming each delegate individually—demonstrates that he views this as a matter of ultimate importance requiring the best counsel available.

word_study.meaning: from the root tsavah, 'to command, order, direct'; the prefix va- indicates past action. The king's command establishes a formal, official delegation.
word_study.significance: The verb indicates royal authority and the establishment of an official mission. This is not a casual suggestion but a binding command from the throne.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'the priest the great'; this is the title of the chief priest of Israel, the highest religious authority in the Temple system. The high priest presided over Temple worship and maintained the sacred rituals.
word_study.significance: Hilkiah's position as high priest gives him unique authority to interpret the scroll's meaning and to access the Temple's sacred spaces. In Israel's religious hierarchy, the high priest was the intermediary between God and the people.

word_study.meaning: Ben ('son of') links individuals to their families and establishes genealogical connection; eved ('servant, attendant') describes a trusted official or personal aide. The mixed terminology reflects different types of relationships and authority.
word_study.significance: The delegation is defined both by formal titles/positions and by personal relationships. Ahikam is identified by his father Shaphan, establishing family connection; Asaiah is identified as the king's personal servant, establishing direct loyalty. This mix suggests both institutional and personal dimensions of authority.

word_study.meaning: An official in the king's household with direct access and personal loyalty to the monarch. Such servants often handled sensitive matters requiring discretion and trustworthiness.
word_study.significance: Asaiah's inclusion suggests the king's desire for direct, personal oversight of the delegation's mission. This is not merely bureaucratic procedure but a matter the king monitors closely.

cross_references.connection: Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah from execution by hostile Temple officials: 'Nevertheless the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, that they should not give him over to the people.' His inclusion in Josiah's delegation suggests he was receptive to prophetic word.

After receiving Huldah's prophecy (v. 15-20), Josiah commands the high priest to bring out pagan vessels from the Temple. Hilkiah immediately executes the king's orders, demonstrating his willingness to act on the scroll's implications.

A parallel account provides the king's specific command to the delegation: 'Go, inquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found.' The delegation's mission is to seek divine wisdom about the scroll.

An earlier king (Ahab) gathers prophets to inquire about a military campaign. Josiah similarly gathers officials for spiritual counsel, but Josiah's inclusion of civil and religious authorities suggests a more balanced approach to seeking God's guidance.

The Lord establishes the principle of seeking counsel: 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.' Josiah's delegation seeks counsel from those he trusts to represent God's will.

commentary.historical_context: The composition of Josiah's delegation reflects the actual power structure of the late Judean monarchy. High priests held significant authority over Temple affairs and religious interpretation. Royal scribes (like Shaphan) held important administrative and advisory roles and often had formal education in law and religious texts. Court officials and the king's personal servants formed an inner circle of trusted advisors. Delegations like this one were a common mechanism in ancient Near Eastern governance for investigating matters of importance. The decision to include both religious and civil authorities suggests an understanding that the scroll's discovery was not merely a religious matter but affected the entire nation—its covenant status, its political legitimacy, and its future. The fact that the king personally names each member of the delegation (rather than simply summoning 'officials') emphasizes the gravity and specificity of the mission. The delegation is not generic but carefully chosen for their particular insights and trustworthiness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 27 describes the coming forth of God's word in the latter days and the need for faithful servants to receive and interpret it. Like Josiah's delegation seeking understanding of the scroll, modern revelation requires authorized recipients and interpreters. Mosiah 11:27 describes King Noah's assembly of priests to make decisions—here Josiah assembles leaders for a righteous purpose.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 establishes that God's word 'shall all be fulfilled, whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants.' Josiah seeks understanding through authorized servants—the high priest and trusted officials. D&C 9:8 invites seeking counsel: 'This is the spirit by which truth is spoken.' The delegation's mission reflects the principle of seeking divine guidance through proper channels.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The delegation's mission will lead them to the Temple to consult with the prophetess Huldah. The Temple becomes the place where covenant matters are resolved and God's will is revealed. In LDS theology, temples are settings for receiving divine direction and understanding God's purposes.

commentary.christological_typology: Josiah's establishment of a commission to understand God's word anticipates Christ's choice of apostles to carry and interpret His message. Matthew 10:1-4 describes Christ calling twelve apostles to whom He gave authority. The delegation chosen by Josiah to interpret the scroll parallels the apostolic office—representatives authorized to understand and communicate God's will. The integration of religious and civil authority in Josiah's delegation foreshadows Christ's role as both priest and king (Hebrews 5:5-6, Revelation 1:6).
commentary.application: This verse emphasizes the importance of seeking wise counsel when confronted with challenging truths or important decisions. Josiah does not respond to his anguished recognition of covenant failure by acting alone; instead, he assembles trusted advisors representing different forms of expertise and authority. Modern members are invited to emulate this pattern: When faced with significant spiritual or moral questions, do we seek counsel from appropriate authorities—ecclesiastical leaders, scripturally knowledgeable members, trusted advisors? The composition of Josiah's delegation also suggests the importance of both religious and practical wisdom. A balanced approach to spiritual matters may require both prophetic insight (represented by the high priest) and administrative wisdom (represented by civil officials). For families and individuals: How do we seek counsel? Do we recognize the need for guidance from more than one perspective? Do we create space for both spiritual and practical wisdom in our decision-making?

text_kjv: Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.

commentary.narrative:
Josiah has just learned that a scroll—the Book of the Law—has been discovered during temple renovation (2 Kings 22:8). The high priest Hilkiah reads it aloud to Shaphan the scribe, who reports it to the king. Upon hearing the contents, Josiah tears his clothes in grief (2 Kings 22:11), a gesture signaling his recognition that Judah has violated covenant commitments. Now he commands his officials to inquire of the LORD about this book's implications.

What is remarkable here is Josiah's theological reasoning. He does not ask whether the scroll is authentic or whether its curses apply to him. Instead, he assumes the worst and acts accordingly. His phrasing—'for me, and for the people, and for all Judah'—includes himself in the collective guilt. He does not exempt the throne from the nation's apostasy. This is covenant thinking at its most mature: a leader who recognizes that disobedience has accumulated across generations, and that he himself stands under judgment along with everyone else.

The 'great wrath' (gedolah chamat YHWH) that Josiah perceives is not theoretical. He has read the scroll's covenant curses—likely the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy—and he understands that these are not merely warnings but descriptions of what will happen if Israel breaks faith. His fathers did not listen; now the consequences are coming due. Josiah's desperate urgency stems from his belief that divine judgment is active and imminent.

word_study.meaning: Heat, burning anger, divine wrath. In covenant contexts, this term describes the active, consuming punishment that God unleashes when His commands are violated. It is not passive anger but kinetic judgment.
word_study.significance: Josiah perceives chama not as a distant threat but as already 'kindled' (nitzta)—already burning. The verb nitzta means to be set on fire or ignited. For Josiah, the scroll is not a theoretical warning; it is a prophecy of judgment already in motion.

word_study.meaning: To hear, listen, obey. In Hebrew, shama encompasses both the physical act of hearing and the moral commitment of obedience. To truly 'hear' God's word is to align one's actions with it.
word_study.significance: Josiah's confession uses the perfect tense: 'our fathers have not hearkened' (lo shamru). This is not a excuse but a diagnosis of generational sin. The fathers heard the law but refused to obey it—they heard but did not listen in the covenant sense.

word_study.meaning: To seek, search, inquire, especially to inquire of God through a prophet or oracle. Darash implies both intellectual seeking and spiritual submission—the inquirer seeks truth and commits to follow the answer received.
word_study.significance: Josiah does not consult the scroll privately; he commands his officials to 'darash et YHWH'—to seek the LORD himself, through prophetic channels. This shows he understands that the question requires divine interpretation, not human speculation.

cross_references.connection: This passage contains the covenant curses that Josiah has just read. The scroll discovered in the temple likely contained this material, explaining why Josiah's response is terror rather than curiosity.
Immediately preceding context: the book is found, Hilkiah reads it, and Shaphan reports to the king, setting up Josiah's urgent command to seek the LORD.
After receiving Huldah's oracle (verses 15-20), Josiah will gather all Judah and Jerusalem and read the book covenant before them, demonstrating how this moment transforms into covenant renewal.

Contrast: Jehoiakim's response to Jeremiah's scroll is to burn it and arrest the prophet. Josiah's response to the Law is to repent and seek God—showing the difference between kings who fear God and those who resist Him.

In the Book of Mormon, sacred records are described as instruments of preservation and judgment—this parallels how Josiah treats the discovered scroll as both a warning and a call to covenant fidelity.

commentary.historical_context:
The scroll discovered during Josiah's reign is almost certainly a version of Deuteronomy or a collection of Deuteronomic law. The temple renovation would have provided opportunity for ancient documents to be found in hidden chambers or beneath debris. Josiah's reaction suggests this was not merely a rare manuscript but a text whose authority was immediately recognized—perhaps because it bore marks of great antiquity or because its language resonated with what the people already knew of covenant law.

Culturally, Josiah's decision to consult a prophetess (not a high priest) about the scroll's significance reflects standard Judean practice. Prophets were the primary means by which God communicated specific, binding messages to the king. A king who inquired of the LORD through proper channels demonstrated his submission to divine guidance. Josiah's urgency also reflects the 8th-century Assyrian threat that had destroyed the northern kingdom (Israel) a century earlier. Judah would have been acutely aware that it too was vulnerable to judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 1:1-8, King Benjamin describes the importance of preserving written records so that future generations might know the words of God and the history of their people. Josiah's discovery and his urgent reading of the scroll mirror this principle—the written word becomes the means of covenant renewal. Also, Alma 37:8-9 teaches that 'small and simple things' (like preserved records) lead to great things, including salvation. The scroll's survival and discovery serves the salvation of Judah (at least temporarily).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 states, 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the covenants which I have made with you shall be enforced.' Josiah's desperate search for the meaning of the covenant text reflects this principle—the commandments are not negotiable, and covenant obligations are binding regardless of how long they have been neglected.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The scroll is found during temple renovation, a work of sanctifying the house of God. In LDS understanding, the temple is the place where covenant relationships are established and renewed. Josiah's journey from discovering the book to renewing the covenant (2 Kings 23:2-3) mirrors the pattern of the endowment—receiving understanding of obligations and then solemnly covenanting to keep them.

commentary.christological_typology: Josiah's response to the discovered Law prefigures the role of prophets and kings in leading people to covenant renewal. Though Josiah himself is not a type of Christ, his urgent action to align the nation with written covenant law reflects Christ's own mission: to call people back to the covenant relationship with God. In Matthew 5:17, Jesus declares, 'I am not come to destroy the law... but to fulfil.' Josiah seeks to fulfill the law after centuries of violation; Jesus comes to fulfill it perfectly and establish a new covenant through His blood.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse challenges us to ask: When we encounter the Lord's word—whether in scripture, conference talks, or personal revelation—do we respond with Josiah's urgency, or do we defer? Josiah understood that a scroll does not sit unread; it demands a response. Similarly, our relationship with scripture and prophetic guidance requires active engagement, not passive possession. The verse also teaches the power of collective responsibility: Josiah does not blame his ancestors and move on; he includes himself in the guilt and seeks mercy for the whole people. This is a model for how communities of faith should approach their heritage—acknowledging past failures while committing to renewed obedience.

text_kjv: So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her.

commentary.narrative:
The king's command to inquire of the LORD is immediately executed. Five of Judah's most powerful officials—including the high priest Hilkiah, the royal scribe Shaphan, and the official Achbor—travel to the home of a woman named Huldah. This detail is extraordinary. In the ancient Near East, prophetic authority was typically, though not exclusively, held by men. Yet when the highest officials of the kingdom need to know God's will, they do not hesitate to go to a woman.

Huldah is identified with remarkable specificity: she is the wife of Shallum, who is keeper of the wardrobe (shomer ha-begadim). This was a palace position of some importance—it could mean oversight of royal garments or, in some interpretations, sacred priestly vestments. That her husband is named at all suggests Huldah's authority was recognized independently of his position, yet the text also establishes her as embedded within the institutional structures of Jerusalem. She lives in the 'Second Quarter' (Mishneh), a newer section of the city on the western hill, developed during the monarchy and populated by officials and the upper class.

The delegation's willingness to travel and consult her—'they communed with her' (va-yedabbru aleha)—demonstrates that prophetic authority transcended gender. The text presents this as entirely natural, requiring no explanation or justification. Later Jewish tradition would venerate Huldah as one of the greatest prophets of Israel, comparable to Jeremiah and Isaiah. Her oracle in the following verses carries the full prophetic formula and binding authority.

word_study.meaning: The feminine form of navi (prophet). A neviah is a woman who receives and communicates messages from God. The term carries the same authoritative weight as its masculine counterpart; there is no diminishment in the title.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's translator notes highlight that neviah appears only a handful of times in the Hebrew Bible (for Miriam, Deborah, Isaiah's wife, and Huldah). Huldah's designation as neviah grants her full prophetic status. She is not a counselor or wise woman but a prophet—someone who speaks on behalf of God. The five officials approach her exactly as they would approach any male prophet.

word_study.meaning: One who guards or maintains garments. In a royal or temple context, this could refer to oversight of priestly vestments, royal robes, or both. It was an administrative position within the palace hierarchy.
word_study.significance: Shallum's position places him within the institutional structure of Jerusalem governance, even if his rank was not the highest. This grounds Huldah not as an isolated mystic but as a person embedded in Judean society—she has a husband, a home, and connections to the palace administration. Yet her prophetic authority stands entirely independent of these social credentials.

word_study.meaning: Second, second part, or second quarter. In Jerusalem's topography, the Mishneh referred to a newer section of the city, developed during the monarchy period, likely on the western hill. It was a residential and administrative center where officials lived.
word_study.significance: The detail that Huldah lived in the Mishneh places her in a prestigious neighborhood. She was not a marginal figure in a remote location but an established resident of Jerusalem's upper class. This reinforces that her prophetic authority was recognized and integrated into the city's institutional and social life.

cross_references.connection: Deborah is described as a prophetess (neviah) who judged Israel. Like Huldah, she held authority that transcended her gender, demonstrating that prophetic calling in Israel was not gender-restricted.
Miriam is called a prophetess (neviah) and leads the women of Israel in song after the exodus. She, too, demonstrates that women could hold full prophetic authority in ancient Israel.
Immediately preceding: Josiah tears his clothes upon hearing the scroll, then commands Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asahiah to inquire of the LORD, setting up this delegation.
After Huldah's oracle, Josiah gathers 'all the elders of Judah and of Jerusalem' to read the book before them, showing how her word catalyzes national covenant renewal.

Saul seeks out the medium at Endor when he needs to consult the dead Samuel. Though this woman is not a prophet but a medium, it shows that in desperate times, kings would seek out women with special spiritual access, even when other channels were unavailable.

commentary.historical_context:
Archaeological evidence supports the existence of a 'Second Quarter' (mishneh) in Jerusalem during the monarchy. Excavations on the western hill have revealed that this area was developed during the 8th-7th centuries BCE as a residential district for the upper classes and officials, expanding Jerusalem beyond the original City of David. This archaeological reality makes Huldah's residence in the Mishneh historically plausible and emphasizes her social standing.

The consultation of a prophetess was not unusual in Israelite practice. The Old Testament records several instances where kings or the people sought out prophets (both male and female) to understand God's will. Prophets were the recognized channels through which God communicated His specific will to the nation. That Huldah is female is presented matter-of-factly in the text, suggesting that by the time this narrative was written, such consultations were simply part of institutional practice. Her recognition by the highest officials of the kingdom—five powerful men—demonstrates that prophetic gift, once recognized, transcended social hierarchies based on gender.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Doctrine and Covenants 25:3-5, the Lord addresses Emma Smith in a revelation and gives her responsibilities comparable to those of male leaders in the Church. Later, in D&C 109:22, the temple is to be a place where 'the veil is taken from our minds.' Huldah's role as a prophet who conveys God's direct word to the leadership of Judah parallels the principle that in God's kingdom, the gift to receive and communicate revelation is not gender-dependent. Similarly, in the Book of Mormon, we see women like Abish (Alma 19) and Sariah (1 Nephi) exercising significant spiritual agency and influence.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 teaches that the President of the Church should 'receive counsel from all those around him.' This principle reflects something Josiah already understood: that seeking God's will requires consulting those whom the Spirit has appointed to receive revelation. Huldah's role in Judah's covenant renewal parallels the function of sustained leaders in the Church—they are instruments through which God communicates His will to the people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In LDS temple theology, women hold priesthood power in partnership with men in the context of covenant ordinances. Huldah's unquestioned authority to receive and communicate God's word to Judah's leadership reflects a principle of shared spiritual authority that is restored in the temple. She is not a priesthood holder in the modern LDS sense, but her role demonstrates that God's communication with His people is not restricted by gender when the Lord calls someone to such service.

commentary.christological_typology: While Huldah is not a type of Christ, her role as a messenger who brings God's word to the nation's leaders prefigures the role of all prophets: to call people to covenant fidelity and warn of consequences. Christ himself is the ultimate Prophet, but He works through subordinate messengers (prophets and apostles) to accomplish His purposes. Huldah's authority to pronounce God's judgment and mercy, even though she is a woman in a male-dominated society, points forward to the principle that in Christ's kingdom, the barriers of gender, class, and status are dissolved in the face of spiritual authority.
commentary.application: This verse teaches modern members that spiritual authority and the capacity to receive revelation are not determined by social status, gender, or institutional rank. Huldah was consulted by the most powerful men in Judah because she had demonstrated the gift to receive God's word. For members today, this is a reminder that seeking truth requires humility—being willing to learn from anyone the Lord has equipped to teach, regardless of their position or background. It also affirms that women's spiritual authority is integral to the covenant community, not supplementary. Finally, the verse demonstrates the importance of establishing and trusting institutional channels through which God's word comes to the people. The delegation did not send just anyone; they sent the high priest and official scribes, treating the consultation with Huldah as a formal inquiry before God.

text_kjv: And she said unto them, Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Tell the man that sent you to me,

commentary.narrative:
Huldah's response begins with the formal prophetic messenger formula: 'Thus saith the LORD God of Israel' (koh amar YHWH Elohei Yisra'el). This language signals that what follows is not Huldah's own interpretation or opinion but a direct communication from God. The formula appears hundreds of times in the prophetic books and carries binding authority. When a prophet says these words, the people are hearing God's voice through a human intermediary.

Notably, Huldah refers to Josiah as 'the man that sent you to me' (ha-ish asher shalach etkhem elai) rather than using his title, 'the king.' This is not disrespect; it is prophetic perspective. In the presence of God's word, all human titles and honors fade. The king is simply a man, answerable to God like anyone else. This detail reflects a crucial principle in ancient Israel: no one—not even the king—stood outside the covenant or above the law. Before God, all are equal subjects.

The oracle is carefully structured: first, a message for the nation (verses 16-17); then, a separate and distinct message for Josiah himself (verses 18-20). This division reflects Huldah's understanding that Josiah, though he rules over the nation, bears his own personal responsibility before God. His individual repentance, though genuine and significant, does not change the corporate judgment coming upon Judah.

word_study.meaning: A formula meaning 'this is what the LORD says' or 'the word of the LORD is.' This is the standard prophetic messenger formula, comparable to the opening of an official proclamation or embassy dispatch. It asserts that the speaker is relaying a message from a higher authority.
word_study.significance: By using this formula, Huldah claims full prophetic authority. She is not offering advice or interpretation but conveying God's direct speech. The formula authenticates her as a true prophet and makes her message binding on all who hear it. This same formula was used by every recognized prophet in Israel—Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others.

word_study.meaning: A man, a person, a human being. When used generically, it emphasizes the person's fundamental humanity rather than their office or status.
word_study.significance: The choice to call Josiah 'the man' (ha-ish) rather than 'the king' (ha-melekh) is deliberate. It signals that before God, institutional authority is secondary to covenant obligation. The king is first and foremost a person responsible to God, just as any subject is. This reflects the covenantal theology of Deuteronomy, where even the king is bound by the same law as everyone else (Deuteronomy 17:18-20).

cross_references.connection: Moses instructs that even the king must make a copy of the law and read it all the days of his life, so he might keep the covenant. Huldah's address to 'the man' (Josiah) echoes this principle—the king is not exempt from the law but bound by it.

When Jeremiah receives his call, God tells him to speak all that the Lord commands, and the formula 'Thus saith the LORD' becomes the mark of his authenticity. Huldah's use of this same formula places her in the same prophetic tradition.
Samuel addresses King Saul with 'Thus saith the LORD,' making clear that even Israel's king is subject to divine judgment communicated through prophets.

In the Book of Mormon, when sealed records are opened, it says the voice of the Lord will come forth, and people will recognize it. Huldah's formula authenticates her message as the voice of God speaking through her, comparable to how prophets in all dispensations authenticate revelation.

commentary.historical_context:
The prophetic messenger formula 'Thus saith the LORD' appears to have been standard in Israel and throughout the ancient Near East. Prophets were understood as messengers (malakhi YHWH, 'messengers of the LORD') conveying a message from the divine realm to the human realm. By beginning with this formula, Huldah situates herself within a recognized institutional and linguistic framework. She is not claiming to be the source of her message but merely its conduit. This language would have been immediately recognizable to the officials consulting her and would have authenticated her as speaking with prophetic authority.

The use of 'the man' (ha-ish) rather than 'the king' also reflects something significant about Judean political theology. Unlike some ancient Near Eastern kingdoms where the king was deified or placed above the law, Israel's covenant framework (based on Deuteronomy) made even the king a subject of the law. Kings were chosen by God (1 Samuel 16:13), but they were not gods themselves and could not exempt themselves from covenant obligation. Huldah's language assumes this framework.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 1:18-20, Lehi is called a prophet and teaches the people with prophetic authority. The text makes clear that his calling came directly from God and carried binding weight. Similarly, when Alma speaks, the narrative often introduces his words with language indicating he speaks with prophetic authority. Huldah's formula and her authority parallel these examples of how the Lord communicates through called servants.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:38 states, 'Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' This principle is embodied in Huldah's oracle. When she says 'Thus saith the LORD,' she is asserting that her voice is delivering God's voice. This same principle authenticates all prophetic speech in the Restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, members hear the voice of the Lord through the words of officiators. The authorization to speak for God—to deliver His message with His authority—is a function of the priesthood. Huldah's authority, though not priesthood in the modern LDS sense, functions analogously: she is authorized to convey God's word to His people, and that word comes with divine power.

commentary.christological_typology: Huldah's use of the prophetic messenger formula, 'Thus saith the LORD,' points to all the Old Testament prophets who spoke on God's behalf, preparing the way for Christ. Christ Himself will later say, 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6), claiming to be not merely a messenger of God but God Himself. In this sense, Huldah represents the line of faithful prophets who testified to God's covenant and prepared the way for the ultimate Word—Christ, who is the Word made flesh (John 1:1-14).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse emphasizes the importance of trusting the words of prophets and apostles who speak with the authority of the Lord. When a prophet uses this language—whether in scripture, general conference, or official declarations—members are hearing God's word, not mere human opinion. The verse also teaches that position and title, while important for order and organization, do not change a person's fundamental standing before God. A king is still a man; a president is still a person. Before God, all are equal. This should humble those in leadership and invite all members to take the Lord's word seriously, whatever their status. Finally, the verse teaches that true prophecy comes with a characteristic mark: it claims to come from God, not from personal insight. Any claim to speak for God without this foundation should be questioned.

text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, even all the words of the book which the king of Judah hath read:

commentary.narrative:
Huldah's oracle now states the first (and worse) part of God's judgment. The word 'evil' (ra'ah in Hebrew) here refers to disaster, calamity, or judgment—the comprehensive term for what befalls a place or people when divine wrath is enacted. This is not moral evil but the concrete experience of judgment: destruction, death, exile, or some combination thereof.

The phrase 'all the words of the book which the king of Judah hath read' is crucial. Huldah confirms that the scroll Josiah has discovered contains words that will come to pass. The book is not an abstract warning or a historical record; it is a prophecy. Every curse written in it will be fulfilled. The discovery of the book does not avert judgment; it merely explains its cause. The judgment is already fixed because the sin is already committed—generations of apostasy under kings like Manasseh and Amon have incurred a debt that cannot be paid by a last-minute reform.

This is one of the most theologically demanding moments in the Bible. Josiah has repented; he has torn his clothes, sought the Lord, and committed to reform (2 Kings 23:1-3). Yet the judgment on the nation is not lifted. Huldah is telling him that his personal righteousness matters—it will spare him from seeing the worst (verse 20)—but it cannot save the nation. This reflects a crucial distinction in Hebrew thought: personal covenant responsibility and corporate judgment are not identical. One person's obedience cannot undo the structural consequences of a nation's long-term disobedience.

word_study.meaning: Evil, disaster, calamity, misfortune. In prophetic contexts, this term refers to the judgment or punishment that God sends in response to covenant violation. It is the opposite of 'good' (tov) and refers to concrete suffering.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'disaster,' which captures the sense better than 'evil' in modern English. Huldah is not saying that God will cause moral wickedness to befall Judah, but that He will send concrete judgment—destruction and suffering. This disaster is not arbitrary but the direct result of covenant violation.

word_study.term_english: all the words of the book
word_study.term_original: אֵת כׇּל־דִּבְרֵי הַסֵּפֶר (et kol divrei ha-sefer)
word_study.meaning: Every word of the book; all the words recorded in the scroll. This phrase indicates that the curses written in the document will be comprehensively fulfilled—not just some, but all.
word_study.significance: Huldah's use of 'all the words' means that every threat, every curse, every judgment recorded in the scroll will come to pass. This is unambiguous and unconditional. The scroll contains not mere advice or conditional warnings but binding prophecies that will be enacted.

cross_references.connection: This passage lists the comprehensive curses that will fall upon Israel if the covenant is broken. Huldah's oracle that 'all the words of the book' will be fulfilled likely refers to these curses being enacted on Judah.

After describing Josiah's reforms, the narrator explains, 'Notwithstanding the LORD turned not from the fierceness of his great wrath... because of all the provocations that Manasseh had provoked him withal.' This verse explains why Josiah's repentance, though genuine, does not avert national judgment.

Jeremiah is called to 'pluck up and break down, to destroy and throw down.' Like Huldah, Jeremiah is a prophet sent to announce that judgment, once decreed, will come to pass, and no human action can prevent it.

After Jerusalem's fall, the poet writes, 'The LORD hath done that which he had devised; he hath fulfilled his word.' This reflects the same principle: divine judgment, once announced through the prophets, is executed.

In the Book of Mormon, Alma teaches that justice cannot be denied—if mercy is extended without justice, law itself is destroyed. Huldah's announcement that God's judgment will proceed reflects this principle: God's justice must be satisfied.

commentary.historical_context:
The judgment Huldah announces aligns with the historical facts: Judah would fall to Babylon in 586 BCE, just decades after Josiah's death. The temple would be destroyed, the people exiled, and Jerusalem left in ruins. Huldah's oracle proves historically accurate. This retrospective accuracy—from the perspective of later readers who knew what happened—would have authenticated her as a true prophet. The text was likely composed after the exile and would have read to that audience as a confirmation that God's word, delivered through Huldah, had indeed come to pass.

The scroll itself, almost certainly a version of Deuteronomy, contained curses for covenant violation (Deuteronomy 28:36-37 explicitly threatens exile to another nation, exactly what happened to Judah). Huldah's authority partly rested on her ability to interpret these ancient curses and apply them to her present moment. She was not inventing judgment but reading it in the text and confirming its relevance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 45:10-14, Alma prophesies that the Nephites will eventually be destroyed because of their wickedness, even though righteous individuals will be preserved. Like Huldah's oracle, this shows that personal righteousness does not guarantee corporate preservation. Also, in 2 Nephi 25:10-13, Nephi teaches that though he and his family are righteous, their descendants will eventually fall away, and judgment will come upon them. This parallels Huldah's distinction between Josiah's personal reward (mercy from judgment) and Judah's corporate fate (destruction).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 95:1-8 contains the Lord's rebuke to the Saints and His command to build a temple. Like Huldah's oracle, it combines warning of judgment with an opportunity for repentance and course correction. However, unlike Huldah's announcement that judgment is already fixed, the Lord's word to the Saints leaves room for intervention through obedience.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The discovery of the book in the temple (2 Kings 22:8) and Huldah's oracle about its curses point to the temple as the place where covenant obligations are most clearly articulated and where their violation is most seriously judged. In LDS understanding, the temple is where covenants are renewed and where understanding of our obligations to God is deepened.

commentary.christological_typology: Huldah's role in announcing judgment foreshadows the role of John the Baptist and the prophets who preceded Christ. They announced that judgment was coming and called for repentance. However, with Christ's atonement, the possibility emerges for judgment to be suspended or transformed through grace. In this sense, Huldah's uncompromising announcement of judgment points to the law's role in revealing humanity's need for redemption—the law condemns; Christ redeems.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern members with a hard truth: personal repentance, though valuable and necessary, does not exempt us from all consequences of collective sin. If we live in a society or community that has drifted from covenant principles, our individual righteousness may save us spiritually but may not prevent us from experiencing the external consequences of corporate judgment. The verse teaches us to take covenant violation seriously—when the Lord has spoken a warning through the scriptures, that warning is not casual or negotiable. It also teaches that judgment can be as much about maintaining justice as about demonstrating mercy. God's character requires that sin have consequences; otherwise, justice itself is destroyed. Finally, the verse urges members to seek understanding of covenants and their obligations. The scroll is found and read because Josiah commits to understanding it. We too must be diligent to understand what God has revealed about covenant keeping.

text_kjv: Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands; therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and shall not be quenched.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 17 provides the reason for the judgment announced in verse 16. The language is unambiguous about Judah's sin: 'they have forsaken me' (azavuni) and 'burned incense unto other gods.' These are comprehensive covenant violations. To forsake the LORD is to break the primary commandment of the covenant—that Israel will have no other gods before Him (Exodus 20:3; Deuteronomy 5:7). Burning incense to other gods violates this at the deepest level, making idolatry not a private preference but an act that directly provokes God's anger.

The phrase 'with all the works of their hands' suggests that idolatry is not a passive sin but something the people have actively constructed and maintained. They have made idols and altars, burned incense in their own temples, and systematically dedicated their energies to gods other than the LORD. This is not a cultural drift but an intentional rebellion. The phrase 'all the works of their hands' recalls the second commandment's warning against carved images made 'by the hands of man' (Deuteronomy 4:28).

The final clause—'my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and shall not be quenched'—is the most devastating. The verb lo tikhbeh ('will not be quenched') indicates that God's anger, once lit, will burn until it consumes what it is meant to consume. The metaphor of unquenchable fire is used elsewhere in Scripture to describe final or ultimate judgment (Jeremiah 4:4, 17:27; Matthew 3:12). In the context of Judah's covenant violation, it means that the judgment is not temporary or reversible but will proceed to completion.

word_study.meaning: To forsake, abandon, leave, desert. In covenant contexts, this verb describes the breach of a relationship—the rejection of a covenant partner and the obligations that bind them together.
word_study.significance: Azab is not merely the sin of adding another god; it is the sin of rejecting the relationship itself. When the text says 'they have forsaken me,' it indicates that Judah has turned away from the LORD as a covenant partner, actively renouncing the relationship. This is the most serious covenant violation possible.

word_study.meaning: To provoke, to irritate, to vex, to arouse anger. This is deliberate provocation, not accidental offense.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures this with 'provoking me'—the intentionality is key. Judah is not inadvertently drifting toward idolatry; they are deliberately provoking God through their choices. This language underscores moral culpability.

word_study.meaning: Wrath (intense anger) and to quench (to extinguish or suppress). The combination suggests fire that, once ignited, cannot be put out.
word_study.significance: The metaphor of unquenchable fire emphasizes the finality of the judgment. God's wrath is not something that can be negotiated away or gradually appeased. It will burn until judgment is complete. This echoes the covenant curses in Deuteronomy 28-29, where disobedience leads to destruction that cannot be reversed by later half-hearted repentance.

cross_references.connection: The first two commandments prohibit idolatry and the worship of other gods. Huldah's indictment directly recalls this foundational covenant requirement and its promised consequence: God's wrath.

This passage describes Manasseh's long reign, during which he 'did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD' and 'built altars for all the host of heaven' (verses 5-6). Huldah's reference to 'other gods' and 'all the works of their hands' directly indicts the idolatry Manasseh institutionalized.

Jeremiah prophesies similar judgment: 'Raise up a lamentation... the generation of his wrath' (verse 29), and 'I will pour out my fury upon this place... and it shall not be quenched' (verse 20). Huldah and Jeremiah speak with one voice about God's unquenchable judgment against idolatry.

The covenant curses in Leviticus promise that if Israel rebels, God will 'walk contrary unto you... in fury' and send such judgment that the land becomes desolate. Huldah's oracle echoes and applies these ancient covenant warnings.

King Benjamin teaches that those who 'knowingly commit sin' against God will 'have brought upon themselves' the wrath of God. This parallels Huldah's language about deliberate provocation—Judah has knowingly chosen idolatry.

commentary.historical_context:
The idolatry Huldah condemns was not invented late in Judah's history but had deep roots, particularly during the long reign of King Manasseh (687-642 BCE), approximately 50 years before Josiah. Manasseh is described in 2 Kings 21:1-17 as having reversed the religious reforms of his father Hezekiah, building altars for Baal and setting up an Asherah pole (a symbol of the goddess Asherah). He is even said to have placed a carved image in the temple itself. Though later he repented (2 Chronicles 33:12-13), his long reign institutionalized idolatry throughout Judah.

When Huldah speaks of 'all the works of their hands,' she is referring to the accumulated religious infrastructure of idolatry: temples, altars, carved images, and the rituals associated with them. This was not marginal practice but the official state religion for much of Judah's recent history. Josiah's discovery of the book and his subsequent reforms (2 Kings 23:4-20) aimed to dismantle this entire system, but Huldah's oracle indicates that the damage has already been done at the level of covenant relationship.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 1:13-17, King Benjamin warns his people about idolatry and the provocation it brings to God. He teaches that to serve 'false gods and the traditions of our fathers' is to 'commit transgression against' God. Also, in Alma 9:9-10, Alma condemns the people for their idolatry: 'Ye have broken the covenant which the Lord made with you.' Both passages, like Huldah's oracle, treat idolatry as the breaking of covenant relationship.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:32-33 states, 'I the Lord am merciful and gracious unto those who fear me and obey my commandments, and revile not against me; but unto those that keep not my commandments a day of wrath awaits them.' This echoes Huldah's principle: those who 'provoke' God through disobedience face unquenchable wrath.
