It prefigures the perfection of worship that Christ would establish—a worship that would not be temporary or subject to subsequent decline but would be eternal and unchanging (Hebrews 10:10-14). Christ's single, perfect sacrifice and his permanent intercession make obsolete all previous priesthoods and sacrifices, establishing a new covenant that supersedes Josiah's restoration of the old one.
commentary.application: This verse haunts us with its irony: spiritual heights can precede spiritual catastrophe. Josiah's people were at their finest at the moment before their worst. This teaches us that covenant faithfulness is not a destination but an ongoing commitment. We cannot rest on past righteousness. The verse challenges modern Latter-day Saints: Are we living as though we are at the apex of covenant restoration, or are we vigilantly maintaining the commitment required to sustain the restoration? Do we treat our own moments of spiritual insight and recommitment as permanent achievements, or do we understand them as current points of alignment that must be maintained through consistent obedience? The verse also invites sobering reflection: What would a future historian say about our spiritual condition? Are we moving toward greater faithfulness or declining from it? The implicit question is: Will this be remembered as a moment of peak covenant devotion, or as a period of decline masquerading as righteousness?

text_kjv: But in the eighteenth year of king Josiah, wherein this passover was holden to the LORD in Jerusalem.

commentary.narrative:
This verse provides a precise chronological anchor: the great Passover occurred in Josiah's eighteenth regnal year. This is the same year in which the scroll was discovered in the temple (mentioned in 2 Kings 22:3), establishing that all of Josiah's religious reforms—the discovery of the law, the temple purification, the destruction of idolatrous sites, and the greatest Passover celebration in Israel's history—transpired within a single year of spiritual revolution. The concentration of these transformative events in one year suggests both the intensity of Josiah's commitment and the completeness of the reformation he attempted to institute.

The dating also has political significance. Josiah was born in 648 BCE and became king around 641 BCE at age eight. If he was in his eighteenth regnal year in approximately 623 BCE, this places the reformation during a period of Assyrian decline and before Babylon had consolidated power. The historical window was narrow—a brief moment when Josiah could act with authority over the northern territories without great power interference. The verse's specificity suggests that the narrator saw the year 623 BCE as historically decisive, the moment when Israel's spiritual restoration peaked before its final collapse.

The verse's placement here, after the summary of how the Passover surpassed all previous ones, emphasizes the historical record: this achievement is dated, placed, fixed in time. It is not mythological or legendary but historical fact—in the eighteenth year of Josiah, this thing happened. The location "in Jerusalem" connects the Passover explicitly to the central sanctuary, the temple, the covenantal center of David's kingdom. The celebration was not scattered throughout the land but unified at the single authorized place of worship.

word_study.meaning: Shmoneh ('eight') esreh ('ten') shanah ('year'). The ordinal counting of Josiah's reign years from his accession. The eighteenth regnal year is the consistent point at which major events occurred in Josiah's reform narrative.
word_study.significance: The specific numbering (eighteenth, not 'many years later') emphasizes historical precision. The narrator is not offering legendary material but datable historical record. The concentration of events—discovery, purification, reformation, Passover—all in this single eighteenth year—highlights the intensity and comprehensiveness of the reform.

word_study.meaning: The Passover is 'made' (performed) 'to/for YHWH.' The preposition la ('to') indicates the Passover's purpose and object—it is performed as an act of worship directed toward YHWH.
word_study.significance: By specifying that the Passover was made 'to YHWH,' the verse emphasizes that despite centuries of confusion and idolatry, Israel is now performing this central act of worship with correct understanding of its object and purpose. It is not offered to Baal or to high place deities but exclusively to YHWH.

cross_references.connection: The scroll's discovery is also dated to Josiah's eighteenth regnal year, establishing that the discovery and the Passover celebration are part of a single, coordinated reformation within one year.
The parallel account in Chronicles also dates the scroll's discovery to Josiah's eighteenth year, confirming the chronological coordination of discovery and reform.
The Passover legislation specified in the discovered scroll is dated here—the eighteenth year marks when that legislation was finally implemented as Deuteronomy required.
The ancient prophecy naming Josiah was uttered approximately three centuries before his reign; verse 23 marks the fulfillment of that prophecy in a precisely dated historical moment.

commentary.historical_context: The eighteenth year of Josiah (approximately 623 BCE) falls at a critical juncture in ancient Near Eastern history. Ashurbanipal, the last great Assyrian emperor, died around 631 BCE, initiating Assyrian decline. By 623 BCE, Babylon had not yet fully consolidated power under Nebopolassar (who became king around 626 BCE). This was a window of opportunity when the great powers were in transition and a determined regional king like Josiah could exercise authority over territories that had been under foreign domination. The year's significance is heightened by this geopolitical context: Josiah's reformation was possible only because external powers were distracted or weakened. The concentration of major events in a single regnal year was possible because Josiah had the political and economic resources to mobilize the nation, coordinate temple repairs, command the priesthood, and require nationwide participation in Passover. This would have been logistically challenging and expensive. The fact that all of this occurred in the eighteenth year suggests careful planning and possibly multiple years of preparation, with the eighteenth year representing the public and ceremonial culmination.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 1:1, Benjamin's reign transitions to his son Mosiah, and the reign of the judges begins—a chronological point marking major spiritual change. Similarly, verse 23's specific dating marks Josiah's eighteenth year as the pivot point of his reign's spiritual significance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 110 records specific details of the Kirtland Temple dedication, including the precise date (April 3, 1836) and the specific manifestations that occurred. Like verse 23's chronological precision, the restoration emphasizes exact dating of significant covenant moments.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Passover in Jerusalem, the central sanctuary, anticipates the role of the temple in the restoration. Both represent centralized worship at a specific, authorized location where covenant people gather at specific times to renew their commitment.

commentary.christological_typology: Just as Josiah's eighteenth year marked a pivotal moment in old covenant history, the life of Christ, particularly his crucifixion and atonement, marks the pivotal moment of covenant history itself. The Passover Josiah commanded was celebrated at the same location (Jerusalem) where Christ would later celebrate a final Passover meal, transforming the festival's meaning and establishing the new covenant.
commentary.application: Verse 23's precise dating reminds us that spiritual transformation is not timeless but happens in specific moments and seasons. We can point to dates when our own covenant commitments were renewed or deepened. The verse invites us to ask: What is my 'eighteenth year'—the moment when I discovered spiritual truth and committed to comprehensive reformation? Have I allowed that moment to remain isolated, or have I sustained it through ongoing commitment? The specificity of the dating also suggests that significant spiritual moments should be remembered and commemorated. In the LDS tradition, we mark significant dates (baptism, temple endowment, mission call, etc.). Josiah's people remembered that in the eighteenth year, everything changed. Do we consciously remember our own defining covenant moments? Finally, the verse notes that while the discovery of truth occurred suddenly (the scroll's finding), its full implementation took work and time (preparation for the great Passover). Spiritual reformation is not instantaneous but requires sustained effort to move from understanding to practice.

text_kjv: Moreover the workers with familiar spirits, and the wizards, and the images, and the idols, and all the abominations that were spied in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, did Josiah put away, that he might perform the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
This final verse of the passage provides a comprehensive summary of Josiah's entire purification campaign. The TCR rendering highlights the catalog of what was eliminated: "mediums, spiritists, household gods, worthless idols, and every abomination." This is not haphazard destruction but systematic removal of every category of idolatrous practice and object. The verb "put away" (bi'er, 'to burn, to consume, to sweep away') suggests aggressive, thorough eradication—nothing was exempted or left standing. The scope extends to the entire land of Judah and Jerusalem itself, emphasizing that no territory was exempt and that even the capital city had harbored these practices.

The verse's structure reveals the theological logic driving all of Josiah's actions: "in order to perform the words of the law." Every destruction, every command, every purification was executed not as arbitrary iconoclasm but as obedience to the discovered text. The discovered scroll is not incidental background; it is the explicit and repeated justification for the entire reformation. Josiah is not innovating or imposing personal religious preference but implementing textual authority. The mention that "Hilkiah the priest found" the scroll in "the house of the LORD" anchors all subsequent action in the temple's authority and the priesthood's discovery of authoritative truth.

The five categories of forbidden practices listed deserve attention. "Mediums" (ovot) and "spiritists" (yid'onim) represent divination and consultation of the dead—practices explicitly forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:11. "Household gods" (terafim) are small figurines used in domestic worship, which Laban kept hidden in his tent (Genesis 31:19) and which represent the persistence of household-level idolatry even in ostensibly monotheistic families. "Worthless idols" (gillulim, literally 'dung-idols' or 'hewn images') and the catch-all "all the abominations" (kol ha-shiqquttsim) suggest that the list is not exhaustive but representative of whatever false religious infrastructure existed. Nothing escaped the purge.

word_study.meaning: From the root ob, referring to persons (particularly women, though not exclusively) who claimed to communicate with the dead or with spirits. The 'ob' itself may have been a bottle or container used in divination, hence the medium 'had an ob.' Familiar spirits are spirits supposedly belonging to or familiar with individual houses or families.
word_study.significance: Mediums represent the religious alternative to prophetic encounter with YHWH. While genuine prophets receive word from YHWH, mediums claim access to spiritual knowledge through other channels (dead ancestors, demons, etc.). Their elimination is part of centralizing all spiritual authority around YHWH and his law.

word_study.meaning: From the root 'yd', meaning 'to know.' The yid'oni is one who claims to 'know' hidden things through esoteric knowledge or divination. Unlike ovot (who consult dead spirits), yid'onim may have used other methods of divination—casting lots, reading entrails, interpreting signs.
word_study.significance: The Deuteronomic law (Deuteronomy 18:10-11) explicitly forbids both ovot and yid'onim as incompatible with faith in YHWH. Their removal from the land represents a commitment to receive guidance exclusively through YHWH's revealed law, not through alternative spiritual practitioners.

word_study.meaning: Small carved figurines used in household religious practice. Found in homes, kept hidden, occasionally consulted for guidance. The exact religious function is debated, but they represent the persistence of idolatrous practice at the family level.
word_study.significance: Terafim are particularly significant because they represent how idolatry persisted in ostensibly monotheistic households. A family might participate in temple worship of YHWH while maintaining household gods for private religious purposes. Josiah's purge extended to this level, demonstrating that reformation required eliminating religious duplicity.

word_study.meaning: From the root gll ('to roll, to dung'). Gillulim may be a pejorative term for carved images, literally suggesting they are 'dung' or worthless. The term appears frequently in Deuteronomy and the prophets as a contemptuous designation for idols.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'worthless idols' captures the intentional contempt in the term. The author uses pejorative language to denote these objects, emphasizing their spiritual emptiness and the foolishness of worshiping them.

word_study.meaning: Shiqquts (abomination) fundamentally means something detestable or ritually disgusting. The term is frequently used for pagan religious practices deemed completely contrary to YHWH's will. The plural form 'shiqquttsim' with the universal quantifier 'kol' ('all') creates a catch-all category.
word_study.significance: The use of 'shiqquts' demonstrates how thoroughly the Deuteronomic narrator rejects pagan religious practice. These are not merely 'different' or 'alternative' but 'abominable'—spiritually repugnant. The comprehensive language ('all abominations') ensures nothing is overlooked.

word_study.meaning: From the root br'h, meaning 'to burn, to consume, to sweep away, to purge thoroughly.' The verb appears in contexts of eliminating what is unclean or dangerous. Used for burning chaff (Matthew 3:12), purging sin, and eliminating threats.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'swept away' captures the thoroughness and finality of bi'er. This is not removal for storage or relocation but destruction—these objects were not preserved or hidden but burned, broken, or otherwise rendered unusable.

word_study.meaning: Le-ma'an ('in order to, for the sake of') expresses purpose. Haqim (from the root qwm, 'to stand, to establish, to fulfill') means 'to establish' or 'to fulfill.' The phrase means 'in order to establish/fulfill.'
word_study.significance: This purpose clause is the theological key to the verse. Every action of destruction and purification is not motivated by arbitrary religious preference or political consolidation but by the single purpose of fulfilling the words of the discovered law. The reforms are explicitly obedience-driven.

cross_references.connection: The law explicitly forbids mediums, spiritists, and those who consult the dead, pronouncing them abominable. Josiah's purge directly implements this law.
The prohibition on carved images and idols in the Ten Commandments forms the legal basis for destroying terafim and gillulim. Josiah's campaign fulfills this foundational covenant law.
Manasseh, Josiah's grandfather, practiced divination, sorcery, and made terafim—exactly the practices Josiah is now eradicating. Josiah reverses and corrects his grandfather's apostasy.
Isaiah condemns Israel for filling its land with idols and consulting spiritists and mediums. Josiah's purge represents the implementation of the prophetic condemnation Isaiah pronounced.
The law forbids divination, and specifically commands that Israel not turn to mediums or spiritists (leviticus 19:31). Josiah's removal of these practitioners aligns with Torah law.

commentary.historical_context: The verse's catalog of forbidden practices reveals the religious landscape of seventh-century Judah before Josiah's reform. The persistence of mediums and spiritists demonstrates that pagan religious specialists maintained social roles and presumably clientele—people consulting them for guidance. The prevalence of terafim in homes suggests household-level idolatry was common enough to be normalized. Archaeologically, carved figurines (likely terafim) have been found in Judahite households from this period, confirming the textual evidence. The fact that these practices had to be actively purged suggests they had social momentum and were not simply the preference of a dissident minority. Josiah had to overcome cultural inertia to eliminate them. The comprehensiveness of the purge implies that it was not passive (waiting for people to stop) but active (searching out practitioners and objects). The phrase "that were spied in the land" may suggest a search or investigation to identify remaining practitioners—a kind of religious inquisition designed to ensure nothing was overlooked. This would have been labor-intensive and required enforcement mechanisms.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 24:25-26, the Lamanites who converted to Christ destroy their weapons of war as a covenant sign. Similarly, Josiah's destruction of idolatrous objects and elimination of false religious practitioners represents a covenant sign—a visible, irrevocable commitment to YHWH exclusive worship. Both involve the material destruction of what previously held religious significance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 109:19-20 describes the temple as a place 'made holy, and consecrated' from which 'all unclean things shall be cast out.' Josiah's purification of the land parallels the temple's consecration, extending the principle of holiness beyond the temple to the entire covenant community.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Just as Josiah purged false religious practitioners and objects from the land to establish exclusive worship at the temple, the restoration teaches that the temple is the exclusive place for covenant ordinances. Other practices and spaces, however well-intentioned, cannot replace temple worship. The purification of what is external (objects, practitioners) reflects the purification of what is internal (hearts and minds) necessary for true covenant commitment.

commentary.christological_typology: Josiah's elimination of false spiritual authorities and competing worship centers anticipates Christ's judgment and elimination of all false religious systems. Revelation 19:11-20 depicts Christ as the righteous judge who purges all that is false and establishes exclusive worship of himself. Josiah's reformation is a type of the ultimate purification Christ will execute at his return, when every false system will be destroyed and only true worship will remain.
commentary.application: This verse addresses us with uncomfortable directness: What are the 'mediums, spiritists, household gods, and abominations' in my own spiritual life? These are not merely ancient problems but timeless temptations to seek spiritual guidance outside of authorized channels, to maintain private religious practices inconsistent with open covenant commitment, to allow worthless substitutes to compete with genuine devotion. The verse invites a searching inventory: Are there sources of guidance I consult other than the revealed word of God? Are there practices I maintain in private that contradict my public devotion? Are there worthless things (habits, media, relationships, ambitions) that I have elevated to quasi-religious status? Josiah's thoroughness—he sought out and destroyed 'all abominations'—challenges us to be similarly comprehensive in our own reformation. The phrase 'in order to perform the words of the law' reminds us that the goal is never destruction for its own sake but obedience to what is true. We purge false things not because we are against them but because we are for something greater—covenant devotion to Christ. Finally, the involvement of Hilkiah the priest reminds us that spiritual authority matters. Josiah did not act on personal whim but in response to an authoritative text discovered by authorized priesthood. In our own reformation, we should similarly seek guidance from those who hold priesthood keys and from the scriptures, not from our own opinions or private revelation that contradicts institutional truth.

text_kjv: And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; neither after him arose there any like him.

commentary.narrative:
This verse stands as the theological climax of Josiah's reign and arguably of the entire Deuteronomistic History. The evaluator (the redactor) uses the most unqualified superlative language in the Kings corpus: no king before him, none after him. This is not merely high praise—it is an absolute, bracketed superlative that seals Josiah as the exemplar of covenantal kingship. The phrase 'turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might' deliberately echoes Deuteronomy 6:5, the Shema—the foundational command that love of God requires total devotion. By using this exact language, the text claims that Josiah achieved what every Israelite was commanded to do: complete, undivided allegiance to YHWH.

The addition 'according to all the law of Moses' specifies the standard: not personal piety or military success (the criteria used for other kings), but total fidelity to Mosaic instruction. This creates a poignant theological moment. Hezekiah (18:5) was praised for trust (bitachon); Josiah is praised for obedience (shmirat ha-mitzvot). The text evaluates him not on outcomes but on interior orientation and external compliance. He succeeded where every other Davidic king failed—he actually kept the whole law.

The closing clause 'neither after him arose there any like him' is not merely predictive but declarative. It closes off the possibility of future reform. The Deuteronomistic historian is saying: this was the maximum. Josiah represents the ceiling of what covenant obedience could achieve under the old order. The reader waits for what comes next—surely God will reward such devotion—and the next verse provides one of the most jarring reversals in biblical literature.

word_study.meaning: to turn, return, repent. In covenantal contexts, it means to return to the path of the law after deviation. The qal form 'turned' (shab) emphasizes a decisive reorientation of the whole self toward YHWH.
word_study.significance: This is the language of repentance in the covenantal sense. Josiah 'turned' in the way that Deuteronomy calls Israel to turn (Deuteronomy 4:30, 30:2). Unlike most kings who 'did evil' or 'did good' in fragmentary ways, Josiah enacted the whole turn.

word_study.meaning: Heart: the seat of will, intellect, and moral agency. Soul: the seat of life-force and desire. Might/strength: physical capacity and power. Together, they denote totality—the whole person in every dimension.
word_study.significance: This exact triad appears in Deuteronomy 6:5 (the Shema). By using it to evaluate Josiah, the text claims he fulfilled the greatest commandment in the most comprehensive way. No other king is evaluated using Deuteronomy's language of total devotion. The Covenant Rendering makes clear this is a direct literary quotation, not mere coincidence.

word_study.meaning: The instruction or teaching of Moses—the written Torah. In Deuteronomistic thought, this is the binding standard for all of Israel's life and governance.
word_study.significance: The Deuteronomistic History repeatedly invokes 'the law of Moses' as the measuring stick (Joshua 1:8, 8:31; 1 Kings 2:3). By explicitly stating that Josiah kept 'all the law of Moses,' the text makes his obedience not merely exemplary but comprehensive—he touched every part of the covenant.

cross_references.connection: Contains the Shema ('love the LORD your God with all your heart, all your soul, all your might'), which verse 25 quotes directly to evaluate Josiah. He is the only king in Kings assessed using Deuteronomy's language of total devotion.

Hezekiah's evaluation: 'he trusted in the LORD God of Israel.' Both are superlative kings, but each praised in different terms—Hezekiah for trust, Josiah for obedience. The text presents two models of ideal kingship.
The law of the king: he must write out the law, read it all his days, and keep all its words. Josiah is presented as the only king who actually fulfilled this prescriptive ideal.
Joshua is commanded to meditate on the law of Moses day and night. Like Joshua, Josiah embodies the leader who lives by the written covenant word.
The Chronicler adds that Josiah 'caused all that were present in Israel to serve the LORD their God.' His obedience was not private but kingly—he led the nation in covenant renewal.

commentary.historical_context: Josiah ruled 640-609 BCE, reigning during the final decline of Assyrian power (Ashurbanipal died in 631 BCE; Assyria fell in 609 BCE). His reform coincided with both the discovery of the law scroll (likely Deuteronomy or a Deuteronomistic text) and a period of international instability that allowed him religious freedom. The Deuteronomistic evaluation is not anachronistic—it reflects genuine memory of comprehensive reform: centralization of worship in Jerusalem, destruction of high places throughout the land, and restoration of the Passover festival. Ancient Near Eastern kings were typically evaluated by military success or piety; Josiah's evaluation is unique in emphasizing obedience to a written law code. This reflects the Deuteronomistic historian's conviction that covenant fidelity, not might, is the true measure of kingship.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:36 resonates with the Shema concept: the command to 'align all thy thoughts unto' God parallels the integrated devotion (heart, soul, might) required of Josiah and all Israel. Both texts insist that covenant obedience is not compartmentalized but total.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:45 speaks of principles that 'flourish...without compulsion or restraint.' Josiah's turning was self-motivated—he sought the Lord without external coercion, modeling the internalized obedience required for full covenant commitment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Josiah's restoration of the Temple and centralization of worship prefigure the Restoration principle that God's house is the center of spiritual life. His obedience to the law, his purification of the Temple, and his focus on proper worship anticipate themes the Restoration emphasizes: authorized ordinances, priesthood clarity, and covenant renewal.

commentary.christological_typology: Josiah is not a type of Christ in the Messianic sense, but rather a type of the idealized covenant keeper—what humanity is called to be under law. He represents obedience as the path to life, even though obedience alone cannot reverse national judgment. In the New Testament paradigm, Jesus fulfills what Josiah typified: total, perfect, undivided alignment of will with God's law. Where Josiah's obedience was still compatible with the nation's doom, Jesus' obedience redeems. The comparison illuminates both the nobility of the law and its insufficiency apart from the Atonement.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Josiah's example raises a searching question: Do I turn to God with all my heart, soul, and might, or in measured portions? His life suggests that covenant loyalty cannot be compartmentalized—religion is not one area of life among others but the organizing principle of all life. His evaluation invites modern readers to examine whether their obedience to the law of God (as revealed in scripture, prophetic counsel, and ordinance) is total and comprehensive, or whether they maintain comfortable reserves. The text also teaches the difficult truth that personal righteousness, however perfect, does not exempt us from living in a fallen world subject to larger consequences. Josiah's greatness did not save the nation. This prepares the reader for the gospel understanding: only Christ's redemptive power, not our own obedience, can ultimately reverse the trajectory of sin and death.

text_kjv: Notwithstanding the LORD turned not from the fierceness of his great wrath, wherewith his anger was kindled against Judah, because of all the provocations that Manasseh had provoked him withal.

commentary.narrative:
The single word 'akh' ('yet,' 'notwithstanding,' 'however') at the opening of this verse performs one of the most devastating reversals in scripture. Verse 25 reaches its absolute apex: the greatest king, total obedience, full law-keeping. Verse 26 overturns it entirely. Despite Josiah's comprehensive reform, God does not relent. The wrath is already fixed; the trajectory is already set. This is not a conditional threat that repentance can still forestall but an announced judgment that perfect obedience cannot reverse. The theological problem is staggering: why would God demand perfect obedience (Deuteronomy) if perfection in obedience cannot change the verdict? The Deuteronomistic historian does not resolve this paradox but holds both truths in tension.

The cause of immutable divine wrath is named explicitly: Manasseh. This connects directly to 21:10-15, where God announced through the prophets that Judah would be destroyed 'as I destroyed Israel' because of Manasseh's sins. Manasseh reigned fifty-five years (697-642 BCE)—nearly three times longer than Josiah (eighteen years). During those decades of institutionalized paganism, temple desecration, and bloodshed, a debt was accumulated. Even though Manasseh repented (2 Chronicles 33:12-13), and even though his grandson became the most righteous king ever, the national debt remained unpaid. The wrath had been kindled; it could not be un-kindled by a single generation's reform.

This verse introduces a somber theology of consequences: sin has weight, momentum, and persistence. A nation's trajectory cannot be reversed by one good reign following generations of rebellion. This is not arbitrary divine punishment but rather the logic of covenant breach—once violated at institutional scale, the covenant relationship enters a new phase. Josiah's obedience earns him personal reprieve (as stated in 22:20: he dies 'in peace'), but it cannot reverse the national sentence. The text refuses sentimentality: righteousness is rewarded, but the nation's fate is sealed.

word_study.meaning: A strong adversative particle meaning 'only,' 'however,' 'yet,' 'notwithstanding.' It introduces a clause that contradicts or qualifies what preceded it. This is the particle of reversal.
word_study.significance: In the mouth of the Deuteronomistic historian, akh is theologically devastating. It asserts the impossibility of undoing what has been done. Josiah's perfection is real; the wrath is equally real. Both statements are true, and akh holds them together in tragic tension.

word_study.meaning: The negation of shub ('turn'). Where Josiah 'turned' (shab) to God, God 'did not turn' (lo shav) from His wrath. The same root word is used ironically for obedience and obstinacy.
word_study.significance: The irony is exquisite: verse 25 uses shub for Josiah's turning toward God; verse 26 uses lo shav for God's not turning from anger. Perfect human turning cannot move divine will when the covenant has been fundamentally violated.

word_study.meaning: A burning of the nose, a flaring of anger. The 'great wrath' (appo ha-gadol) is described as a burning fire that has been kindled and continues to burn. This is not a mild displeasure but an active, consuming anger.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's translation 'the burning of his great anger that blazed against Judah' captures the active, ongoing nature of the wrath. It is not a one-time judgment but a continuous state of alienation.

word_study.meaning: Provocations, vexations, things that provoke wrath. The root ke'es means to provoke to anger. Each provocation is a single infraction; together, they create an accumulation that weighs against the nation.
word_study.significance: The plural 'provocations' (all the provocations) suggests not a single heinous act but a pattern, a lifestyle of rebellion. Manasseh's entire reign was a continuous provocation.

cross_references.connection: God announces through prophets that Judah will be destroyed like Israel because of Manasseh's sins, including shedding innocent blood. Verse 26 confirms this sentence is irrevocable.

Huldah the prophetess tells Josiah that God will bring disaster on the place and its people because of covenant violation, but Josiah will not see it because his heart is tender. This verse explains why: the wrath is fixed; Josiah cannot change it, only be spared from it.
Moses predicts that if Israel forsakes the covenant, God will 'remove them from the land in anger, fury, and great wrath.' Manasseh's reign triggered this curse; Josiah's reform cannot cancel it.
God tells Jeremiah that even if Moses and Samuel interceded, He would not relent toward Judah because of Manasseh's sins. No amount of later righteousness can undo the debt.

Paul's doctrine of justification by faith (rather than works) echoes the Deuteronomistic problem: obedience to law is good, but it cannot reverse the verdict already spoken against sin. Grace, not obedience, is the sole basis of acquittal.

commentary.historical_context: Manasseh (697-642 BCE) represents the antithesis of Josiah. His fifty-five-year reign coincided with the height of Assyrian power under Ashurbanipal (668-631 BCE). Judah was a vassal state; Manasseh's adoption of pagan cultic practices likely reflected both coercion from Assyria and political pragmatism. The 2 Kings account reports he restored pagan worship, made an Asherah pole, practiced divination, and 'shed much innocent blood.' By the time of Josiah (640-609 BCE), Assyria was collapsing, but the institutional idolatry of half a century could not be undone in eighteen years. The Deuteronomistic historian's point is theological: national sin has duration and consequences that outlast any individual reformer. Modern archaeology has not recovered specific evidence of Manasseh's reign, but cuneiform records confirm Judah as an Assyrian vassal during this period.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 9:5-6 teaches that a people cannot escape judgment by later obedience if they have apostatized: 'they were in bondage, and none could deliver them except it were the Lord their God...because of their iniquity they were brought into bondage.' The Nephites faced similar immutability of consequences—reform was good but could not reverse the course of national judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:21-23 reveals that even when the Lord offers repeated calls to repentance, if rejected, the time comes when the door is shut and judgment is set. Manasseh rejected God for decades; by Josiah's time, that window had closed.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant relationship between God and Israel, centered in the Temple, had been broken and could not be unbroken by institutional reform alone. The final destruction of the Temple would soon follow, showing that even the holy house itself could not preserve a people apostate at the national level. This foreshadows how true covenant redemption requires not external reform but internal renewal through the Atonement.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse illustrates the insufficiency of the law and human obedience as a solution to covenant breach. Josiah's perfect obedience stands in relief precisely because it cannot undo Manasseh's rebellion. This typological problem—perfect obedience cannot reverse national judgment—points to the need for something beyond law: vicarious atonement. Only Christ's sacrifice, not any human obedience, can reverse the verdict against sin. Where Josiah's obedience was rewarded personally but could not save the nation, Christ's obedience saves the nation (all who believe) and the world.
commentary.application: This verse teaches a profound lesson about the nature of personal righteousness within community. Josiah's example shows that living righteously is always right and always rewarded personally (he died 'in peace'), but it does not exempt us from the consequences of living in a community that has collectively turned away from God. Modern covenant members face a similar reality: personal faithfulness is essential and will be rewarded, but it does not protect us from living through the consequences of a society's apostasy. The text also warns against the fantasy that individual or generational reform can fully reverse institutional sin. Deep, systemic change requires repentance not just in individuals but in the culture itself—a work that may take generations or, ultimately, divine intervention.

text_kjv: And the LORD said, I will remove Judah also out of my sight, as I have removed Israel, and will cast off this city Jerusalem which I have chosen, and the house of which I said, My name shall be there.

commentary.narrative:
This verse contains the final, explicit divine sentence against Judah. It is God Himself speaking (vayomer YHWH—'the LORD said'), not a prophet, not a narrative voice. The first word 'also' (gam) links Judah's fate to Israel's—the northern kingdom's destruction in 722 BCE is now the precedent for the south. The phrase 'remove from my sight' (asir me'al panai) uses the language of exile: to be removed from God's presence is to be separated from the land, from the Temple, from the covenant relationship itself. The parallel structure is symmetrical and irrevocable: as Israel was removed, so Judah will be removed. The decree is presented as already determined, past tense in its inevitability.

More devastating still is the rejection of what was most precious: Jerusalem and the Temple. 'This city...which I have chosen' (ha-ir ha-zot asher bacharti) invokes the doctrine of Zion's election (found throughout Deuteronomy and the Psalms). Jerusalem was not merely any city but the city God personally selected. The Temple—'the house of which I said, My name shall be there'—invokes the name-theology of Deuteronomy 12, the theological foundation of Deuteronomistic worship. To 'cast off' (ma'asti, from ma'as, 'reject') this city and this house is to revoke both the election of Zion and the presence theology that held Israel together. The 'name of God' (shem YHWH) dwelling in the Temple was the guarantee of divine presence. When that presence is withdrawn, everything is lost.

The theological weight of this verse cannot be overstated. This is not a conditional threat ('if you do not repent, I will remove you') but an announcement of a fixed judgment. It is the answer to the unspoken question at the end of verse 25: 'If Josiah is so righteous, surely God will spare Jerusalem?' The answer is no. Perfect obedience in one generation cannot reverse the verdict spoken against sustained rebellion in the previous generation. The covenant made with David ('your throne shall be established forever'—2 Samuel 7:12-13) now faces annulment. Everything the people believed to be permanent—the city, the Temple, the dynasty, the land—is about to be unmade.

word_study.meaning: To remove, put away, take from sight. The root is asar. The phrase 'from my sight' (me'al panai, 'from my face/presence') means to remove from one's immediate awareness and care.
word_study.significance: This is not mere displacement but a reversal of election. To be 'removed from God's sight' is to lose the status of beloved people. It is the undoing of the covenant relationship that defined Israel's identity.

word_study.meaning: To reject, refuse, despise. This is stronger than 'remove'—it carries the sense of disgust and active rejection.
word_study.significance: The verb ma'as appears in judgment contexts: to be 'cast off' is not just to be displaced but to be rejected as worthless. It is the language of divorce or dissolution of a covenant.

word_study.meaning: To choose, select, elect. This is the language of covenant choice—God's sovereign election of Zion.
word_study.significance: The same word used for Israel's election now is used for the city that God chose. What was chosen can now be unchosen. The stability that chosenness seemed to guarantee dissolves.

word_study.meaning: The divine name dwelling in the Temple was the guarantee of God's presence and accessibility. To have God's name 'dwell' in a place was to have God's character, authority, and blessing localized there.
word_study.significance: This invokes Deuteronomy 12:5, 11, 21 and the entire theology of centralized worship. When the name withdraws, worship becomes impossible and protection is removed.

cross_references.connection: The Davidic covenant promises that David's throne will be established forever and his house secure. This verse revokes that promise: the dynasty and the land will be taken away.
God warns Solomon that if Israel apostatizes, He will cut off Israel from the land and cast off the house He has consecrated. Verse 27 announces the fulfillment of this conditional curse.

The law prescribes that Israel must seek the place where God will cause His name to dwell and bring sacrifices there. This verse announces that God will withdraw that name, ending the system of worship Deuteronomy established.
The psalmist remembers that God rejected the tent of Joseph and chose Mount Zion, loving it. This verse announces that God is now rejecting Zion—the one chosen is being cast off.

Jeremiah warns that as God abandoned the shrine of Shiloh where His name dwelt, so He will abandon the Temple in Jerusalem because of persistent idolatry. This verse is the announcement of that abandonment.

commentary.historical_context: This verse is dated theologically to sometime before 609 BCE (Josiah's death) but most likely reflects the Deuteronomistic historian's retrospective reading after 586 BCE, when Jerusalem fell to Babylon and the Temple was destroyed. The 'choice' theology invoked here—that God elected Zion and the Temple—emerged as a central doctrine during the monarchic period, particularly during the reign of Hezekiah (715-686 BCE) when Jerusalem miraculously survived Assyrian siege (2 Kings 19:34). By the time of the final redaction of Kings, that doctrine had been proven false in political terms: Jerusalem had not been eternally protected. The Deuteronomistic historian reads this as a theological reversal—God's choice was conditional on Israel's obedience, and once violated beyond repair, that choice could be unmade. The 'name theology' invoked here reflects the functional theology of Deuteronomy, not necessarily the more transcendent theology emerging in exilic Judaism (where God's name is distinguished from God's presence).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly cycles through patterns of choice and rejection. Nephi knows that his descendants will eventually be removed from God's sight (2 Nephi 26:15-21). The doctrine that chosenness is conditional and reversible is central to Book of Mormon theology—a people can be chosen and then rejected based on their response to covenant obligations.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 56:3-4 teaches that individuals and peoples are chosen 'by their own agency,' and can be rejected when they rebel. The principle of conditional election appears throughout Restoration scripture. D&C 86 describes the wicked being 'bound in bundles' and 'cast into the fire'—a fate Judah now faces.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: This verse announces the end of the Temple system—the removal of God's name from the house He once sanctified. In Restoration theology, the Temple remains the place where God's name dwells and covenants are made. This verse contrasts the vulnerability of the Aaronic priesthood Temple with the permanence of the restored Temple in the last days. The withdrawal of God's name from Jerusalem foreshadows the centrality of the Temple in the Restoration as the final gathering place.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse presents the ultimate failure of the old covenant: even the Temple, even Zion, even the city God chose cannot survive the apostasy of God's people. In Hebrews 8:13, this obsolescence is interpreted as preparation for the new covenant, where God's presence is no longer localized in a physical temple but in the hearts of the faithful (and ultimately in the body of Christ). Jesus himself became the Temple (John 2:19-21), the dwelling place of God's name. Where the physical Temple could be destroyed, the 'temple' that is Christ's resurrection body is eternal. This verse thus points to the insufficiency of externals (the Temple, the city, the institution) to secure covenant relationship. Only the person and work of Christ can provide the permanent, inviolable presence of God.
commentary.application: This verse delivers a sober truth to modern covenant members: election is not a guarantee but a responsibility. To be chosen by God—as individuals, as members of the restored Church—is conditional on faithfulness. The verse teaches that institutions, even sacred ones, are not self-perpetuating. A people can have been chosen, can have experienced the presence of God, and can then lose that presence through sustained covenant breach. The application is not fearful but clarifying: faithfulness matters; the covenant relationship with God is not automatic but is made and maintained through obedience. For a Church member, this verse asks: Do I treat my membership in the restored Church as a permanent entitlement, or as a conditional privilege requiring sustained covenant-keeping? The Deuteronomistic perspective suggests that complacency about covenants—taking election for granted—is the path to forfeiture.

text_kjv: Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?

commentary.narrative:
This verse follows the standard formula used to close the account of each king in Kings: a reference to a fuller source document (sefer divre ha-yamim le-malke Yehudah, 'the book of the chronicles/annals of the kings of Judah'). Such formulas appear at the end of nearly every royal account and serve a literary function: they signal that the Deuteronomistic History is a selective narrative, not an exhaustive chronicle. The implied reader is directed elsewhere for more details. In Josiah's case, the formula feels almost defensive. The text has just narrated the greatest reformation in Judean history, the discovery of the law scroll, the national Passover, the purification of the Temple—yet it insists that 'all that he did' (et kol asher asah) is recorded in the fuller annals. The formula acknowledges that the sacred history has been selective, that there is more to tell than space permits.

The placement of this formula is strategically significant: it comes after the theological evaluation (verse 25), the divine judgment (verses 26-27), but before Josiah's death (verse 29). The formula thus creates a pause, a moment of narrative transition. It says, in effect, 'the complete record is elsewhere; our focus now turns to how Josiah's reign ends.' This is a marker of literary artistry—the formula is not mere convention but a deliberate pause that heightens what follows: the sudden, shocking death of the greatest king in a single sentence.

For modern readers, the formula raises a historical question: Did such an official chronicle actually exist? Scholars debate whether the 'chronicles of the kings' was an actual document (perhaps official royal records now lost) or a literary convention of the Deuteronomistic historian. Ancient Near Eastern royal archives did exist, and it is plausible that Judean kings kept records. However, no such document survives. The formula may be historically grounded or may be a literary device signaling the limitations of the written record. Either way, the formula functions the same way: it reminds the reader that what we have is interpretation, selection, and theological evaluation, not raw data.

word_study.meaning: The remainder, what is left over. Divre means 'words,' 'acts,' or 'deeds.' The phrase refers to what is not covered in the selective history.
word_study.significance: The word yeter ('rest, remainder') appears consistently in Kings to acknowledge what is not narrated. It is a modest claim: we have selected the theologically significant acts; the complete record is elsewhere.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'the words of the days' or 'the annals.' This phrase refers to official records or chronicles, a form of historical documentation common in the ancient Near East.
word_study.significance: The Deuteronomistic historian claims to draw on earlier sources. Whether the 'chronicles of the kings of Judah' was an actual document or a literary convention, the phrase establishes that the History is not making up Josiah's story but interpreting existing records.

word_study.meaning: A rhetorical question: 'Are they not written?' The question form asserts that the information is written down, publicly accessible, not secret or lost.
word_study.significance: The rhetorical question is a literary device that adds authority. It says: 'Check for yourself; the record is there.' It appeals to an assumption of shared historical knowledge.

cross_references.connection: The same formula is used for Solomon: 'Now the rest of the acts of Solomon...are they not written in the book of the acts of Solomon?' This parallel shows that even the greatest kings' acts are selectively presented; fuller records exist elsewhere.

The Chronicler explicitly references 'the acts of Josiah' and states that they are 'written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.' The Chronicler treats Josiah's acts as historically documented and available for consultation.
The formula is used for Jeroboam II: 'All the rest of his acts...are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?' This shows the formula is standard across both kingdoms.

The formula for Manasseh similarly directs readers to the chronicles: the complete record of his acts is there. This creates consistency in how kings are presented—selectively in Kings, completely in the chronicles.

commentary.historical_context: The reference to an official 'book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah' reflects the practice of ancient Near Eastern kings keeping records of their reigns. Egyptian pharaohs inscribed their deeds on temple walls; Mesopotamian kings commissioned inscriptions recording their accomplishments. The Judean kings likely kept similar records, though none survive as complete documents. The Deuteronomistic historian lived centuries after many of the kings he describes (the final redaction likely occurred in the exilic or early post-exilic period, 6th-5th centuries BCE). His sources for the histories of earlier kings would have been these official chronicles, now lost. The formula acknowledges this gap: 'What I have selected for theological interpretation is available in fuller form in the chronicles.' This adds a note of humility to the History—it is not claiming to be comprehensive but interpretive.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon similarly uses source formulas. Nephi states 'the record is engraven upon the plates of nephi' and repeatedly directs readers to consult fuller records. Mormon edited and selected from vast records (Words of Mormon 1:3-5). Like the Deuteronomistic historian, Book of Mormon editors were selective and theological in their approach, not exhaustive chroniclers.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 speaks of the responsibility to 'be in the church, and attend to all [the Lord's] covenants.' The formula in verse 28 suggests that selective narrative can still convey divine will. Modern revelation in the D&C similarly selects from Joseph Smith's teachings to present what is canonically binding, even though his full teachings are more extensive.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The formula illustrates how the Temple records and the sacred history operate differently. The Temple held complete records; the sacred history presents selected theological interpretation. This mirrors the modern Church's distinction between complete institutional records and the canonized scriptures presented to the membership—both are valuable but serve different purposes.

commentary.christological_typology: The formula does not directly point to Christ, but the principle it embodies—that what is written down is selective and interpretive—applies to all scripture. The Gospels are selective accounts of Jesus' life (John 21:25: 'I suppose...if all were written...the world itself could not contain the books'). Like the Deuteronomistic historian, the evangelists selected from a wider reality to present theological interpretation. Both the Kings narrative and the Gospel accounts are true not by virtue of being exhaustive but by virtue of being faithful interpretations of what matters most spiritually.
commentary.application: This verse teaches readers not to mistake narrative selectivity for completeness. Any historical account—including scripture—is an interpretation, not raw data. The verse invites intellectual humility: we have what is theologically important, but we do not have everything. For modern members, this is a useful principle: the scriptures we have are sufficient for salvation, but they do not answer every historical question or provide every detail. The Deuteronomistic historian's willingness to say 'more is written elsewhere' models intellectual honesty. Applied to Restoration history, it suggests that Church members should welcome both the canonized scriptures and broader historical study, understanding that each serves different purposes. The formula also teaches that what is selectively presented can still be fully true: Josiah's theological significance is not diminished by the existence of fuller records elsewhere.

text_kjv: In his days Pharaohnechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates: and king Josiah went against him; and he slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him.
text_kjv_alt: In his days Pharaoh-nechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria unto the river Euphrates: and king Josiah went against him; and he slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him.

commentary.narrative:
The death of Josiah is reported with stunning narrative minimalism. After twenty-eight verses of detailed theological evaluation, reform narratives, and divine judgment, the greatest king in Judean history dies in a single sentence. 'Pharaoh Neco went up...Josiah went against him...Neco killed him at Megiddo.' The terseness is itself a theological statement: history does not reward virtue; the greatest obedience does not prevent violent death. The narrative refuses to explain, rationalize, or spiritualize Josiah's death. It simply reports the fact.

The geopolitical context is crucial for understanding the event. Pharaoh Neco II (610-595 BCE) was marching northward along the coastal highway to the Euphrates River, where the last remnants of Assyrian power were making a stand against the rising Neo-Babylonian Empire. The Battle of Carchemish (605 BCE) would occur a few years after Josiah's death; Neco was marching to prevent Babylon from consolidating power in the Levant. The phrase 'against the king of Assyria' (al melekh Ashur) almost certainly means 'to assist' or 'in support of,' not 'in opposition to.' Neco's strategy was to prop up Assyria as a counterweight to Babylon. Josiah intercepted Neco at Megiddo (modern Tel Megiddo), a strategically crucial city overlooking the Jezreel Valley and controlling the main highway from Egypt to Syria.

Why did Josiah oppose Neco? The text does not explicitly say. Scholars propose several explanations: (1) Josiah may have been allied with Babylon against Egypt; (2) he may have wanted to prevent Egyptian hegemony over Judah; (3) he may have been reasserting Judean independence after centuries of vassaldom, refusing to allow a foreign army to pass unopposed through his territory. The 2 Chronicles account (35:20-24) adds that Josiah received a direct warning from God through Neco ('God is with me; refrain from opposing God, who is with me, or he will destroy you'), which Josiah ignored. The Kings account provides no such theological explanation—Josiah simply dies. The irony is excruciating: the king who most perfectly obeyed God dies suddenly in a military miscalculation, far from home, cut off in his prime (he was about thirty-nine years old). His greatest obedience did not spare him. Verse 22:20 promised he would die 'in peace' (be-shalom); how does death in battle at a foreign place align with this? The promise was kept in a limited sense—Josiah died before seeing the destruction of Jerusalem—but the manner of death was ignominious. The text holds both truths without resolution: God rewarded Josiah's obedience by not showing him the national destruction, but God also allowed him to die away from his capital, without warning, in an apparently unnecessary military engagement.

word_study.meaning: To go up, ascend. In military contexts, it means to march, to mobilize an army. The direction 'up' (northward) is literal in this case, as Neco is marching from Egypt northward.
word_study.significance: The verb alah is used for both Neco's march and Josiah's opposition ('Josiah went against him'). Both kings are 'going up' militarily. The symmetry suggests equal military commitment on both sides.

word_study.meaning: To meet, encounter, go toward. The preposition liqrat means 'to meet' or 'to encounter.' It can mean either a welcoming meeting or a hostile confrontation. Context determines the sense.
word_study.significance: The same word is used elsewhere for welcoming meetings (e.g., Ruth 3:11, 'go rest... all the people of the city know you are a worthy woman'). Here, in a military context, it means hostile confrontation. But the word itself does not specify hostility—the narrative leaves open the question of motivation.

word_study.meaning: He killed him, caused him to die. This is direct and unambiguous—Neco's soldiers killed Josiah.
word_study.significance: The simplicity of the verb—no heroic resistance, no negotiation, no divine intervention—underscores the finality. Josiah dies suddenly, not as a martyr but as a casualty of international politics.

word_study.meaning: The city of Megiddo, a strategic fortress controlling the Jezreel Valley and main roads between Egypt and Syria. Megiddo was a crucial military checkpoint.
word_study.significance: Megiddo is associated with apocalyptic vision (Armageddon, from Har-Megiddo, 'Mount of Megiddo'). The choice of this location for Josiah's death—a place of strategic importance and later eschatological significance—may not be accident. Kings and battles are determined there (Judges 5:19, 1 Samuel 29:1, 1 Kings 4:12).

cross_references.connection: The Chronicler provides narrative detail absent from Kings: Neco sends a message to Josiah asking him not to interfere, claiming God is with Neco. Josiah disregards the warning and is mortally wounded at Megiddo. The Chronicler adds theological explanation where Kings offers none.

Huldah the prophetess tells Josiah he will be 'gathered to his grave in peace' (be-shalom), not seeing the evil God will bring on Jerusalem. Josiah dies before the exile, but the manner of death—sudden and violent—seems to contradict the promise of 'peace.'
Jeremiah mourns 'Shallum son of Josiah,' Josiah's heir (another name for Jehoahaz), who was taken captive. Jeremiah treats Josiah's death as the moment when doom began to accelerate toward Judah.

The Song of Deborah commemorates battles at Megiddo: 'In heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera.' Megiddo is a place where God fought for Israel; Josiah's death there may suggest divine abandonment.

Though anachronistic, Megiddo later becomes symbolically associated with the final confrontation (Revelation 16:16: Armageddon). Josiah's death at Megiddo foreshadows the ultimate military judgment that comes upon Jerusalem in 586 BCE.

commentary.historical_context: Pharaoh Neco II ruled Egypt 610-595 BCE. Josiah ruled Judah 640-609 BCE, dying at approximately thirty-nine years old (he began his reign at eight years old and ruled twenty-two years before his reform at age twenty-six). The geopolitical crisis was the collapse of Assyria: Ashurbanipal died in 631 BCE, and within a generation, Assyrian power crumbled. By 609 BCE, the last Assyrian forces were besieged at Harran on the Euphrates by the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nabopolassar. Neco marched northward to prevent Babylon from dominating the Levant. Megiddo, located on the main road from Egypt to Syria, was the logical place for Josiah to intercept. The battle's outcome at Megiddo ended Judah's independence; within a few years (by 605 BCE, the Battle of Carchemish), Egypt would be defeated, and Babylon would dominate the region, eventually leading to the exile of Jerusalem in 586 BCE. Josiah's death in 609 BCE thus marks the beginning of Judah's final decline. Archaeologically, Megiddo has been excavated extensively; the city shows evidence of destruction and rebuilding in this period, though the specific battle involving Josiah has not been conclusively identified in the material record.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar deaths of righteous leaders in apparently meaningless circumstances. Captain Moroni dies in his bed without fanfare (Alma 62:51); Alma disappears without record (Alma 45:18-19). The principle emerges that covenant obedience does not guarantee a comfortable death or historical prominence. Righteousness is rewarded spiritually, but the physical world remains subject to chance and mortality.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-9 addresses Joseph Smith's suffering in Carthage Jail: 'All these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good...Thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment.' The principle applies to Josiah: his death was real but was 'a small moment' compared to the spiritual enduring he had already achieved.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Josiah's death, occurring away from the Temple in Jerusalem, symbolically marks the moment when the Temple itself becomes vulnerable. Within a few years, the Temple will stand empty; within seventy years, it will be destroyed. Josiah's absence from Jerusalem at death foreshadows the Temple's loss.

commentary.christological_typology: Josiah's death—sudden, violent, apparently undeserved—lacks any obvious Christological parallel. However, it illustrates the principle that righteousness alone cannot overcome the power of sin and death in the world. Josiah kept the law perfectly, yet he could not save himself or his nation. This points to the need for something beyond obedience to law: redemptive power that overcomes death itself. Christ's resurrection, unlike Josiah's death, overcomes the finality of death and transforms loss into resurrection. Where Josiah's death is an ending, Christ's death is a beginning.
commentary.application: This verse teaches a difficult truth: virtue does not exempt us from suffering or an untimely death. The righteous are not promised exemption from mortality or disaster; they are promised something else. Josiah's death teaches modern covenant members that fidelity to covenant does not mean life will be painless or that we will always understand why suffering comes. The verse also illustrates how individual righteousness is limited in scope. Josiah could not save himself from his own military miscalculation; he could not save the nation from the consequences of past apostasy. The application is both humbling and clarifying: covenant obedience is its own reward (Josiah died 'in peace' spiritually, even if not physically), but obedience does not give us control over circumstances. This prepares the reader for the gospel principle that only Christ's Atonement—not our righteousness—can ultimately overcome death and offer resurrection. For modern members, the verse suggests that we should seek faithfulness for its own sake and for the internal peace it brings, not for the external safety or comfort it might seem to promise.

text_kjv: And his servants carried him in a chariot dead from Megiddo, and brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own sepulchre. And the people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, and anointed him, and made him king in his father's stead.

commentary.narrative:
The verse opens with a somber image: Josiah's body carried by chariot from the battlefield at Megiddo back to Jerusalem. The phrase 'in a chariot dead' (va-yarkibuhu avadav met) emphasizes the reversal—a king who rode in majesty now rides as a corpse. His remains are brought to the capital, and he receives proper royal burial 'in his own sepulchre' (bi-qvurato). This is significant: unlike Manasseh and Amon (21:18, 26), who were buried in the Garden of Uzza (a place outside the royal cemetery), Josiah is buried in the traditional royal tomb. He receives dignity in death; his body is accorded the respect due a king. Yet the funeral cannot alter the reality—the greatest reformer is gone, and with him dies the last hope for Judean independence.

The second half of the verse narrates the succession crisis. 'The people of the land' (am ha-arets)—a term with specific meaning in the Deuteronomistic History referring to the free landowners, the local nobles and property holders, distinct from the Davidic court and the prophetic circles—take initiative in choosing the next king. They select Jehoahaz (also called Shallum in Jeremiah 22:11), one of Josiah's sons, and anoint him, making him king. The bypass of other potential heirs and the popular acclamation suggest either genuine preference or the limited power of the nobility to prevent this choice. Jehoahaz is likely not the eldest surviving son (Eliakim, later renamed Jehoiakim, may have been older), but he is the people's choice. This is the final independent act of Judean resistance—the people choose their king without Egyptian or Babylonian permission. Three months later, Pharaoh Neco deposed Jehoahaz and replaced him with Eliakim (Jehoiakim), reducing Judah to direct vassalage (2 Kings 23:34). The moment of independence sealed in verse 30 is instantly revoked.

Theologically, verse 30 completes the Josiah narrative cycle: a king is born, reforms, dies, and is succeeded. But it also initiates the final decline. Josiah's reign was the exception; what follows is the norm—weak kings under foreign domination, leading inexorably to exile. The verses that follow (31-37) will chart the brief, tragic reigns of the last four kings of Judah. Verse 30 marks the threshold: on one side, Josiah and the possibility of reform; on the other, the last, futile years before destruction.

word_study.meaning: To cause to ride, carry in a chariot. The root rakav means to ride or be carried. In royal contexts, the chariot is the vehicle of status.
word_study.significance: The same word describes royal movement throughout Kings. Here it describes the movement of Josiah's body—a poignant reversal of the living king riding in authority.

word_study.meaning: Dead, deceased. The word emphasizes the state of death, not just the fact of dying. Josiah is carried as a corpse, not a wounded but living man.
word_study.significance: The placement of 'dead' in the phrase 'carried him...dead' emphasizes that there was no hope of recovery, no chance of healing. The king died at Megiddo and is being transported as a body.

word_study.meaning: The people of the land, referring to the free landowners, local nobility, and those with a stake in the land's governance. This is distinct from the urban nobility (sariim) and the prophetic elite.
word_study.significance: Throughout Kings, am ha-arets appears as an independent power broker. Here, they exercise kingmaking authority. Their choice of Jehoahaz suggests they have popular legitimacy but limited political power (their choice will be overturned by Neco within months).

word_study.meaning: To anoint, to consecrate with oil. In Israelite practice, anointing the king was a ritual act conferring divine legitimacy.
word_study.significance: The anointing gives Jehoahaz sacred status as God's anointed (mashiach). Yet this sacred act cannot protect him from imminent displacement by foreign power. The ritual legitimacy is real but powerless against geopolitical reality.

word_study.term_english: made him king in his father's stead
word_study.term_original: וַיַּמְלִיכוּ אֹתוֹ תַּחַת אָבִיו (vayamliku oto tachat abiv)
word_study.meaning: To make/establish as king, in place of/instead of his father. The formula indicates legitimate succession within the dynasty.
word_study.significance: The formula mimics the language used for other successions, but the context is radically different. Jehoahaz succeeds his father not in a stable kingdom but in a kingdom entering its final years.

cross_references.connection: Three months after taking the throne, Pharaoh Neco deposed Jehoahaz and made Eliakim (renamed Jehoiakim) king instead. The independence affirmed in verse 30 is instantly overturned by Egyptian intervention.

Jeremiah laments Jehoahaz (called Shallum), saying 'Do not weep for the dead [Josiah] or mourn him; but weep bitterly for the one exiled, for he shall not return.' The people's choice of Jehoahaz proves disastrous—he will be deported to Egypt.
Manasseh and Amon were buried 'in the garden of Uzza,' outside the royal cemetery. Josiah's burial 'in his own sepulchre' affirms his status as a legitimate and honored king, unlike his predecessors.

The elders of Israel come to Samuel demanding 'Now appoint a king for us.' Like the people of the land in verse 30, they exercise a kingmaking authority, though ultimately subject to divine approval (and, in this case, foreign override).

The Chronicler records the same succession: 'The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah and made him king.' The consistent testimony suggests this was indeed how Jehoahaz came to power—through popular acclamation.

commentary.historical_context: Jehoahaz reigned only three months (609 BCE) before being deposed and exiled to Egypt by Pharaoh Neco, where he died in captivity (2 Kings 23:33-34). The 'people of the land' who anointed him had limited leverage against international powers. The moment captured in verse 30—the last independent choice made by Judean factions—was instantly negated by the arrival of Egyptian authority. Within a generation, Babylon would dominate, and by 586 BCE, Jerusalem would fall. The text thus presents verse 30 as the final act of Judean independence, both elevated (the people retain kingmaking authority) and pathetic (that authority is powerless against foreign powers). Archaeologically, the transition from Josiah to his successors shows a sharp decline in the material evidence of Jerusalem's prosperity and strength. The city, which thrived under Josiah, enters a period of diminishment and vulnerability.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon parallels the moment when a great leader dies and inferior successors take power. After Mormon's death, the Nephites 'did begin to fall into error' (Mormon 1:15). After Mosiah, the people demanded a king (Mosiah 29), rejecting the judges system. The principle appears: when righteous leadership ends, spiritual and political decline often follows. The people may anoint a successor, but without the spiritual stature of the predecessor, degradation occurs.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 speaks of the role of the president of the Church as 'the representative of this church in all things.' When a president dies, the succession is ordained by God, not by popular vote. This contrasts with the am ha-arets anointing Jehoahaz—a human choice that proves disastrous. The Restoration principle is that succession is divinely authorized, not merely popularly affirmed.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Josiah is buried in the royal sepulchre in Jerusalem, affirming the continuity of the Davidic dynasty, even as the dynasty enters its final years. This foreshadows the Restoration principle that even when covenants are broken and institutions fall, the covenant promise to David (2 Samuel 7) is never fully voided. Jesus, as the son of David, ultimately restores what was lost.

commentary.christological_typology: The succession from Josiah to Jehoahaz illustrates the principle of failed human kingship. Josiah was the perfected human king; his successor is weak and powerless. This points to the need for a king who cannot be deposed, displaced, or made irrelevant by time or foreign power. Christ is that king—His throne is eternal; His authority cannot be negated by earthly powers. Where Jehoahaz reigns three months and is then overruled by Pharaoh, Christ's kingdom is 'not of this world' (John 18:36) and therefore not subject to earthly overthrow. The contrast between the powerless succession in verse 30 and the enduring kingdom of Christ illuminates why human kingship, however virtuous, is inherently limited.
commentary.application: Verse 30 teaches several difficult lessons to modern readers. First, it shows that the death of a great leader does not mean the work is finished. Josiah's reform was comprehensive, but the nation was not saved; one generation's righteousness does not guarantee the next generation's fidelity. Church members should not assume that the strength of one leader's vision will automatically be carried forward. Second, the instant displacement of Jehoahaz by Neco (in 23:34) teaches that human authority, however ritually consecrated, is fragile before larger powers. In the Church, this suggests that all positions of authority are stewardships, not permanent holdings. Third, verse 30 illustrates the importance of institutional continuity and the danger of banking everything on a single figure. Josiah's reforms were real and good, but they did not survive his death because they were his reforms, not the people's internalized commitments. For modern members, the lesson is that personal righteousness must be cultivated in oneself and one's household, not merely adopted from a leader. The verse invites reflection: Are my covenants truly my own, or am I riding on the spiritual momentum of Church leaders? What happens to my faith if the leadership structure changes?

text_kjv: Jehoahaz was twenty and three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.

commentary.narrative: Jehoahaz's reign is introduced with a regnal formula that immediately signals catastrophe. At twenty-three years old, he ascends the throne—likely the people's choice, since he was apparently favored over his older brother Eliakim (soon renamed Jehoiakim). Yet the three-month reign represents one of the briefest, most tragic monarchies in Judah's history. This is not a gradual decline but a sudden collapse: Josiah's death at Megiddo in 609 BCE created a power vacuum that Egypt swiftly filled. The notice about his mother Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, grounds his legitimacy in a Judean family and connects him to the southern tribal heartland—but it cannot save him from geopolitical forces beyond Judah's control. The shift from Josiah's transformative reign to Jehoahaz's abrupt exit within weeks underscores how quickly religious reform can be undone when political stability collapses.

word_study.meaning: in/at his kingship; the standard formula marking the beginning of a reign. The preposition be- ('in') emphasizes the state of kingship itself, not just the action of coronation.
word_study.significance: This regnal formula appears throughout 2 Kings to mark each ruler's entry into power. Its brevity here—immediately followed by 'three months'—creates a stark contrast: Jehoahaz 'became king' but did not truly reign. The formula sets up reader expectation for a full narrative arc, which the text immediately frustrates.

word_study.meaning: literally, three lunar months; approximately 90 days. In the ancient Near Eastern world, a reign measured in months rather than years was considered a reign cut short by external force, not by natural succession.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes this signals 'a tragically brief reign.' In the context of 2 Kings, which records most kings' reigns in years (often 10+), three months stands out as virtually stillborn kingship. Jehoahaz never establishes himself; he is swept away by Pharaoh Neco's military campaign before he can even consolidate power or pursue policy.

word_study.meaning: The name likely means 'my father-in-law is dew' (from chatan, 'father-in-law,' and tal, 'dew'). It is a theophoric name expressing blessing through kinship with the divine or with a powerful father-in-law figure.
word_study.significance: Hamutal appears again as the mother of Zedekiah (24:18), meaning she bore Josiah at least two sons who became king—a woman of significant royal influence. Despite her prominence, she could not protect either son from the forces of international politics that engulfed them.

cross_references.connection: Josiah's death at Megiddo is recounted immediately before; his death is the direct cause of the succession crisis that brings Jehoahaz to the throne.
The parallel account in Chronicles adds that the people of the land made Jehoahaz king, emphasizing popular support over Egyptian preference—which made his removal even more humiliating.
Jeremiah explicitly mourns Jehoahaz (called Shallum), predicting he will never return from exile and die in captivity—a lament that confirms the tragic fate alluded to in 2 Kings 23:34.
Zedekiah, Jehoahaz's brother, is also introduced as the son of Hamutal, showing that Josiah's widow bore multiple sons who would sit on Judah's throne during its final years.

commentary.historical_context: The death of Josiah in 609 BCE created a succession crisis at precisely the moment when geopolitical upheaval was reshaping the Near East. Assyria's final collapse (c. 609 BCE) left a vacuum that both Egypt (under Pharaoh Neco II) and Babylon (under Nebuchadnezzar) sought to fill. Egypt initially dominated Judah, and Neco was marching north to support the failing Assyrians when he encountered Josiah at Megiddo. With Josiah dead, the Judean court faced a choice: whom to crown? The people chose Jehoahaz, the younger son (possibly seen as more amenable to popular will), but Neco had other ideas. The three-month reign reflects the reality that a small kingdom caught between imperial superpowers had little autonomy.
