The Covenant Rendering's dating (609 BCE) places this event in the summer of that year, when Neco was consolidating Egyptian control over Judah before marching further north.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of rapid succession and the collapse of religious reform mirrors the cycles described in the Book of Mormon (e.g., Alma 46-62), where political upheaval repeatedly undoes spiritual progress. The people's choice of Jehoahaz parallels moments when Book of Mormon societies chose leaders based on popular will rather than divine guidance, with tragic results.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:36 warns that 'peace shall be taken from the earth, and the devil shall have power over his own dominion.' Jehoahaz's reign illustrates this principle: the peace that Josiah's reforms had created is shattered, and the 'devil'—in the form of imperial violence—sweeps away the young king within months.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Jehoahaz never has time to act on his religious commitment (or lack thereof). The brevity of his reign suggests that even if he had sought to undo his father Josiah's temple reforms, the external crisis would have prevented it. Temple restoration requires stability; empires allow neither.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoahaz's sudden removal from power—unjustly, by foreign force—foreshadows the righteous one who will be unjustly removed. His youth and the people's support for him echo the pattern of the innocent suffering at the hands of worldly power. However, Jehoahaz's subsequent evil (v. 32) distinguishes him from a true type of Christ; he is instead a foil—the king who could have led but was prevented by circumstances beyond his control.
commentary.application: Jehoahaz's story challenges modern believers to recognize that righteous intention is not enough without the time and power to act. His youth and apparent support from the people could not protect him from forces larger than himself. For covenant members, this verse warns that spiritual reform, however sincere, depends partly on circumstances beyond individual control. We are not responsible for geopolitical upheaval, but we are responsible for making the most of whatever platform we are given—no matter how brief. Jehoahaz was given three months; the question for each believer is: what will you do with the time and influence you have?

text_kjv: And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done.

commentary.narrative: Despite Jehoahaz's youth and the apparent hope signaled by his selection, this verse delivers a devastating moral evaluation. The formula 'he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD' appears dozens of times in Kings to mark the spiritual failure of a ruler. What makes this instance startling is the context: Jehoahaz follows immediately after Josiah, described just three chapters earlier as incomparably righteous (23:25). The phrase 'according to all that his fathers had done' is crucial. The translator notes clarify that 'fathers' here refers not to Josiah but to the broader Davidic line—especially the notorious Manasseh and Amon, whose reigns embodied idolatry and apostasy. Jehoahaz, in merely three months, reverts to the pattern of the worst rather than continuing the way of the best. This is the theological scandal of the verse: kinship with Josiah did not instill righteousness; proximity to the temple and its reformed worship did not transform his heart. The brevity of his reign may in fact be God's judgment—a king who rejects reform deserves no long tenure.

word_study.term_english: evil in the sight of the LORD
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'the evil in the eyes of the LORD.' The term ra (evil) in this context refers to spiritual evil—idolatry, covenant-breaking, and injustice—not merely moral evil. 'In the sight of' (be-einei, 'in the eyes of') emphasizes that God sees and judges what is hidden from human sight.
word_study.significance: This formula is the standard deuteronomic evaluation of kings. It appears in 2 Kings 3:2 (Jehoram did evil), 8:27 (Ahaziah did evil), 13:2 (Jehoahaz of Israel did evil), 14:24 (Jeroboam II did evil), and many others. The repetition itself becomes a refrain of failure. For Jehoahaz, despite his apparent promise, this evaluation is immediate and unqualified.

word_study.term_english: according to all that his fathers had done
word_study.term_original: כְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־עָשׂ֖וּ אֲבֹתָֽיו (ke-khol asher asu avotav)
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'just as everything his ancestors had done.' The term avot (ancestors/fathers) can refer to the immediate father or to the broader genealogical line. The phrase ke-khol ('according to everything') suggests complete conformity to the pattern, not partial mimicry.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering translator notes the 'jarring' quality of this statement: Jehoahaz immediately reverts to the worst patterns rather than following Josiah. This suggests that Josiah's reforms never penetrated the royal court's inner circle—the young king, surrounded by the remnants of the old guard, simply continued their ways. The formula implies that evil is the default; righteousness (like Josiah's) is the exception.

cross_references.connection: Josiah is praised as uniquely righteous: 'like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the LORD with all his heart.' The contrast with Jehoahaz's immediate evil demonstrates that righteousness is not inherited but must be personally chosen.
Manasseh's reign, 'according to the abominations of the heathen,' provides the template for evil that Jehoahaz now follows. Jehoahaz abandons Josiah's path and returns to Manasseh's legacy.
The deuteronomic warning against turning to other gods is the theological framework behind the 'evil in the sight of the LORD' formula. Jehoahaz violates the covenant stipulations.

cross_references.reference: 2 Kings 17:2 (parallel formula for Hoshea of Israel)
cross_references.connection: The same evaluation formula appears for northern kings who did evil, showing that apostasy leads to judgment across the divided monarchy.

Jeremiah's oracle on Jehoahaz (called Shallum) does not emphasize his moral evil but his exile; the prophet's focus is on justice and the consequences of his removal, not on religious failure during his brief reign.

commentary.historical_context: The claim that Jehoahaz 'did evil' within three months must be understood carefully. Given that the text provides no specific actions, no mention of idolatry, no narrative detail, the evaluation may be a retrospective theological judgment rather than a historical record of crimes committed. The brief reign—three months—leaves little time for significant action. Some scholars propose that the formula reflects the deuteronomic historian's conviction that any king who fails to eliminate idolatry or who reverts to pre-Josiah patterns is automatically 'evil' in the eyes of the Lord, regardless of what he actually accomplished. The cultural context of the ancient Near East is relevant here: a young king facing immediate foreign domination would have had limited autonomy to pursue any religious policy, good or bad. The judgment may thus be a moral statement about Jehoahaz's heart orientation (what he would have done if he could) rather than a record of his deeds.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that children of righteous parents often fall away (e.g., Alma's son Corianton; Helaman's sons Nephi and Lehi before their conversion). The pattern suggests that covenant faithfulness is not genetic but must be individually chosen. Jehoahaz exemplifies this Nephite pattern: born of a faithful line, he chooses the opposite path.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 93:39-40 teaches that 'every spirit of man was innocent in the beginning; and God cannot take the life of his own image, except it be through the transgression of law.' Jehoahaz's evil is not forced upon him by circumstances but is his own choice, for which he bears responsibility.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Jehoahaz does not engage with the temple reforms his father had championed. His abandonment of Josiah's religious agenda suggests that he either rejected the theological commitments behind it or lacked the will to maintain them. In covenant language, he breaks covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoahaz's reversion to evil contrasts with the typology of the righteous son. He is instead an anti-type: the prince who inherits righteousness but chooses wickedness. This foreshadows the ultimate son, Jesus Christ, who inherits divine righteousness and chooses perfect obedience—the exact opposite of Jehoahaz's trajectory.
commentary.application: This verse confronts believers with an uncomfortable truth: proximity to righteousness does not guarantee personal righteousness. Growing up in a reformed family, in a community of believers, or even in a covenant-keeping household does not automatically make one righteous. Each generation must choose its own spiritual path. The fact that Jehoahaz 'did evil' despite Josiah's example suggests that religious environment influences but does not determine outcome. Modern covenant members must examine their own hearts: Are you following your parents' faith because you have personally chosen it, or merely by inertia? Do you understand the doctrines you profess, or have you inherited them without conviction? Jehoahaz's tragedy is that he had access to Josiah's reforms—the temple, the law, the community of faith—but rejected them. His three-month reign is the physical consequence; the spiritual consequence is judgment.

text_kjv: And Pharaohnechoh put him in bands at Riblah in the land of Hamath, that he might not reign in Jerusalem: and put the land to a tribute of an hundred talents of silver, and a talent of gold.

commentary.narrative: This verse shifts from spiritual judgment to political domination. Pharaoh Neco does not execute Jehoahaz; he imprisons him in bands (shackles) at Riblah, a city on the Orontes River in the region of Hamath (modern Syria/Lebanon). Riblah will become notorious in 2 Kings 25 as the headquarters from which Nebuchadnezzar directs the final destruction of Jerusalem. For now, it serves as Egypt's military and administrative center. The purpose of Jehoahaz's imprisonment—'that he might not reign in Jerusalem'—is clear: Neco removes the king to prevent him from ruling, even if he were released. It is an act of imperial prerogative, executed without trial or negotiation. The financial penalty—one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold—is staggering. The Covenant Rendering translator notes provide scale: approximately 3,400 kg of silver and 34 kg of gold, an immense burden for a small kingdom already traumatized by Josiah's death. The tribute is not simply a fine; it is the cost of Egyptian military occupation and protection against Babylon. Judah has become a vassal state, and this verse marks the moment when the sovereignty of David's line becomes nominal.

word_study.term_english: put him in bands / imprisoned him
word_study.meaning: From the root asar (to bind, to fetter, to imprison). The verb suggests physical restraint with chains or shackles. The qal imperfect form indicates completed action: Neco bound Jehoahaz and held him captive.
word_study.significance: This verb choice emphasizes Jehoahaz's powerlessness. He is not negotiating; he is not in exile by choice. He is a prisoner of war, held by a foreign power. The binding of a king—once the symbol of divine election and power—represents a profound inversion of status.

word_study.term_english: Riblah in the land of Hamath
word_study.meaning: Riblah was a strategic city on the Orontes River, about 70 miles northeast of the Lebanon mountain range. Hamath was a region (and city-state) of central Syria. The phrase marks both a geographic location and a power center.
word_study.significance: Riblah's appearance here and later in 25:6, 20, 21 (as Nebuchadnezzar's headquarters) suggests it was a key administrative and military site for imperial powers operating in the Levant. The fact that Neco chose to imprison Jehoahaz there—rather than in Egypt—suggests that he wanted to maintain control over Judah's foreign policy without physically removing the royal family to Egyptian soil (yet).

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'in his reigning in Jerusalem.' The infinitive construct be-malko emphasizes the act of kingship itself; the phrase specifies the location: Jerusalem, the capital and seat of Davidic authority.
word_study.significance: The phrase clarifies Neco's intent: he is not executing Jehoahaz but removing him from the throne. This suggests Neco respects the institution of kingship (he will install Eliakim in Jehoahaz's place) but asserts his authority to choose who sits on Judah's throne.

word_study.meaning: From the root anash (to fine, to penalize, to punish). The noun means a fine, penalty, or punitive payment. The parallel term in v. 35, me'ah kikkar kesef ('one hundred talents of silver'), specifies the amount as a talent (kikkar), a unit of weight approximately 34 kg.
word_study.significance: The choice of the word onesh (penalty, fine) rather than a neutral economic term (like mas, tax) emphasizes that this is punitive—Neco is penalizing Judah for Josiah's resistance to Egyptian hegemony and for Jehoahaz's brief, unsanctioned reign.

cross_references.connection: Riblah appears again as Nebuchadnezzar's headquarters during the final siege of Jerusalem; the irony is that another imperial power will use the same administrative center to destroy Judah.
This verse records Jehoiakim's later submission to Nebuchadnezzar, marking Judah's shift from Egyptian to Babylonian vassalage—a transition that began with Neco's domination of Judah in 609 BCE.
The parallel account notes that Neco imposed the tribute on Judah and then installed Eliakim (Jehoiakim) as king, showing the sequence: remove the old king, impose penalty, install puppet ruler.

Jeremiah explicitly connects Jehoahaz's exile to God's judgment: 'Weep ye not for the dead...weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more.' The prophet frames Neco's action as a divine sentence.

Isaiah's account of the Assyrian crisis (during Hezekiah's reign) describes Egypt as a 'bruised reed,' a warning about relying on Egyptian protection that proves relevant as Egypt dominates Judah's politics after Josiah's death.

commentary.historical_context: Pharaoh Neco II (r. 610-595 BCE) was an aggressive expansionist who sought to maintain Egyptian control over the Levant in the face of rising Babylonian power. His defeat of Josiah at Megiddo was not accidental but part of his campaign to consolidate Egyptian authority over the coastal kingdoms and trade routes. By imprisoning Jehoahaz (the people's choice) and later installing Eliakim (the compliance candidate) as Jehoiakim, Neco demonstrates the blunt reality of ancient Near Eastern imperialism: a small kingdom's sovereignty is an illusion when a superpower is present. The tribute of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold would have drained Judah's treasury and required heavy taxation of the populace. The Covenant Rendering's note that Riblah was on the Orontes River situates it at a strategic military position controlling the trade routes and movement of armies between Egypt and northern Syria. Neco's choice to imprison Jehoahaz there rather than in Egypt may reflect his intent to maintain direct control over Judah while pursuing campaigns further north against Babylon and the remnants of Assyria.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of conquest and vassal tribute appears in Mosiah 19-22, where Limhi's people are subject to the Lamanites and must pay tribute. Like Jehoahaz, the covenant people of Judah discover that disobedience to covenant leads not just to spiritual judgment but to political subjugation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:80 promises that 'Zion shall escape if she observes to do all things whatsoever I have commanded her.' Jehoahaz and Judah are not observing the commandments; consequently, they do not escape but fall under tributary bondage.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The destruction of Josiah's temple reforms occurs in the political sphere—a foreign power reasserts pagan influence and collects tribute that cannot be used for temple worship or religious observance. The economic cost of vassalage undermines the spiritual restoration that Josiah had initiated.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoahaz's binding and imprisonment at the hands of a foreign oppressor—unjustly, without trial—carries echoes of Christ's binding and trial before Pilate. However, Jehoahaz's imprisonment is a consequence of his own evil (v. 32), whereas Christ's suffering is vicarious and voluntary. The contrast highlights the difference between judgment upon the wicked and redemptive suffering for others.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that spiritual failure has political consequences. Jehoahaz's evil (v. 32) is answered not by a plague or heavenly judgment but by a foreign army and imprisonment. Modern believers should recognize that covenant faithlessness can lead to subjugation in various forms: loss of agency, financial pressure, bondage to poor choices, and dependence on powers that do not honor God. The tributary burden that falls on Judah is borne ultimately by the common people (see v. 35), showing that the sin of leaders cascades downward to affect the vulnerable. Covenant members should also reflect on what 'Riblah' means for them—the places where we are held captive by circumstances beyond our initial control but for which we bear responsibility through our prior choices. True freedom, the verse suggests, comes through covenantal obedience, not through political maneuver or the favor of earthly powers.

text_kjv: And Pharaohnechoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the room of Josiah his father, and turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away: and he came to Egypt, and died there.

commentary.narrative: This verse completes the political transaction. Neco exercises the prerogative of an imperial power: he removes one king and installs another. Eliakim, Josiah's eldest son and brother to Jehoahaz, is made king in place of Jehoahaz. Critically, Neco changes Eliakim's name to Jehoiakim—an act of sovereignty that demonstrates who truly holds power. In the ancient Near East, naming was an assertion of dominion; the one who names rules. The name change from Elyaqim ('God raises up') to Yehoyaqim ('the LORD raises up') is ironic: Neco, an Egyptian pagan, gives his Judean vassal a Yahwistic name. Perhaps Neco understood that Judah's stability required maintaining the appearance of covenant with the God of Israel, or perhaps he simply asserted his authority through the naming itself. Jehoahaz is then taken away to Egypt—not executed on the spot at Riblah but deported. The terse conclusion—'he came to Egypt, and died there'—provides no detail about the manner or timing of his death. The Covenant Rendering's note on Jeremiah 22:10-12 adds weight: the prophet explicitly states that Jehoahaz (called Shallum) will never return and will die in exile. For Judah, the succession has been inverted: the people's choice (Jehoahaz) has been removed and replaced with Neco's puppet. The shift also marks a generational change: Eliakim/Jehoiakim is the eldest brother and will reign for eleven years (v. 36), while Jehoahaz's three-month reign becomes a historical footnote.

word_study.meaning: From the root malak (to reign, to rule, to make king). The hiphil form va-yamlek means 'he made...to be king' or 'he caused...to reign.' The subject is Pharaoh Neco; the object is Eliakim.
word_study.significance: This verb, used of Neco, emphasizes that the Egyptian pharaoh, not the God of Israel or the people of Judah, is determining the succession. In earlier chapters, kings are said to have 'reigned' (malak in qal, passive or intransitive), or they are made king by God (malak in hiphil by divine agents). Here, a foreign power uses the hiphil to assert active control over Judah's throne.

word_study.term_english: in the room of Josiah his father
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'in place of Josiah his father.' The term tachat ('under, beneath, in place of') indicates substitution or succession. The phrase clarifies that Eliakim is succeeding his father Josiah, not his brother Jehoahaz.
word_study.significance: This phrase is significant because it suggests that Neco recognized Josiah's line's legitimacy and was installing Eliakim as his designated successor. However, Eliakim is explicitly not Josiah's chosen successor (that was Jehoahaz, whom the people had made king). Neco is overriding both Josiah's will (if he had designated anyone) and the people's choice. He is imposing his own choice.

word_study.term_original: וַיַּסֵּ֤ב אֶת־שְׁמוֹ֙ יְהוֹיָקִ֔ים (va-yassev et shemo Yehoyaqim)
word_study.meaning: From the root sabab (to turn, to turn around, to change). The phrase 'turned around his name' is a vivid expression of renaming. The new name Yehoyaqim means 'the LORD raises up' (from yeho, 'the LORD,' and yaqim, 'he raises up').
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's translator notes flag the irony: 'the one who names rules.' By renaming Eliakim, Neco asserts dominion. The fact that Neco gives a theophoric (God-referencing) name is either a sign of respect for Judean religion or a calculated political move to make his puppet king appear legitimate to Judeans. The renaming recalls Daniel's experience in Babylon (Daniel 1:7), where captors rename captives to assert cultural and political dominion.

word_study.meaning: Laqach (to take, to seize, to capture) is the verb. The direct object is Jehoahaz. The phrase suggests a deportation or removal, not necessarily violent but definitive.
word_study.significance: The passive voice of Jehoahaz's experience contrasts with the active voice of Neco's actions. Jehoahaz is taken; he does not go willingly. He is an object of imperial will, not a subject with agency.

word_study.meaning: From the root mut (to die, to perish). The word sham (there) specifies the location: Egypt, not Judah. The simple past tense indicates completed action with finality.
word_study.significance: The brevity of this formula—just four Hebrew words—contrasts with the elaborate accounts of some kings' deaths. Jehoahaz's death is noted but not lamented in Kings; the prophet Jeremiah provides the emotional weight (Jer. 22:10-12). The fact that he dies 'there' (in Egypt), far from his homeland, underscores his tragedy: he never returns to Judah.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah explicitly identifies Jehoahaz as Shallum and laments his exile: 'Weep ye not for the dead...weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country.' Jeremiah's oracle confirms Jehoahaz's permanent exile and death in Egypt.
Verse 31 introduces Jehoahaz as the people's choice; verse 34 shows him being displaced by Neco's choice, demonstrating the collapse of popular will before imperial power.
In Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar renames Daniel and his companions, asserting dominion through naming. Neco's renaming of Eliakim operates on the same principle of imperial dominance.
The parallel account provides the same sequence: Neco removes Jehoahaz, imposes tribute, and installs Eliakim/Jehoiakim, emphasizing that the succession was Neco's doing, not Judah's.

Jehoiakim's later submission to Nebuchadnezzar (after a period of Egyptian vassalage) shows that the reigns of Jehoiakim and his successors were determined by the shifting balance of power between Egypt and Babylon, not by any autonomous Judean will.

commentary.historical_context: The sequence of events in verse 34 reflects the geopolitical reality of 609 BCE. After Josiah's death at Megiddo, Neco II faced a choice: execute the entire Davidic line (as the Babylonians would later do) or install a compliant puppet king who would maintain Judah as a stable vassal state. Neco chose the latter, but he needed assurance of loyalty. Jehoahaz, chosen by the people, represented the will of the Judean population—a potential threat to Egyptian interests if he proved independent-minded. Eliakim, by contrast, was apparently more amenable. However, Neco wanted to ensure Eliakim's identification with himself rather than with Judean nationalism, hence the renaming. The renaming of rulers in the ancient Near East was not unique to Neco; it appears in Assyrian vassal treaties and in Babylonian practice. The name change from Elyaqim to Yehoyaqim may also reflect Neco's attempt to legitimize Eliakim in Judean eyes by giving him a name that invoked the God of Israel. Jehoahaz's death in Egypt, though not detailed in 2 Kings, would have been widely known in Judah and would have served as a warning to any future king who might consider resisting Neco's will. The three-month reign of Jehoahaz and his rapid exile would have shocked Judean society, demonstrating the vulnerability of even a king chosen by popular support.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of removing one ruler and installing another appears in Helaman 1-2, where various factions remove and install kings of the Nephites. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that when the people forget their covenant and turn to worldly politics, external powers gain dominance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 123:17 teaches that Saints should 'seek to establish the cause of Zion' against 'the workers of darkness.' Judah's failure to establish and maintain its covenant with the Lord leaves it vulnerable to imperial domination. The loss of agency (both to choose a king and to keep a chosen king) is a consequence of spiritual failure.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Jehoiakim, unlike Josiah, will not prioritize temple restoration. His reign is marked by Jeremiah's opposition and eventual decline. The renaming by a pagan pharaoh symbolizes that Judah's spiritual center—the temple and its God—has lost its cultural and political primacy. An imperial power, not the covenant God, now directs Judah's destiny.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoahaz's removal from the throne by unjust imperial power and his exile and death in a foreign land parallel Christ's suffering under imperial judgment. However, where Jehoahaz's exile and death represent his own judgment (he did evil), Christ's suffering is vicarious redemption. The contrast illuminates the gospel: Christ takes on the exile and death that sinners deserve, whereas Jehoahaz experiences the exile and death his sins warrant.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern believers with a question about power and naming. Who defines your identity? In naming Eliakim 'Jehoiakim,' Neco asserted the right to define the king's identity and purpose. Modern individuals and institutions face similar pressures: the world seeks to rename us, to redefine our identity in its own terms. For covenant members, the question is whether we allow the 'Pharaohs' of our time—cultural forces, media, political powers, economic systems—to rename us and thus to claim dominion over us. Our covenants (like the temple endowment) are acts of reaffirmation: God names us and claims us as his own. Jehoahaz's tragedy is compounded by the fact that he allowed his brother to be renamed by a foreign power and was powerless to prevent it. The verse suggests that spiritual weakness (doing evil, v. 32) leads to political powerlessness. Conversely, spiritual strength and faithfulness (like Josiah's) preserves agency and integrity, even if it does not prevent external pressures. Jehoiakim will be renamed by Neco, but he will later resist Babylon and will ultimately fall. The renaming does not change the underlying covenant reality: Judah belongs to the LORD, not to Pharaoh or Nebuchadnezzar.

text_kjv: And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh: he exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, of every one according to his taxation, to give it unto Pharaohnechoh.

commentary.narrative: This verse reveals the human cost of vassalage. Jehoiakim, newly installed as Neco's puppet king, faces the burden of paying the enormous tribute (one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold) imposed in verse 33. He could theoretically use the royal treasury, but that would deplete his resources and undermine his ability to govern. Instead, he conducts a formal assessment (he'erikh, 'he valued') of the land and its inhabitants, determining each person's tax obligation (erkko, 'his valuation'). The Covenant Rendering translator notes emphasize the method: 'each person was assessed according to his means.' This is not arbitrary taxation but a systematic, almost bureaucratic process. The verb 'exacted' (nagash) carries a note of coercion and pressure—the impression is of aggressive collection, not voluntary payment. Jehoiakim, in effect, has become Neco's tax collector, using the machinery of Judean government to squeeze wealth from his own people. The phrase 'of every one according to his taxation' (ish ke-erkko) suggests that the burden falls on all classes, though in practice the poor and middling classes would have felt the pinch more severely, as they could not secure exemptions or pay in kind through political influence. The verse emphasizes the cascade of judgment: Neco imposes tribute on Jehoiakim; Jehoiakim imposes assessment on the land; the common people bear the cost. This is the practical outcome of a king who 'did evil' (v. 32): the judgment falls not only on him but on the nation he rules.

word_study.term_english: taxed the land / imposed a tax
word_study.meaning: From the root arak (to estimate, to assess, to evaluate, to order). The hiphil form he-erikh means 'he caused to be assessed' or 'he assessed.' The object is the land itself, personifying the nation as the subject of taxation.
word_study.significance: This verb is more precise than simply 'taxed.' It suggests a formal valuation process, as if Jehoiakim were determining the assessed worth of each person or property. The Covenant Rendering's translator notes specify: 'he conducted a formal property assessment to determine each person's tax obligation.' This implies a census, a valuation of assets, and a systematic determination of who owes what—a bureaucratic exercise that would have required time and resources.

word_study.term_english: according to the commandment of Pharaoh
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'upon the mouth of Pharaoh.' The phrase al-pi literally means 'according to the mouth/word of,' denoting obedience to a command or edict. The 'mouth' of the ruler is the source of law and authority.
word_study.significance: This phrase emphasizes that Jehoiakim is not acting autonomously but following Pharaoh's orders. He has no choice but to comply. The 'commandment' is Neco's demand for tribute, and Jehoiakim must implement it at the level of his own people.

word_study.meaning: From the root nagash (to draw near, to approach, to press upon, to drive, to exact, to oppress). In this context, the verb means to extract forcibly or to collect under pressure. The Covenant Rendering uses 'extracted,' suggesting coercive collection.
word_study.significance: The choice of nagash rather than a neutral verb (like 'collected' or 'gathered') implies a harsh, coercive process. The people do not willingly give; they are pressed or driven to pay. This verb appears elsewhere in the Bible to describe oppression and harsh labor (e.g., Exodus 1:11, where the Egyptians 'set taskmasters over them to afflict them with their burdens').

word_study.term_english: of every one according to his taxation
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'man according to his valuation/assessment.' The noun erkko derives from arak (to assess); it means the value assigned or the amount owed based on assessment. The phrase individualizes the taxation: each person (ish) bears a burden proportional to his assessed value.
word_study.significance: This phrase suggests a graduated or proportional tax system, where liability is based on assessed worth. In theory, this is equitable (the wealthy pay more); in practice, it could be manipulated, and the poor often suffered most because they had less ability to hide assets or negotiate exemptions.

cross_references.connection: When Rehoboam threatened to increase taxes on Israel, the northern tribes rebelled and split the kingdom. The burden of taxation is a flashpoint for social and political crisis. Jehoiakim's assessment foreshadows future instability.
Verse 35 implements the tribute imposed in verse 33; Jehoiakim is the intermediary who collects from his own people what Neco demands from him.

The oppression of Israel in Egypt involved 'taskmasters' who 'afflicted them with their burdens.' Jehoiakim's extraction (nagash) of tribute from Judeans echoes this pattern of oppression, with the irony that a Jewish king oppresses his own people on behalf of a pagan pharaoh.

Jeremiah denounces Jehoiakim for building personal luxury while oppressing his people and failing to pay workers justly. This oracle provides moral context for Jehoiakim's systematic taxation: he extracts wealth from the people while using his office for personal gain.

When asked about paying tribute to Caesar, Christ distinguishes between what belongs to Caesar and what belongs to God. Jehoiakim's taxation blurs this boundary: he extracts in Pharaoh's name what rightfully belongs to God's covenant people.

commentary.historical_context: The formal assessment process described in verse 35 reflects ancient administrative practice. When a vassal state was required to pay tribute, the imperial power often demanded a lump sum, and the vassal ruler had to raise the money through whatever means available. The most efficient method was a formal assessment—essentially a census combined with a property evaluation—to determine each subject's taxable capacity. Such assessments are attested in Egyptian, Assyrian, and Babylonian administrative records. Judah itself had conducted such assessments (e.g., 2 Samuel 24, David's census; 1 Kings 4, Solomon's administrative districts). Jehoiakim's assessment would have required officials to visit towns and villages, interview property owners, and record assets. The Covenant Rendering's translator notes that this was a systematic, bureaucratic process—not a simple demand for money but a careful determination of who owed what. The burden of raising one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold from a small, recently traumatized kingdom (Josiah had died only months before) would have been severe. Many families would have had to sell land or assets; some might have fallen into debt slavery to meet the assessment. The social disruption would have been significant, and Jeremiah's later condemnation of Jehoiakim for exploiting the people (Jeremiah 22:13-19) reflects the real resentment this taxation generated.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 60, Moroni criticizes Pahoran for allowing Lamanite taxation and tribute, arguing that a righteous government does not surrender its people's labor and goods to foreign powers. Jehoiakim's acquiescence to Neco's demand represents a failure of leadership comparable to what Moroni condemns.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 31:1 promises the righteous that they 'shall not be deceived, and...shall be blessed in all things.' Conversely, Jehoiakim's disobedience (he 'did evil,' v. 32) leads to a curse of vassalage and oppression. The principle is that covenant faithfulness brings blessing; covenant-breaking brings burdens.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Under the law of Moses, tithes and offerings were to support the temple and the priesthood. Jehoiakim's forced assessment to pay Pharaoh diverts resources from covenant worship to imperial service. The conflict between the claims of Caesar/Pharaoh and the claims of God is a central tension.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoiakim's role as an unjust collector of tribute foreshadows the tax collectors condemned in the Gospels (Matthew 5:46, 18:17, 21:31-32). However, where Gospel tax collectors exploit for personal gain, Jehoiakim is coerced by an imperial master. The typology suggests the cascading nature of injustice: a king oppressed by empire becomes an oppressor of his own people. Christ's teaching about rendering to Caesar (Matthew 22:17-21) provides the countertype: a true king serves God and his people, not an earthly emperor.
commentary.application: This verse presents a sobering picture of how judgment cascades through society. Jehoiakim's personal failure (doing evil, v. 32) is followed by political domination (v. 34) and ultimately results in the oppression of the common people (v. 35). For modern believers, the application is twofold. First, leaders bear a moral responsibility for the consequences of their choices. Jehoiakim did not personally cause the Egyptian occupation, but his spiritual failure may have contributed to it (if Josiah's righteousness had been maintained, perhaps Judah's trajectory would have been different). Second, the burdens of leadership failures fall on the vulnerable. The people who 'are exacted' to pay Pharaoh's tribute are not the architects of Judah's vassalage; they are its victims. This teaches covenant members to be compassionate toward those who suffer the consequences of systemic injustice and to work toward just governance. In personal terms, when we choose to pursue evil, we create burdens not just for ourselves but for those dependent on us. Jehoiakim's three-month successor (Jehoahaz) was unable to chart an independent course; Jehoiakim himself was bound by Neco's demands; the common people bore the costs of both. The verse invites reflection on how our choices affect those around us and those who come after.

text_kjv: Jehoiakim was twenty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Zebudah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah.

commentary.narrative: This verse provides the second major regnal formula of the passage, introducing Jehoiakim in the standard deuteronomic format. Unlike his brother Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim is given a substantial reign: eleven years (approximately 609-598 BCE). At twenty-five years old, he is older and presumably more seasoned than Jehoahaz was. The fact that he reigns for eleven years suggests stability—at least in external appearance—though the historical narrative makes clear that this reign is characterized by conflict with the prophets, especially Jeremiah, and by mounting pressure from Babylon. His mother is Zebudah (Zevidah), daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah. Zebudah's name (meaning 'gift, endowment') appears only here; she is not mentioned again in the biblical record. Rumah is identified as a town in Galilee or Judah, placing her in the Judean heartland. The verse's straightforward presentation contrasts with what we know from the prophetic books: Jehoiakim's reign is marked by injustice (Jeremiah 22:13-19), false prophecy (Jeremiah 28), and the early phase of Babylonian pressure that will eventually destroy him. The regnal formula—which merely records his age, length of reign, and mother's name—gives no indication of the turbulent history that will unfold. This is characteristic of the Kings narrative: the deuteronomic formula provides a framework, but the prophetic books fill in the moral and spiritual detail.

word_study.term_english: twenty and five years old / twenty-five years old
word_study.term_original: בֶּן־עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ (ben esrim ve-chamesh shanah)
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'a son of twenty and five years.' The phrase ben shanah ('a son of years') is the standard biblical expression for age. The Covenant Rendering translates it simply as 'twenty-five years old.' Jehoiakim is older than his brother Jehoahaz (twenty-three) and old enough to have some political experience.
word_study.significance: At twenty-five, Jehoiakim would have been born around 634 BCE, during the reign of his grandfather Amon (643-641 BCE). He is not a young, untested king like Jehoahaz but someone who has lived through Josiah's reformations and has witnessed court politics. His age makes his subsequent spiritual failure (doing evil, presumably, though not stated in v. 32 as it was for Jehoahaz) more morally culpable—he had twenty-five years of life experience and religious instruction.

word_study.term_original: וְאַחַ֤ת עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ (ve-achat esreh shanah malak)
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'and eleven years he reigned.' The verb malak (he reigned) in the qal perfect tense indicates completed action. The eleven-year reign (609-598 BCE) spans a crucial period in international politics.
word_study.significance: Eleven years is a substantial reign—longer than most of Judah's later kings (Jehoahaz: 3 months; Jehoiachin: 3 months; Zedekiah: 11 years). Jehoiakim's reign corresponds to the period during which Egypt's dominance over Judah was gradually eroded by Babylon's rising power. The reign ends with Jehoiakim's death and possibly the beginning of the Babylonian siege (December 598 BCE). The duration suggests that Jehoiakim initially maintained some stability, even if under Egyptian suzerainty and later under Babylonian pressure.

word_study.meaning: The name likely derives from zabid (to give, to endow) and thus means 'gift' or 'endowment.' It is a feminine form expressing the idea of something precious or bestowed. The name appears only once in the biblical record.
word_study.significance: Zebudah's name carries positive connotations, but the biblical text provides no information about her character or influence. She is recorded in the regnal formula but plays no narrative role. This contrasts with Hamutal (Jehoahaz's mother), who bears the same function but whose name carries different theological associations (Chamutal: 'my father-in-law is dew'). The parallel naming of two queens (Hamutal and Zebudah, both mothers of sons of Josiah) suggests the importance of tracking the royal genealogy, especially as multiple claimants to the throne might emerge.

word_study.meaning: A town mentioned only here in the biblical text. It is likely located in Galilee or the northern Judean region, though its precise location is debated among scholars.
word_study.significance: The mention of Rumah grounds Zebudah's family in a specific geographic location and implies that she came from a prominent local family in that town. The identification of the mother's hometown in regnal formulas suggests that she retained connections to her native region and possibly represented political or kinship alliances between the royal court and provincial elites.

cross_references.connection: These verses record the latter part of Jehoiakim's reign, describing his initial vassalage to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar and his eventual death or deposition. The eleven-year reign recorded here encompasses the transition from Egyptian to Babylonian dominance.

The parallel account in Chronicles provides additional detail, noting that Jehoiakim 'did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD' and recording his capture by Nebuchadnezzar and his disgraceful death or exile.

Jeremiah's oracle explicitly condemns Jehoiakim for building his palace with unrighteousness, exacting people's labor without payment, and committing injustice. The prophet predicts that Jehoiakim will be given 'the burial of an ass'—a shameful, disrespectful death.

Jeremiah 36 records a dramatic moment during Jehoiakim's reign when the king burns the scroll containing Jeremiah's prophecies, demonstrating his contempt for the prophetic word. This narrative illustrates the spiritual climate of Jehoiakim's reign.

Verse 31 introduces Jehoahaz with the same regnal formula (age, length of reign, mother's name). The parallel structure invites comparison: Jehoahaz (23 years old, 3 months) vs. Jehoiakim (25 years old, 11 years). The contrast shows that external stability (a longer reign) does not correlate with spiritual faithfulness.

commentary.historical_context: Jehoiakim's eleven-year reign (609-598 BCE) spans one of the most tumultuous periods in Judean history. The first few years (609-605 BCE) were dominated by Egyptian control under Pharaoh Neco II, who had installed Jehoiakim as his puppet king. In 605 BCE, Neco was defeated by the Babylonian army under Nebuchadnezzar at the Battle of Carchemish (in northern Syria), a turning point that shifted dominance in the Levant from Egypt to Babylon. After Carchemish, Jehoiakim initially resisted Babylonian vassalage but eventually submitted (2 Kings 24:1). The later years of his reign were marked by Babylonian pressure, increasing Judean resistance (encouraged by false prophets), and the beginning of the end-game that would result in Jerusalem's destruction. The Covenant Rendering's dating places Jehoiakim's accession in 609 BCE and his death or deposition in 598 BCE. This historical context is crucial for understanding the social tensions recorded in Jeremiah: as Babylon replaced Egypt as the dominant power, Judean society was wracked by competing factions—some favoring Egyptian resistance, some advocating Babylonian accommodation, and prophets like Jeremiah calling for submission to divine judgment rather than political maneuvering. Jehoiakim, as king, was caught in this maelstrom and apparently chose the path of resistance and exploitation of his own people to finance military efforts.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The regnal formulas in 2 Kings parallel the succession accounts in the Book of Mormon (e.g., Mosiah 29-Alma 1), where genealogical and chronological information grounds the narrative in specific time and place. Both texts use similar formulas to mark transitions of power and to track how long each ruler governed.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 87:1-8 (the prophecy on war) describes the upheavals that will come upon the nations. Jehoiakim's reign occurs in a period of similar upheaval, as one empire (Egypt) yields to another (Babylon). The D&C emphasizes that such wars are preparatory to the Second Coming; the historical pattern suggests that political instability often accompanies spiritual decline.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Unlike Josiah, who prioritized temple restoration, or even Hezekiah, who cleansed the temple, Jehoiakim's reign is not marked by significant temple activity. The temple stands, presumably, but its importance in the life of the kingdom is diminished as geopolitical concerns dominate. The covenant people's focus has shifted from the house of the Lord to the survival of the state.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoiakim, despite his eleven-year reign and apparent stability, is ultimately a failed king—one who does not uphold the covenant and is judged by the prophets. Christ, by contrast, is the faithful king who upholds the eternal covenant with his people. Where Jehoiakim reigns in a time of political upheaval and makes wrong choices, Christ reigns eternally and never deviates from righteousness. The contrast illuminates the kingship of Christ: true rulership is measured not by longevity or outward stability but by faithfulness to God's law.
commentary.application: This verse, with its dry recitation of Jehoiakim's age and reign length, conceals a deeper lesson about the insufficiency of outward indicators of success. Jehoiakim reigns for eleven years—a substantial tenure, suggesting stability and legitimacy. Yet the prophetic books reveal that his reign is characterized by injustice, spiritual rebellion, and a refusal to heed the word of the Lord through Jeremiah. Modern believers might ask: Am I measuring success by the right metrics? Jehoiakim's reign 'looks good' on the surface—a full eleven years compared to his brother's three months. But beneath the surface, he is exploiting his people (v. 35), ignoring the prophets (Jeremiah 36), and leading Judah toward destruction. The verse invites introspection: Do we pursue length of tenure, accumulation of power, or outward stability, or do we pursue faithfulness to covenant? The regnal formula—which tells us Jehoiakim's age and how long he reigned—tells us nothing about his spiritual state. That requires reading the prophetic books and the fuller narrative of his reign. For modern believers, the application is to look beyond surface markers of success (career advancement, wealth, longevity, influence) and to examine the spiritual foundation: Are my choices just? Am I serving others, or exploiting them? Am I responding to the prophetic voice, or suppressing it? Jehoiakim's eleven years of apparent stability collapse into shame and judgment because the foundation was rotten. True, lasting success—both personal and institutional—requires a solid covenant foundation, not just outward appearance of power.

text_kjv: And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done.

commentary.narrative: This verse closes the account of Jehoahaz's reign and delivers the theological verdict that defines the entire post-Josiah era of Judah. The phrase 'did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD' echoes the repeated pattern throughout Kings, where every king's reign is measured against the standard of covenant faithfulness. Jehoahaz reigned only three months before Pharaoh Necho deposed him (verse 33-34), yet in that brief time the writer-theologian makes clear that he inherited and perpetuated the spiritual decline of his forefathers. This is not a description of individual moral failure in isolation; it is a theological diagnosis of systemic spiritual disease. The reign of Josiah, the great reformer who had discovered the Book of the Law and led the nation in covenant renewal, had ended. His son immediately reversed course, and from this point forward, every monarch of Judah would be measured by the same condemning standard: they 'did evil in the sight of the LORD.'

word_study.meaning: Bad, evil, or wicked; in covenant terminology, it refers to that which violates the covenant and brings curse. The term encompasses moral, spiritual, and covenantal dimensions—not merely personal sin but faithlessness to the divine law.
word_study.significance: In the Deuteronomistic History, 'doing evil' is the inverse of 'doing good' in the sight of the LORD. It is the condition that triggers divine judgment and removal from the land. Every instance of this phrase in Kings marks a monarch whose reign will end in diminishment or disaster.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'in the eyes of'; used throughout the Deuteronomistic History to denote the divine standard of judgment. It is not merely what appears to human observers, but what stands visible and condemned before the all-seeing God.
word_study.significance: This phrase emphasizes that human justifications or appearances are irrelevant. The LORD sees truly; the historical writer is recording what the divine judge already knows. The 'eyes of the LORD' are the measure of all things.

word_study.term_english: according to all that his fathers had done
word_study.term_original: כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר־עָשׂוּ אֲבֹתָיו (ke-khol asher asu avotav)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'according to all that his fathers did.' This formulaic phrase indicates the continuation of ancestral patterns—not isolated sin, but inherited spiritual corruption. The Covenant Rendering captures this as 'just as his ancestors had done,' emphasizing continuity of faithlessness.
word_study.significance: By the time of Jehoahaz, the evil patterns are no longer individual choices but generational inheritance. The nation has moved beyond isolated lapses into systemic spiritual disease. This refrain, as noted in the translator notes, becomes the darkening theme of the final chapters of Kings—each king repeating his predecessors' failure, and the divine judgment moving inexorably toward exile.

cross_references.connection: Jehoahaz (Shallum) opens with the same negative verdict: 'he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done.' This verse repeats and reinforces the pattern.
The covenant language of 'doing good' and 'doing evil' in the sight of the LORD originates in Moses' covenant renewal discourse. Judgment for covenant violation is the foundational threat.

Manasseh, an earlier evil king, 'did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to the abominations of the heathen.' The pattern is established generations earlier and now becomes the new norm.

The parallel account in Chronicles confirms that post-Josiah kings 'did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD' and 'humbled not themselves before Jeremiah the prophet.' The spiritual decline is documented in both histories.

Israel's final king, Hoshea, 'did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, but not as the kings of Israel that were before him.' This phrase shows how deeply embedded the pattern of evil had become across the entire monarchy.

commentary.historical_context: Jehoahaz reigned during a pivotal moment in ancient Near Eastern politics. After Josiah's death at the Battle of Megiddo (609 BCE), Pharaoh Necho II of Egypt had become the dominant regional power and appointed Eliakim (who became Jehoiakim) over Judah. Jehoahaz, Josiah's younger son, was initially chosen by 'the people of the land' but was quickly deposed after only three months, carried to Egypt, and imprisoned there until his death. The brevity of his reign makes the theological verdict all the more striking—the writer is not recording a long narrative of accumulated sins, but rather making clear that the spiritual descent that would characterize the final decades of Judah was immediate and absolute. From 609 BCE onward, no king of Judah would reverse the trajectory toward exile. The cultural and political autonomy that Josiah had briefly restored was gone, and with it went any hope of sustained covenant renewal. The theological climate of the ancient Near East included the concept of divine judgment manifested through political humiliation; Judah's loss of independence was read by Deuteronomistic historians as the visible expression of spiritual failure.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of generational evil-doing repeats throughout Book of Mormon history. King Noah and his people 'do evil in the sight of the Lord,' and this evil becomes inherited by his sons and corrupts the entire kingdom until judgment comes through Lamanite invasion (Mosiah 11). The Nephites similarly enter cycles where one generation's faithfulness is followed by the next generation's descent into evil, each repeating the sins of their forefathers rather than learning from them (Helaman 7:22-24). Mormon's lamentation over this pattern in his abridged account parallels the Deuteronomistic author's grief.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:33-34 describes the modern covenant people: those who 'do evil in the sight of the LORD' face similar judgments of removal and loss of covenant blessings. The pattern established in ancient Israel remains operative in all dispensations. D&C 82:2-3 reiterates that 'he that sins against the knowledge given shall lose the Spirit,' and each generation must renew its covenant commitment rather than inherit righteousness from ancestors.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant renewal that Josiah had implemented in response to the Book of the Law represented a restoration of sacred knowledge and practice. Jehoahaz's immediate abandonment of that covenant indicates the tragic reality that external reformation without sustained internal commitment is temporary. Modern temple covenants likewise require ongoing personal faithfulness, not mere inherited status. The Lord's house cannot be approached casually; each member must 'do that which is right in the sight of the LORD' individually.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoahaz represents the failure of human kingship to maintain covenant faithfulness across generations. His immediate descent into evil, despite his father's great reforms, prefigures the ultimate insufficiency of any earthly monarchy or human institution to save a people from spiritual decline. Only a king whose reign is eternal and whose righteousness is perfect—the Messiah—can establish a kingdom that does not crumble under the weight of successive generations' unfaithfulness. The closing of the Davidic kingdom in exile foreshadows humanity's need for a king who reigns not through human legitimacy but through divine power to transform hearts and establish an everlasting covenant.
commentary.application: This verse confronts us with the sobering reality that proximity to great spiritual renewal offers no guarantee of personal faithfulness. Jehoahaz had witnessed his father Josiah's dramatic covenant renewal, the discovery of the Book of the Law, and the great Passover celebration. Yet none of that inheritance protected him from doing evil. For modern Latter-day Saints, this is a warning about the sufficiency of inherited membership. One's parents' testimony, one's family's history in the Church, or even one's own previous spiritual experiences are not deposits that earn righteousness for the next generation or the next season of life. Each individual, each generation, must choose 'what is right in the sight of the LORD' for themselves. The refrain 'as his fathers had done' should provoke hard questions: Am I repeating spiritual patterns because I inherited them, or have I genuinely made the covenant my own? The solution is not nostalgia for a previous era of righteousness but present, active choice to 'do good in the sight of the LORD' now, in my own circumstances and generation.

text_kjv: In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant three years: then he turned and rebelled against him.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks the pivot point in Judah's final decades: the arrival of Babylonian dominance under Nebuchadnezzar II (605 BCE onward) and the fatal miscalculation of King Jehoiakim. The phrase 'in his days' refers to the reign of Jehoiakim, who inherited the throne under precarious circumstances following his father Josiah's death at Megiddo (609 BCE). When Nebuchadnezzar 'came up' (invaded with military force), Jehoiakim was forced into vassalage—a subordinate political relationship where he retained his throne but surrendered autonomy and paid tribute to Babylon.

The three-year period of vassalage is crucial chronologically and theologically. Jehoiakim remained loyal until approximately 601 BCE, when Babylon suffered a military setback against Egypt. This apparent weakness emboldened Jehoiakim to believe he could break free. The rebellion was catastrophic miscalculation: Babylon recovered quickly, and Nebuchadnezzar would spend the next decade systematically destroying Judah. The narrative presents this not as geopolitical maneuvering but as covenant violation—Jehoiakim 'turned and rebelled,' language that echoes covenant language throughout the deuteronomistic history.

word_study.meaning: Servant, vassal, slave. The root carries the sense of subordination and obligation. In the context of ancient Near Eastern political relationships, eved describes a client king bound by treaty to serve a suzerain. This is not slavery in the chattel sense but political subjection.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this 'vassal,' which clarifies the political relationship for modern readers. Jehoiakim's status as eved to Nebuchadnezzar echoes language used of Israel's relationship to the covenant itself—they are servants (avadim) of the LORD through covenant obligation. By becoming a servant to a foreign king, Jehoiakim violates the implicit covenant structure that binds Judah to divine law, not to earthly powers.

word_study.meaning: To go up, ascend, invade. In military contexts, alah regularly describes military campaign or invasion, often with a sense of forceful advance. The verb is used of armies moving 'up' toward a geographic target.
word_study.significance: This is the standard Hebrew term for invasion and conquest. It appears throughout the Chronicles of Kings to mark major military interventions. The choice emphasizes that Nebuchadnezzar's arrival was not diplomatic but military—a demonstration of force that compelled submission.

word_study.meaning: To rebel, resist, break covenant bonds. The verb carries connotations of treaty-breaking and defection. It is used elsewhere in Kings to describe Israel's and Judah's rebellion against the LORD—the same moral vocabulary applied to both divine and human authority.
word_study.significance: The use of marad for Jehoiakim's breaking with Babylon parallels his spiritual rebellion against the covenant. The narrative structure equates political and theological rebellion: to turn from the LORD's word is to rebel, and to rebel against Babylon is to commit the same breach of obligation. Both are covenant violations.

cross_references.connection: Jehoiakim's installation as king by Pharaoh Necho and the heavy tribute placed on him, setting the context for later vassalage to Babylon.
Jeremiah's prophecy against Jehoiakim for his oppression, pride, and refusal to hear the prophetic word—the moral backdrop for his rebellion against Babylon.
Jehoiakim's burning of Jeremiah's scroll, demonstrating his rejection of prophetic warning and foreshadowing the catastrophe his rebellion brings.
The parallel account confirming Nebuchadnezzar's invasion, Jehoiakim's vassalage, and his binding with bronze chains.
The same invasion event from the perspective of Jerusalem's fall, marking the beginning of the Babylonian exile and the rise of Daniel's generation.

commentary.historical_context: Nebuchadnezzar II became king of Babylon in 605 BCE and immediately moved to consolidate control over the Levantine states that had been destabilized by the fall of Assyria (612 BCE). Jehoiakim ruled Judah from approximately 609 to 598 BCE, a period of extreme volatility. The power vacuum left by Assyria's collapse created competition between Babylon and Egypt for control of the eastern Mediterranean. Jehoiakim, like other regional kings, was caught in this struggle. The three-year vassalage represents Babylon's initial assertion of control. The Egyptian-Babylonian conflict in 601 BCE (in which neither power achieved decisive victory) created the false impression that Babylon was weakening. This perception, combined with pressure from nationalist elements at court and the prophetic assurances of some (false) prophets, convinced Jehoiakim to attempt defection. Archaeological and textual evidence from Babylonian chronicles confirms Nebuchadnezzar's campaigns in the Levant during this period. The rebellion triggered Nebuchadnezzar's punitive response that would culminate in Jerusalem's siege and fall in 598/597 BCE.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of Jehoiakim's rebellion after a period of forced submission parallels the cycle described in the Book of Mormon, where peoples experience divine judgment, temporary reformation, and then renewed rebellion (Mosiah 29:27; Helaman 13:32-33). The Nephite and Lamanite cycles show that mere external submission to authority without internal covenant renewal leads to renewed transgression.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The principle of divine governance through both consequence and justice appears in D&C 98:37-40, where the Lord describes how He deals with those who break covenants and turn to rebellion. Just as Jehoiakim is given time to repent but ultimately faces judgment, so too does the Lord extend warnings before executing justice.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Jehoiakim's vassalage and rebellion frame the desecration of the temple that will follow. The temple, as the seat of divine presence in Jerusalem, becomes the focal point of the coming judgment. His covenant-breaking has implications for the temple covenant that binds the people to the LORD.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoiakim's three-year vassalage followed by rebellion prefigures the pattern of covenant rejection that leads to exile. Unlike later interpretations of exile as redemptive (exile as purification and preparation for return), Jehoiakim's rebellion represents the human choice to turn away from divine authority. Christ, by contrast, perfectly submits to the Father's will even unto death (Luke 22:42), embodying the covenant loyalty Jehoiakim rejected. The rebellion that triggers judgment points toward the necessity of Christ's perfect obedience to break the cycle of covenant violation and judgment.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Jehoiakim's three years of vassalage followed by rebellion raises a searching question: Do we experience periods of submission to divine authority only to fall away when external pressure seems to diminish? The narrative suggests that genuine covenant strength is not born from fear of consequences alone but from internal alignment with divine purpose. Jehoiakim had the opportunity to use his three years of vassalage to reform his reign, strengthen his people's spiritual commitment, and prepare for the challenges ahead. Instead, he interpreted a moment of Babylonian weakness as permission to rebel. The lesson is that seasons of difficulty, constraint, or humbling are often extended opportunities for genuine transformation—not temporary setbacks to be escaped at the first opportunity. The practical takeaway: When circumstances force us into submission or limitation, ask whether God is working to reshape our priorities rather than assuming He intends only our immediate relief.

text_kjv: And the LORD sent against him bands of the Chaldees, and bands of the Syrians, and bands of the Moabites, and bands of the children of Ammon, and sent them against Judah to destroy it, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by his servants the prophets.

commentary.narrative:
This verse presents the theological interpretation of the military catastrophe that follows Jehoiakim's rebellion. The narrative does not describe Nebuchadnezzar's direct response but rather frames the incoming assault as the LORD's active judgment. The fourfold repetition of 'bands' (gedudim—raiding parties, mobile military units) creates a sense of assault from multiple directions, overwhelm, and inescapability. The raiders include Chaldeans (Babylonians proper), Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites.

The inclusion of Moabite and Ammonite forces is historically significant. These neighboring kingdoms, which had often been Judah's rivals or vassals under earlier kings, now join in the punishment. This may reflect Babylon's strategy of using regional allies as auxiliary forces, or it may indicate the complete isolation of Judah—even former adversaries have joined the assault. The theological heart of the verse lies in its framing: this destruction is not geopolitical consequence but divine action. The phrase 'according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by his servants the prophets' insists that what the eye sees as Babylonian military aggression is actually the fulfillment of prophetic announcements. This principle—that history is shaped by divine word spoken through prophets—is foundational to the deuteronomistic historian's worldview.

word_study.meaning: To send, dispatch, let go. The root can mean sending messengers, armies, or releasing something from control. The subject here is crucial: The LORD (YHWH) is the one who sends—not Nebuchadnezzar, not geopolitical forces, but the God of Israel.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'sent' as the controlling verb with the LORD as subject. This makes explicit what the KJV also conveys but less forcefully: God is the active agent of judgment, commanding the raiding bands as instruments of divine will. This is radical—it claims that even Babylon's expansion and Judah's enemies serve the LORD's purposes.

word_study.meaning: Bands, troops, raiding companies. Gedud describes a mobile military unit, often used for raiding, pillaging, or rapid incursions. It is distinct from a full army (tsava) and suggests smaller, mobile forces meant to harass and weaken rather than conduct formal siege warfare.
word_study.significance: The repeated use of gedudim creates a vivid picture: waves of raiders, likely coming in succession, plundering the countryside and wearing down Judah's defenses. These are not formal military formations but mobile strike forces, which fits the pattern of Babylonian siege strategy—surrounding and harassing a city through auxilliary forces while the main army approaches.

word_study.meaning: To cause to perish, to destroy. The infinitive form of avad in the causative (hiphil) stem emphasizes the deliberate intent to bring ruin. The purpose clause makes clear this is not collateral damage but the intended goal.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'to destroy it' (or 'destroy him,' referring to both the king and the kingdom) expresses divine intention: this is not accidental violence but targeted judgment meant to bring the kingdom to an end. The terminology echoes covenant language—avad is used of what happens when the covenant is broken and blessing is withdrawn.

word_study.term_english: according to the word of the LORD
word_study.meaning: In accordance with, according to. Dvar ('word, matter, thing') links the visible military events to the invisible divine utterance. The preposition ki-da'var ('in accordance with the word/matter of') suggests that prophetic proclamation and historical occurrence are inseparable.
word_study.significance: This phrase is the theological key to the entire verse. It claims that history conforms to what the prophets have announced. The destruction is not random or a mere political consequence—it is the fulfillment of the LORD's word. This conviction lies at the heart of the deuteronomistic history: the prophets speak truth about what will happen, and when destruction comes, it is because the prophetic word is being executed.

cross_references.connection: The pattern of the LORD sending prophets to warn before judgment—a pattern repeated with Judah as it was with Israel, establishing the consistency of divine justice.
The covenant curses that describe a nation coming from afar to besiege and destroy, establishing the legal framework for understanding Babylon's invasion as covenant consequence.
Jeremiah's explicit prophecy that Judah and surrounding nations will serve Babylon, directly interpreting the raiding bands and destruction as fulfillment of his prophetic word.
Jeremiah's initial vision of kingdoms from the north coming against Judah, framed explicitly as the LORD bringing judgment through foreign powers.
The parallel account describing the Chaldeans burning the temple, houses, and carrying away treasures—the concrete fulfillment of the destruction announced in this verse.

commentary.historical_context: The raiding strategy described here reflects Babylonian military tactics of the period. Rather than immediately launching a full siege of Jerusalem, Babylon typically weakened a rebellious kingdom through auxiliary forces, siege camps, and raids on the countryside. The inclusion of Moabite and Ammonite forces suggests either that these kingdoms were Babylonian vassals or that they saw opportunity to exploit Judah's distress (Ezekiel 25 later records their gleeful mockery of Jerusalem's fall). The historical record from Babylonian chronicles and the Bible (Jeremiah 52, 2 Chronicles 36) indicates that the siege of Jerusalem was conducted primarily by Chaldean forces under Nebuchadnezzar, but the surrounding region was harassed by multiple forces. The destruction of the Judean countryside would have been catastrophic—cutting off food supplies to Jerusalem and devastating the agricultural base that supported the kingdom. Archaeologically, evidence from sites throughout Judah shows destruction layers consistent with early 6th-century BCE military campaigns, corroborating the narrative of widespread devastation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:29 describes divine judgment coming upon the Nephites through external enemies as a manifestation of the LORD's justice. The Book of Mormon repeatedly frames enemy invasions as instruments of God's judgment (Mosiah 7:24-26; Helaman 4:11-13), teaching that military defeat is often the physical manifestation of spiritual rebellion. The principle here—that external enemies are sent by God to execute justice—is foundational to Nephite understanding of history.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:37-40 describes how the Lord brings judgment through those who refuse to repent, using the language of surrendering the kingdom into the hands of enemies. The principle that God can and will use external forces to execute judgment on covenant breakers appears throughout the Doctrine and Covenants as well.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The raiding bands that destroy the countryside and ultimately the temple are instruments of the judgment announced against the temple in 23:27. The temple itself becomes the focal point of this destruction—not merely as a building but as the sign of the covenant's rejection and the withdrawal of divine protection from the holy place.

commentary.christological_typology: The pattern of the LORD sending judgment through foreign powers prefigures the ultimate rejection of the covenant community and the necessity of Christ's redemptive work. Just as the prophets warned Judah of coming destruction, Christ's own generation would reject the prophetic word (Matthew 23:37), leading to the destruction of the temple in 70 CE. However, Christ's redemptive sacrifice provides a path beyond judgment—He bears the weight of covenant violation and opens the way to renewal. The raiding bands that come to destroy point toward the necessity of a savior who can address the root cause of judgment (sin and covenant violation) rather than merely experience its consequences.
commentary.application: This verse teaches a profound and difficult truth: God uses external circumstance and even hostile forces to accomplish His purposes and execute His justice. For modern believers, this raises important questions about how we interpret suffering and difficulty. When we experience setback, loss, or apparent defeat—whether personal, familial, or communal—we are invited to ask: Is the LORD using this circumstance to refine me, to turn me from a destructive path, or to accomplish purposes beyond my immediate understanding? This does not excuse those who inflict harm, but it does invite us to see that God's sovereignty extends even over adversity. Practically, when facing hardship, the response should not be to blame external enemies or circumstances but to examine whether we are walking in covenant with God. Jehoiakim's error was to interpret a moment of apparent Babylonian weakness as permission to continue in rebellion. We should instead use seasons of difficulty as opportunities to repent and realign ourselves with divine purpose, recognizing that 'the Lord's ways are mysterious but sure' (Proverbs 3:5-6) and that suffering can accomplish purposes of refinement we do not initially perceive.

text_kjv: Surely at the commandment of the LORD came this upon Judah, to remove them out of his sight, for the sins of Manasseh, according to all that he did;

commentary.narrative:
Verse 3 provides the theological summary of why this catastrophe has come: it is the judgment for sins committed decades earlier by King Manasseh, now finally coming to execution. This is remarkable and troubling to modern sensibilities—why would an entire kingdom suffer destruction for the sins of a king who died more than fifty years prior? The answer reveals the deuteronomistic historian's understanding of covenant community: the nation is a unified body before God, and the sins of a king shape the spiritual character of the entire kingdom. Manasseh's wickedness was so egregious that his repentance (recorded in 2 Chronicles 33:12-16) was insufficient to avert the judgment already set in motion. The phrase 'at the commandment of the LORD' (al-pi YHWH) eliminates any ambiguity—this destruction is not accidental or merely military consequence but deliberately ordered by the God of Israel.

The purpose 'to remove them out of his sight' (le-hasir me'al panav) echoes the language of 23:27, where the same fate was pronounced against Jerusalem itself. This verse reveals that the prophecy announced in 23:27 is now being executed. Judah's removal from God's sight does not mean annihilation but exile—the loss of the land, the temple, and the visible covenant relationship. This will create the conditions for the Babylonian exile that defines the next seventy years of Judah's existence.

word_study.meaning: Akh means 'surely, only, however, nevertheless.' It marks a strong emphatic or contrastive statement. Al-pi means 'according to the mouth/command of,' with pi ('mouth') standing for the word or command that issues from the mouth.
word_study.significance: The combination akh al-pi YHWH is emphatic: 'Surely, only on the command of the LORD.' This eliminates other explanations—the destruction is not chance, not Babylonian ambition alone, not geopolitical consequence, but directly commanded by the God of Israel. The use of 'mouth' to describe God's command personalizes divine will as something spoken and binding.

word_study.term_english: to remove them out of his sight
word_study.meaning: The infinitive of sur (to turn aside, depart) in the causative (hiphil) stem: to cause to depart, to remove. Panav means 'his face' or 'his presence,' with the sense of intimate awareness and relationship.
word_study.significance: To be 'removed from the face' of God is to lose the protective presence of the covenant deity. This language appears in 23:27 as a prophecy and now is revealed as being executed. Removal from divine presence is the ultimate covenant curse—not death but the loss of relationship with the one who sustains life and blessing. This is the theological meaning of exile.

word_study.meaning: Chattot (plural of chattat, 'sin, transgression') refers to willful violations of covenant law. The use of the plural suggests not a single transgression but habitual, systematic covenant violation.
word_study.significance: The reference to Manasseh's sins is historically specific. Manasseh reigned longer than any other king of Judah (approximately 687-642 BCE) and, according to 2 Kings 21, reintroduced idolatry, child sacrifice, and divination—grave covenant violations. His sins created a spiritual atmosphere that, even after his own repentance, left the kingdom spiritually compromised. The narrative suggests that a kingdom shaped by such prolonged wickedness cannot recover its spiritual integrity through a single repentant king.

word_study.term_english: according to all that he did
word_study.meaning: In accordance with everything that he did. Kelal ('all, whole') paired with asher-asah ('that he did') emphasizes the totality and comprehensiveness of Manasseh's actions.
word_study.significance: This phrase insists that the judgment is proportional to the covenant violation.
